        Why Automate Testing? What, When and What Not To

        Test automation means writing programs that check your software for you, so a machine repeats the boring checks while people do the thinking. This page explains what automation really buys you, how to estimate whether it pays for itself, what you should deliberately leave manual, and why a good automation suite is a piece of software engineering in its own right, not a pile of recorded clicks.

        What "test automation" actually is

        Strip away the tools and an automated test is tiny. The "Software Engineering at Google" book defines the simplest test as four ingredients: one behavior you are testing, a specific input, an observable output, and a controlled environment. You run the code, compare what happened with what you expected, and report pass or fail. A framework (Playwright, Selenium, Cypress, JUnit, pytest...) only adds convenience: finding tests, running them in parallel, reporting, retrying.

        The same book breaks the work into three activities that repeat forever: write tests, run them, and react to failures. Beginners focus on "write". Teams that succeed spend most of their effort on "run" (fast pipelines) and "react" (keeping the suite trustworthy so a red build means something).

        # No framework at all: every automated test is just this idea.
def subtract(a, b):
    return a - b

expected = -3
actual = subtract(2, 5)        # known input, controlled environment
assert actual == expected, f"expected {expected}, got {actual}"
        Analogy: the smoke detector. You could walk through the house every hour sniffing for fire (manual testing), or install a detector that watches all day and speaks up only when something is wrong (automation). The detector does not replace a fire inspector who understands the building, but you would not want to live without it.

        Why teams automate

        Several independent sources give consistent reasons. They are listed here with who said it, so you can judge them yourself.

        BenefitWhat it means in practiceSource
        Fast feedbackYou learn "did I break something?" in seconds or minutes instead of days, while the change is still fresh in your head.Vocke (Thoughtworks); Fowler
        Safety to change codeRefactoring and upgrades become routine because a "bug detector" shouts when you goof.Fowler; SWE@Google
        RepeatabilityThe machine runs the same steps in the same order every time and never gets bored or tired.ISTQB CTFL 4.0; SWE@Google
        ScaleOne engineer cannot manually check every language, browser, device and feature on every change.SWE@Google
        Better designCode that is hard to test is usually tightly coupled; tests are the first client of your API.SWE@Google
        Executable documentationA clear test shows what the code does in a specific case, and breaks when the docs go stale.SWE@Google
        Human time freedTesters spend time designing deeper tests and exploring, not re-clicking the same path.ISTQB CTFL 4.0; Vocke

        Martin Fowler goes further: he regards the regression suite as the single biggest benefit of automated tests, even more than the design pressure that test-driven development provides. A regression test is one that re-checks old behavior after a change.

        A story from the Google book shows the effect at scale. In 2005 the Google Web Server team found that more than 80% of production pushes contained user-affecting bugs that had to be rolled back. After they required tests with every change and ran them continuously, emergency pushes dropped by half within a year, even while the team made a record number of changes. The authors' lesson: you cannot rely on programmer talent alone. A hypothetical 100-person team where everyone writes only one bug a month still creates about five new bugs every workday.

        Manual versus automated testing

        Neither is "better". They answer different questions. Automation is excellent at checking: confirming that known expectations still hold. People are excellent at exploring: noticing what nobody thought to write down.

        Manual testing (a person follows steps)
        • Cheap to start, expensive to repeat: the cost is paid again on every run.
        • Slow feedback; usually done late, in batches.
        • Consistency suffers: people skip steps, get bored, make slips.
        • Unbeatable for judgement: "this feels wrong", confusing wording, ugly layout, surprising behavior.

        Best for: exploring new features, usability, one-off checks, anything that changes too fast to script.

        Automated testing (a program checks)
        • Expensive to build, nearly free to repeat: the cost is mostly up front plus maintenance.
        • Runs on every commit, at night, on many browsers in parallel.
        • Perfectly consistent, but only checks what you told it to check.
        • Blind to anything you did not assert: it will not notice an overlapping button unless you test for it.

        Best for: regression checks, stable business rules, data-heavy or cross-browser/device repetition.

        When to automate (a checklist)

        ISTQB says regression suites are a strong candidate because they run many times and keep growing, and that automation should start early. Combine that with common sense and you get a practical checklist. The more boxes a test case ticks, the better the case for automating it.

        • Repeated often: runs every commit, every release, or in many configurations.
        • Stable: the feature and its UI will not be rewritten next sprint.
        • Deterministic: a clear, objective expected result exists (no "looks nice").
        • High value: a failure would hurt (payments, login, data loss).
        • Tedious or error-prone for humans: large data tables, many combinations, precise numeric comparison.
        • Hard to do by hand: load, concurrency, thousands of API calls, many device/browser combinations.
        • Automatable at a low level: if you can check it with a fast unit or API test, do that instead of a slow browser test (see the test pyramid).

        The ROI and cost model

        "ROI" (return on investment) sounds fancy; the idea is a break-even calculation. Automation has an up-front build cost and a per-run maintenance cost; manual testing has a per-run execution cost. Automation wins once you have run the check enough times.

        break-even runs  =  build cost
                    -------------------------------------------
                    manual cost per run - automation cost per run

automation cost per run = machine time (usually ~0)
                        + average maintenance and failure triage per run

        Here is a worked example. The numbers are illustrative, invented for teaching, not measured data from any source.

        ScenarioManual runBuildAvg. maintenance + triage per runBreak-even
        Stable checkout flow, healthy suite20 min6 h (360 min)2 min360 / (20 - 2) = 20 runs
        Same flow, flaky and brittle selectors20 min6 h15 min360 / (20 - 15) = 72 runs
        Same flow, maintenance exceeds manual20 min6 h22 minnever (negative saving)
        Feature rewritten every sprint20 min6 h, redone each sprintn/aruns per sprint must exceed ~20 (the break-even above) just to pay back the rebuild

        If the checkout check runs on every commit (say 10 times a day) the healthy case pays back in two days. The lesson is not the exact numbers but the shape: maintenance cost per run decides everything. A flaky test that costs engineers 15 minutes of triage each time it fails can be a net loss even if it runs a thousand times.

        // A tiny model you can adapt with your own team's numbers.
function breakEvenRuns(buildMin: number, manualMin: number, maintMin: number): number {
  const saving = manualMin - maintMin;       // minutes saved per run
  return saving <= 0 ? Infinity : Math.ceil(buildMin / saving);
}

breakEvenRuns(360, 20, 2);   // 20
breakEvenRuns(360, 20, 15);  // 72
breakEvenRuns(360, 20, 22);  // Infinity
        Hidden costs and benefits the simple formula misses
        • Cost: test data and environments, CI machine time, training, tool licences, upgrade work when browsers or libraries change. ISTQB warns about inaccurate estimates of time, cost and effort to introduce a tool and maintain scripts.
        • Cost: opportunity cost. Hours spent on a fragile UI test are hours not spent on cheaper lower-level tests.
        • Benefit: earlier bug detection. The Google book says the later a bug is caught, the more expensive it is, "exponentially so in many cases" (their wording, citing a general industry claim; treat the exact shape as a rule of thumb).
        • Benefit: confidence and speed of release. Many Google projects ship daily, which the authors say would not be possible without automated testing.
        • Benefit: consistent, always-available documentation of behavior.

        A decision flow: should this check be automated?

        1. Will it run again?Only once or twice? Do it manually.
        2. Is the result objective?"Looks good" is a human judgement.
        3. Is it stable enough?If the UI changes weekly, wait or test lower down.
        4. Can a lower level cover it?Unit or API test beats a browser test.
        5. Does payback beat upkeep?Run the break-even estimate.
        6. Automate, then keep it healthyReview flakiness and relevance regularly.

        What should NOT be automated

        Wanting "100% automation" is a common beginner goal and a bad one. ISTQB lists "using a test tool when manual testing is more appropriate" and "relying on a tool too much, e.g., ignoring the need of human critical thinking" among the risks of automation. Think twice before automating:

        • One-off checks and migrations you will never repeat.
        • Brand-new, fast-changing features whose behavior is still being decided. Explore first, automate once it settles.
        • Subjective quality: usability, "does this feel right", copywriting tone, visual taste. Computers are, in Ham Vocke's words, notoriously bad at checking whether something "looks good". Pixel-comparison tools can catch changes but not judge quality.
        • Checks that cost more to maintain than they save (the break-even table above).
        • Highly non-deterministic scenarios you cannot control (live third-party systems, real payment gateways). Use a test double or a contract test instead.
        • Duplicates: if a unit test already proves the rule, a UI test for the same rule adds cost but little confidence.
        Record-and-playback trap. Fowler calls record-playback tools "almost always a bad idea" for automation because the recordings resist change and block useful abstractions. They are fine for generating a first draft that you then edit as real code. Teams that automate by recording tend to end up with the ice-cream cone described in The Test Pyramid.

        Exploratory testing: the human half of the strategy

        Exploratory testing means a skilled person simultaneously designs, runs and evaluates tests while learning about the product (ISTQB's definition). It is not random clicking. It is often organised in time-boxed sessions guided by a charter (a short mission such as "explore coupon edge cases in checkout") followed by a debrief.

        Why it matters even in a heavily automated team:

        • Automation checks the cases you thought of. Exploration finds the ones you did not. ISTQB notes it is especially useful when specifications are thin or time is short, and it complements formal techniques.
        • Vocke recommends scheduling it regularly and "using a destructive mindset" to provoke problems: bugs, design issues, slow responses, misleading error messages.
        • It feeds automation: when you find a bug by exploring, write an automated regression test so it stays dead. Missed bugs are also feedback on your pipeline, a hint that some kind of test is missing.

        ISTQB's principle "absence-of-defects fallacy" reminds us that passing every test does not prove the product is useful. Exploring with a user's eyes is part of the answer.

        Five myths about test automation
        1. "Automation replaces testers." It replaces repetitive checking, not thinking. ISTQB lists over-reliance on a tool, "ignoring the need of human critical thinking", as a risk.
        2. "Automate everything." The break-even table shows some checks never pay back.
        3. "More tests means more quality." Vocke: every test is baggage, because writing, reading and running it all cost time. Duplicated tests across levels add cost without confidence.
        4. "A high coverage number proves quality." Coverage shows lines executed, not behaviors verified.
        5. "Once written, tests are free." Google's authors note tests derive their value from engineers' trust; a suite that becomes a productivity sink can be worse than none.

        Automation is software engineering

        The most common reason automation projects die is treating test code as second-class. Vocke's guidance is blunt: test code is as important as production code, and "it's only test code" is not an excuse for sloppiness. Concretely this means:

        • Design for change: abstractions (for UI tests, the Page Object pattern; see Page Object Models) so a UI change is fixed in one place.
        • Code review, version control and CI for tests, exactly like product code.
        • Readability: the Google book says "a test should be obvious upon inspection" and discourages loops and conditionals inside tests, because there are no tests for the tests.
        • Hermetic tests: each test sets up and tears down its own world and does not depend on test order or a shared database.
        • Treat the suite as a product with owners, health metrics (run time, flake rate) and a budget for upkeep.
        • Do not worship coverage: Google's authors warn that line coverage only measures that code ran, not that anything useful was checked, and that a target like 80% becomes a ceiling, not a floor.
        Best practice: when you decide to automate a check, also decide where in the pyramid it belongs and who maintains it. A test with no owner becomes a flaky test within months.
        How this maps to Playwright: Playwright gives you the tooling for the "run" and "react" parts: parallelism and sharding make runs fast, the Trace Viewer makes failures cheap to diagnose, and best practices covers keeping tests isolated. The decision of what to automate is still yours.

        Key points

        • Automation is best at fast, repeatable checking; people are best at exploring and judging. You need both.
        • Pay-back = build cost divided by (manual cost per run minus maintenance per run). Maintenance cost decides whether automation wins.
        • Automate stable, repeated, objective, high-value checks, and push them to the lowest level that can prove the behavior.
        • Do not automate one-offs, volatile features, subjective quality or things you cannot control deterministically.
        • Test code is software: design, review and maintain it. A flaky or unloved suite can be worse than none.
        • Found a bug while exploring? Write the regression test, so the human insight becomes permanent protection.

        A manual check takes 10 minutes. Automating it takes 5 hours (300 minutes) and the test will cost about 4 minutes per run in maintenance and triage. Roughly how many runs until automation breaks even?

        Saving per run = 10 - 4 = 6 minutes. Break-even = 300 / 6 = 50 runs. Notice how the 4 minutes of upkeep nearly doubled the break-even compared with a free-to-run test (30 runs).

        Which of these is the BEST candidate for staying manual (at least for now)?

        C needs human judgement about usability, which the sources agree automation cannot provide. A, B and D are objective, repeated and automatable (and B and D are best done below the UI).

        Name three activities that make up automated testing (SWE@Google).
        Write tests, run tests, react to failures. Teams often over-invest in writing and under-invest in running fast and fixing failures quickly.
        What decides whether automation pays back?
        The per-run maintenance and triage cost compared with the manual cost per run. High upkeep (flaky, brittle tests) can make it never pay back.
        Give three things you should not automate.
        One-off checks, fast-changing features, subjective quality (usability, looks), and scenarios you cannot make deterministic.
        What is exploratory testing?
        Simultaneously designing, executing and evaluating tests while learning the product, usually in time-boxed sessions with a charter. It finds what scripted checks miss.
        Why call automation "software engineering"?
        Because tests are code: they need design, reviews, version control, readability, ownership and ongoing maintenance, or they rot.

        The Test Pyramid (and Trophy, Honeycomb, Ice-Cream Cone)

        Not all automated tests are equal: some are tiny, fast and precise, others are big, slow and realistic. The test pyramid is a simple picture for deciding how many of each to write. This page explains the pyramid, its popular rivals (the trophy and the honeycomb), the ice-cream-cone anti-pattern, Google's small/medium/large test sizes, and how to decide for your own project where UI and end-to-end tests belong.

        Start with an analogy: checking a car factory

        Imagine you build cars. You could test each bolt, each subassembly (engine, brakes), and finally drive the finished car on a track. Testing bolts is cheap and instant, and when one fails you know exactly which bolt. Driving the whole car is the most realistic check, but it takes a day, needs a track, and when it fails you only know "something is wrong". A sensible factory does many bolt checks, some subassembly checks and a few track drives. That is the test pyramid.

        Where the pyramid comes from

        Most people know the pyramid from Mike Cohn's 2009 book Succeeding with Agile, where it is called the "Test Automation Pyramid". Martin Fowler's history note says Cohn first drew it in conversation with Lisa Crispin around 2003-2004, and that Jason Huggins independently came up with the same idea around 2006. Cohn's three layers, bottom to top, are unit tests, service tests and user interface (UI) tests. ISTQB's Foundation syllabus (v4.0.1) presents the same idea: the higher the layer, the lower the isolation and the higher the execution time, so a few high-level tests cover a lot of functionality while many small tests are needed at the bottom.

        UI / End-to-endFew. Slowest, most realistic, most brittle.
        Service / IntegrationSome. Real database, real API, one boundary at a time.
        UnitMany. Milliseconds, no I/O, pinpoint failures.

        Both Fowler and Ham Vocke (author of "The Practical Test Pyramid") stress that you should keep only two ideas from the original: write tests with different granularity, and the more high-level you get, the fewer tests you should have. They also say the layer names are not sacred: Vocke notes that "service test" is a confusing term and that, with modern front-end frameworks, UI logic can be unit-tested too, so UI tests do not have to sit at the top.

        Why the shape? Speed, cost and confidence

        Mike Wacker's Google Testing Blog post "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests" explains the reasoning from first principles. A failing test does not help the user; a bug fix does. So a good suite is one that gives developers a good feedback loop with three properties: it is fast, reliable and it isolates failures (tells you where the bug is). Unit tests score well on all three but cannot show that pieces work together. End-to-end tests are the opposite: they best simulate a real user but are slow, flaky and hard to debug.

        PropertyUnitIntegrationEnd-to-end (UI)
        SpeedMilliseconds; Google calls even 0.1 s "slow" for a unit testSecondsMany seconds to minutes
        Reliability (low flakiness)HighMediumLowest: browsers, timing, networks, shared environments
        Isolates failuresPoints to a function or classPoints to one boundary"Somewhere in the whole system"
        Resembles real usageLowMediumHigh
        Cost to write and maintainLowMediumHigh
        Confidence that parts work togetherNone by itselfGood for one seamHighest, but narrow in what it covers

        Wacker's illustration is a composite story: a team requires 90% of nightly end-to-end tests to pass; over a week the pass rate swings between 1% and 89.5% because of a broken sign-in, a bad build from a partner team, hardware failures in the lab and flaky tests. The tests did catch real bugs, but the milestone was a week late. Fowler adds the broader warning that UI tests are "brittle, expensive to write, and time consuming to run" and that even good end-to-end tests are more prone to non-determinism.

        How many of each? The numbers (and why they differ)

        Google gives two rough ratios, from different times and authors:

        • The 2015 blog post suggests "as a good first guess" a 70/20/10 split: 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% end-to-end.
        • The later book chapter (Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11) says they aim for about 80/15/5, by test-case count, adding that "every team's mix will be a little different".

        These are not contradictory laws; they are two shrugs in the same direction. The point is the shape. Treat any percentage as a smell detector, not a target. A commenter on the Google post noted a few E2E tests may produce more coverage than many unit tests, so counting alone can mislead; the Google author replied that deviation shows up in measurable side effects such as longer run time and more flakes.

        Test sizes: small, medium, large

        Google found that arguing "is it a unit or an integration test?" went nowhere. So they classify every test by size (what resources it needs) and separately by scope (how much code it verifies). Size is enforceable by tooling, which is why it is useful.

        SizeWhere it may runAllowedNot allowedTypical use
        SmallA single process (often a single thread)Pure computation, in-memory fakesSleeping, disk or network I/O, starting other programs such as a databaseLogic, algorithms, components with doubles
        MediumA single machine, several processesLocalhost network calls, a real DB, a browser driven by WebDriverCalling other machinesIntegration, UI against a local server
        LargeAnywhere, multiple machinesReal clusters and external systems(few limits)Full-system E2E, legacy parts you cannot fake

        The key insight: size and scope are different axes. A broad-scoped test of a server endpoint can still be "small" if every out-of-process dependency is replaced with an in-process double. Conversely a narrow test of a date-picker may need a whole browser and so be "medium". Google's advice is to write the smallest possible test for each behavior, because small tests are fast and deterministic. Notice how this reframes the pyramid debate: what you want is speed and determinism, whatever you call the test.

        Pyramid, trophy, honeycomb: reconciling the shapes

        Different communities draw different shapes. They disagree less than they seem to, because they use different definitions of "unit" and "integration" and have different architectures in mind.

        ModelProposed byBiggest layerContext it was designed forCore argument
        PyramidMike Cohn (2009); popularised by Fowler, Google, VockeUnitGeneral applicationsLow-level tests are fast, stable and pinpoint failures; keep high-level tests few.
        TrophyKent C. Dodds (2018), after Guillermo Rauch's "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration."Integration (plus a static-analysis base)A single JavaScript front-end codebase; "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you"Best return on investment, where "return" is confidence and "investment" is time. Static checks (types, linting) catch typos for free.
        HoneycombSpotify engineers (André Schaffer, Rickard Dybeck, 2018)Integration tests of a whole microserviceMicroservices, where complexity lives in the interactions between servicesA microservice is itself the "unit". Prefer integration tests through its API, add a few "implementation detail" tests for isolated tricky logic, and avoid "integrated" tests that depend on other systems being correct.
        Ice-cream cone (anti-pattern)Named by Fowler, Google and othersManual and E2E on topTeams that started with record-and-playback or "let QA test it later"Slow, flaky, expensive; the shape to avoid.
        Hourglass (anti-pattern)GoogleUnit and E2E, with a thin middleTightly coupled code that is hard to instantiate in piecesFailures that a medium-scope test would catch fast show up as E2E failures.

        How to reconcile them:

        • Definitions drive the disagreement. Dodds calls a "unit" a single function or object with its dependencies mocked, and an "integration" test anything that combines multiple units, which is broader than Vocke's narrow "one boundary at a time". Fowler suspects the difference between pyramid and trophy advocates is "probably illusory due to different definitions of 'unit test'". Dodds himself quotes the old joke of a trainer who covers 24 definitions of unit test on the first morning, and concludes the exact classification matters less than writing expressive, fast, reliable tests.
        • Architecture matters. Spotify argues that in microservices the risk is in the wiring between services, so a unit-heavy pyramid can be "actively harmful" because many tiny tests lock the internals in place. Google, which prefers keeping real dependencies when feasible and testing narrowly, reaches a more unit-heavy answer in a monorepo. Both measure value as fast and trustworthy feedback.
        • Shared conclusions: few end-to-end tests; tests should survive refactoring (test behavior, not implementation); invest in speed and determinism; do not argue about names.
        A practical rule: pick the shape that fits your architecture, write your team's definitions down ("in this repo, a medium test means..."), and then spend your energy on making tests fast and reliable. Dodds, Vocke and Google all end up saying roughly this.

        The ice-cream cone anti-pattern

        In an ice-cream cone the suite is top-heavy: lots of manual and UI end-to-end tests, a few integration tests, almost no unit tests. Google's book says it often appears in projects that started as prototypes, were rushed to production, and never paid back their testing debt. Fowler traces it to the days of record-and-playback tools. The symptoms are recognizable:

        • CI takes an hour or more, so developers stop running tests before committing.
        • A small change breaks dozens of tests that must be re-recorded or re-fixed.
        • Failures are intermittent ("just re-run it"), so people stop trusting red builds (see Flaky Tests).
        • Nobody can say where a failure originates without a long debugging session.

        Escaping the cone is gradual. Vocke gives a rule of thumb you can apply from tomorrow: if a high-level test finds a bug and no lower-level test fails, write the lower-level test too, and push every check as far down the pyramid as it can go.

        Where UI and end-to-end tests fit

        People often use "UI test", "end-to-end test" and "acceptance test" as synonyms. Vocke argues they are three orthogonal ideas:

        • End-to-end describes scope: the whole deployed system.
        • UI describes how you drive it: through the user interface (a REST API or command line is also a user interface).
        • Acceptance / customer-facing describes purpose: proving a feature works from the user's perspective.

        Testing end to end often means driving the UI, but the reverse is not true: a React component can be tested through the UI with no backend at all, and an acceptance rule can run as a fast low-level test. So a UI test does not automatically belong at the top of the pyramid.

        Where full-stack browser tests earn their cost:

        • A handful of critical user journeys. Vocke's example for an online shop: search for a product, add it to the basket, check out. "Everything more than that will likely be more painful than helpful."
        • Wiring and configuration that cannot be seen at lower levels: is the deployed app reachable, do the front end and back end actually agree, are the flags and environment variables right? The Google book says large tests are mostly about validating configuration rather than code, and should be "sanity checks", not a primary way to catch bugs.
        • Things only a real browser shows: real rendering, cross-browser quirks, real navigation, file uploads, popups.

        And a caveat so you do not over-apply the rule. Fowler's own footnote says the pyramid assumes broad-stack tests are slow, expensive and brittle, "while this is usually true, there are exceptions": if your high-level tests are fast, reliable and cheap to modify, lower-level tests may not be needed. Fowler also points readers to LMAX, a team whose experience showed end-to-end tests can play a large and valuable role. Modern tools (for example Playwright's auto-waiting, parallel workers and tracing) narrow the gap a little, but the 2018-era Vocke and 2015-era Wacker arguments about cost and isolation still apply in kind, if less in degree. Spotify goes the other way too: its Assert(JS) talk says end-to-end tests are flaky by nature and suggests having 5 of them instead of 500.

        Common misreadings of the pyramid
        • "Unit tests are good, everything else is bad." No: Google's own mix still reserves a slice for integration and end-to-end tests, and Spotify argues the middle layer should be the biggest for microservices.
        • "The pyramid is a quota." The percentages are rough guesses by count; what matters is run time, reliability and how fast a failure leads you to the cause.
        • "UI tests must be at the top." A UI test can be small (a rendered component with stubbed data); a non-UI test can be large (a multi-service API journey).
        • "Mock everything to stay at the bottom." Heavy mocking makes tests brittle (Google) and couples them to implementation (Fowler); prefer real in-process objects and fakes when you can.

        Example: one business rule at three levels

        Suppose the rule is "orders of 100 or more get a 10% discount". Testing it at each level shows the trade-off.

        import { discountedTotal } from './pricing';

test('10% off at the 100 threshold', () => {
  expect(discountedTotal(100)).toBe(90);   // boundary
});
test('no discount just below the threshold', () => {
  expect(discountedTotal(99.99)).toBe(99.99);
});
// Runs in about 1 ms. A failure points at one function.
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('POST /orders applies the discount', async ({ request }) => {
  const res = await request.post('/api/orders', { data: { items: [{ sku: 'A1', qty: 1, price: 100 }] } });
  expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  expect((await res.json()).total).toBe(90);
});
// Needs a running server and database, but no browser. About 50 ms.
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('customer sees the discounted total at checkout', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/shop');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to basket' }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-total')).toHaveText('$90.00');
});
// Needs the whole system plus a browser. Seconds, and many things can fail.

        The right amount is: thorough unit tests for the rule's edge cases (99.99, 100, 100.01, negative, zero), one API test proving the rule is wired into the endpoint, and at most one UI test proving the displayed total reaches the customer, usually as part of a broader checkout journey. You do not repeat all the edge cases at the UI level.

        How to decide: a practical procedure

        1. State the behavior"Orders over 100 get 10% off."
        2. Smallest test that can fail for the right reason?Pure logic: unit test (small).
        3. Does the risk live at a boundary?DB, queue, HTTP API, file: narrow integration test.
        4. Does only the full system prove it?Wiring, config, browser: E2E, but only for critical journeys.
        5. Check for duplicationIs a lower test already covering it? Delete or skip the higher one.
        6. Place it in the pipeline by speedFast first, slow later.
        Question to askIf yes, lean towards
        Is the logic pure (inputs to outputs)?Unit test
        Is the risk in how we talk to a database, queue, or other service?Narrow integration test (real DB in a container; fake or contract for others)
        Do two teams share an interface?Contract tests (see Test Types)
        Is it a high-value user journey that must never break?One end-to-end test, kept tiny
        Do I only need to know the UI wiring (button shows data)?Component test with the backend mocked (see mocking)
        Would it break when I refactor without changing behavior?Rewrite it to test behavior, not implementation
        Is the environment shared and unreliable?Lower the level, or make the environment hermetic

        Vocke adds a point about pipelines: stages should be defined by speed and scope, not by the formal test type. A narrow, quick integration test may belong in the same early stage as unit tests simply because it gives fast feedback. Fowler agrees: keep a fast "commit suite" (mostly unit tests) that runs several times a day, and push slower tests to later stages of the deployment pipeline.

        Do not chase the percentages. A suite that is 70/20/10 on paper but whose 10% E2E tests take two hours and flake daily is still unhealthy. Watch the outcomes: total run time, flake rate, how often a failure tells you where the bug is, and how often a refactor breaks tests. Dodds quotes Justin Searls: debating test percentages is a distraction; focus on expressive tests with clear boundaries that run quickly and fail only for useful reasons.
        Best practice: before fixing a bug found by a high-level test, reproduce it with a low-level test first (Fowler's advice). The unit test then keeps that bug dead cheaply, and the high-level test stays a second line of defense.
        How this maps to Playwright: Playwright Test is mostly used at the top of the pyramid, which makes the discipline above important. You can lower the level of many checks without leaving the tool: use the API testing features to test endpoints directly, mock or intercept the network to test UI behavior without a real backend, and reuse login state via authentication so each E2E test does not repeat the same slow sign-in. Decide placement into projects and CI stages with projects and CI.

        Key points

        • Pyramid idea: many fast, narrow tests at the bottom; few slow, broad tests on top. Keep the idea, not the exact layer names.
        • Trade-off triangle: small tests are fast, reliable and pinpoint failures; large tests are more realistic but slower, flakier and harder to debug.
        • Google's rough mixes are 70/20/10 (2015 blog) and 80/15/5 (book): a smell detector, not a quota.
        • Google's size model (small = one process, medium = one machine, large = anywhere) separates resource use from scope and makes speed enforceable.
        • Trophy (Dodds) and honeycomb (Spotify) emphasise integration tests for front ends and microservices; most disagreement is about definitions and architecture.
        • Ice cream cone and hourglass are anti-patterns; escape by writing a lower-level test for every bug a high-level test finds.
        • UI, end-to-end and acceptance are three different axes. Keep E2E to a few critical journeys plus wiring checks.

        A team has 40 unit tests, 5 integration tests and 600 browser-driven tests that take 90 minutes and fail randomly about once a day. Which description fits best?

        The bulk of the effort sits in slow end-to-end tests, with few unit tests. Hourglass needs many unit tests as well; here the unit layer is tiny. The symptoms (slow, flaky, hard to diagnose) match the cone Google and Fowler describe.

        According to Google's testing sizes, which test is "small"?

        Size is defined by how a test runs and what resources it may use, not by lines of code. A browser on localhost is a medium test (multiple processes, same machine).

        What two ideas should you keep from Cohn's pyramid?
        Write tests of different granularity, and the higher-level the test, the fewer of them you should have.
        Size versus scope (Google)?
        Size = resources a test needs (process, machine, network, time). Scope = how much code it verifies. They are independent axes.
        Testing trophy vs honeycomb?
        Trophy (Dodds): front-end, mostly integration tests plus static checks. Honeycomb (Spotify): microservices, mostly integration tests of a whole service via its API.
        Ice-cream cone vs hourglass?
        Cone: mostly manual/E2E, few lower tests. Hourglass: many unit and E2E tests but few integration tests in the middle.
        Rule when a high-level test finds a bug?
        Make sure a lower-level test also fails (write one if needed), and push tests down the pyramid as far as they can go.

        📚 Sources

        • Test Pyramid – Martin Fowler: origins (Cohn, Crispin, Huggins), ice-cream cone, exceptions to the pyramid, UI vs E2E vs customer-facing
        • The Practical Test Pyramid – Ham Vocke (Thoughtworks): layers in practice, UI/E2E/acceptance as orthogonal ideas, few critical journeys, pipeline staging, avoiding duplication
        • Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests – Mike Wacker / Google Testing Blog: fast/reliable/isolating feedback loop, 70/20/10 split, ice cream cone and hourglass
        • Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11 "Testing Overview" – Adam Bender / Google: small/medium/large sizes, size vs scope, 80/15/5 guideline
        • The Testing Trophy and Testing Classifications – Kent C. Dodds: trophy shape, his unit/integration definitions, why definitions differ
        • Testing of Microservices – André Schaffer and Rickard Dybeck / Spotify Engineering: the testing honeycomb
        • Test Flakiness – Methods for identifying and dealing with flaky tests – Jason Palmer / Spotify Engineering: "5 instead of 500" E2E advice
        • ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1 – ISTQB: section 5.1.6, the test pyramid as a granularity model

        Test Levels, Test Types and Test Doubles

        "Unit", "integration", "smoke", "regression", "E2E", "acceptance"... testing vocabulary is a jungle, and the same word often means different things in different teams. This page untangles it: first the difference between a test level (how big a piece you test) and a test type (what quality you check), then a field guide to fourteen common kinds of tests, and finally the toolbox of test doubles (dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake) that lets you test a piece without its real neighbours.

        Two axes: level and type

        The ISTQB Foundation syllabus (v4.0.1) separates two ideas that people constantly mix up:

        • Test levels are groups of test activities organised and managed together, tied to a phase of development: from individual components up to whole systems.
        • Test types are groups of test activities aimed at specific quality characteristics, and most of them can be performed at every level.

        Analogy: levels are the zoom on a map (street, district, city); types are the layer you switch on (roads, traffic, weather). You can look at traffic at street level or city level.

        ISTQB test levelFocusUsual ownerInformal names
        Component testingOne component in isolation, often with a test harness or unit-test frameworkDevelopersUnit testing
        Component integration testingInterfaces and interactions between componentsDevelopersIntegration testing (narrow)
        System testingOverall behavior of the whole system, functional end-to-end tasks plus non-functional characteristicsOften an independent teamE2E, functional testing
        System integration testingInterfaces to other systems and external services, in an environment similar to productionTest / integration teamIntegration environment testing
        Acceptance testingValidation: does the system meet business needs, is it ready to deploy?Ideally the intended usersUAT, alpha/beta, operational, contractual, regulatory

        ISTQB names four test types in the Foundation syllabus: functional (what the system should do), non-functional (how well it behaves), black-box (derived from specifications, not code) and white-box (derived from code structure). Non-functional testing draws on the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model: performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability and safety. On top of these there are change-related tests: confirmation testing (is this defect really fixed?) and regression testing (did the change break anything else?).

        Why two vocabularies? ISTQB's levels come from process-heavy lifecycles. Developers on agile teams more often talk about the "unit / integration / end-to-end" scale in the test pyramid. Ham Vocke's pyramid article admits there is "no right or wrong" and that the community "hasn't managed to settle on well-defined terms". The practical rule he gives: agree names and scope inside your team and write them down.

        A field guide to fourteen kinds of tests

        The table gives a plain definition, the question each test answers, and where it normally sits. Some entries (unit, integration, acceptance, regression, exploratory, performance, security, usability-related) are defined by ISTQB or the cited articles; others (smoke, sanity, component, visual, accessibility) are everyday industry terms whose exact meaning varies by team, and I say so where it matters.

        KindQuestion it answersScope and speedNotes
        UnitDoes this small piece of logic behave correctly?Tiny; millisecondsFowler: low-level, written by programmers, fast. "Unit" is "ill-defined"; the team decides what a unit is (function, class, small cluster).
        ComponentDoes this module or UI component work with its own collaborators but without the rest of the system?Small to mediumAmbiguous word: ISTQB uses it as a synonym for unit; Vocke notes some call narrow integration tests "component" or "service" tests; front-end teams mean "render one UI component".
        IntegrationDo two parts (code and database, service and queue) work together at their boundary?Medium; secondsVocke prefers narrow integration tests: one integration point at a time, real DB, test double for other services.
        ContractDo a provider and its consumers still agree on the interface?Small to mediumConsumer-driven contracts (for example Pact): consumers publish tests of the data they need; the provider runs them in its pipeline. Fowler uses the term differently too: tests that run the same interaction against a real remote system and its test double to check the double stays honest.
        End-to-end (E2E)Does a whole user journey work through the fully deployed system?Large; seconds to minutesHighest confidence, highest cost; keep few. Also called broad-stack or system tests.
        SmokeIs the build alive at all, can we even start testing?A handful of very fast checksCommon usage: a minimal set run first after a deploy. Fowler recommends a smoke test to check that an asynchronous service responds at all, so a broken environment stops the run in seconds instead of waiting for timeouts.
        SanityAfter a small change or fix, does that area plausibly work before we run deeper tests?Narrow and quickThe terms smoke and sanity are used inconsistently across organisations; no source I read defines them formally. Agree your own definition.
        RegressionDid a change break something that used to work?Any level, run oftenISTQB: regression suites grow every release, so they are strong candidates for automation. Confirmation testing is its sibling: "is this one bug fixed?".
        AcceptanceDoes the feature work from the user's or business's point of view?Usually high level, but not necessarilyISTQB forms: user, operational, contractual, regulatory, alpha and beta acceptance. Vocke stresses it is about purpose, orthogonal to the pyramid: if you can prove it at a lower level, do.
        VisualDid the layout or appearance change unexpectedly?Medium to largeUsually screenshot comparison against a baseline. Vocke: computers are bad at judging "looks good"; they detect changes, a human judges quality.
        PerformanceIs it fast enough, and how does it behave under load?Large; needs representative environmentA non-functional type (ISO 25010 "performance efficiency"). Results vary run to run, so it is non-deterministic by nature; Fowler distinguishes such tests from regression tests.
        SecurityCan it be attacked, are secrets and permissions safe?All levels; static scans through pen testsNon-functional type. Google's Beyoncé Rule lists security among properties you must test if you do not want them to break.
        AccessibilityCan people using keyboards, screen readers or zoom use it?Component through systemGenerally part of usability / interaction capability. Automated scanners find only a portion of issues; manual checks with assistive technology are still needed. Google's book lists accessibility among properties to test.
        ExploratoryWhat surprises are hiding that nobody scripted?Human, time-boxed sessionsISTQB: tests are designed, run and evaluated at once while the tester learns. Not automatable by definition, but its findings become automated regression tests.
        Same name, different meaning. Kent C. Dodds calls a test of several units together "integration"; Vocke calls "integration" a test of one boundary; Google would call the same test "small" or "medium" depending only on whether it needs more than one process. Before arguing about a word in a code review, ask "what does it start, and what does it replace with doubles?"

        How levels and types combine

        Because types cut across levels, one cell of a grid can hold many different tests. For a login feature:

        Level / typeFunctionalPerformanceSecurityAccessibility
        Component (unit)Password-rule validator returns correct resultHashing function completes under a time budgetValidator rejects injection stringsForm component exposes labels and error roles
        IntegrationLogin service reads the user row from the real DBQuery uses the index (checked by timing or plan)Stored hashes are salted(rare)
        System / E2EA user logs in and reaches the dashboard100 concurrent logins stay under 1 sAccount locks after repeated failuresLogin is possible by keyboard alone
        AcceptanceA product owner confirms the sign-in matches the agreed storyMeets the contractual response-time SLAPasses the customer's security reviewMeets the regulatory standard

        Typical tools per kind (examples, not an endorsement)

        KindExamples of toolsNotes
        Unit / componentJUnit, pytest, Jest, Vitest, NUnit, Mockito, Testing LibraryLanguage-specific; run in a single process
        IntegrationThe same runners plus Testcontainers, Spring/Django/Express test helpers, WireMockReal DB in a container, fakes for other services
        ContractPact, Spring Cloud ContractConsumer-driven contracts
        UI / E2EPlaywright, Selenium, Cypress, WebdriverIO, TestCafe, Appium (mobile)The tools this course is about
        VisualPlaywright screenshots, Percy, Applitools, BackstopJSBaseline images and tolerances
        Performancek6, JMeter, Gatling, Lighthouse (front-end)Needs realistic data and hardware
        SecurityOWASP ZAP, static analysers, dependency scannersMix of automated and expert manual work
        Accessibilityaxe-core, Lighthouse, Pa11y, plus screen-reader checksAutomation covers only part of the rules

        Test doubles: dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake

        A unit under test usually talks to collaborators: a database, an email service, a payment gateway, the clock. Using the real ones may be slow, random or dangerous. Gerard Meszaros coined test double (think "stunt double") as the umbrella term for anything that replaces a production object for testing. Martin Fowler's short article lists five kinds, and the vocabulary is worth learning because many people say "mock" for all of them.

        DoubleWhat it doesExampleVerified by
        DummyPassed around but never used; fills a parameter list.A Logger the code under test never calls.Nothing
        StubReturns canned answers to calls made during the test.A price service that always returns 100.State of the unit under test
        SpyA stub that also records how it was called.An email sender that counts messages sent.Assert on recorded calls afterwards
        MockPre-programmed with expectations; fails if it gets unexpected calls or misses expected ones."charge() must be called exactly once with 90".The mock itself verifies behavior
        FakeA real, working but simplified implementation, not suitable for production.An in-memory database or in-memory repository.State
        Need nothing from it?Dummy.
        Need fixed answers?Stub.
        Need to see what was sent?Spy (or mock).
        Need realistic behavior without the cost?Fake (in-memory DB, local server).
        Is the call itself the outcome?Mock, with verification.

        Here is one scenario implemented with each kind, to make the differences concrete. The unit under test is OrderService.checkout, which looks up a price, charges a card and sends a receipt.

        // Collaborators (interfaces the production code depends on)
interface PriceService { priceOf(sku: string): number }
interface Gateway      { charge(amount: number): boolean }
interface Mailer       { send(to: string, body: string): void }
interface Logger       { info(msg: string): void }

// DUMMY: required by the constructor, never touched in this test
const dummyLogger: Logger = { info() { throw new Error('should not be called'); } };

// STUB: canned answer
const stubPrices: PriceService = { priceOf: () => 100 };

// SPY: stub that also records calls
class SpyMailer implements Mailer {
  sent: Array<[string, string]> = [];
  send(to: string, body: string) { this.sent.push([to, body]); }
}

// FAKE: working but simplified implementation
class InMemoryOrders { private rows = new Map<string, number>();
  save(id: string, total: number) { this.rows.set(id, total); }
  find(id: string) { return this.rows.get(id); } }

// MOCK (hand-rolled): knows what it expects, verifies itself
class MockGateway implements Gateway {
  calls: number[] = [];
  charge(amount: number) { this.calls.push(amount); return true; }
  verify(expected: number) {
    if (this.calls.length !== 1 || this.calls[0] !== expected) throw new Error('unexpected charge calls: ' + this.calls);
  }
}

test('checkout charges the discounted total and emails a receipt', () => {
  const mailer = new SpyMailer(), gateway = new MockGateway();
  const svc = new OrderService(stubPrices, gateway, mailer, dummyLogger);
  svc.checkout('A1', 'ann@example.com');
  gateway.verify(90);                                        // behavior verification (mock)
  expect(mailer.sent).toEqual([['ann@example.com', expect.stringContaining('90')]]);  // spy
});

        In practice you rarely hand-write these. Mocking libraries generate them, and the same idea exists in every ecosystem:

        const gateway = { charge: jest.fn().mockReturnValue(true) };   // stub + spy in one
svc.checkout('A1', 'ann@example.com');
expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith(90);            // mock-style verification
        Gateway gateway = mock(Gateway.class);
when(gateway.charge(90)).thenReturn(true);                  // stub
svc.checkout("A1", "ann@example.com");
verify(gateway, times(1)).charge(90);                       // mock-style verification
        gateway = Mock()
gateway.charge.return_value = True                          # stub
svc.checkout("A1", "ann@example.com")
gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(90)                  # mock-style verification

        Note the terminology trap: the library object is called a "mock" in all three, yet depending on how you use it, it plays the role of a stub (canned answer), a spy (recording) or a true mock (verifying expectations).

        Using doubles wisely: state versus behavior, classical versus mockist

        Fowler's "Mocks Aren't Stubs" describes two separate differences. First, state verification (run the code, then check the resulting state of the unit and its collaborators) versus behavior verification (check that the unit made the right calls on its collaborators). Second, two styles of test-driven development: the classical style uses real collaborators where practical and doubles only when awkward, while the mockist style isolates each unit with mocks and drives design from the outside in. Related vocabulary from Jay Fields: solitary tests replace all collaborators; sociable tests use real ones.

        Classical / sociableMockist / solitary
        VerificationMostly stateMostly behavior (calls)
        Coupling to implementationLower: only final state mattersHigher: changing how collaborators are called breaks tests
        Refactoring safetyBetterWorse (mock-heavy tests are brittle)
        Failure localizationA bug in a collaborator can fail neighbours' testsFailures point to the one unit
        Design pressureDomain-model outOutside-in; encourages role interfaces and "tell, don't ask"

        Fowler says he is a classicist but presents both fairly. Google's book is more pointed: its codebase "has suffered so badly from an abuse of mocking frameworks" that some engineers declared "no more mocks", and Google generally prefers keeping real dependencies in place when feasible. Vocke is relaxed: using both approaches is fine; he uses mocks and stubs "generously" when real collaborators are awkward, and real ones when they add confidence.

        Rules of thumb that all the sources support:
        • Always replace what is non-deterministic or out of your control: the clock, random numbers, remote services, payment gateways (Fowler's non-determinism article).
        • Prefer fakes and real in-process objects over interaction-verifying mocks when you can: they survive refactoring.
        • Test observable behavior ("given x and y the result is z"), not the sequence of calls inside.
        • Keep doubles honest with contract tests: the same checks run against the double and the real thing, or consumer-driven contracts between teams.
        Over-mocking trap: a test that mocks every collaborator and asserts a list of calls mostly proves that the code does what the code does. When the implementation changes but behavior does not, such tests fail anyway, which trains people to ignore or delete them.
        How this maps to Playwright: in UI tests the "collaborator" is usually the network. Mocking APIs and network interception let you stub backend responses (a stub or fake of your server), API testing covers the integration level without a browser, and the toHaveScreenshot assertion supports visual testing (see assertions). Tag tests (for example smoke versus full regression) and select them with projects.

        Key points

        • Levels answer "how big a piece?"; types answer "which quality?". Most types apply at every level (ISTQB).
        • Terms such as unit, integration, component, smoke and sanity are fuzzy. Define them locally in terms of what the test starts and what it fakes.
        • Regression tests re-check old behavior; confirmation tests check one fix; exploratory tests are human, and their findings should be automated.
        • Contract tests keep provider and consumer (or a double and the real service) in agreement.
        • Test doubles: dummy (unused), stub (canned answers), spy (records calls), mock (verifies expectations), fake (simplified working version).
        • Prefer state verification and fakes for resilience to refactoring; use mocks sparingly and for real boundaries.

        An in-memory implementation of your repository interface that really stores and retrieves data, but is not suitable for production, is a...

        Fowler (after Meszaros): a fake has a working implementation but takes a shortcut. A stub only returns canned answers; a mock verifies expectations; a dummy is never used.

        Which statement about test levels and test types is correct according to ISTQB?

        The syllabus states that test types can be applied at every level, though the focus differs. Regression testing is a change-related activity, not a level.

        Level vs type?
        Level: size of the thing tested (component to system to acceptance). Type: quality being checked (functional, performance, security...).
        Stub vs mock?
        A stub supplies canned answers and you assert on state. A mock holds expectations about calls and verifies them (behavior verification).
        What is a spy?
        A stub that also records how it was called, so you can assert on those calls afterwards.
        Two meanings of "contract test"?
        1) Consumer-driven contract between teams (Pact). 2) A test that runs the same interaction against a real service and its test double to make sure they match.
        Smoke test purpose?
        A few very fast checks to see whether the build or environment is alive before running deeper tests (fail fast).

        Test Design: Choosing Good Test Cases and Writing Them Well

        Automation tools tell a computer how to run a test; test design decides which tests are worth running. Since you can never test everything, you need systematic techniques that pick a small set of cases with a high chance of finding bugs. This page teaches seven classic techniques, each with a worked example, and then how to structure, name and size the test code you write (Arrange-Act-Assert, Given-When-Then, four-phase, FIRST, and the "one assert per test" debate).

        Why we need techniques

        ISTQB's second testing principle says exhaustive testing is impossible: apart from trivial cases you cannot try every input and every path, so you use test techniques, prioritisation and risk to focus effort. A field that accepts an integer from 1 to 1,000,000 has a million valid values; nobody tests them all. The techniques below are ways to choose a handful that stand in for the rest.

        ISTQB groups techniques into families. Black-box techniques derive tests from the specification without looking at the code (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, state transitions). White-box techniques derive tests from the code's structure (statement and branch coverage). Experience-based techniques use the tester's knowledge (error guessing, exploratory, checklists). Risk-based testing is a prioritisation approach that sits above all of them.

        1. Understand the ruleRead the spec, ask questions, find the inputs and outputs.
        2. Pick a techniqueRanges: EP and BVA. Combined rules: decision table. Workflow: state transition.
        3. Derive the casesEach case has input, expected result and a reason.
        4. Prioritise by riskTest the dangerous areas deepest.
        5. Automate at the right levelTable-driven unit tests where possible.

        1. Equivalence partitioning (EP)

        Idea: split the input into groups ("partitions") that the program should treat the same way. If one value from a partition finds a bug, any other value in that partition should find it too, so one test per partition is enough (ISTQB). Partitions must not overlap and must not be empty. Include invalid partitions too: values that should be rejected.

        Worked example. A ticket price depends on age. The spec: ages 0 to 12 are "child", 13 to 17 "teen", 18 to 64 "adult", 65 to 120 "senior"; anything else is invalid.

        PartitionRangeRepresentative valueExpected
        Invalid lowbelow 0-5error
        Child0 to 126child price
        Teen13 to 1715teen price
        Adult18 to 6440adult price
        Senior65 to 12080senior price
        Invalid highabove 120150error

        Six tests cover all partitions: that is 100% partition coverage. You might also add non-numeric partitions (empty, text, decimal) if the input is a free-text field. With several inputs, the simplest criterion is each choice: every partition of every input appears in at least one test (it ignores combinations; see decision tables and pairwise below).

        2. Boundary value analysis (BVA)

        Idea: bugs cluster at the edges of partitions because developers slip on "less than" versus "less than or equal", so test the edges. BVA only applies to ordered partitions (numbers, dates). ISTQB describes two variants:

        • 2-value BVA: each boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition.
        • 3-value BVA: each boundary value and both neighbours. It is stricter. ISTQB's example: if the condition "x is at most 10" is mistakenly coded as "x equals 10", the 2-value test values 10 and 11 both pass, but the 3-value neighbour 9 exposes the bug.

        For the age example the boundaries are 0, 12, 13, 17, 18, 64, 65 and 120, with neighbours -1 and 121 at the outer edges:

        Boundary2-value pair3-value adds
        invalid | child-1, 01
        child | teen12, 1311, 14
        teen | adult17, 1816, 19
        adult | senior64, 6563, 66
        senior | invalid120, 121119

        Notice the code you would actually write is a table-driven test: one function, many rows.

        import { ticketCategory } from './ticket';

test.each([
  [-1, 'invalid'], [0, 'child'], [12, 'child'], [13, 'teen'],
  [17, 'teen'], [18, 'adult'], [64, 'adult'], [65, 'senior'],
  [120, 'senior'], [121, 'invalid'],
])('age %i is %s', (age, expected) => {
  expect(ticketCategory(age)).toBe(expected);
});
        import pytest
from ticket import ticket_category

@pytest.mark.parametrize("age, expected", [
    (-1, "invalid"), (0, "child"), (12, "child"), (13, "teen"),
    (17, "teen"), (18, "adult"), (64, "adult"), (65, "senior"),
    (120, "senior"), (121, "invalid"),
])
def test_ticket_category(age, expected):
    assert ticket_category(age) == expected
        @ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"-1,invalid", "0,child", "12,child", "13,teen", "17,teen",
            "18,adult", "64,adult", "65,senior", "120,senior", "121,invalid"})
void ticketCategory(int age, String expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, Ticket.category(age));
}

        3. Decision table testing

        Idea: when the outcome depends on combinations of conditions (business rules), list the conditions as rows and each rule as a column; every column becomes a test case. ISTQB notes the table "provides a systematic approach to identify all the combinations" and exposes gaps or contradictions in the requirements. The number of rules grows exponentially (n yes/no conditions give 2n columns), so you simplify by merging columns where a condition is irrelevant, marked with a dash.

        Worked example. Shop rules: members get 10% off; non-members who have a coupon get 5% off (coupons do not stack with membership); orders of 100 or more ship free. Three conditions give 8 combinations, but when the customer is a member the coupon does not matter, so the table reduces to 6 columns.

        Conditions / actionsR1R2R3R4R5R6
        Member?TTFFFF
        Has coupon?--TTFF
        Total >= 100?TFTFTF
        10% offXX
        5% offXX
        Free shippingXXX

        Six tests achieve 100% decision-table coverage (all feasible columns). Writing the table often reveals questions for the product owner ("what if a member also has a coupon?") before a single line of test code exists.

        4. State transition testing

        Idea: for anything with a lifecycle (orders, tickets, user accounts, wizards), model the states, the events that cause transitions, and sometimes guards (conditions). A transition is written event [guard] / action. A test is a sequence of events and the resulting states.

        Createdpay
        Paidship
        Shippeddeliver
        Deliveredfinal

        The state table shows every state and event; an empty cell is an invalid transition that should be refused.

        State / eventpayshipdelivercancel
        CreatedPaidCancelled
        PaidShippedCancelled (refund)
        ShippedDelivered
        Delivered
        Cancelled

        ISTQB defines three coverage levels, from weakest to strongest:

        • All states: visit every state (5 states here). Cheap but weak.
        • Valid transitions (0-switch): exercise every valid transition once. Here: pay, ship, deliver, cancel-from-Created, cancel-from-Paid = 5 transitions. This is the most widely used criterion.
        • All transitions: also attempt every invalid transition (for example "ship" on a Created order, "cancel" on a Shipped order). ISTQB recommends testing only one invalid transition per test to avoid defect masking, and treats this as a minimum for safety-critical software.
        test('a shipped order cannot be cancelled', () => {
  const order = new Order();       // Created
  order.pay();                     // Paid
  order.ship();                    // Shipped
  expect(() => order.cancel()).toThrow(/cannot cancel/i);
  expect(order.state).toBe('Shipped');   // state unchanged
});

        5. Pairwise (all-pairs) testing

        Idea: when many parameters each have several values, the full cross-product explodes. Pairwise (also called all-pairs) testing picks a small set of tests so that every pair of values from any two parameters appears at least once. The premise, widely reported in the combinatorial-testing literature, is that most failures are triggered by one or two parameters interacting, not by all of them at once. It is a heuristic, not a guarantee. (Pairwise is not part of the CTFL v4.0.1 syllabus that I read for this page, so treat this subsection as general industry practice rather than ISTQB content.)

        Worked example. A checkout has Payment (Card, PayPal, Voucher), Delivery (Standard, Express, Pickup) and Currency (USD, EUR, VND). The full set is 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 tests. Nine rows are enough to cover every pair:

        #PaymentDeliveryCurrency
        1CardStandardUSD
        2CardExpressEUR
        3CardPickupVND
        4PayPalStandardEUR
        5PayPalExpressVND
        6PayPalPickupUSD
        7VoucherStandardVND
        8VoucherExpressUSD
        9VoucherPickupEUR

        Check one pair: (PayPal, VND) occurs in row 5 only, and (Voucher, Pickup) in row 9. You do not generate these by hand in real work: tools such as Microsoft's PICT or the AllPairs family produce the set and let you declare constraints (for example "Voucher cannot be combined with Pickup"). Combine pairwise with the highest-risk full combinations that you add manually.

        6. Error guessing

        Idea: use experience to predict where defects hide. ISTQB defines it as anticipating errors, defects and failures from how the application behaved in the past, the mistakes developers typically make, and failures seen in similar applications. A structured version is the fault attack: build a list of likely faults and design tests to expose them. Build the list from past defects.

        AreaIdeas to try
        Text inputempty, only spaces, very long, emoji, accents, right-to-left text, quotes and angle brackets, leading and trailing whitespace
        Numbers0, negative, decimal, huge, NaN, thousands separator, locale comma versus dot
        Dates and time29 February, end of month or year, time zones, daylight-saving jumps, midnight (see flaky tests)
        Collectionsempty, one item, many items, duplicates
        Workflowdouble-click submit, browser back button, refresh mid-operation, two tabs, session expiry
        Interfacesmissing field, extra field, wrong type, timeout, 500 error from a dependency

        7. Risk-based testing

        Idea: since you cannot test everything equally, spend effort where failure would hurt most. ISTQB defines risk by two factors: likelihood (probability it happens) and impact (the harm if it does). Quantitatively, risk level = likelihood x impact; qualitatively you place each risk in a matrix. Risk analysis then decides test scope, which levels and types, which techniques and how much coverage, and in what order to test.

        FeatureLikelihood of defect (1-5)Impact if it fails (1-5)Risk (L x I)Test approach
        Payment capture3515Decision tables, boundaries, contract tests, one E2E, exploratory sessions
        Newly rewritten search4312Component and integration tests, error guessing
        Profile photo upload326A few EP/BVA cases
        Footer links111A smoke check or none

        Likelihood inputs come from complexity, change frequency, and history; ISTQB's "defects cluster together" principle says a few components usually contain most defects, so past defect data is an input. Risk-based testing also decides what not to automate (see Why Automate?). The numbers above are invented for illustration.

        Structuring a test: AAA, Given-When-Then, four-phase

        All three are the same idea at different levels of formality: get into a known situation, do one thing, check the outcome.

        NamePhasesOrigin and typical use
        Arrange, Act, Assert (AAA)set up data, call the code under test, check resultsUnit-test mnemonic; Vocke recommends it for all tests, not just unit tests
        Given, When, Thencontext, event, outcomeBehavior-driven development (BDD) wording; reads like a business scenario; Vocke: nice for acceptance tests, even without a BDD tool
        Four-phasesetup, exercise, verify, teardownxUnit pattern (Meszaros, cited by Fowler); explicitly adds cleanup
         
        test('member gets 10% off', () => {
  // Arrange
  const cart = new Cart({ member: true });
  cart.add({ sku: 'A1', price: 50 }, 2);
  // Act
  const total = cart.total();
  // Assert
  expect(total).toBe(90);
});
        def test_member_gets_ten_percent_off():
    # given a member with two items worth 50 each
    cart = Cart(member=True)
    cart.add(Item("A1", 50), qty=2)
    # when we total the cart
    total = cart.total()
    # then a 10% discount is applied
    assert total == 90
        @BeforeEach void setUp()    { db = new InMemoryDb(); db.save(member("ann")); }   // setup
@Test void memberGetsTenPercent() {
    Cart cart = new Cart(db.find("ann"));
    cart.add(item("A1", 50), 2);
    double total = cart.total();                                                // exercise
    assertEquals(90.0, total, 0.001);                                           // verify
}
@AfterEach void tearDown()  { db.close(); }                                     // teardown

        Practical guidelines from the sources: keep tests short and expressive; do not put loops and conditionals inside tests, because "there are no tests for the tests" (Google); readability beats strict DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), and Vocke suggests balancing DRY with DAMP ("descriptive and meaningful phrases"): some duplication is fine if it makes each test understandable on its own.

        FIRST: qualities of a good test

        FIRST is a mnemonic popularised by the Clean Code literature (Tim Ottinger and Jeff Langr); I did not read that source for this page, so I attribute it only by name and I map each letter to ideas that the sources I did read state explicitly.

        LetterMeaningSupported by
        FastRuns in milliseconds to seconds so people run it constantly.Fowler (compile and commit suites); Google (0.1 s is slow for a unit test)
        Independent / isolatedDoes not depend on other tests or run order; can run alone, in any order, in parallel.Fowler (non-determinism: isolation); Google (hermetic tests)
        RepeatableSame result every time, in any environment: no dependence on clock, network, randomness.Fowler (non-determinism); see Flaky Tests
        Self-validatingThe test itself says pass or fail; no human reading logs.Google (a test verifies output)
        TimelyWritten at about the same time as the code (often before, as in TDD), not months later.Fowler (tests give design feedback; fix bugs with a test first)

        Naming tests

        A good name tells the reader, without opening the body, what scenario is covered and what is expected. When a test fails in CI, the name is often the only thing people see. Vocke's examples describe behavior: shouldReturnFullNameOfAPerson and shouldTellIfPersonIsUnknown.

        ❌ Vague
        test1
testLogin
checkCart

        When one fails, you must open the code to learn what broke.

        ✅ Specific
        rejects_login_after_five_failed_attempts
member_gets_ten_percent_off
shipped_order_cannot_be_cancelled

        Reads as a specification: situation plus expected behavior. Nested describe blocks or a sentence string work equally well.

        The "one assert per test" debate

        The rule has a strong and a weak form, and the sources lean toward the weak one.

        • Strong form: literally one assertion per test method. Upside: a failure points at exactly one expectation; no assertion hides behind an earlier failing one. Downside: lots of repeated setup, and slower suites when setup is expensive.
        • Weak form: one logical behavior or condition per test, with as many assertions as needed to describe that outcome. Vocke says "test one condition per test", and Google says tests should exercise one behavior at a time. Fowler's own examples assert both that an order is filled and that the warehouse stock dropped: two assertions, one behavior.

        Recommendation: ask "if this test fails, will the name tell me what is wrong?" If yes, several assertions on one outcome are fine. If a test checks unrelated things (login works, and the cart is empty, and the footer renders), split it, or the first failure masks the rest. For end-to-end tests, where every setup costs seconds, teams reasonably assert a few related things per test (this is common practice rather than a claim from the sources). Many frameworks offer soft assertions that report all failed checks at once, which reduces the cost of multiple asserts.

        Best practice: test observable behavior, not implementation. Vocke's formulation: ask "if I enter x and y, will the result be z?" rather than "will it call class A and then class B?". Tests tied to internals break on every refactoring and lose their value as a safety net.
        Coverage is not design. 100% line coverage can still miss boundary bugs, because executing a line is different from verifying it. Google's book warns that coverage only shows lines were invoked, not that anything useful was checked. Use techniques to choose meaningful inputs, and use coverage only to find untested code.
        How this maps to Playwright: data-driven loops over rows are easy to write in test.describe with for (const row of rows) test(...); keep each generated test independent (see fixtures for per-test setup and teardown, a direct analogue of the four-phase pattern). Group steps within a test using test.step, and prefer behavior-focused names. Cover the dense business-rule tables (EP, BVA, decision tables) with fast API tests or unit tests, and reserve browser tests for the journey itself. See best practices for test isolation.

        Key points

        • Exhaustive testing is impossible; techniques pick a small, effective set of cases.
        • EP: one value per group of inputs treated alike (include invalid groups). BVA: test the edges; 3-value BVA catches errors that 2-value misses.
        • Decision tables handle combinations of rules (n conditions give 2n columns before merging); state-transition testing handles lifecycles, including invalid transitions.
        • Pairwise cuts large parameter combinations drastically but is a heuristic; use constraints and add risky combinations by hand.
        • Error guessing uses past defects and experience; risk-based testing spends effort by likelihood x impact.
        • Structure: Arrange-Act-Assert, Given-When-Then or setup-exercise-verify-teardown. Keep tests fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating and timely (FIRST).
        • Name tests after behavior; aim for one logical behavior per test rather than a rigid single assertion.

        A quantity field accepts whole numbers from 1 to 50. How many values does 3-value boundary value analysis test for this valid range's two boundaries?

        Each boundary contributes itself and both neighbours: 1 gives 0, 1, 2 and 50 gives 49, 50, 51. That is 6 values (2-value BVA would give 0, 1, 50, 51 = 4).

        A pricing rule has 4 independent yes/no conditions. How many columns does the full (unminimised) decision table have?

        Each condition doubles the combinations: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16. ISTQB notes the rule count grows exponentially, so merge irrelevant combinations or prioritise by risk.

        EP vs BVA in one sentence each?
        EP: one test per group of inputs the program treats alike. BVA: test the values at the edges of those ordered groups, where off-by-one bugs live.
        Three state-transition coverage levels?
        All states, valid transitions (0-switch), all transitions (also attempt invalid ones, one per test).
        What does pairwise guarantee?
        Every pair of values from any two parameters appears at least once. It does not guarantee coverage of 3-way interactions.
        Risk level formula?
        Likelihood x impact (quantitative), or a risk matrix (qualitative). Higher risk gets deeper and earlier testing.
        Good test structure?
        Arrange-Act-Assert / Given-When-Then / setup-exercise-verify-teardown: known state, one action, check outcome; one logical behavior per test.

        📚 Sources

        • ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1 – ISTQB: definitions and coverage of EP, BVA (2- and 3-value), decision tables, state transitions, error guessing, exploratory testing, risk likelihood x impact, exhaustive testing principle
        • The Practical Test Pyramid – Ham Vocke (Thoughtworks): Arrange-Act-Assert, Given-When-Then, test naming, one condition per test, DRY vs DAMP, test behavior not implementation
        • Mocks Aren't Stubs – Martin Fowler: four-phase test structure (setup, exercise, verify, teardown), state verification examples with several asserts
        • Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11 "Testing Overview" – Adam Bender / Google: clear tests, no logic in tests, hermetic tests, limits of code coverage
        • Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests – Martin Fowler: isolation and repeatability (clock, ordering) behind FIRST
        • Unit Test – Martin Fowler: speed expectations for unit-test suites

        Flaky Tests: Causes, Detection and Cures

        A flaky test is one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on exactly the same code. It is the single most corrosive problem in test automation, because it teaches people to ignore red builds.
