This page defines flakiness precisely, shows why even a tiny flake rate wrecks a big suite, walks through seven root-cause families with fixes, explains how to detect flaky tests, compares quarantining with fixing, and ends with a step-by-step deflaking playbook and decision flow, with real numbers from Google, Spotify and Uber.

        What flakiness is

        Different organisations word it slightly differently, but the core is the same:

        • Google (John Micco): a flaky result is a test that "exhibits both a passing and a failing result with the same code".
        • Martin Fowler calls the same thing a non-deterministic test: it passes sometimes and fails sometimes, "without any noticeable change in the code, tests, or environment".
        • Spotify (Jason Palmer): a test that "both passes and fails periodically without any code changes".
        • Uber: a test that returns different results on any two executions without changes to the source code, caused either by non-determinism inside the test or the code under test, or by variability in the environment (the machine, or the set of tests running concurrently).

        Analogy: a smoke detector that sometimes beeps for no reason. After the third false alarm you stop leaving the room when it beeps, and then one day there is a real fire. Fowler states the consequence bluntly: once people start ignoring a regression test failure, "that test is useless". Google's engineers add the human-nature point: it is natural to ignore alarms that have a history of false signals, citing airline pilots who ignored a 737 alarm.

        Why a tiny flake rate is a big problem

        The Google book gives a simple calculation: if each of 10,000 daily test runs has a 0.1% chance of failing when it should not, you investigate about 10 flakes a day. But the damage to whole-suite reliability is worse. If every test independently flakes with probability p, a suite of n tests is green with probability (1 - p)n. This is a simplification (real flakes cluster), but it shows the shape:

        Per-test flake rate pChance a 1,000-test suite is all greenWhat it feels like
        0.001% (1 in 100,000)about 99%Rare, easy to trust
        0.01%about 90%A red build every few days: investigate
        0.1%about 37%Most runs red; people start re-running
        0.15% (Google's overall rate)about 22%Mostly red; requires big infrastructure to cope
        1%effectively 0%Suite is useless; green is a coincidence

        Fowler makes the same point in words: in a suite of 100 tests with 10 non-deterministic ones, the suite will often fail; at first people check that the failures are in the known-flaky tests, but "soon they'll lose the discipline" and failures in healthy tests get ignored too. He calls flaky tests a "virulent infection".

        1. A few tests flake"Just re-run it."
        2. Re-runs become routineCI time and cost go up.
        3. Red stops meaning "bug"Failures are shrugged off.
        4. A real bug is dismissedShipped to users.
        5. Trust in the suite collapsesPeople skip or delete tests.

        Real numbers, with attribution

        OrganisationFigureSource
        Google (2016)About 1.5% of all test runs report a flaky result; almost 16% of tests have some level of flakiness (more than 1 in 7); about 84% of observed pass-to-fail transitions involve a flaky test. Insertion rate of new flakiness is about the same as the fix rate.John Micco, Google Testing Blog, May 2016
        Google (book)Flake rate "hovers around 0.15%", implying thousands of flakes a day; "as you approach 1% flakiness, the tests begin to lose value".Adam Bender, Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11
        Google (2016)An average project has about 1,000 tests; at 1.5% flaky runs, about 15 tests will fail and need investigation before a release.John Micco
        Spotify (2019)Making a simple table of flaky and slow tests visible, and doing nothing else, reduced flakiness from 6% to 4% in two months.Jason Palmer, Spotify Engineering
        Uber (2021)Targeted infrastructure fixes, reproducer tools and crowdsourced fixes reduced flaky tests by around 85% in their Java monorepo (hundreds of thousands of unit tests).Uber Engineering blog, "Handling Flaky Unit Tests in Java"
        Reading these numbers carefully: they measure different things (percent of runs, percent of tests, percent of transitions), at different scales and test mixes. Do not compare them directly or use them as targets; use them to calibrate your intuition that flakiness is common even at world-class companies, and that it needs continuous effort. Google's authors add that they do not keep an accurate count of how often flaky tests mask real bugs.

        Root-cause taxonomy

        The sources use slightly different lists. Here they are merged into seven families, with the source that emphasises each. Most real flakes come from the first two or three.

        FamilyTypical symptomTypical fixSource emphasis
        1. Async and waitingAssertion runs before the page or service is ready; passes on a fast machine, fails on a slow one; fixed sleep.Wait for a condition (poll or callback), not for time; auto-waiting assertions.Fowler, Spotify, Google book, Uber (bounded waits)
        2. Concurrency and racesThreads or processes interleave differently each run; occasional deadlock or wrong value; may be a real bug in the product.Synchronise properly, remove shared mutable state, fix the production race.Google, Uber
        3. Test-order dependencePasses alone but fails in the full run, or vice versa; changes when ordering or parallelism changes.Make every test set up its own state; reset between tests; randomise order to expose it.Spotify, Fowler, Uber (run test alone)
        4. Shared stateLeftover data in a database, static or singleton variables, logged-in user, files; parallel tests collide.Fresh state per test, unique data, transactions rolled back, isolated resources.Fowler (lack of isolation), Google (hermetic)
        5. Time and randomnessFails around midnight, month-end, daylight saving; depends on now(); random data hits an edge case; duplicate ids from clock ticks.Inject a clock and freeze it; seed random generators and log the seed.Fowler (time, seeded randomiser), Google book
        6. Environment and infrastructureCPU or memory contention under parallel load, port collisions, slow disks, full disk, browser or driver version differences, resource leaks, network blips.Dynamic ports, containers, resource limits, pinned versions, better CI capacity.Uber (parallelism, ports, embedded DBs), Fowler (resource leaks), Spotify (infra columns)
        7. External servicesThird-party API slow, rate limited, or returning different data; a shared test environment is down; partner team deploys a bad build.Replace with a test double or recorded response; add contract tests to keep the double honest.Fowler (remote services), Google (third-party code), Wacker (partner and lab failures)

        One more theme cuts across all of them: scope. Fowler notes non-determinism "is particularly prone to affect tests with a broad scope". Spotify's blunt version: end-to-end tests are flaky by nature, so write fewer of them. Vocke lists the UI-specific suspects: browser quirks, timing issues, animations and unexpected popup dialogs. This is why the test pyramid is partly an anti-flakiness strategy.

        Cause by cause: bad versus good

        1. Async and waiting

        Fowler's rule: "never use bare sleeps". A sleep is either too long (slow suite) or too short (random failures). Poll for a condition with a generous upper limit instead, so the test proceeds the instant the condition holds.

        ❌ Fixed sleep
        await page.click('#save');
await page.waitForTimeout(2000);        // hope 2 s is enough
expect(await page.textContent('#status')).toBe('Saved');

        Too slow on a good day, too fast on a bad day.

        ✅ Wait for the condition
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Saved');   // retries until true or timeout

        Proceeds as soon as it is true; timeout is only a safety net.

        Every major tool has its own way to express "wait for the condition":

        await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Saved');   // web-first assertion auto-retries
        WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(
    EC.text_to_be_present_in_element((By.ID, "status"), "Saved"))   # explicit wait polls
        cy.get('[data-testid=status]').should('have.text', 'Saved')   // commands and assertions retry
        deadline = now() + LIMIT          # a named constant, never a literal
while not condition():
    if now() > deadline: raise TestTimeout("status never became Saved")
    sleep(POLL_INTERVAL)           # small: bounds the wasted time

        Fowler adds details worth copying: use a clearly named timeout exception, keep wait limits as shared constants (so you can tune all at once), and use a callback instead of polling if the system under test can provide one. Uber goes further for Java: a lint rule that forbids short timed waits such as latch.await(100, MILLISECONDS) in tests, because 100 ms is fine alone but too short under CPU load; they prefer unbounded waits plus a global test timeout.

        3 and 4. Order dependence and shared state

        ❌ Tests share a user
        test('create user ann', async ({ request }) => {
  await request.post('/users', { data: { name: 'ann' } });
});
test('ann can log in', async ({ page }) => {
  await login(page, 'ann');    // only works if the test above ran first
});

        Passes serially, fails when run alone, sharded or in parallel.

        ✅ Each test owns its data
        test('user can log in', async ({ page, request }) => {
  const name = `ann-${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`;
  await request.post('/users', { data: { name } });   // setup inside the test
  await login(page, name);
  await expect(page.getByText(`Hi ${name}`)).toBeVisible();
});   // unique data; cleanup in a fixture or by resetting the environment

        Independent of order and parallelism.

        Fowler's guidance: either rebuild the starting state from scratch for each test or clean up after each one; he prefers the former because when a test fails to build state you can see which test is at fault, whereas a bad cleanup breaks a different test later. A handy trick for databases: run each test in a transaction and roll back at the end. Beware exceptions in teardown: they can let the test pass while corrupting the next one, so make teardown failures loud.

        5. Time and randomness

        // Production code takes a clock instead of calling Date.now() directly.
interface Clock { now(): Date }
function isExpired(expiresAt: Date, clock: Clock) { return clock.now() > expiresAt; }

// Test: a frozen clock makes the result deterministic, even at 23:59:59.
const frozen: Clock = { now: () => new Date('2030-01-31T23:59:59Z') };
test('coupon expires at month end', () => {
  expect(isExpired(new Date('2030-01-31T23:59:59Z'), frozen)).toBe(false);
});

        Fowler: "always wrap the system clock" so it can be substituted, and even suggests a static check that fails the build on direct clock calls. A colleague of his deliberately forces a test run just before and after midnight to catch tests that assume the date does not change. For randomness: seed the generator and print the seed on failure so any failure can be replayed. Fowler also describes the opposite trick of stubbing the randomiser to a constant, to surface collision bugs.

        6 and 7. Environment and external services

        Uber's analysis of its Java monorepo found most flaky tests came from external factors: highly parallel execution causing CPU and memory contention, embedded databases and servers (Cassandra, MariaDB, Redis) with buggy start-stop logic, hard-coded ports that collided across parallel tests, and Spark's default UI server grabbing a fixed port. Their central fix: run databases in containers via the Testcontainers library, each on a random free port, and disable the Spark UI in tests. For remote services Fowler says to use a test double and keep it honest with contract tests, which run the same interaction against the real service and the double (periodically, not on every build); he notes that any advantage of talking to the real system "is overwhelmed by the need to stamp out non-determinism".

        Detecting flaky tests

        • Repeat and compare. Run the same test many times on the same commit. Any mixed result is a flake. Uber labels a test stable only after 100 consecutive successes on the main branch.
        • Track history. Google's CI notices when a passing test transitions to failing and checks whether the test is known to flake; another tool detects changes in a test's flakiness level and tries to find the change that caused it. Uber's Test Analyzer keeps the last k results per test.
        • Visualise. Spotify's "Odeneye" shows tests down the side and CI runs across the top: a scatter of orange dots is test flakiness, while a solid column of failures is an infrastructure problem. Their plain table of flaky and slow tests alone cut flakiness from 6% to 4%.
        • Stress the environment. Uber's reproducer runs each test alone, with its class, with its whole target, with ports already occupied (a "Port Claimer" process), and under added CPU load. This catches isolation, port and timing flakes systematically.
        • Check before merge. Spotify's "Flakybot" lets an engineer exercise their tests repeatedly in a pull request to gain confidence the flakiness is really fixed.
        • Randomise order, parallelise, shard. Anything that changes ordering or timing will flush out hidden dependencies.
        # Playwright example: run a suspect test 50 times, in parallel, and see the failures
npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts --repeat-each=50 --workers=4

# Retries make flaky tests visible in reports rather than hiding them:
npx playwright test --retries=2     # a test that fails then passes is reported as "flaky"
        A retry is a bandage, not a cure. Google's book says automatic reruns trade CPU cycles for engineer time and "only delay the need to address the root cause". Google also notes that marking tests "flaky" so they fail only after three failures in a row discourages owners from fixing them, and slows real feedback: a 15-minute test marked flaky takes 45 minutes to report a real break. Use retries to keep the pipeline moving and to measure, never as the final answer.

        Quarantine versus fix

        When a test flakes you have two competing needs: keep the main pipeline trustworthy now, and eventually restore the lost coverage. Quarantine serves the first; fixing serves the second. The sources agree quarantine is acceptable only as a short-lived holding pen.

        ApproachWhat it isBenefitRiskWho does it
        Quarantine suiteMove flaky tests to a separate suite that does not block merging (Fowler).Healthy tests keep giving clear signals.Quarantined tests are forgotten and coverage silently erodes.Fowler: advises time or count limits (for example no more than 8 tests, or no longer than a week)
        Automatic quarantineA tool monitors flakiness and removes a test from the critical path, filing a bug.Developers are unblocked."Could easily mask a real race condition" in the product (Google).Google
        Disable and re-qualifyA job disables flaky tests; they return after 100 consecutive passes.Keeps merges flowing at huge scale.Functionality is untested while disabled: Uber calls this "a deliberate tradeoff".Uber
        Rerun on failureAutomatically retry a failing test and pass if it succeeds.Cheap and fast.Hides the problem; costs CI time; can mask real intermittent bugs.All; Uber enabled it only after cutting flakes by about 85%
        Fix the root causeDiagnose and eliminate the non-determinism.Permanent; improves product quality when the cause is a real race.Takes effort; long tail of causes.Test owners, with tooling support
        Delete or push downRemove the test or recreate it at a lower, more deterministic level.Removes recurring cost.Lost coverage if not replaced.Team decision

        Fowler adds an organisational detail: his Mingle team ran the quarantine suite one stage after the healthy tests in the pipeline, forcing quick cleanup, but he cautions that this only works for highly disciplined teams, and for most teams advises keeping quarantined tests out of the main pipeline. Uber also found that centralised fixing does not scale to the long tail of causes, so it crowdsourced with "Fix It Week" events and by engaging the teams with the highest share of flaky tests.

        The deflaking playbook

        1. ReproduceRepeat many times; alone; in the full suite; in parallel; under CPU load.
        2. Gather evidenceTrace, screenshots, logs, the random seed, timing, environment.
        3. ClassifyWhich of the seven families? Test bug, product bug or infra?
        4. Fix the causeWait for conditions, isolate data, freeze time, replace the service.
        5. Prove itMany consecutive green runs under stress (Uber uses 100).
        6. PreventLint rules, review checklist, flake dashboard.
        1. Reproduce it. If you cannot reproduce, you cannot know you fixed it. Run the test alone, as part of its file, as part of the full suite, with parallel workers and with a loaded CPU. Different results between these runs already point at a family (alone passes but suite fails means order or shared state; only fails under load means timing or resources).
        2. Capture evidence at the moment of failure. A recorded trace, video and console and network logs are worth far more than a stack trace. In Playwright, set trace collection on first retry so a failure that happens only occasionally is still recorded (see Trace Viewer and retries). Uber notes that similar exceptions can come from very different root causes, so look earlier in the run than the failing line.
        3. Decide whose bug it is. Is the test wrong (bad wait, shared state), the environment wrong (port, CPU, version), or the product wrong (a real race condition)? Google's commenters raise this point and Google replies that they do not track how often flaky tests hide real bugs. Do not assume it is the test.
        4. Fix the family-specific cause using the taxonomy above. Prefer the structural fix (isolate data, inject time, wait on conditions) over tuning numbers (longer sleeps, bigger timeouts).
        5. Verify. Run the fixed test many times, in parallel, under load. The proof is a long streak of passes, not one green run.
        6. Prevent recurrence. Add a static check or review rule (ban fixed sleeps, ban direct clock calls, ban hard-coded ports), a fast feedback tool such as Spotify's Flakybot, and a visible dashboard. Uber's analytics track how often each lint check fires and is suppressed.
        7. Reduce what you must deflake. The best flake is the one never written: push checks down the pyramid, keep E2E tests few, and make every test hermetic.

        Decision flow: what do I do when a test fails intermittently?

        Test failed in CIIs the failure reproducible on the same commit? Re-run a few times.
        Always fails?Then it is not flaky: a real regression or a broken test. Fix now.
        Sometimes fails?It is flaky. Open an issue with owner and deadline.
        Is it blocking the team?Yes: quarantine it (time-boxed) so healthy tests stay trusted.
        Investigate with the playbookReproduce, classify, find root cause (test, product or infra).
        Fixed within the deadline?Yes: return it to the main suite after a long green streak. No: delete it or rewrite at a lower level.
        Best practice policy: (1) Treat a flaky test as a bug with an owner. (2) Quarantine only with an expiry date or a size cap. (3) Never "fix" with a longer sleep. (4) Measure flake rate and run time as suite-health metrics, as Spotify and Google do. (5) Keep E2E tests few; as Spotify's talk puts it, "instead of having 500 end to end tests... have 5".
        How this maps to Playwright: many causes above are handled by design. Actionability checks and web-first assertions remove most async flakes; each test gets a fresh browser context and fixtures give per-test setup, which tackle shared state; parallel workers expose hidden order dependence early; retries report "flaky" tests instead of hiding them; the Trace Viewer records evidence; mocking and network control cut external-service flakes; the clock API lets you control time. Keep CI resources stable (and consider Docker images pinned to the Playwright version) to limit environment flakes.

        Key points

        • Flaky = different results on the same code. It destroys trust in the suite far beyond the cost of each failure.
        • A 0.1% per-test flake rate across 1,000 tests leaves only about 37% of runs green; Google reports about 1.5% of runs flaky and 84% of pass-to-fail transitions involving flaky tests.
        • Seven root-cause families: async and waiting, concurrency, test order, shared state, time and randomness, environment and infrastructure, external services. Broad-scope (E2E) tests are the most exposed.
        • Never use bare sleeps; wait for conditions. Give each test its own data; inject and freeze time; replace unreliable services with doubles kept honest by contract tests.
        • Detect by repetition, history and visualisation; reproduce under stress (alone, in parallel, under load).
        • Retries and quarantine are temporary measures that buy time; quarantine needs an owner and an expiry; the goal is root-cause fixes or deleting or lowering the test.
        • Prevention beats cure: lint rules, hermetic tests, fewer E2E tests, and visible flake metrics.

        A test passes when run alone but fails when the entire suite runs. Which root-cause family is the MOST likely?

        Passing alone and failing in the suite is the classic signature of another test leaving state behind (Spotify: "you cannot run a test in isolation and it only passes when the whole suite is run"). Fix by giving each test its own state.

        A team marks a flaky 20-minute integration test as "fail only if it fails 3 times in a row" and calls the problem solved. What is the main problem with this?

        Google's flaky-test post warns of exactly this: the breakage is not discovered until all executions finish, and owners are encouraged to ignore flakiness. Retries buy time; they do not remove the cause.

        Define a flaky test.
        A test that both passes and fails on the same code and environment, without any relevant change (Google, Fowler, Spotify, Uber).
        Name the seven root-cause families.
        Async/waiting, concurrency, test-order dependence, shared state, time/randomness, environment/infrastructure, external services.
        Why avoid bare sleeps?
        Too long slows the suite; too short fails randomly. Poll or use a callback with a high timeout limit instead (Fowler).
        Quarantine rules of thumb?
        Separate the flaky test from the main pipeline, give it an owner, and cap the time or the count (Fowler: for example a week, or 8 tests); then fix, rewrite lower, or delete.
        How do you prove a flake is fixed?
        Many consecutive green runs under stress (parallel, loaded CPU, random order). Uber requires 100 consecutive successes to re-classify a test as stable.

        📚 Sources

        • Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them – John Micco / Google Testing Blog: 1.5% flaky runs, 16% flaky tests, 84% of transitions, rerun, quarantine and monitoring tools
        • Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11 "Testing Overview" – Adam Bender / Google: flakiness case study (0.1% x 10,000 runs, 0.15% rate, 1% loses value), reruns as trading CPU for engineer time, sleep() as a naive heuristic, hermetic tests
        • Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests – Martin Fowler: quarantine, isolation, async waits, remote services and contract tests, time, resource leaks
        • Test Flakiness – Methods for identifying and dealing with flaky tests – Jason Palmer / Spotify Engineering: causes, Odeneye, flake table (6% to 4%), Flakybot
        • Handling Flaky Unit Tests in Java – Uber Engineering (June 2021): Test Analyzer, 100-consecutive-pass rule, Testcontainers, reproducers, Error Prone checks, about 85% reduction. (Read via a regional mirror of the same post; the canonical URL may return an error to automated clients.)
        • Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests – Mike Wacker / Google Testing Blog: why E2E feedback loops are unreliable (partner and lab failures, flaky tests)
        • The Practical Test Pyramid – Ham Vocke (Thoughtworks): UI test flakiness (browser quirks, timing, animations, popups)

        Anatomy of a Test Automation Framework (layers & separation of concerns)

        A test suite that lives for years needs the same thing a healthy application needs: a clear structure in which every piece has one job and knows as little as possible about the others. This section shows the layers almost every mature framework converges on, the dependency rule that keeps them honest, and how to decide what to build and what to simply adopt.

        Why a framework needs an architecture at all

        Imagine a restaurant. The customer says "I'd like the soup". A waiter turns that into an order. The kitchen knows recipes. The suppliers deliver ingredients. If the customer had to walk into the kitchen and chop onions, every change to a recipe would require re-educating every customer. That is what a suite of "record and replay" scripts looks like: every test knows every locator, every wait and every URL.

        Gerard Meszaros, in xUnit Test Patterns, names the resulting disease Fragile Test. One of its causes, Interface Sensitivity, is "a test fails to find a user interface element it needs". His recommended cure is to place a layer between the tests and the system under test, so that tests speak a higher-level language and only that layer knows the technical details. Martin Fowler describes the same idea for web UIs as the Page Object. Layering is simply this cure applied systematically.

        The layers

        Different books name the layers differently (Screenplay talks about tasks and interactions, Robot Framework about test cases and keywords), but the roles are stable. Read the diagram from top (closest to a human's intention) to bottom (closest to the browser).

        Test layerScenarios: arrange, act, assert. Reads like a requirement.
        Flow / steps layerBusiness actions: "sign in", "place order". Composes pages.
        Page & component layerScreens and widgets: the only code that knows locators.
        Driver / wrapper layerBrowser, HTTP client, mobile driver; thin helpers, retries, logging.
        System under testThe real application, reached through a browser or an API.
        LayerResponsibilityMay depend onMust NOT know
        TestState one behaviour; own the assertions; choose dataFlows, data builders, fixturesLocators, waits, driver API
        Flow / stepsName a business action; sequence several screens or API callsPages, API clientsCSS/XPath, assertions about the test's purpose
        Page / componentHide HTML structure; expose actions and readable stateDriver layerWhich test is running, test data origin
        Driver / wrapperTalk to the browser, HTTP, device; common logging and error contextThe tool's libraryAnything about the application's domain
        UtilitiesPure helpers: random strings, dates, file parsingNothing in the frameworkEverything else
        ConfigBase URL, timeouts, browser matrix, feature toggles, secrets by referenceEnvironment variablesTest logic
        Test dataFixtures, factories, builders, seeding helpersAPI clients, utilitiesThe UI
        ReportingLogs, screenshots, traces, result files, tagsRunner hooksBusiness rules

        The same idea in code

        Below, each layer is a few lines. Notice that only the page object contains anything that looks like markup.

        import { test, expect } from '../fixtures';

test('a returning customer can pay by card', async ({ shop, customer }) => {
  // Arrange: data layer builds a valid customer through an API
  const order = await shop.api.createCart(customer, { items: ['Backpack'] });

  // Act: flow layer, business vocabulary
  await shop.flows.signIn(customer);
  const receipt = await shop.flows.payByCard(order);

  // Assert: the TEST owns the assertion
  expect(receipt.total).toBe('$29.99');
  expect(receipt.status).toBe('Paid');
});
        export class CheckoutPage {
  constructor(private readonly ui: Ui) {}           // driver layer, injected

  async payWithCard(card: Card) {
    await this.ui.fill('Card number', card.number);   // label-based, not CSS
    await this.ui.fill('Expiry', card.expiry);
    await this.ui.press('Pay now');
  }
  async receipt(): Promise<Receipt> {                // returns data, not assertions
    return { total: await this.ui.text('Total'), status: await this.ui.text('Status') };
  }
}

        The dependency rule

        Draw an arrow from A to B when A uses B. In a healthy framework all arrows point downwards in the diagram above (tests use flows, flows use pages, pages use the driver) and never upwards. A page object that imports a test helper, or a driver wrapper that mentions "checkout", is a sign that a concern has leaked into the wrong layer. The cross-cutting boxes (config, data, reporting, utilities) can be used from many layers, but they themselves depend on almost nothing.

        Why does direction matter? Things at the bottom change for technical reasons (a new browser version, a tool migration) and things at the top change for business reasons (a new checkout rule). If the top never reaches into the bottom, a technical change touches one layer. Fowler states the benefit in two parts: UI-manipulation logic is confined to one place, and the test code becomes easier to read because it expresses intention instead of widgetry.

        Do not skip layers "just this once". A page.locator('#btn-7') inside a test is the first crack. Simon Stewart's remark, quoted by Fowler, is blunt: if WebDriver calls appear in your test methods, you are doing it wrong. A lint rule or an import restriction that forbids the tool's API in the tests/ folder is cheap and effective.

        SOLID, DRY and KISS applied to tests

        These are principles for production code, and tests are code too. Here is what each means in a test framework. Be careful with the last column: following a principle to the extreme is itself a failure mode.

        PrincipleIn a test frameworkOver-applied looks like
        Single responsibilityA page object models one screen or component; a flow models one business action; a data builder builds one entityFifty one-method classes nobody can navigate
        Open/closedAdd a new payment method by adding a class, not by editing an if chain in the checkout pagePlugin systems for a suite with three payment methods
        Liskov substitutionA MobileLoginPage can replace WebLoginPage in a flow without the flow noticingDeep inheritance trees just to share two helpers
        Interface segregationA test needing only "get the price" is handed a small interface, not the whole 60-method pageOne interface per method
        Dependency inversionFlows depend on an abstract Ui or Api contract that is injected, so a fake or a different tool can be swapped inAbstracting a tool you will never replace, hiding its best features
        DRYOne place knows the login button's locator; one place knows how to build a valid userMerging two tests that merely look alike, so a change for one breaks the other
        KISSPlain functions and straight-line tests; a test should be understood at a glanceA clever generic "do anything" step that nobody dares to touch

        Meszaros adds a test-specific twist on DRY and KISS. A test should be a readable specification: the Four-Phase Test (set up the fixture, exercise the system, verify the outcome, tear down) makes each test's intent visible, and "Test Code Duplication" and "Obscure Test" appear in his list of test smells. His catalogue also lists "Conditional Test Logic" (a test containing code that may or may not execute) as a smell. The usual argument is that nobody writes tests for the tests, so a test should stay simple enough to be verified by reading it.

        Cross-cutting concerns, one by one

        • Config. The Twelve-Factor guidance applies directly: everything that varies between deploys (base URL, credentials, feature toggles) comes from the environment, not from constants in code. Details in test data and environments.
        • Test data. Builders and API helpers create exactly what a test needs. Tests should not rely on a pre-existing "golden" database row.
        • Reporting. Logs, screenshots and traces are attached by runner hooks, not copy-pasted into tests. Naming and tagging conventions belong here too; see reporting and debugging.
        • Utilities. Pure functions with no knowledge of the application: formatting a date, parsing a downloaded CSV. If a utility needs the app, it is not a utility; it is a flow or a page.

        An example folder structure

        One layout that works for a UI-plus-API suite. Names are conventions, not rules; what matters is that each folder maps to one layer or concern and that the tests/ folder imports from the others, never the reverse.

        repo/
├─ tests/                 # TEST layer: only scenarios, grouped by feature
│  ├─ checkout/
│  ├─ account/
│  └─ smoke/
├─ src/
│  ├─ flows/              # FLOW layer: signIn(), payByCard(), registerUser()
│  ├─ pages/              # PAGE layer: one class per screen
│  ├─ components/         # reusable widgets: NavBar, DataGrid, DatePicker
│  ├─ api/                # API clients used for fast setup and verification
│  ├─ driver/             # DRIVER layer: browser factory, Ui wrapper, HTTP client
│  ├─ data/               # builders, factories, static fixtures (JSON)
│  └─ support/            # UTILITIES: random, dates, waits for non-UI things
├─ config/
│  ├─ base.ts             # defaults
│  └─ env.ts              # reads environment variables; no secrets in files
├─ fixtures/              # wiring: creates and injects objects per test
├─ reports/               # generated, git-ignored
└─ ci/                    # pipeline definitions

        Build or adopt?

        "Framework" is a loaded word. Teams often say they will "build a framework" when they mean "pick a runner and add a thin domain layer". The first is months of work the community has already done; the second is a few days. A useful rule of thumb (this is the author's opinion, but widely shared): adopt everything that is generic, build only what encodes your product.

        ConcernAdopt (generic)Build (specific to you)
        Runner, parallelism, retriesPlaywright Test, Cypress, JUnit/TestNG, pytest, MochaNothing
        Assertions and waitingThe tool's built-in auto-retrying assertionsDomain assertions ("order is paid")
        Browser/device driverSelenium, Playwright, Appium, CypressA thin factory and a few helpers
        ReportingHTML reporter, Allure, trace viewerTags and naming conventions
        Pages, flows, data-All of it: this is your product's vocabulary
        Wrap less than you think. The Selenium documentation presents the "Bot" pattern, an action-oriented helper around the raw API, as an alternative to page objects for teams who find them uncomfortable. Wrapper helpers are fine when they add something (consistent logging, an unusual widget). They become harmful when they re-implement what the tool already does, for example custom polling loops on top of an engine that already auto-waits: now two retry mechanisms stack and timeouts become unpredictable. See synchronisation and locators.
        Test the framework by using it. Keep the framework's own unit tests tiny (builders, utilities, parsers). The real proof of a layer is that a new teammate can write a working test by reading three existing ones.

        Common architecture failures

        • Utility dumping ground. Helpers.ts grows to 2,000 lines. Split by concern, and move anything domain-related into flows or data.
        • Base-class gravity. A BaseTest that does login, data setup, logging and screenshots for every test. Prefer composition (fixtures, injected objects) over inheritance.
        • The "mega flow". A flow called doEverything() with twelve boolean parameters. Split into small named flows and compose them.
        • Hidden state shared between layers. Static variables or singletons that outlive a test cause Meszaros's "Interacting Tests" smell. More in design patterns.
        • Architecture before the first test. Start with three real tests, extract the duplication you see, and let the layers emerge. Premature abstraction is the commonest overengineering.

        How the architecture grows with the suite

        Suite sizeSensible structureWarning sign that it is time to evolve
        Under about 20 tests, one personPlain specs plus one or two helper functionsThe same locator appears in a third test
        Dozens of tests, a small teamPage and component objects, a data builder, fixtures for setupTests repeat the same four-step journey; set-up dominates runtime
        Hundreds of tests, several teamsFull layering, flows or Screenplay tasks, API clients, shared library versioned like a productTeams copy each other's helpers; releases of the shared code break other teams

        The numbers above are illustrative, not research findings: they are a way to say "do not build the third row on day one". The consistent message in the sources is that structure should follow demonstrated duplication, which is why even Fowler's description of the Page Object is framed as an encapsulation technique rather than a mandate.

        Quick self-check

        ❌ Everything in the test
        test('pay', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://shop.test/login');
  await page.fill('#u', 'ann'); await page.fill('#p', 'x1');
  await page.click('.btn.btn-primary');
  await page.waitForTimeout(3000);
  await page.click('div.cart > a:nth-child(2)');
  // ... 40 more lines
});

        Hard-coded URL, secrets, structural CSS, a hard sleep, no business meaning. Every UI change breaks every test that logs in.

        ✅ Intent in the test, detail below
        test('pay', async ({ shop, customer }) => {
  await shop.flows.signIn(customer);
  const receipt = await shop.flows.payByCard(customer.cart);
  expect(receipt.status).toBe('Paid');
});

        Four lines that read like the requirement. Locators, URLs, waits and credentials live exactly once, in the layer that owns them.

        Key points

        • Layers: test, flow/steps, page/component, driver, plus cross-cutting utilities, config, data and reporting.
        • Dependencies point downwards only; the top changes for business reasons, the bottom for technical ones.
        • Only the page/component layer knows locators; only tests own assertions (with a small exception for "is this the right page" checks).
        • Adopt generic machinery, build only the product vocabulary; avoid re-implementing what the tool already does.
        • Principles such as SOLID, DRY and KISS help, but each has an over-applied failure mode.
        • Let structure emerge from real duplication rather than designing it all up front.
        How this maps to Playwright: the test layer is a spec file; the flow and page layers are plain classes or functions (Page Object Models); the wiring layer is fixtures; config lives in playwright.config with projects; reporting is reporters. The driver layer is mostly unnecessary because locators already auto-wait (actionability). See also best practices.

        A page object class imports a helper called createRandomCustomer() from the test-data folder and calls it inside its register() method. What is the main problem?

        B. The page's job is to hide the UI structure and offer actions such as "fill the registration form with these values". Choosing or creating the values belongs to the test or flow layer. Mixing them makes the page harder to reuse and the test harder to understand.

        Your team wants to write its own retry and polling engine on top of a tool that already auto-retries assertions. What is the best advice?

        B. Build only what encodes your product. Stacked waits are a documented hazard (Selenium warns against mixing implicit and explicit waits for the same reason).

        State the dependency rule of a layered framework.
        Arrows point downwards: tests use flows, flows use pages, pages use the driver. Lower layers never import upper ones.
        Which layer is allowed to contain locators?
        Only the page/component layer (and nothing above it).
        What does "adopt generic, build specific" mean?
        Use existing runners, assertions, drivers and reporters; write only the pages, flows and data builders that express your own product.
        Name the Fragile Test cause that layering cures.
        Interface Sensitivity: tests break because the UI or API changed. Cure: encapsulate the interface behind a higher-level layer.
        Why prefer composition to a giant BaseTest class?
        Inheritance couples every test to hidden setup and shared state; injected objects (fixtures) make dependencies explicit and swappable.

        📚 Sources

        • Page Object – Martin Fowler: encapsulation of UI widgetry, benefits of confining UI logic to one layer, layering a DSL over page objects
        • Design patterns and development strategies – Selenium project: Page Objects, LoadableComponent and the Bot (command) alternative
        • Page object models – Selenium project: separation of tests from page-specific code, composition with components
        • Test Smells and Fragile Test – Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: smell catalogue, Interface Sensitivity and SUT API Encapsulation
        • Four-Phase Test – Gerard Meszaros: structuring each test so its intent is obvious
        • Screenplay Pattern – Serenity/JS: a layered alternative organised around actors, tasks and interactions
        • The Twelve-Factor App: III. Config – Adam Wiggins et al.: config belongs in the environment, not in code
        • Best Practices – Playwright docs: isolation, user-facing locators, built-in auto-waiting as a reason not to re-wrap

        Design Patterns for Test Code

        A design pattern is a named, reusable answer to a problem that keeps coming back. Test automation has its own recurring problems: locators scattered everywhere, test data that is painful to build, tests that depend on global state. This section walks through the patterns that matter (Page Object, Component, App Actions, Screenplay, Factory, Builder, Facade, Strategy, Dependency Injection) and explains when each one earns its keep and when it is just ceremony.

        Why patterns, and why be skeptical of them

        Patterns give a team a shared vocabulary: saying "put that behind a page object" is faster than explaining the idea again. But every pattern adds indirection, and indirection has a cost every time someone reads the code. The honest test is: does this pattern remove more duplication or fragility than the reading cost it adds? For a 10-test suite, a plain script with one helper function may be the right design. For a 2,000-test suite maintained by six people, it almost never is.

        One login flow, four designs

        Seeing the same behaviour written several ways is the quickest way to feel the difference. The scenario: sign in with valid credentials and see a greeting. The first two tabs use a Playwright-style API; the third uses the Screenplay pattern as implemented by Serenity/JS (simplified for clarity).

        test('valid login', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://app.test/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Username').fill('ann');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('s3cret');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText('Hello ann');
});
// Fine for one test. With 50 tests, the login steps and locators are copied 50 times.
        export class LoginPage {
  constructor(private page: Page) {}
  async open() { await this.page.goto('/login'); }
  async loginAs(user: string, pass: string) {
    await this.page.getByLabel('Username').fill(user);
    await this.page.getByLabel('Password').fill(pass);
    await this.page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    return new HomePage(this.page);          // navigation returns the next page
  }
}
export class HomePage {
  constructor(private page: Page) {}
  greeting() { return this.page.getByRole('heading'); }  // exposes, does not assert
}
// test
test('valid login', async ({ page }) => {
  const login = new LoginPage(page);
  await login.open();
  const home = await login.loginAs('ann', 's3cret');
  await expect(home.greeting()).toHaveText('Hello ann');   // the TEST asserts
});
        // Task: a business-level step composed of lower-level interactions
const LogIn = {
  as: (name: string, password: string) =>
    Task.where(`#actor logs in as ${name}`,
      Enter.theValue(name).into(UsernameField),
      Enter.theValue(password).into(PasswordField),
      Click.on(SignInButton),
    ),
};
// Question: how an actor reads the system
const Greeting = () => Text.of(PageElement.located(By.css('h1')));

test('valid login', async ({ actorCalled }) => {
  await actorCalled('Ann').attemptsTo(
    Navigate.to('/login'),
    LogIn.as('ann', 's3cret'),
    Ensure.that(Greeting(), equals('Hello ann')),
  );
});
// Actor 'Ann' has the ability BrowseTheWeb; the same Task could run
// on another driver because only the Ability knows the tool.
        // When login is NOT what you are testing, skip the UI entirely.
async function signInViaApi(request: APIRequestContext, context: BrowserContext, user: User) {
  const res = await request.post('/api/session', { data: user });
  const { token } = await res.json();
  await context.addCookies([{ name: 'session', value: token, url: BASE_URL }]);
}
test('profile shows my name', async ({ page, request, context }) => {
  await signInViaApi(request, context, aUser());   // milliseconds, not seconds
  await page.goto('/profile');
  await expect(page.getByText('Ann')).toBeVisible();
});

        Notice what changes as you move right. Plain script: everything is visible, nothing is reusable. Page Object: locators live once, the test is shorter, but the unit of reuse is still "a screen". Screenplay: the unit of reuse is "something a person does", and tools hide behind abilities. App Action: for set-up, you do not use the UI at all.

        The catalogue at a glance

        PatternProblem it solvesPays off whenOverkill when
        Page ObjectLocators and UI mechanics duplicated across testsThe same screen is touched by many testsOne-off throwaway checks
        Component ObjectRepeating widgets (nav bar, grid row, date picker) appear on many pagesA widget is reused or appears many times on one pageA widget used once
        App ActionsSlow, fragile UI steps used only as set-upSet-up (login, create data) dominates test timeThe set-up is the behaviour under test
        ScreenplayBusiness language and tool independence across UI, API, mobileLarge suites, several interfaces, business-readable reportsSmall teams without time to learn the vocabulary
        FactoryChoosing which concrete object (browser, user type, page) to createCreation depends on config, platform or roleOnly one possible implementation
        BuilderObjects with many fields where each test cares about only a fewRich domain data (orders, invoices, users)Entities with two fields
        FacadeA complicated sequence hidden behind one simple callFlows spanning several pages or APIsWrapping a single call
        StrategySame step, interchangeable behaviour (pay by card / PayPal / voucher)Variants differ in "how", not "what"Two variants that will never grow
        Dependency Injection / fixturesObjects creating their own collaborators and hiding stateAlways, in some formNever overkill if kept light
        Singleton"Just one shared driver / config"Rarely; see belowUsually harmful

        Page Object and Component Objects in depth

        The two best sources agree on the basics. Martin Fowler says a page object should let the client "do anything and see anything that a human can", and that changing the concrete control should not change its interface: a text box takes and returns strings, a checkbox uses booleans, a button is an action-named method. The Selenium documentation lists the practical rules:

        • Public methods represent services the page offers, not individual clicks ("sign in", not "click button 3").
        • Do not expose the driver or raw elements; the page object should be the only place with deep knowledge of the HTML.
        • Methods return other page objects, component objects, or themselves (for fluent style), or plain data.
        • Different outcomes of the same action are different methods: loginAs() returns the home page, loginAsExpectingError() returns the login page again.
        • A page object need not represent a whole page. Fowler himself regrets the name, suggesting "panel object" would be better; the Selenium docs call the smaller pieces Page Component Objects and model a products page as having a list of product components (composition, not inheritance).

        Fowler cites a study (Leotta et al., ICSTW 2013) in which a suite with page objects took slightly longer to update for the first test case after a software upgrade, but much less time for the rest. This matches intuition: the pattern is an investment that repays as the suite grows.

        Where the experts disagree: assertions in page objects

        Fowler and the Selenium guide both say no assertions in page objects; the page offers data (isUnread(subject)) and the test decides what is correct. Supporters of assertions in pages argue it removes duplicated checks and allows friendlier error messages. Fowler's answer is to share assertion helpers in a library instead, which achieves the same without bloating the page. Both sources allow one exception: a check, usually in the constructor or an open() method, that the right page actually loaded, and invariants that hold for the page regardless of the test.

        A second disagreement concerns navigation. Returning the next page object from an action (as above) is the common advice, but Fowler's footnote notes some teams prefer the page to return a generic context so the test decides which page object to build, especially with conditional flows. Statically typed languages favour returning typed pages because the flow is visible in the signatures. Pick one convention and stay consistent.

        ❌ God page object with assertions
        class AccountPage {
  // 80 methods: profile, billing, orders, security, ...
  async verifyBalanceIs(x) { expect(await this.bal.text()).toBe(x); }
  async updateAddressAndCheckEmailSentAndLogOut() { /* 30 lines */ }
}

        It models a whole area of the app, mixes assertions with access, and its methods do several things, so tests cannot compose them.

        ✅ Small, composed, assertion-free
        class AccountPage {
  readonly billing = new BillingPanel(this.page);
  readonly security = new SecurityPanel(this.page);
}
class BillingPanel {
  balance(): Promise<string> { /* returns text */ }
  async updateAddress(a: Address) { /* one job */ }
}

        Each panel is a component object with one job. The test asserts on await billing.balance().

        App Actions and Screenplay: two ways beyond page objects

        App Actions means driving the application through a faster, more stable route (API call, direct state seeding, a test-only endpoint) whenever the UI journey is not what the test is about. Fowler makes the same general point: a scripting interface underneath the UI is usually simpler and faster than going through it. Use the UI for the behaviour under test, and everything else (login, data creation) through the side door. Caveat: you still need some tests that exercise login through the UI.

        Screenplay, as described in the Serenity/JS handbook, organises tests around people and goals instead of pages. Its five building blocks:

        ElementMeaningExample
        ActorA person or external system interacting with the system under testWendy the customer, Apisitt the data manager
        AbilityA thin wrapper around an integration library (browser driver, HTTP client)BrowseTheWeb, CallAnApi
        InteractionA low-level action using an abilityClick, Enter, Send a request
        TaskA named sequence of activities that is meaningful in the domain"Add product to basket"
        QuestionRetrieves information from the system or environmentPage title, last response status

        The handbook's key claim is that tests should express what actors must do to reach their goals in domain language, so failures can be tied to business impact. Its second claim is portability: because only the ability knows the tool, the same tasks can run under different runners. Note the trade-off: Screenplay adds vocabulary and boilerplate, and it is a stronger fit for large, long-lived suites than for a small team's first framework. Also note that the Serenity/JS documentation is naturally written by advocates of the pattern.

        Factory, Builder, Facade, Strategy

        Builder: the test-data pattern

        Nat Pryce's article contrasts two ways to create test objects. An Object Mother is a class of factory methods such as newDeerstalkerAndCapeInvoice(); it reads nicely but grows a new method for each variation until it becomes "bloated, messy and hard to maintain". A Test Data Builder has a field per constructor parameter with safe defaults, chainable withX() overrides, and a build() method. A test then states only what matters to it.

        class UserBuilder {
  private u: User = { name: 'Ann Tester', email: `ann+${uid()}@test.io`, role: 'member', verified: true };
  withRole(r: Role)        { this.u.role = r; return this; }
  unverified()             { this.u.verified = false; return this; }
  build(): User            { return { ...this.u }; }
}
const admin = new UserBuilder().withRole('admin').build();
const newbie = new UserBuilder().unverified().build();   // everything else is irrelevant and defaulted

        Pryce also notes that named parameters make intent clear: a positional newAddress("Sherlock", "221b Baker St", "London", "NW1") hides which argument is which, while .withCity("London") cannot be mixed up. See test data and environments.

        Factory

        A factory decides which object to build. The classic test use is a driver factory that reads configuration ("chromium", "firefox", "android") and returns the right object, so no test mentions a browser name. Keep it small: a switch over config is enough.

        Facade

        A facade offers one simple call over a complicated sequence: shop.flows.payByCard(order) hides four pages and two API calls. It is the pattern behind the "flow layer" in layered architecture. Danger: a facade with a dozen boolean flags is a god object in disguise.

        Strategy

        Strategy passes behaviour as a parameter. The Selenium guide uses it quietly: productsPage.getProduct(p -> p.getName().equals("Backpack")) passes a predicate so the page does not need a method for every way of searching. Similarly, a PaymentMethod interface with CardPayment and VoucherPayment implementations lets one checkout flow serve many tests.

        Dependency injection, fixtures and the Singleton trap

        Instead of an object creating its own browser or config, you hand them in. Modern runners do this for you: Playwright and pytest fixtures, JUnit extensions, and Spring or Guice in Java. The benefits are that each test gets fresh objects, dependencies are visible in the signature, and a fake can replace a real thing.

        Why Singleton is risky in tests. A singleton, a static variable or a global registry outlives the test that created it. Gerard Meszaros lists "anything that outlives the lifetime of the test" as a mechanism for Interacting Tests: test B passes only because test A left a value behind, and fails when run alone, reordered, or in parallel. He names Singletons and Registries as things to avoid, and says that if you must keep them, reinitialise them at the start of each test. A "shared driver singleton" is the classic example: parallel runs fight over one browser and a leftover cookie from test 14 fails test 15. Prefer a fresh object per test supplied through a fixture.

        Pitfalls checklist

        • God page objects. Split by component or area; prefer composition.
        • Assertions hidden in pages or flows. The test should show what is being verified.
        • Leaking the driver. If tests receive the raw page or WebElement from a page object, locators will creep back into tests.
        • Inheritance for reuse. LoginPage extends BasePage extends AbstractPage hides behaviour; share via composition.
        • Hard sleeps in pages. They hide timing bugs for everyone; see synchronisation.
        • Pattern for its own sake. Introduce a pattern the second or third time you feel the pain, not before.
        Same locator in 3+ tests?Introduce a Page or Component Object.
        Setup slow or noisy?Use App Actions: API, seeded state.
        Data painful to build?Add a Builder with sensible defaults.
        Multi-page steps repeated?Hide them in a Facade / flow or Screenplay Task.
        Global state creeping in?Replace with injected fixtures.

        Key points

        • Page objects hide HTML; they expose services and data, return typed next pages, and (by the main references) do not assert.
        • Page objects should model significant UI regions, composed from component objects, not one giant class per site area.
        • App Actions use a faster route for set-up; Screenplay models actors, abilities, tasks and questions in domain language.
        • Builders beat Object Mothers when data varies; factories choose implementations; facades hide sequences; strategies pass behaviour.
        • Prefer injection (fixtures) to Singletons: shared state is a main cause of tests that interact.
        • Add a pattern when duplication or fragility hurts, not in advance.
        How this maps to Playwright: see Page Object Models for the official take, fixtures for injection (each test gets its own page), authentication and API testing for App Actions style set-up, and locators, which are already lazy and auto-waiting so page objects can stay thin.

        A page object has a method verifyWelcomeMessage() that calls expect(...) internally. According to Fowler and the Selenium documentation, what is the preferred design?

        B. Mixing data access with assertion logic bloats pages and hides what a test verifies. The accepted exception is a "page loaded correctly" check.

        Two tests pass in the normal order but one fails when run alone or in parallel. A shared static Config.currentUser is set by the first test. Which smell is this?

        B. Meszaros names static variables, Singletons and Registries as typical mechanisms. The cure is a fresh fixture per test.

        Page Object: what do public methods represent?
        Services the page offers (e.g. loginAs), not individual clicks; the HTML structure stays hidden.
        Object Mother vs Test Data Builder?
        Mother: many named factory methods that bloat with variations. Builder: safe defaults plus chainable overrides, so each test states only what matters.
        Name the five Screenplay elements.
        Actors, Abilities, Interactions, Tasks, Questions.
        What are App Actions?
        Setting up state through APIs or direct manipulation instead of the UI when the UI path is not what the test checks.
        Why is a Singleton driver risky?
        It outlives tests, so state leaks between them and parallel runs collide; use per-test injected instances.

        📚 Sources

        • Page Object – Martin Fowler: definition, "panel object" naming, assertions debate, navigation footnote, Leotta et al. study
        • Page object models – Selenium project: rules for page objects, component objects, strategy via predicates
        • Design patterns and development strategies – Selenium project: LoadableComponent and the Bot pattern as an alternative style
        • Screenplay Pattern – Serenity/JS handbook: actors, abilities, interactions, tasks, questions and portability
        • Test Data Builders: an alternative to the Object Mother pattern – Nat Pryce: builder vs mother trade-offs
        • Erratic Test – Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Interacting Tests, shared fixtures, Singletons and Registries
        • Best Practices – Playwright docs: isolation and user-facing locators

        Synchronisation and Locators: the two causes of most flaky UI tests

        Almost every UI automation tool has to answer two questions: "When is the page ready for my next command?" (synchronisation) and "How do I point at the right element and keep pointing at it after the UI changes?" (locators). Get these two right and most flakiness disappears. This section explains the ideas once, then shows how Selenium, Cypress and Playwright each implement them.

        The root problem: a race between your test and the app

        A browser test is two programs running side by side: your script, which is fast and impatient, and the web application, which loads data, animates and re-renders at its own pace. The Selenium documentation puts it directly: the process often ends up in a race condition where sometimes the browser gets into the right state first and sometimes the code executes first, and this is "one of the primary causes of flaky tests".

        Think of ordering at a restaurant. A hard sleep is "I will ask for my soup exactly five minutes from now, whatever happens". Sometimes the soup is not ready (too early, error); sometimes it has been ready for four minutes (wasted time). Smart synchronisation is glancing at the pass every few moments and reaching for the soup the instant it appears, but giving up after a sensible limit.

        Navigation commands already wait for the page's readyState (by default, "complete"), but that only covers assets listed in the HTML. Scripts that run afterwards add elements, reveal fields and swap content, so after the page "loads" the DOM can still change. That is the gap your waits must cover.

        The waiting strategies

        Hard sleepPause for a fixed time. Brittle and slow.
        Implicit waitGlobal "keep looking for the element for N seconds".
        Explicit waitPoll a specific condition until true or timeout.
        Fluent waitExplicit wait plus polling interval and ignored errors.
        Auto-wait / retry-abilityThe tool checks readiness itself before each action and re-runs assertions.
        StrategyHow it worksStrengthWeakness
        Hard sleepsleep(3000)Trivial to writeCannot know the right duration: too short fails, too long wastes time on every run
        Implicit waitSession-wide timeout (default 0 in Selenium) applied to every element lookup; returns as soon as the element is foundOne line of configOnly waits for presence; global, so hard to reason about; must not be mixed with explicit waits
        Explicit waitA loop that polls a condition (title is X, element visible, text present) until timeoutWaits for exactly the condition you needVerbose; easy to wait for the wrong condition
        Fluent waitExplicit wait with custom polling frequency and a list of exceptions to ignoreFine control for unusual widgetsMore code; same condition risk
        Auto-waitBefore each action the tool verifies the element is ready; assertions retry until they pass or time outWaiting is built in, tests stay shortDoes not know your business readiness (e.g. "data finished loading") unless you assert it

        Why hard sleeps fail

        • They are a guess. The Selenium docs: because the code cannot know exactly how long to wait, a sleep can fail when it is not long enough, and if the value is set high everywhere the session duration "can become prohibitive".
        • They multiply. Illustrative arithmetic: 300 tests each carrying two 3-second sleeps spend 30 minutes doing nothing, before any parallelism.
        • They hide bugs. The test passes on a fast laptop and fails on a loaded CI machine, so the failure looks random and gets blamed on "flakiness".
        • They test time, not state. What you care about is "the confirmation message is visible", never "three seconds have passed".
        Never mix implicit and explicit waits. Selenium's documentation warns that doing so can cause unpredictable wait times; its example is an implicit wait of 10 seconds with an explicit wait of 15 seconds possibly timing out after 20. Choose explicit waits (or an auto-waiting tool) and leave the implicit wait at 0.

        The same wait in three tools

        The scenario (taken from Selenium's own demo page): click "Add a box!", after which a new element #box0 appears a moment later. We want to verify its class.

        driver.findElement(By.id("adder")).click();

// Explicit wait: poll until the condition holds, at most 2 seconds
Wait<WebDriver> wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(2));
WebElement box = wait.until(d -> d.findElement(By.id("box0")));
assertEquals("redbox", box.getDomAttribute("class"));

// Fluent variant: custom polling, ignore a specific error
Wait<WebDriver> fluent = new FluentWait<>(driver)
    .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .pollingEvery(Duration.ofMillis(300))
    .ignoring(ElementNotInteractableException.class);
        cy.get('#adder').click()

// No explicit wait: .should() re-runs the query chain until it passes
// or the command timeout (default 4 s) expires.
cy.get('#box0').should('have.class', 'redbox')
        await page.locator('#adder').click();   // auto-waits: visible, stable, enabled, receives events

// Web-first assertion: retries until it passes or times out
await expect(page.locator('#box0')).toHaveClass('redbox');
        await page.locator('#adder').click();
await page.waitForTimeout(3000);            // guess
expect(await page.locator('#box0').getAttribute('class')).toBe('redbox');  // no retry either

        Retry-ability: how modern tools remove most waiting

        Cypress's documentation gives the clearest model. Commands split into queries (find something), assertions (a kind of query) and non-queries such as clicks, which run only once. When an assertion fails, Cypress re-runs the whole linked chain of queries from the top and re-checks until success or timeout. The page is allowed to change in the meantime: a three-second artificial delay in the app's rendering did not break the example test. Action commands additionally wait until the element is actionable (visible, not covered, not disabled) and then perform the action once.

        Playwright applies the same idea: before an action it checks the element is visible, stable (same bounding box for two animation frames), receives events (not hidden behind an overlay), enabled, and not inert; assertions like toBeVisible() are "auto-retrying". Testing Library draws the same line with its query families: getBy fails immediately, queryBy returns null (to assert absence), and findBy returns a promise that retries (default 1000 ms in that library).

        IdeaSeleniumCypressPlaywright
        Wait before actionYou write it (explicit wait)Built in (actionability)Built in (actionability)
        Retry assertionYou write a polling wait around it.should() re-runs the query chainexpect(locator) web-first assertions
        Default timeout0 s implicit; you pass explicit timeouts4 s per retrying commandConfigurable action and assertion timeouts
        Element referenceA live handle to a DOM node (can go stale)Re-queried from the chainA lazy locator, resolved at each use

        Stale elements

        A stale element reference appears when you hold a pointer to a node that the application later replaced. The page looks identical, but the old node is gone. Cypress documents the same trap: a .should() in the middle of a chain acts as a "retry boundary", so if the page re-renders after it passes, later queries operate on a detached element; the fix is to split the chain or use a single callback assertion that re-queries. Two general cures: do not store elements, store how to find them (locators), and re-find after any action that can re-render. Tools with lazy locators (Playwright) or re-queried chains (Cypress) mostly do this for you. Selenium users need to keep the lookup inside the wait condition.

        Waiting for something the page does not show

        Sometimes the UI gives no visible signal, for example a background save. Then wait for the observable cause: the network response the app sends.

        # No built-in network wait: poll something observable, e.g. a status element or an API you can call.
WebDriverWait(driver, 5).until(
    lambda d: d.find_element(By.ID, "save-status").text == "Saved")
        cy.intercept('POST', '/api/save').as('save')
cy.contains('button', 'Save').click()
cy.wait('@save').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 200)
        const saved = page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/save') && r.ok());
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
await saved;                       // start listening BEFORE the click to avoid a race

        What should you wait for?

        • An element is visible, enabled or contains specific text (user-visible state).
        • The URL or title changed after navigation.
        • A specific network call finished (an API response), when the UI gives no visible signal.
        • A loading indicator disappeared.

        Avoid waiting for "network idle" or fixed times as your only signal; wait for the thing a user would see.

        Diagnosing timing failures

        What you seeLikely causeBetter approach
        "Element not found" right after a clickThe element is added a moment later; no wait, or only a presence waitWait for the visible, usable state, or use an auto-waiting tool
        "Element not interactable / click intercepted"Element exists but is hidden, animating or covered by an overlay or spinnerWait for the overlay to disappear; rely on actionability checks
        Stale element referenceRe-render replaced the node after you located itRe-locate inside the wait; avoid storing elements
        Assertion reads old textAssertion ran once, before the UI updatedUse a retrying assertion, not a one-shot read of the value
        Passes locally, fails on CICI is slower; fixed sleeps or tight timeoutsCondition-based waits; raise the timeout of the specific slow step only
        Test takes minutes of nothingAccumulated sleeps or a very long implicit waitRemove sleeps; set implicit wait to 0
        Read versus assert. A one-shot read such as "get the text, then compare" cannot retry, because the value was already captured. A retrying assertion receives the locator and re-reads it. Playwright's best-practice guide uses this exact contrast (expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true) returns immediately, while await expect(locator).toBeVisible() waits). The same principle applies to Cypress's .should() versus .then(), which Cypress documents as not retried.

        Locators: pointing at the right element, durably

        A locator is a rule that finds an element. The strategy that matters is not syntax but what the rule depends on: the more it depends on things users and assistive technology rely on (role, name, label), the less it breaks when developers restyle or restructure the page.

        Testing Library's priority order

        Testing Library's guiding principle is that "the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you". From it follows an ordered list of queries:

        1. Accessible to everyone: getByRole (with name), getByLabelText, getByPlaceholderText, getByText, getByDisplayValue.
        2. Semantic: getByAltText, getByTitle (title is not consistently read by screen readers).
        3. Test IDs: getByTestId, recommended only when you cannot match by role or text or it does not make sense, e.g. dynamic text.

        Playwright's documentation reaches nearly the same ranking: prefer user-facing attributes and explicit contracts; role first, label for form fields, text for non-interactive elements, test ids when needed, and CSS or XPath as a last resort because "the DOM can often change".

        RankLocator typeDepends onBreaks whenNotes
        1Role + accessible nameWhat the element is and what it is calledControl is renamed or its role changesMirrors users and screen readers; failure can signal an accessibility bug
        2Label / placeholder / textVisible copyCopy edits, translationsGreat for forms; use regexes or test language for multi-language apps
        3Test id (data-testid)An explicit contract with developersSomeone deletes the attributeVery stable but invisible to users; needs team agreement
        4id / nameDeveloper-chosen identifiersGenerated or renamed idsFine when they are stable and meaningful
        5CSSClasses and structureAny redesign or refactorCommon in legacy suites; keep short and inside page objects
        6XPath (positional)Exact DOM pathAlmost any layout changeLast resort; useful for axis queries the others cannot express
        Where the sources differ. Testing Library ranks test ids last; Playwright's locator guide calls test ids "the most resilient way of testing" because role and text can change, while also noting they are not user-facing. These are compatible: roles and labels are best for interactive controls because they verify accessibility, while test ids suit dynamic content, repeated structures and teams that want an explicit contract. Whichever you choose, agree on it as a team and write it down.

        The accessibility tree as the stable contract

        Browsers build an accessibility tree from the DOM: a simplified tree of roles, names and states (button "Submit", textbox "Password", heading level 1) used by screen readers. Role locators query this tree. It is stable because it describes meaning, not markup: turning a <div class="btn"> into a <button> or changing its CSS class leaves "button named Submit" unchanged. Testing Library says of getByRole that there is not much you cannot get with it, and "if you can't, it's possible your UI is inaccessible". That is a bonus: fragile role locators often point to real accessibility defects (unlabelled icon buttons, clickable divs).

        // Core API: id, name, CSS, XPath, link text. No built-in role locator.
driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("form button[type='submit']"));
driver.findElement(By.xpath("//button[normalize-space()='Sign in']"));   // text-based XPath: better than positional
// Tip: keep these only inside page objects, so a change is a one-line fix.
        cy.get('[data-testid="signin"]').click()      // explicit contract
cy.contains('button', 'Sign in').click()      // text-based
cy.findByRole('button', { name: /sign in/i }).click()  // with @testing-library/cypress
        await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();   // role + accessible name
await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret');             // label
await page.getByTestId('signin').click();                     // data-testid
await page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Product 2' })
          .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();   // chain + filter

        Strictness and ambiguity

        A locator that matches several elements is a bug waiting to happen. Playwright locators are strict: an action on a locator that matches more than one element throws, and the documentation discourages first(), nth() and last() because they silently pick a different element when the page changes. Testing Library behaves similarly: getBy throws if there is more than one match. Narrow with context ("the row containing Product 2") rather than an index.

        Make testability a team agreement. Ask developers to use semantic HTML, label every control and add a test id where role and text are ambiguous. Testing Library describes a test id as a way to "establish a stable API contract in the HTML". Cheaper than rewriting 300 CSS selectors after each redesign.
        Common mistakes: locators built from auto-generated class names (.css-1x2y3z), absolute XPaths (/html/body/div[3]/div[2]/button), locating by visible text in a multilingual app, and storing located elements in fields across page transitions.

        Key points

        • Flakiness is mainly a race between the test and the app; solve it by waiting for conditions, never for time.
        • Hard sleeps are guesses: too short is flaky, too long is slow. Implicit waits only cover presence; do not mix them with explicit waits.
        • Cypress and Playwright build retry-ability and actionability into commands and assertions; Selenium makes you write explicit or fluent waits.
        • Stale elements come from holding references to DOM nodes; hold locators instead.
        • Prefer role/label/text locators, then test ids; CSS and XPath are a last resort kept inside page objects.
        • The accessibility tree is the most stable contract because it describes meaning, and it doubles as an accessibility check.
        How this maps to Playwright: read auto-waiting (actionability), locators, web-first assertions and best practices. Test-id attribute naming is configurable in test configuration.

        A test clicks "Save" then runs sleep(2000) before checking for a toast. It passes locally and fails on CI about once in ten runs. What is the best fix?

        B. The sleep guesses a duration; CI is slower than the laptop. Waiting for the toast waits only as long as necessary and fails with a useful message if it never appears. A long implicit wait only covers element presence and slows every missing-element check.

        Which locator is generally the most resilient to a visual redesign, according to Testing Library and Playwright?

        B. Role plus name depends on meaning, not on markup, so restructuring or restyling does not break it. A and C depend on DOM structure.

        Why does a hard sleep make tests flaky and slow?
        It guesses a fixed duration: too short fails on slow runs, too long wastes time on every run.
        Difference between implicit and explicit waits?
        Implicit: global session setting for element lookups. Explicit: a polled condition with its own timeout. Do not mix them.
        What is retry-ability?
        The tool re-runs a query or assertion until it passes or times out, so the app may change in between.
        What causes a stale element?
        A stored DOM reference whose node was removed or replaced by a re-render; re-find it via a locator.
        State the Testing Library locator priority.
        Role, label, placeholder, text, display value; then alt text, title; then test id; CSS/XPath only as a manual escape hatch.
