        • Auto-waiting – Playwright docs: actionability checks and auto-retrying assertions

        Test Data, Isolation and Environments

        A test is only as trustworthy as the world it starts in. Most "mysterious" failures come not from the test steps but from the data they run against (someone changed a record) or the environment they run in (a different URL, a missing flag, a shared database). This section covers how to create and clean up data, how to keep tests independent, and how to manage environments, configuration and secrets safely.

        Why data and environment decide whether tests are reliable

        Picture a chemistry lab. A good experiment starts with clean glassware and measured ingredients; if the previous student left residue in the flask, your result tells you nothing. A test with a pre-existing "golden" customer shared by thirty tests is a flask that is never washed.

        Gerard Meszaros calls the starting state the test fixture and structures each test into four phases: fixture setup, exercise the system, verify the result, and fixture teardown, which returns the world to the state in which you found it. Everything in this section is about doing the first and last phase well.

        Set upCreate exactly the data this test needs, with unique values.
        ExerciseDrive the system under test. Data is not changed by the test harness.
        VerifyAssert on outcomes that relate to this test's data only.
        Tear downRemove or isolate the data, even if the test failed.

        Test data strategies

        StrategyWhat it isGood forRisks
        Static fixturesFiles (JSON, CSV, SQL) with fixed data loaded before the testReference data, small stable inputs, expected outputsGo stale; tests share and mutate them; hard to see which fields matter
        Factories / buildersCode that builds valid objects with safe defaults and overridesRich domain objects; unique values per runBuilders drift from the real model if not maintained
        SeedingScripts that load a known data set into a database before a runA stable baseline for read-only testsSeed changes can silently break many tests (data sensitivity)
        API-driven setupTests create entities through the app's own API before touching the UIFast, realistic, goes through business rulesDepends on the API; it must itself be tested
        DB snapshot / restoreRestore a known database image (or container) before a run or testComplex relational states; fully isolated environmentsSlow for large databases; snapshots must be regenerated on schema change
        Synthetic dataGenerated fake data (e.g. a faker library), optionally seededPrivacy-safe, unlimited volume, edge casesMay not reflect real-world messiness
        Masked production dataA copy of production with personal data replaced or scrambledRealistic volumes and weird casesCompliance risk if masking is incomplete; broken referential integrity; stale quickly

        Builders: say only what matters

        Nat Pryce's Test Data Builder article explains why simple helpers are not enough. An Object Mother grows a new factory method for every variation until it is "bloated, messy and hard to maintain". A builder starts with sensible defaults and lets a test override only the field it cares about, so a reader can see what is significant. Adding a new required field means changing the builder once, not forty tests.

        export const anOrder = () => new OrderBuilder();

class OrderBuilder {
  private o = { customerId: '', lines: [{ sku: 'BACKPACK', qty: 1 }], coupon: null as string | null };
  forCustomer(id: string) { this.o.customerId = id; return this; }
  withLine(sku: string, qty = 1) { this.o.lines.push({ sku, qty }); return this; }
  withCoupon(code: string) { this.o.coupon = code; return this; }
  build() { return structuredClone(this.o); }
}
// A test states only the interesting part:
const order = anOrder().forCustomer(user.id).withCoupon('SAVE10').build();

        API-driven setup (and where the UI still matters)

        export const test = base.extend<{ customer: Customer }>({
  customer: async ({ request }, use) => {
    // setup: unique data through the API, milliseconds instead of a UI journey
    const res = await request.post('/api/customers', { data: aCustomer().build() });
    const customer = await res.json();
    await use(customer);                        // the test runs here
    await request.delete(`/api/customers/${customer.id}`);   // teardown, also runs after failures
  },
});

        Use the UI to create data only when the UI path is the behaviour under test (for example, the registration form). Everywhere else, the fastest, most stable route wins; see "App Actions" in design patterns.

        Synthetic versus masked production data

        Synthetic data is created from scratch: safe and flexible, but you must deliberately include the ugly cases (long names, accents, nulls, time zones). Masked production data brings realistic shape and volume, but "masked" has to mean irreversibly altered, with consistent replacement so that relationships between tables survive. If you cannot guarantee that, treat the copy as production data under the same access rules. A practical combination is synthetic data for functional tests and a masked, periodically refreshed copy for performance or data-migration rehearsals. (This paragraph is general practice, not a claim from a single source; check your organisation's data-protection rules.)

        Randomness needs a seed. Meszaros's "Nondeterministic Test" smell is caused by using different random values each run, which makes failures impossible to reproduce. If you use generated data, print the seed (or the generated values) in the test output, so a failing run can be replayed exactly. A cleaner alternative is "distinct generated values": unique but deterministic-looking identifiers such as ann+<runId>@test.io.

        Isolation and independence

        Test independence means any test can run alone, in any order, in parallel, any number of times, and give the same result. Meszaros's catalogue of Erratic Tests reads like a list of what happens when it does not hold:

        Smell (Meszaros)SymptomTypical data/environment cause
        Interacting TestsPasses alone, fails after another test (or when reordered)Test B relies on rows or state created by test A
        Unrepeatable TestPasses the first run, fails the next (or the reverse)Fixture outlives the run; leftovers from last time
        Test Run WarRandom failures when several people or pipelines run at onceA shared database or file everyone writes to
        Resource LeakageGets slower, then fails, until something is restartedTests allocate sessions, connections or records and never free them
        Resource OptimismPasses in one environment, fails in anotherAssumes a file, service or setting that is not everywhere
        Nondeterministic TestRandom failures even in a single runRandom values, time, uncontrolled concurrency

        The preferred cure in his book is the Fresh Fixture: each test builds its own data and does not rely on what exists. Where a shared fixture is unavoidable, he suggests making it immutable or partitioning the database so tests cannot overlap. He also offers a cheap diagnostic: run the tests in a different order, and any test that now fails depends on another. Another useful technique he names for verification is the delta assertion: compare "before" and "after" snapshots so unrelated rows added by others do not matter.

        The Fragile Test chapter names the matching pain Data Sensitivity: a test breaks because the data it assumed was changed, typically in a shared database. Its fix is the same: tests should not depend on the existing contents of the database.

        ❌ Shared golden data
        test('update address', async () => {
  await login('testuser1');   // shared by all tests
  // changes testuser1's address ...
});
test('show address', async () => {
  await login('testuser1');   // fails after the test above
});

        Order-dependent, breaks under parallel runs, and a second run starts from the first run's leftovers.

        ✅ Own your data
        test('update address', async ({ customer }) => {
  await login(customer);      // unique per test, created by a fixture
  // ...
});
test('show address', async ({ customer }) => {
  await login(customer);      // a different customer, no interference
});

        Any order, any parallelism, repeatable. Cleanup lives in the fixture.

        Parallel-safe data in practice

        Running tests in parallel is the fastest way to expose hidden sharing. Three habits keep parallel runs safe without locks:

        1. Namespace by run and worker. Embed a run id and worker index in generated names (order-r481-w3-17), so two pipelines or workers never collide, and so leftovers can be traced to a run for cleanup.
        2. Partition unavoidable shared resources. If tests must share one database, give each worker its own tenant, schema or account range. Meszaros calls this a database partitioning scheme.
        3. Assert on your own data. Verify "my order is listed", not "the list has 5 items". The second form breaks as soon as another test adds a row (Data Sensitivity).
        // Unique, traceable identifiers; no shared mutable state between workers
let counter = 0;
const runId = process.env.RUN_ID ?? Date.now().toString(36);
export const uid = (prefix: string) => `${prefix}-${runId}-${test.info().workerIndex}-${counter++}`;

// Weak: depends on what everyone else has done
await expect(rows).toHaveCount(5);
// Strong: depends only on this test's data
await expect(rows.filter({ hasText: order.reference })).toHaveCount(1);

        A quick data-health audit

        Question to ask of a failing or flaky testIf "yes", suspect
        Does it pass alone but fail in the suite?Interacting Tests: another test changes shared state
        Does it pass on the first run after a database reset only?Unrepeatable Test: leftovers from previous runs
        Does it fail more often when colleagues or other pipelines run?Test Run War on a shared environment
        Does it use "the first user in the list" or "any product"?Hidden assumptions about data content
        Does the failure vary with the clock, time zone or random values?Nondeterministic Test: control time and seeds
        Does it assume a file, service or flag that exists only somewhere?Resource Optimism

        Cleanup strategies

        StrategyHowProsCons
        Inline teardowntry/finally or afterEach deletes what the test createdSimple; Meszaros notes it must run even when assertions failEasy to forget; leaks when the test crashes early
        Automated (fixture-managed) teardownA fixture creates data, hands it over, deletes it afterCentralised; guaranteed by the runnerNeeds a deletion API or direct DB access
        Unique data, no cleanupDistinct values per test; a nightly job purges old rowsFast; parallel-safeDatabase grows; the "janitor" must be trusted and monitored
        Ephemeral environmentSpin up a database or whole stack per run or per branch, destroy afterPerfect isolation; no leakageCosts time and money; needs infrastructure
        Snapshot restoreReset to a known image between runsDeterministic baselineSlow for big data; hard for parallel tests in one database

        A defensive habit (the author's recommendation, not a quotation): make setup tolerant of leftovers, for example by generating unique identifiers, because teardown is the phase most likely to be skipped when a pipeline is killed. Cleanup is then hygiene rather than a hidden dependency.

        Environments and configuration

        The Twelve-Factor App defines config as everything likely to vary between deploys (staging, production, a developer's machine): resource handles, credentials, hostnames. It requires strict separation of config from code and stores it in environment variables, which are easy to change without touching code, unlikely to be committed by accident, and independent of language and OS. Its litmus test is neat: could the codebase be open-sourced at any moment without leaking credentials? A test repository should pass the same test.

        One 12-factor idea is a little counter-intuitive for testers, who often keep dev.json, qa.json, staging.json. The authors warn that named groups of config ("environments") do not scale: new names such as staging, qa or joes-staging multiply until config is brittle, and prefer granular variables managed independently per deploy. A pragmatic compromise is a few presets that only set variables, each of which can still be overridden individually from the command line or the pipeline.

        function required(name: string): string {
  const v = process.env[name];
  if (!v) throw new Error(`Missing environment variable ${name}`);   // fail fast, with a clear message
  return v;
}
export const config = {
  baseUrl: required('BASE_URL'),
  apiUrl: process.env.API_URL ?? `${required('BASE_URL')}/api`,
  adminToken: required('ADMIN_TOKEN'),            // injected by the CI secret store
  headless: process.env.HEADED !== '1',
};

        Secrets

        • Never commit credentials. Commit an .env.example with names only, and git-ignore the real .env.
        • Inject secrets from the CI system's secret store; do not print them (most CI tools mask known secrets, but not transformed ones).
        • Give automation accounts least privilege and separate them per environment, so a leaked staging token cannot touch production.
        • Rotate tokens; prefer short-lived ones obtained at the start of the run.

        Parity and hermetic tests

        Twelve-Factor's "dev/prod parity" principle says to keep environments as similar as possible, because gaps in time, people and tools cause surprises. The test equivalent: if staging runs a different database version or lacks a service, your staging results predict little about production.

        A hermetic test goes further: it controls everything it touches. Playwright's best-practices guide gives a concrete rule: do not test third-party services you do not control; instead intercept and fulfil the network call so the response is guaranteed, and for databases make sure you control the data. Consequences, as a spectrum:

        LevelWhat is realSpeed / reliabilityConfidence
        Hermetic UI testYour front end; back end and third parties stubbedFast, very stableFront-end behaviour only
        Integrated testYour front end and back end in a test environment; third parties stubbedModerateMost business flows
        Production smokeEverything; read-only or synthetic-user checksSlowest, least controllableDeployment health

        Feature flags

        A feature flag changes behaviour without a deploy, so a test's result may depend on a flag it never mentions. Rules of thumb (practice, not a single-source claim): pin the flags a test depends on explicitly in setup (via config or a flag API) instead of trusting the environment default; run the important flows in both states while a rollout is in progress; tag tests with the flag they need so a pipeline can skip them when the flag is not available; and delete tests and flags together once the flag is retired.

        Beware "it works on staging". Staging databases accumulate data, flags drift, and several teams deploy at once. A failure that disappears on re-run is a data or environment smell until proved otherwise: check for Interacting Tests, leftover rows and concurrent runs before blaming the framework.
        Checklist: every test creates its own data; values are unique; cleanup is automatic; config comes from variables; secrets come from the store; third parties are stubbed; flags are pinned; the suite passes when run in random order and with 4 workers.

        Key points

        • Structure each test as setup, exercise, verify, teardown; the first and last phases decide reliability.
        • Prefer fresh data per test (builders plus API setup) over shared golden records.
        • Static fixtures and seeds suit stable reference data; snapshots suit complex states; masked production data needs strong masking.
        • Interacting, unrepeatable and run-war tests are all symptoms of shared state; run tests reordered and in parallel to find them.
        • Config belongs in the environment (12-factor); secrets in a secret store; presets may only set variables.
        • Hermetic tests stub what you do not control; pin feature flags explicitly.
        How this maps to Playwright: data setup and cleanup are naturally written as fixtures; API-driven set-up uses API testing; reusing a signed-in state is covered in authentication; stubbing third parties uses mocking and network; isolation per test comes from browser contexts; environments map to projects and configuration; parallel safety is explained in parallelism.

        A suite passes when run once, then two tests fail on the second run against the same database; resetting the database fixes it. Which smell fits best?

        B. This is Meszaros's pass-then-fail pattern, usually from a persistent shared fixture. The cure is fresh data per test, distinct generated values, or automated teardown.

        According to the Twelve-Factor App, where should values like a database URL or an API token live?

        B. Config varies between deploys while code does not. Environment variables are hard to commit by accident and language-agnostic; grouping into named environments does not scale.

        What is a Fresh Fixture?
        Each test builds its own data from scratch rather than relying on shared pre-existing records.
        Builder vs Object Mother?
        A builder has defaults plus overrides so each test states only what matters; a mother grows a method per variation.
        Name three Erratic Test causes.
        Interacting Tests, Unrepeatable Test, Test Run War (also Resource Leakage, Resource Optimism, Nondeterministic Test).
        What is a hermetic test?
        One that controls everything it depends on, stubbing third parties and creating its own data.
        12-factor rule for config?
        Store config in environment variables, strictly separate from code; the repo should be open-sourceable without leaking secrets.

        📚 Sources

        • Four-Phase Test – Gerard Meszaros: setup, exercise, verify, teardown; try/finally teardown
        • Erratic Test – Gerard Meszaros: Interacting Tests, Unrepeatable Test, Test Run War, Resource Leakage and related causes and cures
        • Fragile Test – Gerard Meszaros: Data Sensitivity and Fresh Fixture
        • Test Data Builders: an alternative to the Object Mother pattern – Nat Pryce: builders with defaults and overrides
        • The Twelve-Factor App: III. Config – Adam Wiggins et al.: config in environment variables; why named environments do not scale
        • The Twelve-Factor App: X. Dev/prod parity – Adam Wiggins et al.: keeping environments similar
        • Best Practices – Playwright docs: test isolation, avoid testing third-party dependencies, control database data

        Data-driven, Keyword-driven and BDD Styles (and Hybrids)

        Besides "how is the code structured" there is a second design question: "in what form do we write the tests down?" Three popular answers are data-driven tests (one flow, many inputs), keyword-driven tests (a vocabulary of reusable actions) and Behaviour-Driven Development (examples that the whole team writes in business language). They solve different problems, and mixing them up is a common cause of expensive, unloved test suites.

        The three styles at a glance

        StyleCore ideaTypical toolsMain audienceBest for
        Data-drivenSeparate the test logic from its data; run the same logic over many rowsJUnit/TestNG parameters, pytest parametrize, Robot Test Templates, Scenario Outlines, CSV loopsTesters and developersValidation rules, boundaries, combinations
        Keyword-drivenBuild tests from named actions ("keywords") that hide the implementationRobot Framework, Selenium-based keyword librariesTesters, analysts, partly businessWorkflows shared by many people, long-lived acceptance suites
        BDDSpecify behaviour with concrete examples in shared language, then automate themCucumber, SpecFlow/Reqnroll, Behave, Robot with Given/When/Then styleWhole team including businessBuilding shared understanding; living documentation
        HybridCombine them: BDD-style scenarios built from keywords, parametrised with dataRobot Framework, Cucumber + page objects + Scenario OutlineMixedMost real suites

        Data-driven testing

        Many checks differ only in their inputs: is an empty username rejected? A password of 7 characters? Writing one test per row by copy and paste creates exactly the duplication that layering is meant to remove. Data-driven testing stores the data in a table, a file or a parameter list and runs the same flow once per row.

        import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize("user,password,message", [
    ("",      "valid-pw",  "Username is required"),
    ("ann",   "",          "Password is required"),
    ("ann",   "wrong",     "Invalid credentials"),
])
def test_login_rejected(login_page, user, password, message):
    login_page.login(user, password)
    assert login_page.error_text() == message
        const cases = [
  { user: '',    pass: 'valid-pw', msg: 'Username is required' },
  { user: 'ann', pass: '',         msg: 'Password is required' },
  { user: 'ann', pass: 'wrong',    msg: 'Invalid credentials' },
];
for (const c of cases) {
  test(`login rejected: ${c.msg}`, async ({ loginPage }) => {   // one real test per row
    await loginPage.login(c.user, c.pass);
    await expect(loginPage.error).toHaveText(c.msg);
  });
}
        *** Settings ***
Test Template    Login with invalid credentials should fail

*** Test Cases ***                  USERNAME         PASSWORD
Invalid User Name                   invalid          ${VALID PASSWORD}
Invalid Password                    ${VALID USER}    invalid
Empty User Name                     ${EMPTY}         ${VALID PASSWORD}
Empty Password                      ${VALID USER}    ${EMPTY}
        Scenario Outline: rejected logins
  When I sign in with "<user>" and "<password>"
  Then I see the error "<message>"

  Examples:
    | user | password | message              |
    |      | valid-pw | Username is required |
    | ann  |          | Password is required |
    | ann  | wrong    | Invalid credentials  |

        The Robot Framework user guide shows two ways to organise the same table: one test per row (readable names, but many entries in statistics) or one test containing all rows, and says the right choice depends on context and preference. It also notes that templated tests are special: all rows are executed even if one fails, and the overall result is FAIL if any row failed. Check what your own tool does, because many runners stop at the first failing assertion inside a loop.

        Data-driven pitfalls. (1) Giant tables become a second, unreviewed test suite; keep rows meaningful and named. (2) Putting if statements inside the loop (Meszaros's Conditional Test Logic smell) means rows no longer test the same thing. (3) A failure in "row 37" with no description wastes triage time; give each row a readable name. (4) Do not use a table to hide that you are testing ten unrelated behaviours.

        Keyword-driven testing (Robot Framework)

        In a keyword-driven suite, tests are written as sequences of keywords: named actions such as Open Login Page or Welcome Page Should Be Open. Keywords come from two places: libraries (implemented in a programming language, e.g. Python) and user keywords that combine other keywords. Robot Framework describes itself as a Python-based, extensible keyword-driven automation framework for acceptance testing, ATDD, BDD and RPA, with a tabular syntax, reusable higher-level keywords, variables for different environments, tags, setup and teardown, and HTML reports.

        *** Settings ***
Resource    resources/login.resource       # keyword implementations live here

*** Test Cases ***
Valid Login
    Open Login Page
    Input Username    demo
    Input Password    mode
    Submit Credentials
    Welcome Page Should Be Open

*** Keywords ***                           # in the resource file
Input Username
    [Arguments]    ${username}
    Input Text     id:username_field    ${username}

        This is the same layering you saw in layered architecture, written as a language. The test case reads like a workflow: first take the system to an initial state, then act on it, finally verify. The lowest-level keywords wrap a library (Selenium, Playwright, HTTP), while the keywords in between are your business vocabulary.

        ❌ Keywords that are just clicks
        Valid Login
    Click Element    id:u
    Input Text       id:u    demo
    Click Element    id:p
    Input Text       id:p    mode
    Click Button     id:go
    Page Should Contain    Welcome

        This is a script in a table: no abstraction, locators in every test, and it is no easier for a non-programmer to read than code.

        ✅ Keywords that name intent
        Valid Login
    Given login page is open
    When valid credentials are submitted
    Then welcome page should be open

        Each line is a user keyword built from lower-level ones. Locators live once, in the resource file.

        Strengths: non-programmers can compose tests from existing keywords; keywords are reused across suites; reports show business steps. Costs: you are still programming, just in a restricted language, so you need code-review, naming conventions and refactoring discipline for the keyword library; debugging across several layers of keywords can be slower than debugging plain code; and a library of 800 poorly named keywords is as hard to navigate as any large codebase.

        BDD and Gherkin

        BDD is a collaboration practice first

        The Cucumber documentation, written by the tool's own authors, is explicit: "there's much more to BDD than just using Cucumber". BDD is a way of working that closes the gap between business and technical people by (1) encouraging collaboration to build shared understanding, (2) working in small rapid iterations, and (3) producing documentation that is automatically checked against the system's behaviour. Day-to-day it is three practices, in this order:

        DiscoveryWhat it could do. Structured conversations about concrete examples of a user story.
        FormulationWhat it should do. Write the agreed examples in a readable, automatable format (Gherkin).
        AutomationWhat it actually does. Connect each example to the system as a test; implement until it passes.

        The docs stress that the documentation and automated tests are "nice side-effects"; the real goal is valuable, working software reached through conversation, and "if you're new to BDD, discovery is the right place to start". The corollary is uncomfortable for many teams: if testers alone write Gherkin after the code is finished, with no conversation with product and development, you have bought the syntax and skipped the benefit.

        Gherkin in practice

        Feature: Multiple site support
  Only blog owners can post to a blog, except administrators,
  who can post to all blogs.

  Example: Dr. Bill posts to his own blog
    Given I am logged in as Dr. Bill
    When I try to post to "Expensive Therapy"
    Then I should see "Your article was published."

  Example: Dr. Bill tries to post to somebody else's blog, and fails
    Given I am logged in as Dr. Bill
    When I try to post to "Greg's anti-tax rants"
    Then I should see "Hey! That's not your blog!"

        The keywords carry meaning. Feature groups examples; Rule (since Gherkin 6) groups examples that illustrate one business rule; an Example (or Scenario) is a concrete case that is also a test. Given sets the context (things that happened in the past, not user interactions), When is the event or action, Then is an observable outcome. Background shares Given steps, Scenario Outline plus Examples runs a template once per row.

        The reference includes advice that is worth treating as rules of thumb:

        • Aim for 3 to 5 steps per example; many steps lose their value as specification and documentation.
        • Imagine it is 1922: describe what the user does without assuming a UI technology; hide "click the blue button" in step definitions.
        • A Then should check an outcome observable from outside (a message, a report), not a database row. The reference says to "resist that temptation".
        • Keep Background short (more than about four lines suggests irrelevant detail) and vivid, so readers can remember it.
        • Cucumber ignores the keyword when matching steps, so Given and Then with identical text are duplicates; this pushes you toward clearer wording ("my account has a balance of £430" vs "my account should have a balance of £430").
        • One Feature per file; use tags (@smoke) to group across files; write in the language your domain experts speak.

        Declarative versus imperative scenarios

        ❌ Imperative (UI script in English)
        Given I go to "/login"
And I type "ann" into the field "username"
And I type "s3cret" into the field "password"
And I click the "Sign in" button
Then I should see the text "Hello ann" in the "h1" element

        Tied to UI details; business readers skim it; any UI change rewrites many scenarios.

        ✅ Declarative (behaviour)
        Given Ann is a registered customer
When she signs in with valid credentials
Then she is greeted by name

        States intent. The step definitions call a flow (signIn(customer)), which uses page objects.

        // Step definitions are thin glue: they translate sentences into calls on the flow layer.
Given('{word} is a registered customer', async function (name: string) {
  this.customer = await this.data.createCustomer({ name });      // API-driven setup
});
When('she signs in with valid credentials', async function () {
  await this.shop.flows.signIn(this.customer);
});
Then('she is greeted by name', async function () {
  expect(await this.shop.home.greeting()).toBe(`Hello ${this.customer.name}`);
});

        Martin Fowler gives the same architectural advice: if you write tests with a DSL such as Cucumber, layer the DSL over the page objects, so a parser translates statements into calls on them.

        When BDD hurts

        BDD has real costs: every example needs a step definition, a regular expression or pattern to maintain, and an extra translation layer between the sentence and the code. The following failure modes are widely reported by practitioners (this list is synthesis and opinion, supported by the Cucumber docs' emphasis on collaboration and short examples):

        • No one reads the files. If product people never review the feature files, the plain English is overhead; use ordinary test code instead.
        • Scenarios as UI scripts. Imperative steps duplicate what page objects already do and are harder to refactor than code.
        • Step-definition explosion and regex tangles. Hundreds of near-duplicate sentences, hidden shared state between steps (a "world" object that grows forever).
        • Huge scenario counts. Exhaustive input combinations belong in data-driven or unit tests, not in Gherkin; use BDD for the representative examples.
        • Treating it as a test tool. Using Cucumber only to automate test cases written by a tester after the fact, skipping discovery.
        A simple decision rule. Use Gherkin when business stakeholders will actually take part in writing or reviewing the examples and the examples are worth keeping as documentation. Otherwise write the same checks as well-named tests over page objects and flows: you keep the architecture and drop the translation layer.

        Hybrid designs

        The styles compose. Robot Framework's guide describes exactly this division: workflow tests can be written in keyword-driven or behaviour-driven style, and data-driven style is used to run the same workflow with varying data. It also lets you drop the Given/When/Then/And/But prefixes when implementing keywords, so the same keyword can be used with different prefixes (Then welcome page should be open, and welcome page should be open).

        *** Test Cases ***
Valid Login                                 # workflow, BDD style, built from keywords
    Given login page is open
    When valid username and password are inserted
    and credentials are submitted
    Then welcome page should be open

Invalid Logins                              # same workflow, data-driven rows
    [Template]    Login with invalid credentials should fail
    invalid          ${VALID PASSWORD}
    ${VALID USER}    invalid
    ${EMPTY}         ${EMPTY}
        NeedReach for
        Same check over many inputsData-driven table (parameters, Test Template, Scenario Outline)
        Reusable vocabulary for a mixed-skill teamKeyword-driven (Robot Framework or a keyword library on top of page objects)
        Shared understanding with the business, living documentationBDD with discovery sessions, then Gherkin
        Developer-only team, fast feedbackPlain tests + page objects + builders

        Key points

        • Data-driven separates logic from data; keep rows named and logic free of conditionals.
        • Keyword-driven builds tests from named actions; value comes from good abstraction, not from the file format.
        • BDD is Discovery, Formulation, Automation; the conversation is the point, the tool is a side-effect.
        • Write declarative Gherkin: 3 to 5 steps, no UI details, outcomes observable from outside.
        • Step definitions should be thin glue to the flow layer; do not duplicate page-object logic.
        • BDD hurts when nobody reads the scenarios; then plain code is cheaper.
        How this maps to Playwright: data-driven tests are plain loops over cases or projects with parameters; keyword-style reuse comes from page objects and test.step (see fixtures); Gherkin is available through third-party packages that sit on top of Playwright (a choice, not a requirement). General guidance is in best practices.

        Which Then step best follows the Gherkin reference's advice?

        B. An outcome should be observable by the user or an external system; checking database rows (A) or UI mechanics (C) couples the specification to implementation.

        A team writes Gherkin files alone after development finishes, and no product owner ever reads them. Which statement fits the Cucumber documentation?

        B. The docs say there is much more to BDD than Cucumber and that discovery is the place to start; without it, the extra layer is mostly overhead.

        What are the three BDD practices?
        Discovery, Formulation, Automation.
        Given / When / Then?
        Context (known state), event or action, expected observable outcome.
        What does a Robot Framework Test Template do?
        Turns a keyword-driven test into a data-driven one: rows supply arguments to one template keyword, and all rows run.
        Declarative vs imperative scenario?
        Declarative states behaviour and intent; imperative lists UI steps. Prefer declarative.
        When should you skip Gherkin?
        When nobody from the business will write or review the examples; use plain tests over page objects.

        📚 Sources

        • Behaviour-Driven Development – Cucumber: BDD as collaboration; Discovery, Formulation, Automation
        • Gherkin Reference – Cucumber: keywords, Rule, Background, Scenario Outline, guidance on step count and observable outcomes
        • Robot Framework User Guide – Robot Framework Foundation: keyword-driven, data-driven (test templates) and behaviour-driven styles
        • Page Object – Martin Fowler: layering a testing DSL over page objects
        • Test Smells – Gerard Meszaros: Conditional Test Logic, Obscure Test
        • Screenplay Pattern – Serenity/JS: how Cucumber step definitions can delegate to reusable tasks

        Reporting, Observability and Debugging of Test Runs

        An automated test that fails but cannot explain why has moved the work from the machine to a human, who must now reproduce the problem by hand. Good reporting turns every failure into a short investigation: what happened, where, with what data, in which environment, and whose problem is it. This section covers the evidence a run should collect, how reports like Allure organise it, a triage workflow, and the naming and retention rules that keep it useful.

        Why reporting is part of the framework, not an extra

        Think of the flight recorder in an aircraft. Nobody expects to use it, but when something goes wrong it decides whether the cause is found in an hour or never. The same goes for CI: the run may happen at 3 a.m. on a machine nobody can log into, and the only thing you will have in the morning is the artifacts it left behind.

        The Allure documentation expresses the goal precisely: when investigating an unexpected failure, it is convenient to not just read the list of completed steps but to see the same data the test saw; a screenshot just before failure often answers "is the page loaded", "is the form filled correctly" and "is an unexpected popup in the way?" at a glance. The aim of everything below is to reduce the time from "red build" to "root cause".

        The evidence a run can collect

        EvidenceAnswers the questionCostTypical capture policy
        Step log / structured stepsWhat did the test do, in what order, and which step failed or was slow?Very lowAlways
        Error message + stackWhat exactly failed (expected vs actual)?FreeAlways
        ScreenshotWhat did the page look like at the moment of failure?LowOn failure (optionally every step)
        VideoWhat happened between steps, including animations, redirects, popups?Medium (disk, CPU)On failure or first retry
        Trace (action timeline with DOM snapshots, network, console)What was the page state before and after each action? Which request failed?MediumOn first retry, or on failure
        Console captureDid the page throw JavaScript errors or warnings?LowOn failure
        Network capture / HARWhich API calls were made, with what status and payload?Medium to high; may contain secretsOn failure; scrub before sharing
        DOM / page source dumpWhat did the markup look like (for locator problems)?LowOn failure
        Application logs / correlation idWhat did the server do for this request?Depends on infrastructureLink by id; attach excerpt
        Environment infoWhich build, browser, OS, URL, flags, user?FreeAlways, once per run
        Traces are the new default for UI tests. Playwright's trace viewer lets you go back and forward through each action and see a DOM snapshot you can interact with, plus log, source, network, errors and console for each step. Its starter configuration records a trace on-first-retry, with retries set to 2 on CI and 0 locally, so the cost is paid only when something has already failed.

        Capture on failure: three tools

        export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  reporter: [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['junit', { outputFile: 'results/junit.xml' }]],
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',        // DOM snapshots + network + console for the retry
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',     // keep videos only for failed tests
  },
});
        @Test
void checkoutShowsReceipt() {
  Allure.step("Sign in as customer", () -> shop.flows().signIn(customer));
  try {
    Allure.step("Pay by card", () -> shop.flows().payByCard(order));
  } catch (Throwable t) {
    // post-failure hook: attach what the test saw (Allure Java 2.x name)
    byte[] png = ((TakesScreenshot) driver).getScreenshotAs(OutputType.BYTES);
    Allure.addAttachment("Screenshot at failure", "image/png", new ByteArrayInputStream(png), "png");
    throw t;                       // never swallow the failure
  }
}
        import allure, pytest

@pytest.hookimpl(hookwrapper=True)
def pytest_runtest_makereport(item, call):
    outcome = yield
    report = outcome.get_result()
    driver = item.funcargs.get("driver")
    if report.when == "call" and report.failed and driver:
        allure.attach(driver.get_screenshot_as_png(),
                      name="screenshot at failure",
                      attachment_type=allure.attachment_type.PNG)
        allure.attach(driver.page_source, name="DOM",
                      attachment_type=allure.attachment_type.HTML)

        Allure's own guidance adds a refinement: taking a screenshot when you detect a failure is the common approach, but if you do not mind the disk use, a screenshot on every step helps in long scenarios, and sometimes a video is even more informative.

        Anatomy of an Allure-style report

        Allure Report is framework-agnostic: an integration for your test framework writes result files into a results folder (allure-results by default), the command-line tool turns them into a static HTML report, and you can enrich results with environment data, CI links, history and custom categories. Several ideas in it are useful whatever tool you use:

        • Steps. Structured logging: each step is an interval with its own status and duration and can nest, so you can find the block that started but did not finish, or took too long. Steps double as documentation of what the test does. They work best when named in business language ("Create a customer"), which is also why flow layers and Screenplay tasks map to them neatly.
        • Attachments. Screenshots, logs, HTML dumps and visual diffs (expected, actual and diff images) are attached to the test or to a step.
        • Statuses. Passed, Failed, Skipped, Broken, Unknown. The Failed/Broken split is a triage hint: failed means the test ran validly and an assertion was false (likely a product problem), while broken means the test could not check the behaviour, for example because of an exception unrelated to the assertion or a missing configuration file (likely a test or environment problem). Integrations decide the boundary differently, so treat it as a clue, not a verdict.
        • Categories. Failures are grouped by status and message: Product errors (failed tests) and Test errors (broken tests) by default, plus custom rules that match message or trace text. Grouping by category answers "how many tests did this one problem break?".
        • History, retries and stability marks. The report can compare with earlier runs and mark tests as flaky, retried, newly failed (regressed), newly passed or newly broken.
        • Environments and timeline. Results are grouped by browser or OS or deployment; a timeline shows parallelisation and slow tests.
        • Quality gate. Rules can fail a run when a standard is violated, for example too many failures in critical tests.
        // Allure Report 3: a custom category groups failures by cause (simplified)
export default defineConfig({
  historyPath: "./history.jsonl",       // needed for flaky and status-transition detection
  categories: { rules: [{
    name: "Timeouts waiting for elements",
    matchers: { statuses: ["failed", "broken"], message: /Timeout .* exceeded/ },
  }]},
});
        Identity matters. For History and Retries to work, Allure identifies "the same test" across runs using the test case id or its fully qualified name plus parameters (and environment in Allure 3). Renaming a test or generating parameters that change every run (random values, timestamps) breaks the history. This is a strong argument for stable, deliberate test names.

        Failure triage workflow

        Triage means deciding quickly what kind of failure this is, because each kind has a different owner and a different fix. A repeatable workflow prevents two bad habits: re-running until green, and blaming "flakiness" for everything.

        Read the messageExpected vs actual, failing step, timeout or assertion?
        Look at the evidenceScreenshot, trace, console, network at the failing step.
        Check historyNew failure or old? Flaky mark? Failed in other environments?
        ClassifyProduct bug, test bug, data, environment, or genuinely flaky.
        Act and recordFile a defect, fix the test, repair the environment, or quarantine with a ticket.
        ClassTypical signalsOwnerAction
        Product defectAssertion fails consistently; the screenshot shows wrong behaviour; a 500 in the network log; same failure across browsersDevelopmentFile a bug with the attached trace; link the test
        Test defectLocator not found after a UI change; broken status; fails everywhereAutomationUpdate locator or flow; add a missing wait condition
        Data problemPasses after a reset; "user already exists"; 404 for a recordAutomation / data ownerMake setup create its own unique data
        Environment problemMany unrelated tests fail at once; timeouts everywhere; 503s; one machine onlyOps / platformCheck service health first; rerun after fix
        Flaky testAlternating pass/fail on the same code; retry passes; timing-relatedAutomationFind the race (see synchronisation); quarantine with deadline

        Allure's stability analysis gives a concrete definition of "flaky": in Allure 3 a test is marked when its status keeps changing back and forth across recent runs, and a single failure after a series of passes, or a single recovery, is not enough. In Allure's words, unstable tests cause "alarm fatigue" and time spent chasing non-existing bugs.

        Retries are a diagnostic, not a cure. Automatic retries keep a pipeline green, but they hide the information that a test is unstable. Record and report the retried-then-passed tests (Allure marks them "changed on retry"), and track their number over time. Meszaros warns that removing an erratic test to "keep the bar green" creates a lost test, and that leaving a known failure in the suite can hide other problems because a second failure is much harder to notice than a green-to-red change.

        Making failures actionable

        ❌ Unhelpful
        AssertionError: expected true to be false
  at CheckoutTest.test (CheckoutTest.java:57)

        No idea what was checked, with which data, on which page, or what the page showed.

        ✅ Actionable
        Order total mismatch for order ORD-r481-w3-17 (customer ann+r481@test.io)
  expected: $29.99
  actual:   $39.99   (shipping added?)
  step:     Pay by card  >  Confirm
  url:      https://staging.shop.test/checkout/confirm   build: 2b9f1c7
  attached: screenshot, trace.zip, network.har, server correlation id c-91ab

        Says what, with which data, where, and where to look next.

        Practical rules for good failure output:

        • One reason to fail. Meszaros's Assertion Roulette smell: when a test has many assertions it is hard to tell which one failed. Keep tests focused or give assertions messages.
        • Show expected versus actual. Use matchers that print both. Allure can render a diff view for assertion failures and an image diff for visual comparisons.
        • Include context in the failure: test data ids, URL, build or commit, browser, flags. Add them as report labels or in the message, never rely on someone guessing.
        • Correlate with the back end. Pass a correlation or request id header from the test and print it on failure, so developers can find the server logs for exactly that request (general observability practice).
        • Keep screenshots and traces tied to steps. An artifact belongs next to the step that produced it.
        • Fail fast with a clear cause for setup problems (missing environment variable, unreachable URL) instead of 200 identical timeouts.

        Naming and tagging

        Test names are what people read in dashboards and what tools use as identity. Name tests for the behaviour: customer can pay by card beats test_checkout_03, and Allure's history depends on the name being stable. Tags and labels turn a flat list into slices you can filter, schedule and report on:

        Label / tagExample valuesUsed for
        Feature / epiccheckout, accountGrouping failures by product area; Allure categories can group by label
        Severity / prioritycritical, normal, minorQuality gates; deciding what blocks a release
        Layerui, api, componentSeeing where failures cluster
        Owner / teamteam-paymentsRouting a failure to the right people
        Suite@smoke, @regression, @nightlyChoosing what runs in each pipeline stage
        Status flags@quarantine, @flaky-TICKET-123, @needs-flag-XVisible exceptions with a ticket and an end date
        Keep tag vocabularies small and documented. Twenty tags nobody remembers are worse than five that everyone uses. Treat the list like code: review changes, remove dead tags.

        Artifact retention and hygiene

        • Keep evidence for failures longer than for passes. A sensible pattern (illustrative, adjust to your storage budget): all results summary for 90 days, failing-test artifacts for 14 to 30 days, nothing but the status for passing tests, and the last N full reports per branch.
        • Mind the size. Videos and traces can be large; record on failure or first retry, not for every passing test.
        • Scrub secrets and personal data. HAR files, traces and logs can contain cookies, authorization headers, tokens and personal data. Treat artifacts as sensitive, restrict access, and redact before sharing outside the team.
        • Make artifacts reachable. Publish the report to a URL linked from the CI job and from failure notifications; a zip buried in a build agent is rarely opened.
        • Preserve history deliberately. If you want flaky detection and trend charts, persist the history file between runs; Allure notes that cleaning the results directory affects retry data.
        • Report suite health, not only counts. Track flaky rate, retry count, duration and mean time to triage; they show whether the suite is trusted.

        Key points

        • Collect evidence automatically: steps, error, screenshot, trace, console, network, environment.
        • Pay for heavy artifacts (video, trace) only on failure or first retry.
        • Structured steps with business names turn logs into readable documentation and show where time is spent.
        • Triage by class (product, test, data, environment, flaky) and route to an owner; Failed vs Broken is a clue.
        • Retries are diagnostic: report them; do not let them hide instability.
        • Stable names, small tag vocabularies and scrubbed, time-limited artifacts keep reporting trustworthy.
        How this maps to Playwright: start with trace viewer and reporters (HTML, JUnit, and third-party Allure), enable retries with trace on first retry, run in CI and upload the report as an artifact, and use sharding with merged reports for large suites. Log in-test context with test.step and attachments.

        A suite has retries set to 2. A test fails, passes on retry and the build is green. What is the best practice?

        B. Retries stabilise the pipeline but hide instability. Reporting tools such as Allure mark tests that changed status on retry so they can be investigated; deleting the test creates a lost test.

        In an Allure report, a test shows status Broken rather than Failed. What does that most likely indicate?

        B. Allure uses Broken for test defects (an exception unrelated to normal assertion failures), with the caveat that integrations draw the line differently.

        When should a trace or video be recorded?
        On failure or first retry, to limit cost while keeping evidence for the runs that matter.
        What are Allure steps?
        Nestable, timed, status-bearing blocks of a test: structured logging that also documents what the test does.
        Failed vs Broken?
        Failed: a valid test with a false assertion. Broken: the test could not do its check (test or environment defect).
        Why are retries only a diagnostic?
        They mask instability; report retried-then-passed tests and watch the trend.
        What risk do HAR files and traces carry?
        They may contain cookies, tokens and personal data; scrub and restrict access.

        Automation Protocols: How Code Drives a Browser

        Every browser-automation tool, however friendly its API, is really just sending messages to a browser over some wire protocol. Knowing the three protocols that matter – classic WebDriver, the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) and WebDriver BiDi – explains why tools behave the way they do, why some features exist only in some tools, and why the industry is converging on BiDi.

        The 60-second analogy

        Think of a browser as a car and your test as a driver who is not sitting inside it. You need a way to give orders from outside. Classic WebDriver is a walkie-talkie with strict turns: you say “turn left”, you wait for “done”, only then can you say the next thing. CDP is a direct line into the engine room: powerful, chatty, and the car maker may rearrange the pipes at any time. WebDriver BiDi is the standardised version of that chatty line: both sides can talk at any moment, and all car makers agreed on the wording.

        Test codeYour script or test runner
        Client libraryLanguage binding that builds messages
        Wire protocolHTTP+JSON or WebSocket+JSON
        Driver / browser endpointChromeDriver, geckodriver, or the browser itself
        Browser engineRenders the page, runs JS

        1. Classic WebDriver (W3C, HTTP + JSON)

        The W3C WebDriver specification defines a protocol between a local end and a remote end. The remote end is, in the spec's own words, an HTTP server reading requests and writing responses. Every command is one HTTP request with a JSON body, and every answer is one HTTP response with a JSON value.

        The spec distinguishes two kinds of remote node. An endpoint node is the final server (in practice a browser driver). An intermediary node is a proxy that looks like a remote end to the client but forwards commands upstream – this is exactly what a Selenium Grid or a cloud provider is. The spec requires that all node types be black-box indistinguishable to the client, which is why the same test can run locally or on a grid by changing one URL.

        Driver binaries

        Browsers do not natively speak classic WebDriver over HTTP, so each vendor ships a small executable that translates: ChromeDriver for Chrome, geckodriver for Firefox, Edge Driver, SafariDriver and so on (WebdriverIO's protocol page lists these). The driver runs on the same machine as the browser, which may or may not be the machine running your tests (Selenium documentation, “Selenium components”).

        Sessions and capabilities

        Nothing works until you create a session with POST /session. In the request you describe what you want using capabilities; the server answers with the capabilities it actually granted plus a sessionId. Every later URL contains that id.

        Standard capabilityMeaning
        browserName, browserVersion, platformNameWhich browser, version and OS you need
        acceptInsecureCertsWhether invalid TLS certificates are tolerated
        pageLoadStrategyWhen navigation counts as finished (normal, eager, none)
        timeoutsScript, page-load and implicit-wait timeouts
        unhandledPromptBehaviorWhat to do with an unexpected alert (default: dismiss and notify)
        proxy, setWindowRect, strictFileInteractabilityNetwork proxy, window resizing support, strictness for file inputs
        webSocketUrlOpt in to BiDi (see below)

        Vendors add their own keys with a prefix ending in a colon – the spec's example is moz:experimental-webdriver, and Appium uses appium:. Capabilities can be given as alwaysMatch (all must be satisfied) and firstMatch (a list of alternatives; first workable one wins). Capabilities are fixed for the life of the session.

        A minimal raw example

        This is what Selenium, Appium and WebdriverIO do under the hood. You can reproduce it with curl against a running ChromeDriver (default port 9515) or a Selenium server.

        # 1. Create a session
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9515/session \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"capabilities":{"alwaysMatch":{"browserName":"chrome","pageLoadStrategy":"normal"}}}'
# => {"value":{"sessionId":"a1b2c3","capabilities":{"browserName":"chrome", ...}}}

# 2. Navigate
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9515/session/a1b2c3/url \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://example.com"}'
# => {"value":null}

# 3. Find an element (note: one round trip)
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9515/session/a1b2c3/element \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"using":"css selector","value":"a"}'
# => {"value":{"element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf":"node-42"}}

# 4. Click it, then read the title, then end the session
curl -s -X POST   http://localhost:9515/session/a1b2c3/element/node-42/click -d '{}'
curl -s           http://localhost:9515/session/a1b2c3/title
curl -s -X DELETE http://localhost:9515/session/a1b2c3

        Two details are worth noticing. First, an element is not the DOM node itself but a small JSON reference keyed by a constant string defined in the spec (element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf). Second, if that node later leaves the DOM, using the reference returns the spec's stale element reference error (HTTP 404) – the origin of the famous “StaleElementReferenceException” in Selenium.

        Client builds requestPOST /session/{id}/element + JSON body
        Driver receivesValidates session id, parses JSON
        Driver talks to browserVendor-specific internal channel
        Driver replies200 + {"value": ...} or 4xx/5xx + {"value":{"error":...}}
        Client unblocksOnly now can the next command be sent

        2. Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)

        CDP is the protocol Chrome's own DevTools uses. The official site describes it as a JSON-based protocol connecting debug and automation targets (pages, workers) with trusted clients, divided into domains – Page, DOM, Network, Fetch, Runtime, Tracing and many more. Each domain has commands (you call them) and events (the browser pushes them to you). It is carried over a persistent WebSocket, so there is no per-command connection set-up.

        // client -> browser (a command: has an id)
{ "id": 1, "method": "Page.navigate", "params": { "url": "https://example.com" } }

// browser -> client (the reply: same id)
{ "id": 1, "result": { "frameId": "F1", "loaderId": "L7" } }

// browser -> client (an event: no id, pushed whenever it happens)
{ "method": "Network.requestWillBeSent",
  "params": { "requestId": "R1", "request": { "url": "https://example.com/", "method": "GET" } } }

// turning on request interception (Fetch domain)
{ "id": 2, "method": "Fetch.enable", "params": { "patterns": [{ "urlPattern": "*/api/*" }] } }
// ...then events Fetch.requestPaused arrive; you answer with Fetch.fulfillRequest / continueRequest / failRequest

        Because events stream in at any time, CDP lets a tool observe console output, network traffic, exceptions, performance traces and coverage without polling. The price is stability: the CDP site states plainly that CDP is not a public or supported API for third parties, that it gives no backwards-compatibility guarantee, and that third-party tools should go through supported products such as Puppeteer or ChromeDriver. It is also, by name, a Chromium protocol – Firefox and Safari do not implement it the same way.

        Connectws://host:9222/devtools/page/<id>
        Enable a domain{"method":"Network.enable"}
        Send a commandPage.navigate with id=1
        Events stream inrequestWillBeSent, responseReceived, loadEventFired…
        Reply arrives{"id":1,"result":...} matched by id

        3. WebDriver BiDi (bidirectional, standardised)

        The W3C WebDriver BiDi specification extends WebDriver “by introducing bidirectional communication”: instead of strict command/response, events can stream from the browser to the controller. It is carried over a WebSocket and uses three message shapes – a command (id, method, params), a response (type: "success" or "error"), and an event (type: "event"). The Selenium documentation calls it the cross-browser replacement for CDP and says it was created together with the browser vendors.

        Commands are grouped in modules. The spec defines, among others: session, browsingContext (navigate, create tabs, screenshots, print), network (intercepts, extra headers, cache behaviour), script (evaluate, call functions, preload scripts), log, input, storage (cookies), emulation (geolocation, locale, timezone, user agent) and browser.

        // 1. opt in when creating the classic session:  capabilities: { "webSocketUrl": true }
//    the reply then contains a ws:// URL to connect to.

// 2. subscribe to events
{ "id": 1, "method": "session.subscribe",
  "params": { "events": ["log.entryAdded", "network.beforeRequestSent"] } }

// 3. navigate and wait for the load
{ "id": 2, "method": "browsingContext.navigate",
  "params": { "context": "ctx-1", "url": "https://example.com", "wait": "complete" } }

// 4. intercept requests before they leave the browser
{ "id": 3, "method": "network.addIntercept",
  "params": { "phases": ["beforeRequestSent"], "urlPatterns": [{ "type": "string", "pattern": "https://example.com/api/x" }] } }

// events arrive without being asked for:
{ "type": "event", "method": "log.entryAdded",
  "params": { "level": "error", "text": "Uncaught TypeError ...", "type": "javascript" } }

        Notice the design choice: BiDi keeps WebDriver's user-centric commands (navigate, click via input.performActions) and adds the introspection features that previously required CDP. Selenium enables it with the webSocketUrl capability; Appium supports it as opt-in with the same capability; WebdriverIO starts local sessions over BiDi by default; Puppeteer can drive Chrome or Firefox over either CDP or BiDi.

        Classic sessionPOST /session with webSocketUrl:true
        Open WebSocketURL returned in the capabilities
        session.subscribeChoose events: log, network, context…
        Drive + listenCommands and events interleave freely
        session.end / closeSocket and session end

        The same feature through each layer

        “Fail the test if the page logs a JavaScript error” is a good probe because it needs a pushed event. Here is how it looks at three levels of abstraction (the exact method names vary by version – treat these as illustrations of the idea).

        // You manage the socket, enable domains, and match events yourself
ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id: 1, method: 'Runtime.enable' }));
ws.on('message', (raw) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(raw);
  if (msg.method === 'Runtime.exceptionThrown') {
    throw new Error(msg.params.exceptionDetails.text);
  }
});
        // The library wraps the protocol (CDP or BiDi) into a friendly event
page.on('pageerror', (err) => { throw err; });
await page.goto('https://example.com');
        // Same idea; the runner reports it as a test failure with a trace attached
const errors: Error[] = [];
page.on('pageerror', (e) => errors.push(e));
await page.goto('https://example.com');
expect(errors).toEqual([]);

        The lesson: the higher the layer, the less you see of the protocol – but every layer is still doing the same three things: open a channel, subscribe to an event, react to a message.

        What each protocol enables, at a glance

        • Network interception – CDP: Fetch.enable + Fetch.requestPaused. BiDi: network.addIntercept with phases beforeRequestSent, responseStarted and authRequired, then continueRequest, provideResponse or failRequest. Classic: not possible, so older Selenium suites used a separate proxy such as BrowserMob.
        • Console / log events – CDP Runtime/Log events; BiDi log.entryAdded (levels error, warn, info, debug). Classic: browser-specific log endpoints at best.
        • Script access – Classic: Execute Script (sync/async). BiDi: script.evaluate, script.callFunction, preload scripts that run before page code. CDP: Runtime.evaluate.
        • Tracing and profiling – CDP only (for now): the Tracing and Profiler domains feed performance traces, which is why Lighthouse and DevTools depend on it.
        • Emulation – CDP Emulation domain; BiDi has dedicated emulation.* commands such as geolocation, locale, timezone and user-agent overrides.

        Side-by-side comparison

        AspectClassic WebDriverCDPWebDriver BiDi
        TransportHTTP request per command, JSONWebSocket, JSONWebSocket, JSON
        DirectionClient asks, server answersBoth waysBoth ways
        GovernanceW3C standardChromium project, no compatibility guaranteeW3C standard (in progress; modules still being added)
        BrowsersAll major, via driversChromium familyCross-browser, vendor-committed
        Network interceptionNoYes (Fetch, Network)Yes (network.addIntercept …)
        Console / JS-error eventsNo (poll logs at best)Yes (Runtime, Log)Yes (log.entryAdded)
        Tracing / profilingNoYes (Tracing, Profiler)No dedicated tracing module in the current spec
        Input modelDispatched by the browser as real user inputSynthetic events via Input domainSame user-centric actions as WebDriver
        Typical usersSelenium, Appium, WebdriverIOPuppeteer, Playwright (Chromium), DevToolsSelenium 4+, WebdriverIO, Puppeteer, Appium
        What about Playwright? Playwright is not a thin client of any single protocol above. It ships browser builds and its own client/server layer between your test process and the browsers, so the same API works for Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. The practical consequence is that features like page.route work identically across browsers without waiting for a standard.

        Why modern tools moved

        1. Events beat polling. With strict request/response the only way to learn the page logged an error is to ask repeatedly. A pushed event is both faster and impossible to miss.
        2. Fewer round trips. One persistent WebSocket avoids a fresh HTTP request, header parsing and driver hop for every command. Cypress's docs argue the same point from the other extreme: tools outside the browser execute “remote commands across the network”.
        3. Features users now expect – mocking APIs, asserting there were no console errors, throttling the network, capturing traces – require browser introspection that classic WebDriver never offered.
        4. Standardisation. CDP is powerful but Chromium-only and explicitly unsupported for third parties. BiDi aims to give the same power through a standard every vendor implements; WebdriverIO's docs note that vendors implement and test the W3C protocols against real user-facing browser builds.

        Reconciling the sources: classic WebDriver is not dead – it remains the base for session creation, for Appium's mobile world and for grids – but Selenium's own docs describe its CDP support as temporary until BiDi is implemented, and the BiDi page says it is moving its whole implementation toward BiDi while keeping backwards compatibility. Expect “classic for the session, BiDi for the conversation” for several years.

        Do not build on raw CDP unless you must. Chrome's own documentation says CDP has no backwards-compatibility promise and that direct third-party use is unsupported. If a test suite talks to CDP directly (for example through cdpSession.send helpers), pin the browser version and expect breakage on upgrade. Prefer the tool's high-level API or BiDi.
        Debug at the wire level once. When a command behaves strangely, run the same call with curl (classic) or watch messages in Chrome's Protocol Monitor (CDP). Seeing the actual JSON removes much of the mystery from tool-specific errors.

        Key points

        • Classic WebDriver = HTTP + JSON, one command at a time, via a browser-specific driver executable; sessions and capabilities are negotiated by POST /session.
        • CDP = WebSocket + JSON, organised in domains with commands and events; very powerful but Chromium-only and officially unsupported for third-party direct use.
        • WebDriver BiDi = W3C standard WebSocket protocol combining WebDriver's user-centric commands with event streams (network, log, script); enabled via the webSocketUrl capability.
        • Network interception, console events and tracing need a bidirectional protocol; that is the main reason tools moved away from pure classic WebDriver.
        • Intermediary nodes (grids, cloud vendors) are possible because every node must look like a normal remote end to the client.
        How this maps to Playwright Playwright exposes the same capabilities through high-level APIs: network and mocking replace raw Fetch.requestPaused handling, the trace viewer replaces manual Tracing calls, and browser contexts replace manual target management.

        Which statement best explains why Selenium Grid and cloud vendors can sit between your test and the browser?

        The W3C spec defines intermediary and endpoint nodes; because both must look identical to the local end, a client only has to change the server URL.

        You need to fail a test whenever the page logs a JavaScript error. Which protocol feature makes this natural?

        Pushed events let the controller react the moment the error occurs; classic request/response has no push channel.

        What is an intermediary node in WebDriver?
        A proxy that acts as both local and remote end and forwards commands upstream (e.g. Selenium Grid); it must be indistinguishable from a real remote end.
        Which capability turns on BiDi?
        webSocketUrl: true; the new-session response then contains the WebSocket URL.
        CDP: command vs event?
        A command carries an id and gets a matching reply; an event has no id and is pushed by the browser when something happens.
        Why is raw CDP risky for long-lived test suites?
        It is not a public/supported API and offers no backwards-compatibility guarantee, so browser upgrades can break it.

        📚 Sources

        • WebDriver Level 2 (W3C specification) – W3C Browser Testing and Tools WG: nodes, HTTP processing model, endpoints, capabilities, error codes, element reference
        • WebDriver BiDi (W3C draft) – W3C: message shapes, module list, network.addIntercept, log.entryAdded, session.subscribe
        • Chrome DevTools Protocol – Chrome DevTools team: domains, commands/events, support policy
