        Install the VS Code extension, then click the green triangle next to the test you want to run, or run everything from the testing sidebar. See Getting Started with VS Code.

        GoalCommand / flag
        Run everythingnpx playwright test
        UI Mode--ui
        Show the browser--headed
        Select browser/project--project webkit (repeatable)
        A single file / multiple directories / keywordslanding-page.spec.ts, tests/a/ tests/b/, landing login
        By title-g "add a todo item"
        Only tests that failed last time--last-failed
        Custom last-run file--last-failed-file=<path> or PLAYWRIGHT_LAST_RUN_OUTPUT_FILE
        Debug with the Inspector--debug

        Debugging tests

        Since Playwright runs on Node.js, you can debug with familiar tools: console.log, your IDE, or directly in VS Code with the extension. Playwright offers UI Mode (see each step, logs, errors, network requests, DOM snapshots...) and the Playwright Inspector (step through each API call, view debug logs, explore locators).

        Debugging in UI Mode

        npx playwright test --ui

        While debugging, use the Pick Locator button to select an element and see the locator Playwright would use. You can edit the locator in the locator playground and see the highlight live in the browser. Use the Copy Locator button to copy it and paste it into your test.

        Debugging with the Playwright Inspector

        To debug the entire test run, add the --debug flag:

        npx playwright test --debug

        The command opens a browser window together with the Playwright Inspector. Use the step over button at the top of the Inspector to go step by step, or the play button to run from start to finish. When the test finishes, the browser window closes.

        Debug a single test file:

        npx playwright test example.spec.ts --debug

        Debug a specific test at the line where test(.. is defined — add :line-number after the file name:

        npx playwright test example.spec.ts:10 --debug

        The Inspector also has Pick Locator/Copy Locator as above. See the debugging guide for more on the VS Code debugger, UI Mode, the Inspector and Browser Developer Tools.

        Tip: UI Mode is the recommended debugging option; use --debug when you want to step through each Playwright API call.

        Test reports

        The HTML Reporter gives a full report you can filter by browser, passed, failed, skipped and flaky tests. By default the report opens automatically if any test fails; otherwise, open it with:

        npx playwright show-report

        You can filter and search tests, and click an individual test to see its errors along with the test steps.

        1. npx playwright testQuick run, headless
        2. --headedWhen you want to see the browser
        3. --uiSteps, trace, locator picker
        4. --debugInspector, step over each API call
        5. show-reportView the HTML report

        What's next

        • Generate tests with Codegen
        • View traces
        • Explore all UI Mode features
        • Run your tests on CI with GitHub Actions

        Key takeaways

        • Default: parallel + headless; --headed, --ui, --project change the behavior.
        • Filtering tests: by file, directory, keyword, -g (title), file:line.
        • --last-failed re-runs failed tests; the state is stored in .last-run.json in the outputDir.
        • --debug opens the Inspector; file.spec.ts:10 --debug debugs exactly one test.
        • The HTML report opens automatically on failures; open it manually with show-report.

        How do you re-run only the tests that failed in the previous run?

        --last-failed reads the list from .last-run.json and runs only the failed tests.

        Which command debugs exactly the test defined at line 10 of example.spec.ts?

        Add :line-number after the file name together with --debug to open the Inspector for that test.

        Trace viewer

        Trace Viewer is a GUI tool for exploring recorded traces of your tests: you move forward and backward through each action and see visually what happened — very useful for finding why a test failed on CI.

        Introduction

        You will learn: how to record a trace, how to open the HTML report, and how to open/view a trace.

        Recording a trace

        By default, playwright.config contains the configuration needed to create a trace.zip file for your tests. Trace is set to on-first-retry, meaning it is only recorded on the first retry of a failed test. Also, retries is 2 when running on CI and 0 when running locally. So a trace is recorded on the first retry of a failed test, but not on the first run and not on the second retry either.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0, // set to 2 when running on CI
  // ...
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry', // record traces on first retry of each test
  },
});

        See the full list of trace recording options in the detailed Trace Viewer guide.

        Traces are normally run in a CI environment because locally you already have UI Mode for development and debugging. However, if you want to record traces locally without UI Mode, force them on with --trace on:

        npx playwright test --trace on
        ScenarioValueResult
        Default configurationtrace: 'on-first-retry'Records a trace on the first retry of a failed test
        CIretries: 2Retries happen, so a trace exists
        Localretries: 0No retries, so by default there is no trace
        Force on locally--trace onRecords a trace for every test
        Common mistake: running locally with retries: 0 and wondering why there is no trace — by default a trace is only recorded on the first retry. Use --trace on or UI Mode.

        Opening the HTML report

        The HTML report shows a report of all the tests that ran, on which browser, and how long they took. You can filter by passed, failed, flaky or skipped, and search by name. Click a test to open its details: errors, test steps and the trace.

        npx playwright show-report

        Opening the trace

        In the HTML report, click the trace icon next to the test file name to open that test's trace directly. Alternatively, open the test's detail page, scroll down to the 'Traces' tab and click the trace screenshot.

        Learn more about reporters, including the HTML Reporter.

        Viewing the trace

        View the trace by clicking through each action or by hovering over the timeline to see the page state before and after the action. You can inspect the log, source, network, errors and console at each step. The trace viewer creates a DOM snapshot so you can fully interact with it and open the browser DevTools to inspect HTML, CSS...

        • Actions + timeline: navigate through each step.
        • Before / After: the page state before and after an action.
        • Log, Source, Network, Errors, Console: detailed information for each step.
        • DOM snapshot: interact with it and open DevTools.
        1. Test fails on CIretries: 2
        2. First retryon-first-retry trace is recorded
        3. show-reportOpen the HTML report
        4. Click the trace iconOr the Traces tab on the detail page
        5. Inspect each actionLog, network, console, DOM snapshot

        What's next

        • Run your tests on CI with GitHub Actions
        • Learn more about Trace Viewer

        Key takeaways

        • Default is trace: 'on-first-retry'; CI retries: 2, local 0.
        • Force it on locally: npx playwright test --trace on.
        • Open a trace from the icon in the HTML report or the Traces tab of the detail page.
        • A trace has a timeline, before/after, log, source, network, errors, console and an interactive DOM snapshot.

        With the default configuration, when is a trace recorded?

        on-first-retry records a trace on the first retry of a failed test — not on the first run and not on the second retry.

        What do you do to record a trace when running locally without UI Mode?

        --trace on forces tracing on for every test.

        Setting up CI

        Playwright tests can run on any CI provider. This page shows one way to run tests on GitHub using GitHub Actions: the workflow, viewing logs, downloading the HTML report, viewing traces and publishing the report to the web.

        Introduction

        You will learn: setting up GitHub Actions, viewing test logs, viewing the HTML report, viewing traces, and publishing the report to the web. To configure other CI providers, see the detailed Continuous Integration documentation.

        Setting up GitHub Actions

        When you install Playwright using the VS Code extension or npm init playwright@latest, you are asked whether to add a GitHub Actions workflow. It creates a playwright.yml file in the .github/workflows folder, containing everything needed to run tests on every push and pull request to the main/master branch. The file looks like this:

        name: Playwright Tests
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
      with:
        node-version: lts/*
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    - name: Install Playwright Browsers
      run: npx playwright install --with-deps
    - name: Run Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
      with:
        name: playwright-report
        path: playwright-report/
        retention-days: 30

        The workflow performs these steps:

        1. Clone the repository
        2. Install Node.js
        3. Install NPM dependencies
        4. Install Playwright Browsers
        5. Run Playwright tests
        6. Upload the HTML report to the GitHub UI
        1. checkoutClone the repo
        2. setup-nodeNode lts/*
        3. npm ciInstall dependencies
        4. playwright install --with-depsDownload browsers + system libraries
        5. playwright testRun the tests
        6. upload-artifactPush playwright-report/ (if !cancelled())

        Workflow timeout

        This workflow does not set timeout-minutes at the job level. Instead, set globalTimeout in the config:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Fail the run after an hour, so that the reporters still produce a report.
  globalTimeout: 60 * 60 * 1000,
});
        Why use globalTimeout? When the run fails because time ran out, the reporters still have time to generate the report; whereas if GitHub cancels the job through timeout-minutes, you may lose the report.

        Learn more: Understanding GitHub Actions.

        Create a repo and push to GitHub

        Once you have the workflow, you just need to create a repository on GitHub or push your code to an existing one. Follow GitHub's instructions and don't forget to initialize a git repository with git init so you can add, commit and push your code.

        Opening Workflows

        Click the Actions tab to see the workflows; there you can see whether tests passed or failed. For a Pull Request, you can also click the Details link in the PR status check.

        Viewing test logs

        Click a workflow run to see every action GitHub performed; click Run Playwright tests to see the error message, the expected and received values, and the call log.

        HTML Report

        The HTML Report gives a full report of your tests; filter by browser, passed, failed, skipped and flaky.

        Downloading the HTML Report

        In the Artifacts section, click playwright-report to download the report as a zip file.

        Viewing the HTML Report

        Opening the report directly from a local file will not work properly because it needs a web server. First, unzip it (preferably into a folder where Playwright is installed). On the command line, change into the folder containing the report and use npx playwright show-report with the name of the extracted folder; the command serves the report for viewing in the browser.

        npx playwright show-report name-of-my-extracted-playwright-report

        See more about the HTML Reporter.

        Viewing the trace

        Once the report is being served with npx playwright show-report, click the trace icon next to the test's file name. You can view the trace and inspect each action to find out why the test failed. See again the Trace Viewer.

        Publishing the report to the web

        Downloading the HTML report as a zip is inconvenient. You can use Azure Storage's static website hosting feature to serve the HTML report on the Internet with minimal configuration.

        1. Create an Azure Storage account.
        2. Enable Static website hosting for the storage account.
        3. Create a Service Principal in Azure and grant it access to Azure Blob storage. When it succeeds, the command prints the credentials used in the next step. 
          az ad sp create-for-rbac --name "github-actions" --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" --scopes /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/resourceGroups/<RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME>/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/<STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME>
        4. Use the credentials from the previous step to create encrypted secrets in the GitHub repository (Settings, GitHub Actions secrets section) with these secrets:
          • AZCOPY_SPA_APPLICATION_ID
          • AZCOPY_SPA_CLIENT_SECRET
          • AZCOPY_TENANT_ID
        5. Add a step that uploads the HTML report to Azure Storage: 
          ...
    - name: Upload HTML report to Azure
      shell: bash
      run: |
        REPORT_DIR='run-${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}'
        azcopy cp --recursive "./playwright-report/*" "https://<STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME>.blob.core.windows.net/\$web/$REPORT_DIR"
        echo "::notice title=HTML report url::https://<STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME>.z1.web.core.windows.net/$REPORT_DIR/index.html"
      env:
        AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE: SPN
        AZCOPY_SPA_APPLICATION_ID: '${{ secrets.AZCOPY_SPA_APPLICATION_ID }}'
        AZCOPY_SPA_CLIENT_SECRET: '${{ secrets.AZCOPY_SPA_CLIENT_SECRET }}'
        AZCOPY_TENANT_ID: '${{ secrets.AZCOPY_TENANT_ID }}'

        The contents of the $web container can be accessed from a browser through the website's public URL.

        Note: this step does not work for pull requests created from a forked repository because those workflows do not have access to secrets.

        Handling Secrets with care

        Artifacts such as trace files, the HTML report or even console logs contain information about the test run. They may contain sensitive data such as test user credentials, access tokens for a staging backend, test source code, and sometimes even application source code. Treat these files with the same care as that sensitive data.

        If you upload reports and traces in a CI workflow, only upload them to a trusted artifact store, or encrypt the files before uploading. Likewise, when sharing artifacts with teammates, use a trusted file-sharing location or encrypt them first.

        What's next

        • How to use Locators
        • How to perform Actions
        • How to write Assertions
        • Learn more about Trace Viewer
        • More ways to run tests on GitHub Actions
        • Run tests on other CI providers

        Key takeaways

        • Default workflow: checkout, setup-node, npm ci, playwright install --with-deps, playwright test, upload artifact.
        • if: ${{ !cancelled() }} ensures the report is still uploaded when tests fail.
        • Use globalTimeout instead of timeout-minutes so the reporters can still produce a report.
        • A downloaded report must be served with npx playwright show-report <folder>, not opened directly as a file.
        • Reports/traces/logs can contain sensitive data: only upload them to a trusted location or encrypt them.

        Why set globalTimeout in the config instead of the job's timeout-minutes?

        When the run fails because of globalTimeout, the reporters still run and create a report; a job that is hard-cancelled may lose the report.

        How do you view an HTML report downloaded from an artifact?

        The report needs a web server to work properly; show-report serves the extracted folder.

        Playwright Test Agents

        Playwright ships with three agents: planner, generator and healer. Use them independently, in sequence or in a loop so AI can explore your app, generate tests and automatically fix failing tests.

        Introduction

        Playwright comes with three Playwright Test Agents: 🎭 planner, 🎭 generator and 🎭 healer. They can be used independently, in sequence, or as chained calls in an agentic loop. Used in sequence, they produce test coverage for your product.

        AgentRoleOutput
        🎭 plannerExplores the app and produces a Markdown test planspecs/*.md
        🎭 generatorTurns the Markdown plan into Playwright Test filestests/*.spec.ts
        🎭 healerRuns the test suite and automatically fixes failing testsPassing (or skipped) tests
        1. PlannerExplores the app, writes specs/*.md
        2. GeneratorGenerates tests/*.spec.ts, verifies selectors live
        3. Run testsDetects failing tests
        4. HealerReplays, inspects the UI, patches, re-runs
        5. Pass or skipGuardrails stop the loop

        Getting started

        Add the agent definitions to your project with the init-agents command. These definitions should be regenerated whenever you update Playwright to pick up new tools and instructions.

        npx playwright init-agents --loop=vscode
        npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude
        npx playwright init-agents --loop=codex
        npx playwright init-agents --loop=opencode
        VS Code: requires VS Code v1.105 (released 9 Oct 2025) or later for the agentic experience to work properly.

        Once the agents are generated, use your preferred AI tool to instruct them to build Playwright Tests.

        🎭 Planner

        The planner explores the app and produces a test plan for one or more scenarios and user flows.

        Input

        • A clear request sent to the planner (for example: "Generate a plan for guest checkout.").
        • A seed test that sets up the environment needed to interact with the app.
        • (optional) A Product Requirement Document (PRD) for context.

        Prompt

        Note: seed.spec.ts is included in the planner's context. The planner runs this test to perform any initialization your tests need, including global setup, project dependencies and any required fixtures and hooks. The planner also uses the seed test as an example for all generated tests. Alternatively, you can mention the file name in the prompt.

        import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('seed', async ({ page }) => {
  // this test uses custom fixtures from ./fixtures
});

        Output

        • A Markdown test plan saved at specs/basic-operations.md.
        • The plan is readable by humans, yet precise enough to generate tests from.
        Example: specs/basic-operations.md 
        # TodoMVC Application - Basic Operations Test Plan

## Application Overview

The TodoMVC application is a React-based todo list manager that demonstrates standard todo application functionality. The application provides comprehensive task management capabilities with a clean, intuitive interface. Key features include:

- **Task Management**: Add, edit, complete, and delete individual todos
- **Bulk Operations**: Mark all todos as complete/incomplete and clear all completed todos
- **Filtering System**: View todos by All, Active, or Completed status with URL routing support
- **Real-time Counter**: Display of active (incomplete) todo count
- **Interactive UI**: Hover states, edit-in-place functionality, and responsive design
- **State Persistence**: Maintains state during session navigation

## Test Scenarios

### 1. Adding New Todos

**Seed:** `tests/seed.spec.ts`

#### 1.1 Add Valid Todo

**Steps:**
1. Click in the "What needs to be done?" input field
2. Type "Buy groceries"
3. Press Enter key

**Expected Results:**
- Todo appears in the list with unchecked checkbox
- Counter shows "1 item left"
- Input field is cleared and ready for next entry
- Todo list controls become visible (Mark all as complete checkbox)

#### 1.2 Add Multiple Todos
...

        🎭 Generator

        The generator uses the Markdown plan to create runnable Playwright Tests. It verifies selectors and assertions live while executing the scenarios. Playwright supports generation hints and has a catalog of assertions for effectively checking structure and behavior.

        Input

        • The Markdown plan in specs/.

        Prompt

        Note: basic-operations.md is included in the generator's context — that is how the generator knows where to get the test plan. Alternatively, you can mention the file name in the prompt.

        Output

        • A test suite in tests/.
        • Generated tests may have initial errors; the healer agent can fix them automatically.
        Example: tests/add-valid-todo.spec.ts 
        // spec: specs/basic-operations.md
// seed: tests/seed.spec.ts

import { test, expect } from '../fixtures';

test.describe('Adding New Todos', () => {
  test('Add Valid Todo', async ({ page }) => {
    // 1. Click in the "What needs to be done?" input field
    const todoInput = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'What needs to be done?' });
    await todoInput.click();

    // 2. Type "Buy groceries"
    await todoInput.fill('Buy groceries');

    // 3. Press Enter key
    await todoInput.press('Enter');

    // Expected Results:
    // - Todo appears in the list with unchecked checkbox
    await expect(page.getByText('Buy groceries')).toBeVisible();
    const todoCheckbox = page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Toggle Todo' });
    await expect(todoCheckbox).toBeVisible();
    await expect(todoCheckbox).not.toBeChecked();

    // - Counter shows "1 item left"
    await expect(page.getByText('1 item left')).toBeVisible();

    // - Input field is cleared and ready for next entry
    await expect(todoInput).toHaveValue('');
    await expect(todoInput).toBeFocused();

    // - Todo list controls become visible (Mark all as complete checkbox)
    await expect(page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: '❯Mark all as complete' })).toBeVisible();
  });
});

        🎭 Healer

        When a test fails, the healer agent:

        • Replays the failing steps.
        • Inspects the current UI to find an equivalent element or flow.
        • Proposes a patch (for example: updating a locator, adjusting a wait, fixing data).
        • Re-runs the test until it passes or until guardrails stop the loop.

        Input

        • The name of the failing test.

        Output

        • A passing test, or a test that is skipped if the healer believes the functionality is broken.
        Careful: the healer may skip a test instead of fixing it when it believes the app's functionality is broken — review skipped tests and don't assume they are "handled".

        Artifacts and conventions

        The static agent definitions and generated files follow a simple, easy-to-audit structure:

        repo/
  .github/                    # agent definitions
  specs/                      # human-readable test plans
    basic-operations.md
  tests/                      # generated Playwright tests
    seed.spec.ts              # seed test for environment
    tests/create/add-valid-todo.spec.ts
  playwright.config.ts

        Agent Definitions

        Under the hood, an agent definition is a collection of instructions and MCP tools. They are provided by Playwright and should be regenerated whenever you update Playwright. Example command for the agents (the original documentation illustrates the Claude Code subagents section):

        npx playwright init-agents --loop=vscode

        Specs in specs/

        Specs are structured plans that describe scenarios in human-readable language. They include steps, expected results and data. Specs can start from scratch or be extended from a seed test.

        Tests in tests/

        The generated Playwright tests, corresponding one-to-one with specs whenever feasible.

        Seed tests: seed.spec.ts

        A seed test provides a ready-to-use page context to bootstrap execution.

        ComponentLocationNotes
        Agent definitions.github/ (depends on --loop)Instructions + MCP tools; regenerate when upgrading Playwright
        Specsspecs/Markdown test plans
        Teststests/Generated from specs, 1-to-1 where possible
        Seedtests/seed.spec.tsProvides page + initialization fixtures/hooks

        Key takeaways

        • Three agents: planner (Markdown plan), generator (test code), healer (auto-fixes failing tests).
        • Initialize with npx playwright init-agents --loop=vscode|claude|codex|opencode; regenerate when upgrading Playwright.
        • The planner needs a clear request + a seed test (+ optional PRD); its output goes in specs/.
        • The generator reads specs/, verifies selectors/assertions live, and outputs to tests/.
        • The healer takes the name of a failing test, patches it and re-runs; it may skip if the functionality is genuinely broken.
        What does the planner produce?
        A Markdown test plan in specs/.
        What is a seed test used for?
        It provides a ready-to-use page, runs global setup/fixtures/hooks, and serves as the template for generated tests.
        When does the healer end its loop?
        When the test passes, or when guardrails stop it; it may skip the test if the functionality is broken.

        Which agent turns a Markdown test plan into Playwright test files?

        The generator reads the plan in specs/ and generates tests in tests/; the planner creates the plan; the healer fixes failing tests.

        Which command adds the agent definitions for Claude to a project?

        Use init-agents with the --loop flag to choose the tool (vscode, claude, codex, opencode).

        Command line – the Playwright CLI

        Playwright provides a powerful CLI for running tests, viewing reports, installing browsers, generating code, debugging traces and merging reports. The latest list of commands/arguments is always available with npx playwright --help.

        Run Tests

        The main command for running tests. See also Running tests.

        npx playwright test [options] [test-filter...]

        Commonly used examples

        # Run all tests
npx playwright test

# Run a single file
npx playwright test tests/todo-page.spec.ts

# Run multiple files / directories
npx playwright test tests/todo-page/ tests/landing-page/

# Run the test at a specific line
npx playwright test my-spec.ts:42

# Run tests by title
npx playwright test -g "add a todo item"

# Run with a visible browser (headed)
npx playwright test --headed

# Run a specific project
npx playwright test --project=chromium

# Show help
npx playwright test --help
        # Disable parallelization
npx playwright test --workers=1

# Debug with the Playwright Inspector
npx playwright test --debug

# Run in interactive UI mode
npx playwright test --ui

        Common Options

        OptionDescription
        --debug [mode]Run tests with the Playwright Inspector. A shortcut for the PWDEBUG=1 environment variable along with the options --timeout=0 --max-failures=1 --headed --workers=1. The optional mode is "inspector" (default) or "cli" (allows attaching and debugging through the CLI).
        --headedRun tests in a headed browser (default: headless).
        -g <grep> / --grep <grep>Only run tests matching this regex (default ".*").
        --project <project-name...>Only run tests belonging to the specified projects, supports the * wildcard (default: run all projects).
        --uiRun in interactive UI mode.
        -j <workers> / --workers <workers>Number of parallel workers or a % of logical CPU cores; use 1 to run in a single worker (default: 50%).

        All Options

        OptionDescription
        Non-option argumentsEach argument is a regex matched against the full path of test files; only tests in matching files run. Special characters such as $ or * must be escaped with \; many shells require the argument to be quoted.
        --add-reporter <reporter>Add reporters on top of those in the config, separated by commas. Can be the name of a built-in reporter or the path to a custom reporter file. Unlike --reporter: it keeps the configured reporters instead of replacing them.
        -c <file> / --config <file>The config file, or a test directory that already contains playwright.config.{m,c}?{js,ts}. Defaults to playwright.config.ts or .js in the current directory.
        --debug [mode]As in the table above (Inspector, PWDEBUG=1, "inspector" | "cli").
        --fail-on-flaky-testsFail if any test is marked flaky (default false).
        --forbid-onlyFail if any test.only is present (default false). Useful on CI.
        --fully-parallelRun all tests in parallel (default false).
        --global-timeout <timeout>Maximum time for the whole test suite, in ms (unlimited by default).
        -g / --grep <grep>Only run tests matching the regex (default ".*").
        -G / --grep-invert <grep>Only run tests that do NOT match the regex.
        --headedRun headed browsers (default headless).
        --ignore-snapshotsIgnore screenshot and snapshot expectations.
        -j / --workers <workers>Number of workers or a % of logical CPU cores (default 50%).
        --last-failedOnly re-run the tests that failed.
        --last-failed-file <file>Override the last-run JSON path for --last-failed (default <outputDir>/.last-run.json). Equivalent to the PLAYWRIGHT_LAST_RUN_OUTPUT_FILE environment variable.
        --listCollect and list all tests but do NOT run them.
        --max-failures <N> / -xStop after the first N failures. -x stops after the first failure.
        --no-depsDo not run project dependencies.
        --output <dir>Folder for output artifacts (default "test-results").
        --only-changed [ref]Only run test files that changed between 'HEAD' and 'ref'. Defaults to all uncommitted changes. Git only.
        --pass-with-no-testsAllow the run to succeed even if no tests are found.
        --project <project-name...>Only run the specified projects, supports the * wildcard.
        --quietSuppress stdio.
        --repeat-each <N>Run each test N times (default 1).
        --reporter <reporter>The reporter to use, comma-separated: "dot", "line", "list", "failures"... (default "list" locally, "dot" on CI). You can pass the path to a custom reporter file.
        --retries <retries>Maximum number of retries for flaky tests, 0 = no retries (no retries by default).
        --run-agents <mode>Run agents to generate code for page.perform. Values: "missing", "all", "none" (default "none"). See the test-agents page.
        --shard <shard>Split tests into shards and only run the selected shard, in the form "current/all", counted from 1, for example "3/5".
        --shuffle [seed]Schedule tests in random order: test files are shuffled, and so are individual tests in parallel mode. Tests that must run together (for example within a serial suite) keep their order. The seed is printed at the start of the run; pass the seed again to reproduce the exact order.
        --test-list <file>Path to a file containing the list of tests to run (see the Test list section below).
        --test-list-invert <file>Path to a file containing the list of tests to skip.
        --timeout <timeout>Per-test timeout in ms, 0 = unlimited (default 30 seconds).
        --trace <mode>Force a trace mode: on, off, on-first-retry, on-all-retries, retain-on-failure, retain-on-first-failure, retain-on-failure-and-retries.
        --tsconfig <path>Path to a single tsconfig applied to all imported files (default: look up a separate tsconfig for each file).
        --uiRun UI mode.
        --ui-host <host>Host to serve the UI on; specifying this option opens the UI in a browser tab.
        --ui-port <port>Port to serve the UI on, 0 = any free port; specifying this option opens the UI in a browser tab.
        -u / --update-snapshots [mode]Update snapshots with the actual results. Values: "all", "changed", "missing", "none", "default". No flag = "default"; the flag without a value = "changed".
        --update-source-method <method>How to update the source: "patch" (default, creates a unified diff file to apply later), "3way" (generates conflict markers in the source), "overwrite" (overwrites the source with the new snapshot values).
        -xStop after the first failure.
        Positional arguments are regexes. npx playwright test todo runs every file whose path contains "todo". The :42 suffix selects the test at line 42.
        1. Read the config-c or playwright.config.ts
        2. Select projects--project, plus dependencies (unless --no-deps)
        3. Filter by file/linepositional arguments, --test-list, --only-changed, --last-failed
        4. Filter by title--grep / --grep-invert, --shard
        5. Run--workers, --retries, --repeat-each, --shuffle
        6. Report--reporter / --add-reporter, artifacts in --output

        Test list – a list of tests from a file

        --test-list and --test-list-invert accept the path to a file that lists tests in a format similar to the output of --list mode.

        # This is a test list file.
# It can include comments and empty lines.

# Run ALL tests in a file:
path/to/example.spec.ts

# Run all tests in a file for a specific project:
[chromium] › path/to/example.spec.ts

# Run all tests in a specific group/suite:
path/to/example.spec.ts › suite name

# Run all tests in a nested group:
path/to/example.spec.ts › outer suite › inner suite

# Fully qualified test with a project:
[chromium] › path/to/example.spec.ts:3:9 › suite › nested suite › example test

# This test is included for all projects:
path/to/example.spec.ts:3:9 › example test

# Use "›" or ">" as a separator:
[firefox] > example.spec.ts > suite > nested suite > example test

# Line/column numbers are completely ignored, you can omit them.
# Three entries below refer to the same test:
example.spec.ts › example test
example.spec.ts:15 › example test
example.spec.ts:42:42 › example test

        Show Report – view the HTML report

        Displays the HTML report of the previous run. See also Test reporters.

        npx playwright show-report [report] [options]

# The latest report
npx playwright show-report

# A specific report
npx playwright show-report playwright-report/

# Custom port
npx playwright show-report --port 8080
        OptionDescription
        --host <host>Host to serve the report on (default localhost)
        --port <port>Port to serve the report on (default 9323)

        Install Browsers

        Installs the browsers Playwright needs. See also Browsers.

        npx playwright install [options] [browser...]
npx playwright install-deps [options] [browser...]
npx playwright uninstall

# Install all browsers
npx playwright install

# Chromium only
npx playwright install chromium

# Pick multiple browsers
npx playwright install chromium webkit

# Install along with system dependencies
npx playwright install --with-deps

        Install options

        OptionDescription
        --forceForce reinstall of already installed browsers
        --with-depsAlso install the browsers' system dependencies
        --dry-runDo not install, just print information
        --listPrint the list of browsers from all Playwright installations
        --only-shellOnly install chromium-headless-shell instead of full Chromium
        --no-shellDo not install chromium-headless-shell
        --no-progressDo not show the download progress bar
        --no-removeDo not remove browsers that are no longer used

        Install-deps options

        OptionDescription
        --dry-runDo not modify the system. On Linux: simulates the installation via apt-get and exits with a non-zero code if a required package is missing (useful for non-interactive check scripts). On Windows: prints the install commands.

        Code Generation – codegen

        Records your actions and generates tests for multiple languages. See Codegen.

        npx playwright codegen [options] [url]

# Record with the interactive UI
npx playwright codegen

# Record on a site
npx playwright codegen https://playwright.dev

# Generate Python code
npx playwright codegen --target=python
        OptionDescription
        -b, --browser <name>chromium, firefox or webkit (default chromium)
        -o, --output <file>Output file for the generated script
        --target <language>Language: javascript, playwright-test, python, etc.
        --test-id-attribute <attr>Attribute to use as the test id

        Trace Viewer – show-trace

        Analyze and view traces for debugging. See Trace Viewer.

        npx playwright show-trace [options] [trace]

# Open the viewer without a trace (load a trace via the UI)
npx playwright show-trace

# View a trace file
npx playwright show-trace trace.zip

# View a trace from a directory
npx playwright show-trace trace/
        OptionDescription
        -b, --browser <name>chromium, firefox or webkit (default chromium)
        -h, --host <host>Host to serve the trace on
        -p, --port <port>Port to serve the trace on
        Security. When you pass --port, other users on your machine can open the trace on that port. When you pass --host, anyone who can reach this address and port can open the trace, for example other machines on the network if you use --host=0.0.0.0.

        Merge Reports

        Reads blob reports and merges them (usually after sharding). See Sharding.

        npx playwright merge-reports [options] <blob dir>

# Merge reports
npx playwright merge-reports ./reports
        OptionDescription
        -c, --config <file>Config file; used to specify additional configuration for the output report
        --reporter <reporter>Reporter, comma-separated: "list", "line", "dot", "failures", "json", "junit", "null", "github", "html", "blob", "perfetto" (default "list" locally, "dot" on CI)

        Clear Cache

        npx playwright clear-cache

        Playwright stores transpiled test files in the system's temp directory. To store them elsewhere (for example on a Linux machine shared with other people), set the PLAYWRIGHT_TRANSFORM_CACHE_DIR environment variable:

        PLAYWRIGHT_TRANSFORM_CACHE_DIR=~/.cache/playwright-transform npx playwright test

        Key takeaways

        • npx playwright test [options] [test-filter...]: positional arguments are regexes on the file path, and file:line is supported.
        • --debug = PWDEBUG=1 + timeout 0 + headed + 1 worker + stop after 1 failure.
        • --reporter replaces, --add-reporter adds extra reporters.
        • --last-failed, --only-changed, --test-list, --shard help you run a subset of tests.
        • --no-deps skips project dependencies; --shuffle [seed] shuffles the order and prints the seed for reproduction.
        • Other commands: show-report, install/install-deps/uninstall, codegen, show-trace, merge-reports, clear-cache.

        Which command do you use to run exactly the test at line 42 of the file my-spec.ts?

        Positional arguments support the :line suffix. -g filters by a regex on the test title, and there is no --line flag.

        What is the difference between --reporter and --add-reporter?

        According to the docs, --add-reporter keeps the configured reporters instead of replacing them.

        Configuration – configuring the test runner

        Playwright has many options to control how tests run, declared in the config file. Important note: test runner options are top-level, NOT placed in the use section.

        Introduction

        The playwright.config.ts file uses defineConfig. Runner options (testDir, retries, workers, ...) live at the top level; browser/context options (baseURL, trace, ...) go inside use (see Configuration (use)).

        Common mistake. Putting retries or timeout inside use has no effect. They must be top-level.

        Basic Configuration

        The most common options:

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Look for test files in the "tests" directory, relative to this configuration file.
  testDir: 'tests',

  // Run all tests in parallel.
  fullyParallel: true,

  // Fail the build on CI if you accidentally left test.only in the source code.
  forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI,

  // Retry on CI only.
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,

  // Opt out of parallel tests on CI.
  workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined,

  // Limit the whole test run, so that it fails with a report instead of hanging.
  globalTimeout: 60 * 60 * 1000,

  // Reporter to use
  reporter: 'html',

  use: {
    // Base URL to use in actions like `await page.goto('/')`.
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',

    // Collect trace when retrying the failed test.
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  // Configure projects for major browsers.
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
  // Run your local dev server before starting the tests.
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        forbidOnlyExit with an error if any test is marked test.only. Useful on CI.
        fullyParallelRun all tests in all files in parallel. See Parallelism and Sharding.
        globalTimeoutMaximum time for the whole run. When the limit is reached, Playwright stops the run but the reporters still produce a report. See Timeouts.
        projectsRun tests with multiple configurations or on multiple browsers.
        reporterThe reporter to use. See Test Reporters.
        retriesMaximum number of retries for each test. See Test Retries.
        testDirThe directory containing test files.
        useThe options inside use{}.
        webServerLaunch a server while the tests run.
        workersMaximum number of worker processes running in parallel. Can be set as a % of logical CPU cores, for example '50%'.
        CI/local pattern. Use process.env.CI to enable forbidOnly, retries: 2, workers: 1 only on CI, while locally you run fast and with maximum parallelism.

        Filtering Tests

        Filter test files with glob patterns or regular expressions.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Glob patterns or regular expressions to ignore test files.
  testIgnore: '*test-assets',

  // Glob patterns or regular expressions that match test files.
  testMatch: '*todo-tests/*.spec.ts',
});
        OptionDescription
        testIgnoreGlob or regex used to IGNORE when looking for test files, for example '*test-assets'.
        testMatchGlob or regex that matches test files, for example '*todo-tests/*.spec.ts'. By default Playwright runs files matching **/*.@(spec|test).?(c|m)[jt]s?(x).

        Advanced Configuration

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Folder for test artifacts such as screenshots, videos, traces, etc.
  outputDir: 'test-results',

  // path to the global setup files.
  globalSetup: require.resolve('./global-setup'),

  // path to the global teardown files.
  globalTeardown: require.resolve('./global-teardown'),

  // Each test is given 30 seconds.
  timeout: 30000,
});
        OptionDescription
        globalSetupPath to the global setup file. The file is required and run before all tests; it must export exactly one function.
        globalTeardownPath to the global teardown file, run after all tests; it must export exactly one function.
        outputDirFolder for artifacts: screenshots, videos, traces...
        timeoutTimeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. The time spent in the test function, test fixtures and the beforeEach hook all counts toward this timeout.

        See also Global setup and teardown.

        Expect Options

        Configuration for the expect assertion library.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    // Maximum time expect() should wait for the condition to be met.
    timeout: 5000,

    toHaveScreenshot: {
      // An acceptable amount of pixels that could be different, unset by default.
      maxDiffPixels: 10,
    },

    toMatchSnapshot: {
      // An acceptable ratio of pixels that are different to the
      // total amount of pixels, between 0 and 1.
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.1,
    },
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        expectWeb-first assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own timeout, 5 seconds by default: the maximum time expect() waits for the condition to be true. See Timeouts.
        expect.toHaveScreenshotConfiguration for toHaveScreenshot().
        expect.toMatchSnapshotConfiguration for toMatchSnapshot().
        globalTimeoutthe whole run (unlimited by default)
        timeoutper test: 30s, includes fixtures + beforeEach
        expect.timeoutper web-first assertion: 5s
        actionTimeout / navigationTimeoutin use; default 0 = unlimited

        Key takeaways

        • Runner options are top-level; browser/context options go in use.
        • Default testMatch: **/*.@(spec|test).?(c|m)[jt]s?(x).
        • timeout defaults to 30s per test; expect.timeout defaults to 5s.
        • globalTimeout makes the run fail with a report instead of hanging indefinitely.
        • forbidOnly, retries, workers are usually tied to process.env.CI.

        Where should the retries option go in playwright.config.ts?

        Test runner options are top-level and do not go inside use.

        Configuration (use) – Browser/Context options

        Besides the runner configuration, you can configure Emulation, Network and Recording for the Browser/BrowserContext through the use: {} object in the config.

        Basic Options

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Base URL to use in actions like `await page.goto('/')`.
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',

    // Populates context with given storage state.
    storageState: 'state.json',
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        baseURLBase URL for every page in the context; lets you navigate with just a path, for example page.goto('/settings').
        storageStateLoads a storage state into the context; handy for authentication (see Authentication).

        Emulation Options

        Playwright can emulate real devices (phones, tablets) - see Projects. You can also emulate geolocation, locale, timezone, grant permissions (for example notifications) or change colorScheme for all tests or for individual tests. See Emulation.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Emulates `'prefers-colors-scheme'` media feature.
    colorScheme: 'dark',

    // Context geolocation.
    geolocation: { longitude: 12.492507, latitude: 41.889938 },

    // Emulates the user locale.
    locale: 'en-GB',

    // Grants specified permissions to the browser context.
    permissions: ['geolocation'],

    // Emulates the user timezone.
    timezoneId: 'Europe/Paris',

    // Viewport used for all pages in the context.
    viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        colorSchemeEmulates the prefers-color-scheme media feature: 'light' or 'dark'
        contrastEmulates prefers-contrast: 'no-preference' or 'more'
        forcedColorsEmulates forced-colors: 'active' or 'none'
        geolocationGeographic location of the context
        localeEmulates the user locale, for example en-GB, de-DE
        permissionsList of permissions granted to every page in the context
        reducedMotionEmulates prefers-reduced-motion: 'reduce' or 'no-preference'
        timezoneIdChanges the timezone of the context
        viewportViewport size for every page in the context

        Network Options

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Whether to automatically download all the attachments.
    acceptDownloads: false,

    // An object containing additional HTTP headers to be sent with every request.
    extraHTTPHeaders: {
      'X-My-Header': 'value',
    },

    // Credentials for HTTP authentication.
    httpCredentials: {
      username: 'user',
      password: 'pass',
    },

    // Whether to ignore HTTPS errors during navigation.
    ignoreHTTPSErrors: true,

    // Whether to emulate network being offline.
    offline: true,

    // Proxy settings used for all pages in the test.
    proxy: {
      server: 'http://myproxy.com:3128',
      bypass: 'localhost',
    },
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        acceptDownloadsAutomatically downloads all attachments, defaults to true. See Downloads.
        clientCertificatesTLS Client Authentication: the server requests and verifies a client certificate.
        extraHTTPHeadersAdditional HTTP headers sent with every request. All header values must be strings.
        httpCredentialsHTTP authentication credentials.
        ignoreHTTPSErrorsIgnores HTTPS errors during navigation.
        offlineEmulates the network being offline.
        proxyProxy settings for every page in the test.
        serviceWorkersWhether to allow sites to register Service workers, defaults to 'allow'. See Network.
        Network mocking needs no configuration. Just define a custom Route for the browser context. See the network mocking guide.

        Recording Options

        You can capture screenshots, record videos and record traces while tests run. These are off by default; turn them on with the screenshot, video and trace options. Traces, screenshots and videos are placed in the output directory, usually test-results.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Capture screenshot after each test failure.
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',

    // Record trace only when retrying a test for the first time.
    trace: 'on-first-retry',

    // Record video only when retrying a test for the first time.
    video: 'on-first-retry'
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        screenshotCaptures a screenshot. Values: 'off', 'on', 'only-on-failure'
        traceRecords a trace to view in the Trace Viewer. See the modes below.
        videoRecords a video for the test; it has the same set of modes as trace.

        Trace modes

        The modes differ in which runs are recorded and which recordings are kept. A test's first execution is the "first run"; later executions caused by retries are "retries".

        ModeRecords trace onKeeps trace when
        'off'never-
        'on'every runalways
        'retain-on-failure'every runthat run fails
        'retain-on-first-failure'first run onlythe first run fails
        'retain-on-failure-and-retries'every runthat run fails, or it is a retry
        'on-first-retry'first retry onlyalways
        'on-all-retries'every retryalways

        Traces retained in a few common scenarios, assuming retries: 2:

        ModePasses on the first runFails, then passes on retryFails every time
        'off'---
        'on'first runfirst run + retryall three runs
        'retain-on-failure'-first runall three runs
        'retain-on-first-failure'-first runfirst run
        'retain-on-failure-and-retries'-first run + retryall three runs
        'on-first-retry'-first retryfirst retry
        'on-all-retries'-first retryboth retries

        Video modes

        The video option supports the same set of modes as trace and uses the same record/keep rules.

        ModeRecords video onKeeps video when
        'off'never-
        'on'every runalways
        'retain-on-failure'every runthat run fails
        'retain-on-first-failure'first run onlythe first run fails
        'retain-on-failure-and-retries'every runthat run fails, or it is a retry
        'on-first-retry'first retry onlyalways
        'on-all-retries'every retryalways

        Videos retained in common scenarios, assuming retries: 2:

        ModePasses on the first runFails, then passes on retryFails every time
        'off'---
        'on'first runfirst run + retryall three runs
        'retain-on-failure'-first runall three runs
        'retain-on-first-failure'-first runfirst run
        'retain-on-failure-and-retries'-first run + retryall three runs
        'on-first-retry'-first retryfirst retry
        'on-all-retries'-first retryboth retries
        Best practice. trace: 'on-first-retry' is a balanced choice: it costs no resources on the first run, but gives you a full trace for flaky/failing tests when they retry.

        Other Options

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Maximum time each action such as `click()` can take. Defaults to 0 (no limit).
    actionTimeout: 0,

    // Name of the browser that runs tests. For example `chromium`, `firefox`, `webkit`.
    browserName: 'chromium',

    // Toggles bypassing Content-Security-Policy.
    bypassCSP: true,

    // Channel to use, for example "chrome", "chrome-beta", "msedge", "msedge-beta".
    channel: 'chrome',

    // Run browser in headless mode.
    headless: false,

    // Change the default data-testid attribute.
    testIdAttribute: 'pw-test-id',
  },
});
        OptionDescription
        actionTimeoutTimeout for each action (ms). Defaults to 0 (no limit). See Timeouts.
        browserNameBrowser that runs the tests, defaults to 'chromium'; chromium, firefox or webkit.
        bypassCSPBypasses Content-Security-Policy; useful when the CSP contains production origins. Defaults to false.
        channelBrowser channel (for example chrome, chrome-beta, msedge, msedge-beta). See Browsers.
        headlessWhether to run headless, defaults to true.
        navigationTimeoutTimeout for each navigation operation (ms). Defaults to 0 (no limit).
        testIdAttributeChanges the default data-testid attribute used by Playwright locators.

        More browser and context options

        Any option of BrowserType.launch, Browser.newContext or BrowserType.connect can be set in launchOptions, contextOptions and connectOptions inside use.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    launchOptions: {
      slowMo: 50,
    },
  },
});

        That said, common options such as headless or viewport are available directly in use.

        Explicit Context Creation and Option Inheritance

        While a test or hook is running, every browser context created through the Playwright instance the test runner uses inherits the context options from use. This includes contexts created with the built-in browser fixture, a separately launched browser, BrowserType.launchPersistentContext, or a direct import of playwright-core that points to the same instance. Explicitly passed options take precedence.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    userAgent: 'some custom ua',
    viewport: { width: 100, height: 100 },
  },
});
        test('should inherit use options on context when using built-in browser fixture', async ({
  browser,
}) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();
  expect(await page.evaluate(() => navigator.userAgent)).toBe('some custom ua');
  expect(await page.evaluate(() => window.innerWidth)).toBe(100);
  await context.close();
});

        Configuration Scopes

        You can configure Playwright globally, per project, or per test. For example, set locale in the global use, override it for one project, then override it again for a file/describe with test.use({}).

        1. Globaluse in config: locale 'en-GB'
        2. Projectprojects[].use: locale 'de-DE'
        3. File / describetest.use({ locale: 'fr-FR' })
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    locale: 'en-GB'
  },
});

        Override for one project:

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        locale: 'de-DE',
      },
    },
  ],
});

        Override for a test file with test.use():

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({ locale: 'fr-FR' });

test('example', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        The same approach works inside a describe block:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('french language block', () => {

  test.use({ locale: 'fr-FR' });

  test('example', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });
});

        Reset an option

        You can reset an option back to the value in the config file. Suppose the config sets baseURL:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    baseURL: 'https://playwright.dev',
  },
});

        Configure baseURL for the file, then opt out for one test:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Configure baseURL for this file.
test.use({ baseURL: 'https://playwright.dev/docs/intro' });

test('check intro contents', async ({ page }) => {
  // This test will use "https://playwright.dev/docs/intro" base url as defined above.
});

test.describe(() => {
  // Reset the value to a config-defined one.
  test.use({ baseURL: undefined });

  test('can navigate to intro from the home page', async ({ page }) => {
    // This test will use "https://playwright.dev" base url as defined in the config.
  });
});

        If you want to reset it completely to undefined, use the long-form fixture syntax:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Completely unset baseURL for this file.
test.use({
  baseURL: [async ({}, use) => use(undefined), { scope: 'test' }],
});

test('no base url', async ({ page }) => {
  // This test will not have a base url.
});
        Know the difference. test.use({ baseURL: undefined }) returns to the value in the config; to remove it entirely (no baseURL at all) you must use the long-form fixture syntax.

        Key takeaways

        • use holds Browser/Context options: emulation, network, recording and other options.
        • 3 scopes: global (config) < project < file/describe (test.use); the narrower scope overrides.
        • trace/video share the same 7 modes; 'on-first-retry' is the most common.
        • Manually created contexts still inherit use; explicitly passed options take precedence.
        • launchOptions/contextOptions/connectOptions cover less common options (for example slowMo).

        Which trace mode records EVERY run but only keeps the recording of a run that fails?

        'retain-on-failure' records a trace on every run and keeps it only when that run fails. The other two modes only record on retries.

        How do you make one describe block use the French locale?

        test.use() overrides options for a file or a describe block.

        Projects – grouping tests with the same configuration

        A project is a logical group of tests that run with the same configuration. Use projects to run tests across multiple browsers/devices, multiple environments, or to run the same tests under different configurations.

        Introduction

        Projects are configured in playwright.config.ts; you can then run tests on all projects or on a single project. You can also use projects to run the same tests under different configurations, for example logged-in and logged-out states.

        Projects also let you run groups of tests with different timeouts or retries, or against different environments (staging, production), split tests by package/feature, and more.

        Configure projects for multiple browsers

        Use projects to run tests on chromium, webkit, firefox as well as branded browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. Playwright can also run on emulated tablet/mobile devices. See the registry of device descriptors in Playwright's GitHub repository for the full list.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },

    {
      name: 'firefox',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] },
    },

    {
      name: 'webkit',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] },
    },

    /* Test against mobile viewports. */
    {
      name: 'Mobile Chrome',
      use: { ...devices['Pixel 5'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'Mobile Safari',
      use: { ...devices['iPhone 12'] },
    },

    /* Test against branded browsers. */
    {
      name: 'Microsoft Edge',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Edge'],
        channel: 'msedge'
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'Google Chrome',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        channel: 'chrome'
      },
    },
  ],
});

        Run projects

        By default Playwright runs all projects.

        npx playwright test

Running 7 tests using 5 workers

  ✓ [chromium] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [webkit] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Mobile Chrome] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Mobile Safari] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Microsoft Edge] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Google Chrome] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)

        Use the --project option to run a single project:

        npx playwright test --project=firefox

Running 1 test using 1 worker

  ✓ [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)

        The VS Code test runner runs on Chrome by default. To run on a different browser or on several browsers, click the dropdown of the play button in the Testing sidebar and pick another profile, or edit the default profile via Select Default Profile and choose the browsers you want to run. You can select one profile, several profiles or all of them.

        Configure projects for multiple environments

        You can run a group of tests with different timeouts/retries or against different environments. For example: run staging with 2 retries and production with 0 retries.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  timeout: 60000, // Timeout is shared between all tests.
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'staging',
      use: {
        baseURL: 'staging.example.com',
      },
      retries: 2,
    },
    {
      name: 'production',
      use: {
        baseURL: 'production.example.com',
      },
      retries: 0,
    },
  ],
});

        Splitting tests into projects

        Split tests into projects and use filters to run a subset. For example, one project matches every test with a specific file name, while another project ignores those files. The example below defines a shared timeout and two projects: "Smoke" runs a small set with no retries, "Default" runs all remaining tests with retries.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  timeout: 60000, // Timeout is shared between all tests.
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'Smoke',
      testMatch: /.*smoke.spec.ts/,
      retries: 0,
    },
    {
      name: 'Default',
      testIgnore: /.*smoke.spec.ts/,
      retries: 2,
    },
  ],
});

        Dependencies

        dependencies is a list of projects that need to run BEFORE the tests of another project. It is useful for configuring global setup actions: a project depends on a setup project that runs first. When you use project dependencies, the test reporter shows the setup tests, the trace viewer records traces of the setup (you can use the inspector to view DOM snapshots), and you can also use fixtures in the setup.

        Example: the chromium, firefox and webkit projects depend on a setup project.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'setup',
      testMatch: '**/*.setup.ts',
    },
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
    {
      name: 'firefox',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
    {
      name: 'webkit',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
  ],
});

        Running Sequence

        Dependencies always run first; once all tests in that project pass, the other projects run in parallel.

        1. setuptests of the 'setup' project run; all must pass
        2. chromium + firefox + webkitrun in parallel, limited by the maximum number of workers

        If there are several dependencies, they run first and in parallel with each other. If a test in a dependency fails, the tests that depend on that project will NOT run.

        1. Tests in the 'Browser Login' and 'DataBase' projects run in parallel: 'Browser Login' passes, but 'DataBase' fails.
        2. The 'e2e tests' project (which depends on both) does NOT run.

        Teardown

        You can tear down the setup by adding a teardown property to the setup project. Teardown runs after all the projects that depend on it have finished. See also the teardown guide.

        Test filtering

        All ways of filtering tests, such as --grep/--grep-invert, --shard, filtering by location on the command line, or test.only(), directly select the "main" tests to run. If those tests belong to a project with dependencies, all tests of the dependencies run as well.

        Pass --no-deps to skip all dependencies and teardown; only the projects you select directly will run.

        npx playwright test --project=chromium --no-deps

        Custom project parameters

        Projects can also be used to parameterize tests with custom configuration. See Parameterize tests – Parameterized Projects.

        Key takeaways

        • Project = group of tests + configuration (use, retries, timeout, testMatch, testIgnore...).
        • devices['...'] provides desktop/mobile presets; channel selects real Chrome/Edge.
        • --project=name runs one project; by default all projects run.
        • dependencies: the dependent project runs only after all dependencies pass; if they fail, the dependent project is skipped.
        • teardown runs last; --no-deps skips dependencies and teardown.

        A dependency project fails. What happens to the project that depends on it?

        If a test in the dependency fails, the tests that rely on that project do not run.

        You filter with --grep and the selected test belongs to a project with dependencies. What happens?

        The filter only selects the main tests; dependencies are still pulled in. Use --no-deps to avoid that.

        Global setup and teardown

        There are two ways to run code once before/after the entire test run: project dependencies (recommended) or the globalSetup/globalTeardown options in the config.

        Introduction

        With project dependencies, you define a project that runs before all other projects. This is the recommended approach because it integrates better with the test runner: the HTML report includes the global setup, traces are recorded, and fixtures are available. A comparison table:

        FeatureProject Dependencies (recommended)globalSetup (config option)
        Runs before all tests✅ Yes✅ Yes
        Shown in the HTML report✅ Appears as a separate project❌ Not shown
        Trace recording✅ Full trace❌ Not supported
        Playwright fixtures✅ Fully supported❌ Not supported
        Browser management✅ Through the browser fixture❌ Fully manual via browserType.launch()
        Parallelism and retries✅ Supported through the standard config❌ Not applicable
        Options such as headless or testIdAttribute✅ Applied automatically❌ Ignored
        1. setup dbglobal.setup.ts: creates the database (like a regular test)
        2. chromium with dbruns the real tests, depends on 'setup db'
        3. cleanup dbteardown: global.teardown.ts, runs after the dependent projects finish

        Option 1: Project Dependencies

        Project dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests of another project; they help you configure global setup actions. Using dependencies lets the global setup produce traces and other artifacts.

        Setup

        First add a project named 'setup db' and set testMatch to match the global.setup.ts file:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  // ...
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'setup db',
      testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/,
    },
    // {
    //   other project
    // }
  ]
});

        Then add dependencies to the dependent projects, passing the name of the project you defined:

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  // ...
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'setup db',
      testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/,
    },
    {
      name: 'chromium with db',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      dependencies: ['setup db'],
    },
  ]
});

        The 'chromium with db' project depends on 'setup db'. Next, create the setup test in the project's root directory. Note: setup and teardown code must be defined like regular tests using the test() function.

        import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';

setup('create new database', async ({ }) => {
  console.log('creating new database...');
  // Initialize the database
});
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('menu', async ({ page }) => {
  // Your test that depends on the database
});

        Teardown

        Tear down the setup with the teardown property of the setup project; it runs after all the dependent projects have finished. Add teardown: 'cleanup db' to the setup project, where 'cleanup db' is the name of the teardown project:

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  // ...
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'setup db',
      testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/,
      teardown: 'cleanup db',
    },
    {
      name: 'cleanup db',
      testMatch: /global\.teardown\.ts/,
    },
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      dependencies: ['setup db'],
    },
  ]
});

        Then create global.teardown.ts in the tests directory, and use it to delete data from the database after all tests have finished:

        import { test as teardown } from '@playwright/test';

teardown('delete database', async ({ }) => {
  console.log('deleting test database...');
  // Delete the database
});

        Test filtering

        All test-filtering options (--grep/--grep-invert, --shard, filtering by location, or test.only()) directly select the main tests. If they belong to a project with dependencies, all tests of the dependencies run as well. Use --no-deps to skip all dependencies and teardown; only the directly selected projects run.

        More examples

        • The Authentication guide
        • The blog post A better global setup in Playwright reusing login with project dependencies
        • The v1.31 release video has a demo

        Option 2: Configure globalSetup and globalTeardown

        Use the globalSetup option in the config file to set something up once before all tests. The global setup file must export a single function that takes the config object; the function runs once before all tests. Similarly, globalTeardown runs once after all tests. Alternatively, let globalSetup return a function to be used as the global teardown. You can pass data (ports, auth tokens...) from the global setup to tests through environment variables.

        Limitations. globalSetup and globalTeardown lack some features (see the comparison table at the top of the page). Prefer project dependencies to get the full feature set.
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: require.resolve('./global-setup'),
  globalTeardown: require.resolve('./global-teardown'),
});

        Example

        An example global setup that authenticates once and reuses the authentication state in tests, using baseURL and storageState from the config:

        import { chromium, type FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const { baseURL, storageState } = config.projects[0].use;
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto(baseURL!);
  await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill('user');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');
  await page.getByText('Sign in').click();
  await page.context().storageState({ path: storageState as string });
  await browser.close();
}

export default globalSetup;

        Declare globalSetup, baseURL and storageState in the config:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: require.resolve('./global-setup'),
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000/',
    storageState: 'state.json',
  },
});

        Tests start in a signed-in state because storageState was produced by the global setup:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  // You are signed in!
});

        You can pass arbitrary data from the global setup to tests using process.env:

        import type { FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  process.env.FOO = 'some data';
  // Or a more complicated data structure as JSON:
  process.env.BAR = JSON.stringify({ some: 'data' });
}

export default globalSetup;
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('test', async ({ page }) => {
  // environment variables which are set in globalSetup are only available inside test().
  const { FOO, BAR } = process.env;

  // FOO and BAR properties are populated.
  expect(FOO).toEqual('some data');

  const complexData = JSON.parse(BAR);
  expect(complexData).toEqual({ some: 'data' });
});
        Note. Environment variables set in globalSetup are only available inside test().

        Capturing trace of failures during global setup

        Sometimes you need to record a trace of failures in the global setup. Call tracing.start in the setup and make sure to call tracing.stop if an error occurs before rethrowing it, by wrapping the setup in try...catch.

        import { chromium, type FullConfig } from '@playwright/test';

async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig) {
  const { baseURL, storageState } = config.projects[0].use;
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();
  try {
    await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });
    await page.goto(baseURL!);
    await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill('user');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');
    await page.getByText('Sign in').click();
    await context.storageState({ path: storageState as string });
    await context.tracing.stop({
      path: './test-results/setup-trace.zip',
    });
    await browser.close();
  } catch (error) {
    await context.tracing.stop({
      path: './test-results/failed-setup-trace.zip',
    });
    await browser.close();
    throw error;
  }
}

export default globalSetup;
        ❌ Avoid (when possible)
        export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: require.resolve('./global-setup'),
});

        No trace, not in the HTML report, no fixtures, and you have to manage the browser yourself.

        ✅ Do this
        projects: [
  { name: 'setup db', testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/, teardown: 'cleanup db' },
  { name: 'cleanup db', testMatch: /global\.teardown\.ts/ },
  { name: 'chromium', dependencies: ['setup db'] },
]

        Setup is a regular test: you get reports, traces, fixtures and retries.

        Key takeaways

        • Recommended: project dependencies + teardown; write setup/teardown like regular tests with test().
        • globalSetup/globalTeardown: each file exports a function; no report/trace/fixtures, and options such as headless are ignored.
        • globalSetup can return a function to act as the teardown; pass data through process.env.
        • --no-deps skips dependencies and teardown.
        • To record a trace of setup failures: tracing.start, wrap in try...catch, and call tracing.stop in both branches.

        What is the main advantage of project dependencies over globalSetup?

        Setup is a regular test, so it integrates fully with the runner: reports, traces, fixtures, retries.

        Which property of the setup project specifies the cleanup project that runs last?

        teardown: 'cleanup db' points to the teardown project, which runs after the dependent projects finish.

        Parameterize tests

        You can parameterize tests at the test level (generate many tests from data) or at the project level (the same tests run with different option values). There are also environment variables, .env files and CSV data.

        Parameterized Tests

        Loop over an array of data and generate one test per element. Test names must be unique.

        [
  { name: 'Alice', expected: 'Hello, Alice!' },
  { name: 'Bob', expected: 'Hello, Bob!' },
  { name: 'Charlie', expected: 'Hello, Charlie!' },
].forEach(({ name, expected }) => {
  // You can also do it with test.describe() or with multiple tests as long the test name is unique.
  test(`testing with ${name}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`https://example.com/greet?name=${name}`);
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText(expected);
  });
});
        Test names must be unique. If two tests have the same name (in the same file/describe), Playwright reports an error. Put the parameter into the title, like `testing with ${name}`.

        Before and after hooks

        Normally you should put beforeEach, beforeAll, afterEach and afterAll OUTSIDE the forEach so the hooks run only once:

        test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

test.afterEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

[
  { name: 'Alice', expected: 'Hello, Alice!' },
  { name: 'Bob', expected: 'Hello, Bob!' },
  { name: 'Charlie', expected: 'Hello, Charlie!' },
].forEach(({ name, expected }) => {
  test(`testing with ${name}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`https://example.com/greet?name=${name}`);
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText(expected);
  });
});

        If you want separate hooks for each test (each loop iteration), put them in a describe() inside the loop:

        [
  { name: 'Alice', expected: 'Hello, Alice!' },
  { name: 'Bob', expected: 'Hello, Bob!' },
  { name: 'Charlie', expected: 'Hello, Charlie!' },
].forEach(({ name, expected }) => {
  test.describe(() => {
    test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
