      await page.goto(`https://example.com/greet?name=${name}`);
    });
    test(`testing with ${expected}`, async ({ page }) => {
      await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText(expected);
    });
  });
});

        Parameterized Projects

        Playwright Test supports running multiple projects at the same time. The following example runs two projects with different options: declare a person option and set its value in the config; the first project runs with Alice, the second with Bob.

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export type TestOptions = {
  person: string;
};

export const test = base.extend<TestOptions>({
  // Define an option and provide a default value.
  // We can later override it in the config.
  person: ['John', { option: true }],
});
        JavaScript (CommonJS) version of my-test.js 
        const base = require('@playwright/test');

exports.test = base.test.extend({
  // Define an option and provide a default value.
  // We can later override it in the config.
  person: ['John', { option: true }],
});

        Use the option in a test, similar to fixtures:

        import { test } from './my-test';

test('test 1', async ({ page, person }) => {
  await page.goto(`/index.html`);
  await expect(page.locator('#node')).toContainText(person);
  // ...
});

        Now run the tests under multiple configurations using projects:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import type { TestOptions } from './my-test';

export default defineConfig<TestOptions>({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'alice',
      use: { person: 'Alice' },
    },
    {
      name: 'bob',
      use: { person: 'Bob' },
    },
  ]
});
        JavaScript version of playwright.config 
        // @ts-check

module.exports = defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'alice',
      use: { person: 'Alice' },
    },
    {
      name: 'bob',
      use: { person: 'Bob' },
    },
  ]
});

        You can also use the option inside a fixture (overriding the page fixture). Learn more in fixtures:

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export type TestOptions = {
  person: string;
};

export const test = base.extend<TestOptions>({
  // Define an option and provide a default value.
  // We can later override it in the config.
  person: ['John', { option: true }],

  // Override default "page" fixture.
  page: async ({ page, person }, use) => {
    await page.goto('/chat');
    // We use "person" parameter as a "name" for the chat room.
    await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill(person);
    await page.getByText('Enter chat room').click();
    // Each test will get a "page" that already has the person name.
    await use(page);
  },
});
        Changed in v1.18. The behavior of parameterized projects changed in version 1.18. See the "custom config options" breaking change in the release notes.
        1. Declare the optionbase.extend: person: ['John', { option: true }]
        2. Override it in the configprojects[].use: { person: 'Alice' }
        3. Use it in a test/fixture({ page, person })
        4. Run each projectthe same tests run once per project

        Passing Environment Variables

        Use environment variables to configure tests from the command line. For example, a test needs a username and password; you should avoid storing secrets in source code, so you need a way to pass them in from outside.

        test(`example test`, async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
  await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill(process.env.USER_NAME);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.PASSWORD);
});

        Run the tests with the username/password set on the command line:

        USER_NAME=me PASSWORD=secret npx playwright test
        set USER_NAME=me
set PASSWORD=secret
npx playwright test
        $env:USER_NAME=me
$env:PASSWORD=secret
npx playwright test

        Similarly, the config file can also read environment variables passed on the command line:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.STAGING === '1' ? 'http://staging.example.test/' : 'http://example.test/',
  }
});

        Now you can run against staging or production:

        STAGING=1 npx playwright test
        set STAGING=1
npx playwright test
        $env:STAGING=1
npx playwright test

        .env files

        To manage environment variables more easily, use a .env file. For example, use the dotenv package to read it directly in the config file:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import dotenv from 'dotenv';
import path from 'path';

// Read from ".env" file.
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, '.env') });

// Alternatively, read from "../my.env" file.
dotenv.config({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, '..', 'my.env') });

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.STAGING === '1' ? 'http://staging.example.test/' : 'http://example.test/',
  }
});

        Now you only need to edit the .env file:

        # .env file
STAGING=0
USER_NAME=me
PASSWORD=secret

        Run the tests as usual and the environment variables will be picked up:

        npx playwright test
        Security. Do not commit a .env file containing secrets to Git; add it to .gitignore.

        Create tests via a CSV file

        The Playwright test runner runs in Node.js, so you can read files directly from the file system and parse them with your favorite CSV library. For example, an input.csv file:

        "test_case","some_value","some_other_value"
"value 1","value 11","foobar1"
"value 2","value 22","foobar21"
"value 3","value 33","foobar321"
"value 4","value 44","foobar4321"

        From it, generate tests with the NPM library csv-parse:

        import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';
import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import { parse } from 'csv-parse/sync';

const records = parse(fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, 'input.csv')), {
  columns: true,
  skip_empty_lines: true
});

for (const record of records) {
  test(`foo: ${record.test_case}`, async ({ page }) => {
    console.log(record.test_case, record.some_value, record.some_other_value);
  });
}

        Key takeaways

        • Test level: loop over an array of data and call test() with a unique name.
        • Hooks placed outside the loop run once; for per-test hooks, wrap them in test.describe() inside the loop.
        • Project level: declare an option with [default, { option: true }] in base.extend, and override it in projects[].use.
        • Environment variables (process.env) are used for secrets and URLs; dotenv reads the .env file in the config.
        • Tests run in Node.js, so you can read CSV/JSON with fs and then generate tests.

        You want beforeEach to run separately for each test generated from a forEach loop. What should you do?

        A hook outside the loop is declared only once; inside a describe in each iteration, every iteration gets its own hook.

        How do you declare an option that can be overridden per project?

        The pair [default value, { option: true }] turns a fixture into an option that can be overridden in projects[].use.

        TypeScript

        Playwright supports TypeScript out of the box: you write tests in TS, and Playwright reads them, converts them to JavaScript and runs them. However, it does NOT type-check.

        Introduction

        Playwright does not check types and will still run tests even when there are non-critical TypeScript compile errors. You should run the TypeScript compiler alongside Playwright, for example on GitHub Actions:

        jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    ...
    - name: Run type checks
      run: npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit
    - name: Run Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test

        During local development, run tsc in watch mode:

        npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit -w
        1. Reads the .ts filealong with the nearest tsconfig.json
        2. Transforms to JSno type-checking
        3. Runs the testseven when there are non-critical type errors
        4. tsc --noEmitrun separately (CI/watch) to catch type errors

        tsconfig.json

        Playwright reads tsconfig.json for every source file it loads. Playwright only supports the following options: allowJs, baseUrl, paths, jsx, jsxFactory, jsxFragmentFactory, jsxImportSource, useDefineForClassFields, references and extends. The target option is only used to determine useDefineForClassFields.

        It is recommended to place a separate tsconfig.json in the tests directory to change settings just for tests. An example directory structure:

        src/
    source.ts

tests/
    tsconfig.json  # test-specific tsconfig
    example.spec.ts

tsconfig.json  # generic tsconfig for all typescript sources

playwright.config.ts
        Supported optionNotes
        allowJsAllows JS files
        baseUrl, pathsPath mapping (import aliases)
        jsx, jsxFactory, jsxFragmentFactory, jsxImportSourceCompiles JSX in .tsx/.jsx
        useDefineForClassFieldsClass fields semantics; target only affects this option
        references, extendsInherit/reference other tsconfigs

        tsconfig path mapping

        Playwright supports path mapping declared in tsconfig.json. Here is an example tsconfig that works with Playwright:

        {
  "compilerOptions": {
    "paths": {
      "@myhelper/*": ["packages/myhelper/*"] // This mapping is relative to the tsconfig.
    }
  }
}

        Now you can import using the mapped path:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { username, password } from '@myhelper/credentials';

test('example', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
});

        tsconfig JSX options

        Playwright compiles JSX in .tsx and .jsx files according to the jsx, jsxFactory, jsxFragmentFactory and jsxImportSource options. When jsx is not specified, or is preserve/react-native, Playwright uses the automatic runtime from react/jsx-runtime.

        {
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "preact"
  }
}

        tsconfig class fields

        Playwright compiles TypeScript class fields according to useDefineForClassFields. Like tsc: when not specified, this option is on for the ES2022 target and above, and when target is not specified.

        When enabled, class fields follow JavaScript semantics: field initializers run before the constructor body and cannot access constructor parameter properties. Turn it off to keep the legacy TypeScript semantics.

        {
  "compilerOptions": {
    "useDefineForClassFields": false
  }
}

        tsconfig resolution

        By default Playwright looks for the nearest tsconfig for each imported file by walking up the directory tree to find a tsconfig.json or jsconfig.json. This way, tests/tsconfig.json applies only to tests and is picked up automatically.

        # Playwright will choose tsconfig automatically
npx playwright test

        Or specify a single tsconfig file on the command line; Playwright uses it for every imported file, not just test files.

        # Pass a specific tsconfig
npx playwright test --tsconfig=tsconfig.test.json

        You can specify a tsconfig in the config file; it is used when loading test files, reporters and so on, but is NOT used when loading the Playwright config file itself or the files imported from it.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  tsconfig: './tsconfig.test.json',
});

        Manually compile tests with TypeScript

        Sometimes Playwright Test does not transform TypeScript code correctly, for example when you use experimental or very new TypeScript features (usually configured in tsconfig.json). In that case you can compile TypeScript yourself before handing the tests to Playwright.

        First add a tsconfig.json in the tests directory:

        {
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "ESNext",
        "module": "commonjs",
        "moduleResolution": "Node",
        "sourceMap": true,
        "outDir": "../tests-out",
    }
}

        In package.json add two scripts:

        {
  "scripts": {
    "pretest": "tsc --incremental -p tests/tsconfig.json",
    "test": "playwright test -c tests-out"
  }
}

        The pretest script runs TypeScript on the tests. test runs the generated tests in the tests-out directory; the -c argument tells the runner to look for tests in tests-out. After that, npm run test will build the tests and then run them.

        1. npm run testnpm runs pretest first automatically
        2. pretest: tsccompiles tests/ into tests-out/
        3. playwright test -c tests-outruns the compiled JS files

        Key takeaways

        • Playwright runs TS but does not type-check; run tsc --noEmit in CI (and -w during development).
        • Only a subset of tsconfig options is supported: allowJs, baseUrl, paths, jsx*, useDefineForClassFields, references, extends.
        • It finds the nearest tsconfig for each file; force a single file with --tsconfig or the tsconfig option in the config (which does not apply to the config itself).
        • Path mapping (paths) enables import aliases such as @myhelper/*.
        • If you need a TS feature that is too new: run tsc yourself into tests-out, then run playwright test -c tests-out.

        A test has a non-critical TypeScript type error. What happens when you run npx playwright test?

        Playwright only transforms TS to JS and does not type-check. Run tsc --noEmit separately.

        The tsconfig option in playwright.config.ts is NOT used when loading which of the following?

        This tsconfig applies to test files, reporters and so on, but is not used when loading the config itself or files imported from the config.

        Fixtures (a ready-made environment for each test)

        Playwright Test is built on the concept of a fixture: each test receives exactly what it needs, and fixtures are isolated between tests. This lets you group tests by meaning instead of by shared setup.

        Introduction and built-in fixtures

        You have already used fixtures since your very first test: the { page } parameter tells the runner to set up the page fixture and pass it into the test function.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('basic test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Playwright/);
});
        FixtureTypeDescription
        pagePageIsolated page for this test run.
        contextBrowserContextIsolated context for this test; page belongs to this context. See the configuration on the test-configuration page.
        browserBrowserBrowser shared between tests to save resources.
        browserNamestringName of the browser running the test: chromium, firefox or webkit.
        requestAPIRequestContextIsolated APIRequestContext instance for this test.

        Without fixtures (traditional hooks)

        The old way: declare a variable in describe, set up TodoPage in beforeEach and clean up in afterEach. TodoPage is a Page Object that wraps page (following the Page Object Model pattern).

        TodoPage code (shared by the examples below) 
        import type { Page, Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export class TodoPage {
  private readonly inputBox: Locator;
  private readonly todoItems: Locator;

  constructor(public readonly page: Page) {
    this.inputBox = this.page.locator('input.new-todo');
    this.todoItems = this.page.getByTestId('todo-item');
  }

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/todomvc/');
  }

  async addToDo(text: string) {
    await this.inputBox.fill(text);
    await this.inputBox.press('Enter');
  }

  async remove(text: string) {
    const todo = this.todoItems.filter({ hasText: text });
    await todo.hover();
    await todo.getByLabel('Delete').click();
  }

  async removeAll() {
    while ((await this.todoItems.count()) > 0) {
      await this.todoItems.first().hover();
      await this.todoItems.getByLabel('Delete').first().click();
    }
  }
}
        import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import { TodoPage } from './todo-page';

test.describe('todo tests', () => {
  let todoPage: TodoPage;

  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    todoPage = new TodoPage(page);
    await todoPage.goto();
    await todoPage.addToDo('item1');
    await todoPage.addToDo('item2');
  });

  test.afterEach(async () => {
    await todoPage.removeAll();
  });

  test('should add an item', async () => {
    await todoPage.addToDo('my item');
  });

  test('should remove an item', async () => {
    await todoPage.remove('item1');
  });
});

        With fixtures

        The same problem as above, but with setup + teardown gathered in one place: everything before await use(...) is setup, and everything after it is teardown.

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { TodoPage } from './todo-page';

// Extend the base test with the "todoPage" fixture.
const test = base.extend<{ todoPage: TodoPage }>({
  todoPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    const todoPage = new TodoPage(page);
    await todoPage.goto();
    await todoPage.addToDo('item1');
    await todoPage.addToDo('item2');
    await use(todoPage);
    await todoPage.removeAll();
  },
});

test('should add an item', async ({ todoPage }) => {
  await todoPage.addToDo('my item');
});

test('should remove an item', async ({ todoPage }) => {
  await todoPage.remove('item1');
});

        Advantages of fixtures over before/after hooks:

        • Encapsulate: setup and teardown live in the same place. If you have an after-hook that cleans up something a before-hook created, consider turning it into a fixture.
        • Reusable: define it once and use it in every test file (just like the built-in page fixture works).
        • On-demand: declare as many as you like; the runner only sets up the fixtures a test actually needs.
        • Composable: fixtures depend on each other to build more complex behavior.
        • Flexible: a test picks the combination of fixtures that suits it without affecting other tests.
        • Simplify grouping: no need to wrap tests in describe just for setup; group by meaning.
        1. Test requests itThe fixture name appears in the parameters of a test/hook
        2. Set up dependenciesFixtures it depends on are set up first (e.g. page)
        3. SetupCode before await use() runs
        4. use(value)The value is passed into the test; the test runs
        5. Test finishesafterEach runs, the fixture is no longer used
        6. TeardownCode after await use() runs, in the reverse order of setup

        Creating a fixture

        Use test.extend() to create a new test object that contains your fixtures. The example below creates todoPage and settingsPage following the Page Object Model.

        import type { Page } from '@playwright/test';

export class SettingsPage {
  constructor(public readonly page: Page) {}

  async switchToDarkMode() {
    // ...
  }
}
        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { TodoPage } from './todo-page';
import { SettingsPage } from './settings-page';

// Declare the types of the fixtures.
type MyFixtures = {
  todoPage: TodoPage;
  settingsPage: SettingsPage;
};

// This new "test" can be used in multiple files, and each of them will get the fixtures.
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({
  todoPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Set up fixture.
    const todoPage = new TodoPage(page);
    await todoPage.goto();
    await todoPage.addToDo('item1');
    await todoPage.addToDo('item2');

    // Pass the value into the test.
    await use(todoPage);

    // Clean up fixture.
    await todoPage.removeAll();
  },

  settingsPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(new SettingsPage(page));
  },
});
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
        Naming rules. A custom fixture name must start with a letter or an underscore, and contain only letters, digits and underscores.

        Using a fixture

        Just mention the fixture name in the test function's parameters. Fixtures can also be used in hooks and in other fixtures; with TypeScript they are type-checked.

        import { test, expect } from './my-test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ settingsPage }) => {
  await settingsPage.switchToDarkMode();
});

test('basic test', async ({ todoPage, page }) => {
  await todoPage.addToDo('something nice');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('todo-title')).toContainText(['something nice']);
});

        Overriding fixtures

        You can override an existing fixture. The example below overrides page to automatically open baseURL; the page fixture can depend on other built-in fixtures/options such as baseURL.

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  page: async ({ baseURL, page }, use) => {
    await page.goto(baseURL);
    await use(page);
  },
});

        Now you can configure baseURL in the config, or locally in a file with test.use():

        test.use({ baseURL: 'https://playwright.dev' });

        A fixture can also be replaced completely, for example to provide your own storageState:

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  storageState: async ({}, use) => {
    const cookie = await getAuthCookie();
    await use({ cookies: [cookie] });
  },
});

        Worker-scoped fixtures

        Playwright runs test files in worker processes. Just as test-scoped fixtures are set up for each test, a worker fixture is set up once per worker process: the ideal place to set up services, run servers and so on. The runner reuses a worker for several files if the worker fixtures match (identical environment).

        Example: an account fixture shared by all tests in the same worker (a unique username thanks to workerInfo.workerIndex), and an override of page to sign in. Note the tuple syntax and { scope: 'worker' }; the types of worker fixtures are passed as the second generic parameter.

        import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type Account = { username: string; password: string };

// The worker fixture type is the second generic parameter.
export const test = base.extend<{}, { account: Account }>({
  account: [async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
    const username = 'user' + workerInfo.workerIndex;
    const password = 'verysecure';

    const page = await browser.newPage();
    await page.goto('/signup');
    await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
    await page.getByText('Sign up').click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('result')).toHaveText('Success');
    await page.close(); // remember to clean up

    await use({ username, password });
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  page: async ({ page, account }, use) => {
    const { username, password } = account;
    await page.goto('/signin');
    await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
    await page.getByText('Sign in').click();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('userinfo')).toHaveText(username);
    await use(page);
  },
});
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
        Separate timeout. A worker-scoped fixture has its own timeout equal to the default test timeout; change it with the timeout option (see the Fixture timeout section).

        Automatic fixtures

        An automatic fixture is set up for every test/worker even if the test does not list it. Use the tuple syntax with { auto: true }. Example: automatically attach a debug log when a test fails, using the TestInfo object to learn the test metadata.

        import debug from 'debug';
import fs from 'fs';
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ saveLogs: void }>({
  saveLogs: [async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    // Collect logs while the test runs.
    const logs: string[] = [];
    debug.log = (...args) => logs.push(args.map(String).join(''));
    debug.enable('myserver');

    await use();

    // After the test: check whether it passed or failed.
    if (testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus) {
      // outputPath() guarantees a unique file name.
      const logFile = testInfo.outputPath('logs.txt');
      await fs.promises.writeFile(logFile, logs.join('\n'), 'utf8');
      testInfo.attachments.push({ name: 'logs', contentType: 'text/plain', path: logFile });
    }
  }, { auto: true }],
});
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

        Fixture timeout

        A fixture is considered part of the test, so its setup/teardown time counts toward the test timeout. A slow fixture can cause a timeout; give it its own larger timeout and keep the overall test timeout small.

        import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const test = base.extend<{ slowFixture: string }>({
  slowFixture: [async ({}, use) => {
    // ... perform a slow operation ...
    await use('hello');
  }, { timeout: 60000 }],
});

test('example test', async ({ slowFixture }) => {
  // ...
});

        Unlike regular test-scoped fixtures, each worker-scoped fixture has its own timeout equal to the test timeout, and it is adjusted the same way. See also Timeouts.

        Fixtures-options (option fixtures)

        Playwright runs multiple projects with their own configuration. Use "option" fixtures to make configuration declarative and type-safe. Below we create a defaultItem option along with a todoPage fixture; note the tuple syntax and { option: true }.

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { TodoPage } from './todo-page';

// Declare the option so the config is type-checked.
export type MyOptions = {
  defaultItem: string;
};
type MyFixtures = {
  todoPage: TodoPage;
};

export const test = base.extend<MyOptions & MyFixtures>({
  // Option + default value (can be overridden in the config).
  defaultItem: ['Something nice', { option: true }],

  // todoPage depends on the option.
  todoPage: async ({ page, defaultItem }, use) => {
    const todoPage = new TodoPage(page);
    await todoPage.goto();
    await todoPage.addToDo(defaultItem);
    await use(todoPage);
    await todoPage.removeAll();
  },
});
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import type { MyOptions } from './my-test';

export default defineConfig<MyOptions>({
  projects: [
    { name: 'shopping',  use: { defaultItem: 'Buy milk' } },
    { name: 'wellbeing', use: { defaultItem: 'Exercise!' } },
  ],
});

        Array as an option value

        If the option value is an array (e.g. [{ name: 'Alice' }, { name: 'Bob' }]), you must wrap it in an extra array together with a scope when passing the value.

        type Person = { name: string };
const test = base.extend<{ persons: Person[] }>({
  // Defaults to an empty array.
  persons: [[], { option: true }],
});

const actualPersons = [{ name: 'Alice' }, { name: 'Bob' }];
test.use({
  // CORRECT: wrap in an array and pass the scope.
  persons: [actualPersons, { scope: 'test' }],
});

test.use({
  // WRONG: passing the array directly will not work.
  persons: actualPersons,
});

        Resetting an option

        Set the option to undefined to go back to the value in the config. Suppose the config has baseURL: 'https://playwright.dev':

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Configure baseURL for this file.
test.use({ baseURL: 'https://playwright.dev/docs/intro' });

test('check intro contents', async ({ page }) => {
  // Uses the baseURL "https://playwright.dev/docs/intro".
});

test.describe(() => {
  // Reset to the value in the config.
  test.use({ baseURL: undefined });

  test('can navigate to intro from the home page', async ({ page }) => {
    // Uses the baseURL "https://playwright.dev" from the config.
  });
});

        To remove the value completely (truly undefined), use the long-form fixture syntax:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Completely unset baseURL for this file.
test.use({
  baseURL: [async ({}, use) => use(undefined), { scope: 'test' }],
});

test('no base url', async ({ page }) => {
  // This test has no baseURL.
});

        Execution order

        Each fixture has a setup phase (before await use()) and a teardown phase (after it). Setup runs before the test/hook that needs it; teardown runs when the fixture is no longer used. The rules:

        • Fixture A depends on B: B is set up before A and torn down after A.
        • Non-automatic fixtures run lazily, only when a test/hook needs them.
        • Test-scoped fixtures are torn down after each test; worker-scoped ones are torn down only when the worker process ends.
        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

const test = base.extend<{
  testFixture: string,
  autoTestFixture: string,
  unusedFixture: string,
}, {
  workerFixture: string,
  autoWorkerFixture: string,
}>({
  workerFixture: [async ({ browser }, use) => {
    // workerFixture setup...
    await use('workerFixture');
    // workerFixture teardown...
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  autoWorkerFixture: [async ({ browser }, use) => {
    await use('autoWorkerFixture');
  }, { scope: 'worker', auto: true }],

  testFixture: [async ({ page, workerFixture }, use) => {
    await use('testFixture');
  }, { scope: 'test' }],

  autoTestFixture: [async ({}, use) => {
    await use('autoTestFixture');
  }, { scope: 'test', auto: true }],

  unusedFixture: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use('unusedFixture');
  }, { scope: 'test' }],
});

test.beforeAll(async () => { /* ... */ });
test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
test('first test', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
test('second test', async ({ testFixture }) => { /* ... */ });
test.afterEach(async () => { /* ... */ });
test.afterAll(async () => { /* ... */ });

        When all tests pass, the order is as follows:

        • Worker setup + beforeAll: set up browser (needed by autoWorkerFixture) → set up autoWorkerFixture (an automatic worker fixture always runs before everything else) → run beforeAll.
        • first test: set up autoTestFixture → set up page (needed by beforeEach) → beforeEach → test → afterEach → tear down page → tear down autoTestFixture.
        • second test: set up autoTestFixture → page → beforeEach → set up workerFixture (needed by testFixture) → set up testFixture → test → afterEach → tear down testFixture → page → autoTestFixture.
        • afterAll + worker teardown: afterAll → tear down workerFixture → autoWorkerFixture → browser.
        Worker setupbrowser, autoWorkerFixture
        beforeAllruns once
        first test: setupautoTestFixture, page, beforeEach
        first test runsafterEach, then teardown of page, autoTestFixture
        second test: setupautoTestFixture, page, beforeEach, workerFixture (lazy), testFixture
        second test runsafterEach, teardown of testFixture, page, autoTestFixture
        afterAllthen teardown of workerFixture, autoWorkerFixture, browser

        A few observations:

        • page and autoTestFixture are set up/torn down for each test (test-scoped).
        • unusedFixture is never set up because no test/hook uses it.
        • testFixture depends on workerFixture, so it pulls in its setup.
        • workerFixture is set up lazily right before the second test but is torn down only once when the worker shuts down.
        • autoWorkerFixture is set up for beforeAll, whereas autoTestFixture is not.

        Combining fixtures from multiple modules (mergeTests)

        Merge fixtures from multiple files/modules with mergeTests:

        import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as dbTest } from 'database-test-utils';
import { test as a11yTest } from 'a11y-test-utils';

export const test = mergeTests(dbTest, a11yTest);
        import { test } from './fixtures';

test('passes', async ({ database, page, a11y }) => {
  // use the database and a11y fixtures.
});

        Box fixtures

        By default, custom fixtures appear as separate steps in UI mode, the Trace Viewer, reports, and even in error messages. For frequently used fixtures, that is noise. "Boxing" hides these steps.

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  helperFixture: [async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    // ...
  }, { box: true }],
});

        Useful for helper fixtures that are not interesting, for example an automatic fixture that sets up common data. Use box: 'self' to hide only the fixture itself while keeping its inner steps in the report.

        Custom fixture title

        Instead of the fixture name, you can set a title that is displayed in the report and in error messages.

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  innerFixture: [async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    // ...
  }, { title: 'my fixture' }],
});

        Adding global beforeEach/afterEach hooks

        test.beforeEach/afterEach only apply to tests in the same file and the same describe. To have a hook run for every test in every file, declare it as an auto fixture:

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ forEachTest: void }>({
  forEachTest: [async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Runs before each test.
    await page.goto('http://localhost:8000');
    await use();
    // Runs after each test.
    console.log('Last URL:', page.url());
  }, { auto: true }], // starts automatically for every test
});
        import { test } from './fixtures';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('basic', async ({ page }) => {
  expect(page).toHaveURL('http://localhost:8000');
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
});

        Adding global beforeAll/afterAll hooks

        beforeAll/afterAll run once per worker process within the same file/describe. To have a hook that runs in every file, use an auto fixture with scope: 'worker':

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{}, { forEachWorker: void }>({
  forEachWorker: [async ({}, use) => {
    // Runs before all tests in the worker process.
    console.log(`Starting test worker ${test.info().workerIndex}`);
    await use();
    // Runs after all tests in the worker process.
    console.log(`Stopping test worker ${test.info().workerIndex}`);
  }, { scope: 'worker', auto: true }], // starts automatically for every worker
});
        Note. The fixture still runs once per worker process; you just do not have to declare it again in every file.
        Fixture options (2nd tuple element)Meaning
        scope: 'test' | 'worker'Set up per test (default) or per worker.
        auto: trueAlways set up, even if the test does not mention it.
        option: trueThe fixture is an option; set its value in the config/test.use.
        timeout: msA separate timeout for the fixture.
        box: true | 'self'Hides the fixture's steps from the report/trace.
        title: stringCustom display name.

        Key takeaways

        • Fixture = setup + await use(value) + teardown, gathered in one place, set up on demand (lazily) and isolated between tests.
        • Create with test.extend(); merge several sets with mergeTests; override built-in fixtures (page, storageState...) when needed.
        • scope: 'worker' sets up once per worker; auto: true runs even when not mentioned; option: true enables per-project configuration.
        • Dependencies are set up first and torn down last; an unused fixture is never set up.
        • Fixtures count toward the test timeout; a slow fixture should have its own timeout. Use box/title to keep reports tidy.
        • For global hooks across all files: use an auto fixture (test-scoped in place of beforeEach/afterEach, worker-scoped in place of beforeAll/afterAll).
        Which fixture is set up only once per worker?
        A fixture with { scope: 'worker' }; it is torn down when the worker process shuts down.
        How do you make a fixture run for every test even if it is not declared?
        { auto: true }.
        How do you hide a helper fixture from the trace/report?
        { box: true } (or box: 'self' to keep the inner steps).

        The testFixture fixture depends on workerFixture. What is the correct setup/teardown order?

        A dependency is always set up before, and torn down after, the fixture that depends on it; since workerFixture has worker scope, it is torn down only once when the worker finishes.

        An option fixture has an array value. What is the correct way to pass it in test.use?

        The array must be wrapped in an extra array together with a scope; otherwise Playwright mistakes it for a tuple that defines a fixture.

        Annotations (labeling and tagging tests)

        Playwright supports tags and annotations that show up in reports: skip, fail, fixme, slow, only, tags for filtering, and custom annotations for notes (issue, category...). They help you manage tests by configuration, browser, or stability.

        Introduction: built-in annotations

        AnnotationBehaviorUse when
        test.skip()Marks the test as irrelevant; it is not run.The test does not apply in a given configuration.
        test.fail()Marks the test as expected to fail; Playwright still runs it and confirms it fails, and reports an error if it passes.A known bug, and you want to know when it gets fixed.
        test.fixme()Marks the test as failing but does not run it.The test is slow or crashes.
        test.slow()Marks the test as slow and multiplies its timeout by 3.The test is valid but takes a long time.

        Annotations can be applied to a single test or to a group. They can be conditional (applied when the condition is truthy, and they can use fixtures), and a single test can have several annotations, which may differ per configuration.

        Focus a test (only)

        When a test is focused, only the focused tests run.

        test.only('focus this test', async ({ page }) => {
  // Only focused tests run across the whole project.
});
        Be careful. Don't commit test.only; on CI, enable forbidOnly in the config so the run fails early if one slips through.

        Skip a test

        test.skip('skip this test', async ({ page }) => {
  // This test does not run
});

        Conditional skip

        Call test.skip(condition, reason) inside the test body.

        test('skip this test', async ({ page, browserName }) => {
  test.skip(browserName === 'firefox', 'Still working on it');
});

        Group tests (describe)

        Group tests to give them a logical name or to scope before/after hooks.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('two tests', () => {
  test('one', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });

  test('two', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });
});

        Tag tests

        Add tags such as @fast or @slow to filter in the report or to run only tests with certain tags. There are two ways: pass a details object when declaring the test, or add an @... token to the title. A tag must start with @.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('test login page', {
  tag: '@fast',
}, async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

test('test full report @slow', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        Tag a whole group, or use multiple tags:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('group', {
  tag: '@report',
}, () => {
  test('test report header', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });

  test('test full report', {
    tag: ['@slow', '@vrt'],
  }, async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });
});

        Run tests by tag with --grep; exclude them with --grep-invert:

        npx playwright test --grep @fast
npx playwright test --grep-invert @fast
# OR: has either tag
npx playwright test --grep "@fast|@slow"
# AND: has both tags (regex lookahead)
npx playwright test --grep "(?=.*@fast)(?=.*@slow)"
        npx playwright test --grep "@fast"
npx playwright test --grep-invert "@fast"
# OR
npx playwright test --grep --% "@fast^|@slow"
# AND
npx playwright test --grep "(?=.*@fast)(?=.*@slow)"
        npx playwright test --grep @fast
npx playwright test --grep-invert @fast
:: OR
npx playwright test --grep "@fast^|@slow"

        You can also filter directly in the config through testConfig.grep and testProject.grep (for example, filtering per project).

        1. Add tagstag: '@fast' or "@slow" in the title
        2. Run the CLInpx playwright test --grep @fast
        3. Match the regexgrep is matched against each test's title + tags
        4. Filteronly matching tests are included in the run (grep-invert does the opposite)
        5. Reporttags are shown in the report

        Annotate tests (type and description)

        When you need more information than a tag provides, use an annotation with a type and a description; these are available in the reporter API. The HTML reporter shows all annotations, except those whose type starts with _.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('test login page', {
  annotation: {
    type: 'issue',
    description: 'https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/23180',
  },
}, async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        Annotate a whole group, or use multiple annotations:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('report tests', {
  annotation: { type: 'category', description: 'report' },
}, () => {
  test('test report header', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });

  test('test full report', {
    annotation: [
      { type: 'issue', description: 'https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/23180' },
      { type: 'performance', description: 'very slow test!' },
    ],
  }, async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });
});

        Conditional skip for a whole group

        Pass a callback to test.skip() at the describe level, e.g. to run the group only in Chromium.

        test.describe('chromium only', () => {
  test.skip(({ browserName }) => browserName !== 'chromium', 'Chromium only!');

  test.beforeAll(async () => {
    // This hook only runs in Chromium.
  });

  test('test 1', async ({ page }) => {
    // Only runs in Chromium.
  });

  test('test 2', async ({ page }) => {
    // Only runs in Chromium.
  });
});

        Using fixme in beforeEach

        To avoid running beforeEach, put the annotation right inside the hook.

        test.beforeEach(async ({ page, isMobile }) => {
  test.fixme(isMobile, 'Settings page does not work in mobile yet');

  await page.goto('http://localhost:3000/settings');
});

test('user profile', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByText('My Profile').click();
  // ...
});

        Runtime annotations

        While a test is running, push extra annotations into test.info().annotations.

        test('example test', async ({ page, browser }) => {
  test.info().annotations.push({
    type: 'browser version',
    description: browser.version(),
  });

  // ...
});
        Best practice. Use tags for filtering and selective runs (smoke, regression), annotations for context (issue links), and test.fixme instead of commenting tests out so they still appear in the report.

        Key points

        • skip does not run; fixme does not run (broken/slow test); fail still runs and expects a failure; slow triples the timeout.
        • Tags start with @, are declared with { tag } or in the title, and are filtered with --grep/--grep-invert (OR with |, AND with lookaheads).
        • An annotation has a type + description; the HTML report hides types that start with _.
        • Conditions can use fixtures (browserName, isMobile); call them in a test, a hook, or a describe.
        • Add annotations at runtime via test.info().annotations.push(...).

        Which command runs the tests that have BOTH the @fast and @slow tags?

        The | character is OR. AND uses a regex lookahead for each tag.

        What is the difference between test.fail() and test.fixme()?

        fail confirms the test is still broken (and reports an error if it passes); fixme skips running it, which is useful when a test is slow or crashes.

        Parallelism

        Playwright Test runs tests in parallel using multiple worker processes. By default it parallelizes by file; you can tune the number of workers, parallelism within a file, serial mode, locks on shared resources, and execution order.

        Introduction

        • By default, test files run in parallel; tests in the same file run sequentially, in the same worker.
        • test.describe.configure lets you run tests within a single file in parallel.
        • fullyParallel (config or project) makes every test in every file run in parallel.
        • To disable parallelism: limit to a single worker.

        You can also control the number of workers and cap the number of failing tests in the whole suite to save resources.

        Worker processes

        All tests run in worker processes: independent OS processes orchestrated by the runner. All workers have an identical environment, and each worker launches its own browser.

        • Workers do not communicate with each other.
        • The runner reuses a worker as much as possible, so several test files often run one after another in the same worker.
        • A worker is always shut down after a failed test to guarantee a clean environment for the following tests (see Retries).
        1. Runner startsCollects test files and creates N workers (N defaults to the CPU count)
        2. Assign filesEach worker gets a test file, and each worker has its own browser
        3. Run sequentially within a fileTests in a file run in declaration order
        4. File finishedThe worker takes the next file (reused if fixtures match)
        5. A test failsThe worker is shut down and a new worker (same parallelIndex) is created
        6. AggregateThe runner collects results from all workers

        Limit the number of workers

        The maximum number of workers can be controlled from the command line or the config:

        npx playwright test --workers 4
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Limit workers on CI, use the default locally
  workers: process.env.CI ? 2 : undefined,
});

        Disable parallelism

        To allow only one worker, set workers: 1 in the config or pass --workers=1.

        npx playwright test --workers=1

        Parallelize tests in a single file

        By default, tests in a single file run in order. If they are independent, use test.describe.configure. Note: parallel tests run in separate worker processes and cannot share state or global variables; each test runs all the relevant hooks for itself, including beforeAll and afterAll.

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' });

test('runs in parallel 1', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
test('runs in parallel 2', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });

        Or enable fully-parallel mode for all tests in the config:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  fullyParallel: true,
});

        Or only for some projects:

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // run all tests in all files of this project in parallel
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
      fullyParallel: true,
    },
  ],
});

        Serial mode

        Mark interdependent tests as serial: if one test fails, the subsequent tests are skipped, and the whole group is retried together.

        Not recommended. It is better to make tests isolated so they can run independently.
        import { test, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

// Mark the whole file as serial.
test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

let page: Page;

test.beforeAll(async ({ browser }) => {
  page = await browser.newPage();
});

test.afterAll(async () => {
  await page.close();
});

test('runs first', async () => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
});

test('runs second', async () => {
  await page.getByText('Get Started').click();
});

        Test locks (locking shared resources)

        Some tests access resources that do not support concurrent access (external services, global account settings). Declare a named lock: tests that share a lock name never run at the same time, while other tests still run in parallel. Locks work across files, workers, and projects.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('update user settings', { lock: 'user-settings' }, async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Never runs concurrently with 'update user settings',
// even in a different project.
test('rename user', { lock: 'user-settings' }, async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        A test can declare multiple locks and only runs once it can acquire all of them. You can declare locks for a whole group with test.describe, and they apply to every test inside.

        test('reset the database', { lock: ['database', 'external-api'] }, async () => {
  // ...
});

        You can also add locks to the current file/describe with test.describe.configure; calling it repeatedly adds locks rather than clearing the old ones.

        test.describe.configure({ lock: 'user-settings' });

        Playwright acquires all of a test's locks before the test starts and releases them when it finishes.

        The built-in -exclusive- lock runs a test in isolation: it only starts when no other test is running, and no other test starts until it is done. This is useful for tests that are sensitive to concurrent activity (performance measurements, restarting a shared service).

        test('restart the server', { lock: '-exclusive-' }, async () => {
  // No other test runs while this test is running.
});
        Note. In default and serial modes, all tests in a file run together in order, so a lock declared on any test is held for the entire duration of the file.
        1. Test A needs the lockWorker 1 acquires the 'user-settings' lock
        2. Test B has the same lockWorker 2 must wait, while unrelated tests keep running
        3. A finishesThe lock is released
        4. B acquires the lockB starts running

        Opt out of fully parallel mode

        If the config enables fullyParallel but some tests still need to run in the default mode, override the mode per describe:

        test.describe('runs in parallel with other describes', () => {
  test.describe.configure({ mode: 'default' });
  test('in order 1', async ({ page }) => {});
  test('in order 2', async ({ page }) => {});
});

        Avoid shared state in parallel tests

        Each worker has its own isolated BrowserContext, so cookies, storage, and in-memory variables are already separated. Flakiness comes from state that lives outside a test. Three recipes:

        Give each test its own backend data

        Two tests that create/modify the same record will race each other. Generate a unique ID from testInfo.testId:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('creates an order', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  const orderId = `order-${testInfo.testId}`;
  await page.goto(`/orders/new?id=${orderId}`);
  await expect(page.getByText(orderId)).toBeVisible();
});

        If many tests share one dataset, create it once per worker (see the section "Isolate data between parallel workers" below).

        Write to unique file paths

        Multiple tests writing to the same path will overwrite each other. testInfo.outputPath() returns a path tied to the current test:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'fs';

test('exports a CSV', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  const file = testInfo.outputPath('export.csv');
  await fs.promises.writeFile(file, 'a,b,c', 'utf8');
});

        Keep tests independent

        Above all, keep tests isolated. Tests that leak state through module-level variables or depend on another test's side effects will work fine when run sequentially but break when run in parallel or in a shuffled order. Set up everything a test needs inside that test or in a fixture, and never rely on another test having run first.

        Shard tests across multiple machines

        Playwright can shard the suite to run it across multiple machines (details in Sharding).

        npx playwright test --shard=2/3

        Limit failures and fail fast

        Set maxFailures in the config or --max-failures on the CLI: once this many tests have failed, Playwright stops and skips the tests that haven't run yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on a suite that is already broken.

        npx playwright test --max-failures=10
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Limit the number of failures on CI to save resources
  maxFailures: process.env.CI ? 10 : undefined,
});

        Worker index and parallel index

        Each worker process has two ids: a unique worker index starting from 0, and a parallel index in the range 0 to workers - 1. When a worker restarts (e.g. after a failed test), the new worker keeps the same parallelIndex but gets a new workerIndex.

        You can read them through the environment variables process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX and process.env.TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX, or through testInfo.workerIndex and testInfo.parallelIndex.

        Isolate data between parallel workers

        Use workerIndex to isolate user data in the database between workers; all tests in one worker share one user. Create a playwright/fixtures.ts file with a dbUserName fixture (worker-scoped):

        import { test as baseTest, expect } from '@playwright/test';
// Utilities for managing users in the project's test database.
import { createUserInTestDatabase, deleteUserFromTestDatabase } from './my-db-utils';

export * from '@playwright/test';
export const test = baseTest.extend<{}, { dbUserName: string }>({
  // Returns a unique user name for the worker.
  dbUserName: [async ({ }, use) => {
    const userName = `user-${test.info().workerIndex}`;
    await createUserInTestDatabase(userName);
    await use(userName);
    // Clean up when the tests are done.
    await deleteUserFromTestDatabase(userName);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

        Each test file imports test from the fixtures file instead of from @playwright/test:

        // Important: import our fixtures.
import { test, expect } from '../playwright/fixtures';

test('test', async ({ dbUserName }) => {
  // Use the user name in the test.
});

        Control test order

        Within a file, tests run in declaration order (unless you parallelize within the file). The order between files is not guaranteed because files run in parallel by default. If you disable parallelism, you can control the order by naming files alphabetically or by using a "test list" file.

        Sort files alphabetically

        When parallelism is disabled, files run in alphabetical order; use a naming convention such as 001-user-signin-flow.spec.ts, 002-create-new-document.spec.ts.

        Use a "test list" file

        Not recommended. Test lists are only supported on a best-effort basis; some features such as the VS Code Extension and tracing may not work correctly.

        Put the tests inside a wrapper function in several files:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export default function createTests() {
  test('feature-a example test', async ({ page }) => {
    // ... tests go here
  });
}
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

export default function createTests() {
  test.use({ viewport: { width: 500, height: 500 } });

  test('feature-b example test', async ({ page }) => {
    // ... tests go here
  });
}

        Create a test list that controls the order: run feature-b first, then feature-a. Each file is wrapped in test.describe() that calls the test-defining function, so test.use() only affects the tests of that file.

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';
import featureBTests from './feature-b.spec.ts';
import featureATests from './feature-a.spec.ts';

test.describe(featureBTests);
test.describe(featureATests);

        Then disable parallelism (workers = 1) and point to the test list:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  workers: 1,
  testMatch: 'test.list.ts',
});
        Note. Don't define tests directly in helper files: the tests would depend on the order of the import/require statements. Wrap tests in a function that the test list calls explicitly.
        GoalHow
        Limit workers--workers N or workers in the config
        Disable parallelism--workers=1
        Parallel within a filetest.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' })
        Fully parallelfullyParallel: true (config or project)
        Interdependent testsmode: 'serial' (use sparingly)
        Shared resources{ lock: 'name' }, '-exclusive-'
        Stop earlymaxFailures / --max-failures

        Key points

        • Default: files run in parallel, tests within a file run sequentially; a worker is an independent OS process, they don't communicate, and a worker is shut down after a failed test.
        • workers limits the number of processes; fullyParallel or mode: 'parallel' parallelizes down to the test level; use mode: 'serial' only as a last resort.
        • Parallel tests don't share state; use testInfo.testId, outputPath(), and a worker fixture + workerIndex to isolate data.
        • lock prevents tests that share a resource from running at the same time; -exclusive- runs a test alone.
        • Order is only guaranteed within a single file; to get an order between files you must disable parallelism.

        When you use test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' }), which statement is true?

        Parallel tests are distributed across different worker processes, so they cannot share global variables; hooks also run separately for each test.

        Two tests modify the same global setting of an external service. What is the best way to avoid running them at the same time?

        A lock only serializes the tests that share the resource; other tests still run in parallel.

        Sharding (splitting tests across multiple machines)

        Sharding splits the suite into several parts (shards) that run as independent jobs, usually on multiple CI machines, to cut total run time. You then merge the shards' blob reports into a single HTML report.

        Introduction

        By default Playwright runs files in parallel and makes full use of the machine's CPU. To parallelize even further, you run tests on several machines at once: this is "sharding". Each shard is like a separate job that runs independently and uses the cores available to it; in CI, each shard can be one job.

        Shard tests across multiple machines

        Pass --shard=x/y: x is the shard index (starting from 1) and y is the total number of shards. For example, to split into 4 parts:

        npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4

        If you run these 4 commands in parallel on different jobs, the suite finishes roughly 4 times faster. Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can run in parallel; by default that means sharding by file.

        1. Matrix jobshardIndex 1..4, shardTotal 4
        2. Each job runsnpx playwright test --shard=i/4
        3. Blob reportEach shard produces blob-report/report-...-i.zip
        4. Upload artifactblob-report-i is uploaded to artifacts (if: !cancelled())
        5. merge-reports jobneeds: [playwright-tests], downloads all artifacts into all-blob-reports
        6. merge-reportsnpx playwright merge-reports --reporter html
        7. HTML reportA single report in playwright-report

        Balancing shards

        There are two levels of granularity depending on whether you enable fullyParallel; this affects how tests are balanced across shards.

        With fullyParallel: trueWithout fullyParallel
        Unit of splittingIndividual testsIndividual files (the same file can land in different shards in different projects)
        BalanceEvenly distributed, optimalDepends on file size; a shard can be heavy, light, or even empty
        Recommendation. Use fullyParallel: true for an even distribution, especially on CI. Otherwise, keep test files small and of similar size.
        • Statically skipped tests (test.skip, test.fixme) are not counted when balancing shards because they don't run.

        Merging reports from multiple shards

        Each shard has its own report. To get one combined report, merge them. Start by adding the blob reporter when running on CI:

        export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
});

        A blob report contains information about every test that ran, the results, and all attachments (traces, screenshot diffs). Blob reports can be merged and converted to any Playwright report. By default it is written to the blob-report directory (see Blob reporter).

        To merge: put the blob files into one directory (e.g. all-blob-reports). Blob file names contain the shard number, so they don't collide. Then run:

        npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports

        The result is a standard HTML report in the playwright-report directory.

        GitHub Actions example

        GitHub Actions supports splitting tests into multiple jobs with jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix, running one job per combination. Here is an example that runs on 4 machines in parallel and then merges:

        1. Add a matrix with shardTotal: [4] and shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4].
        2. Run the tests with --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}.
        3. Upload the blob report to GitHub Actions Artifacts so other jobs can use it.
        name: Playwright Tests
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
jobs:
  playwright-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        shardTotal: [4]
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
      with:
        node-version: lts/*
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    - name: Install Playwright browsers
      run: npx playwright install --with-deps

    - name: Run Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}

    - name: Upload blob report to GitHub Actions Artifacts
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
      with:
        name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
        path: blob-report
        retention-days: 1

        After the shards finish, a separate job merges the reports. To guarantee the order, merge-reports depends on (needs) the playwright-tests job:

        jobs:
...
  merge-reports:
    # Merge after playwright-tests, even if some shards fail
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    needs: [playwright-tests]

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
      with:
        node-version: lts/*
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Download blob reports from GitHub Actions Artifacts
      uses: actions/download-artifact@v5
      with:
        path: all-blob-reports
        pattern: blob-report-*
        merge-multiple: true

    - name: Merge into HTML Report
      run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports

    - name: Upload HTML report
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
      with:
        name: html-report--attempt-${{ github.run_attempt }}
        path: playwright-report
        retention-days: 14

        The report is now merged and available in the Artifacts tab of GitHub Actions.

        Merging reports from multiple environments

        If you run the same set of tests on several environments (rather than splitting tests across machines), you need to tell the environments apart. Set tag in the config to tag every test with the environment name; this tag is automatically picked up by the blob report and the merge tool.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
  tag: process.env.CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME, // for example "@APIv2"
});

        Merge-reports CLI

        npx playwright merge-reports path/to/blob-reports-dir reads all the blob reports in the directory and combines them into one report. When merging reports from different operating systems, you must provide an explicit merge config to determine the root directory of the tests.

        OptionMeaning
        --reporter reporter-to-useThe report to produce; separate multiple reporters with commas.
        --config path/to/configA config file containing the output reporters; use it to pass extra configuration to the output reporters. It can differ from the config used when generating the blobs.
         
        npx playwright merge-reports --reporter=html,github ./blob-reports
npx playwright merge-reports --config=merge.config.ts ./blob-reports
        export default {
  testDir: 'e2e',
  reporter: [['html', { open: 'never' }]],
};

        Key points

        • --shard=x/y: x is the current shard (starting from 1), y is the total; run the shards in parallel on different jobs/machines.
        • Enable fullyParallel: true to split by test, which gives the best balance; otherwise the split is by file.
        • On CI, use the blob reporter, upload each shard's blob, then merge-reports into HTML.
        • The merge job must needs the shard job and use if: ${{ !cancelled() }} so you still get a report when a shard fails.
        • Multiple environments: set tag in the config; different OSes: you need an explicit merge config.

        The suite has a few very large files and many small ones, and the shards are unevenly loaded. What is the simplest improvement?

        Without fullyParallel, shards are split by file, so large files cause imbalance; fullyParallel splits at the level of individual tests.

        Which reporter should each shard use so the results can later be merged into one HTML report?

        A blob report contains the full details of the run (including attachments) so it can be merged and converted to any report format.

        Retries (automatically re-running failed tests)

        Retries automatically re-run a test when it fails, which helps deal with flaky tests (sometimes fail, sometimes pass). Understanding how the worker is restarted after a failure will help you understand how hooks and state behave during a retry.

        Introduction

        Test retries are configured in the config file (or the CLI). They are useful when a test fails intermittently.

        Failures: what happens when a test fails

        Tests run in worker processes (independent OS processes with an identical environment, and each worker has its own browser). Consider this snippet:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('suite', () => {
  test.beforeAll(async () => { /* ... */ });
  test('first good', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
  test('second flaky', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
  test('third good', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
  test.afterAll(async () => { /* ... */ });
});

        When all tests pass, they run one after another in the same worker:

        • Worker starts → beforeAll → first good passes → second flaky passes → third good passes → afterAll.

        When a test fails, Playwright discards the entire worker along with its browser and starts a new worker; testing continues from the next test:

        • Worker #1: beforeAll → first good passes → second flaky fails → afterAll.
        • Worker #2: beforeAll runs again → third good passes → afterAll.

        When retries are enabled, the second worker begins by re-running the failed test and then continues:

        • Worker #1: beforeAll → first good passes → second flaky fails → afterAll.
        • Worker #2: beforeAll runs again → second flaky is retried and passes → third good passes → afterAll.

        This mechanism works perfectly with independent tests and ensures that a failing test doesn't affect healthy ones.

        1. Worker #1 runsbeforeAll, first good (pass)
        2. second flaky FAILSafterAll runs; worker #1 is discarded along with its browser
        3. Worker #2 startsNew process + browser, beforeAll runs again
        4. Retrysecond flaky runs again, testInfo.retry = 1
        5. Pass: flakyMarked flaky (failed the first time, then passed)
        6. Continuethird good passes, afterAll

        Configuring retries

        By default, failed tests are not retried. When enabled, a failed test is re-run several times until it passes or the maximum number of retries is reached.

        # Give failing tests 3 retry attempts
npx playwright test --retries=3
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Give failing tests 3 retry attempts
  retries: 3,
});

        Playwright Test classifies tests as follows:

        CategoryMeaning
        passedPassed on the very first run.
        flakyFailed the first time but passed on a retry.
        failedFailed the first time and failed all the retries.
         
        Running 3 tests using 1 worker

  ✓ example.spec.ts:4:2 › first passes (438ms)
  x example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky (691ms)
  ✓ example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky (522ms)
  ✓ example.spec.ts:6:2 › third passes (932ms)

  1 flaky
    example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky
  2 passed (4s)

        Detect a retry at runtime with testInfo.retry (usable in a test, hook, or fixture). For example, clearing a server-side cache before retrying:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('my test', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  if (testInfo.retry)
    await cleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();
  // ...
});

        Specify retries for a group of tests or a file with test.describe.configure:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe(() => {
  // All tests in this group get 2 retries.
  test.describe.configure({ retries: 2 });

  test('test 1', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });

  test('test 2', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });
});

        Conditional retries

        The number of retries can depend on the error. Provide a list of entries, each with a count and an optional condition (a regex). After each failure, the largest count among the entries whose condition matches that attempt's error message is applied; an entry without a condition always applies.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  retries: [
    // Retry every failure once.
    { count: 1 },
    // Retry up to three times when the browser or worker crashes.
    { count: 3, condition: /Target crashed|worker process exited unexpectedly/ },
  ],
});

        Worker crashes and timeouts are matched by their error message like any other failure. The most recent failure decides: a test that first crashes and later fails on an assertion only gets the retry count for assertion errors.

        Serial mode

        Use test.describe.serial (or mode: 'serial') to group interdependent tests and make sure they always run together, in order. If one test fails, the subsequent tests are skipped. The whole group is retried together.

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

test.beforeAll(async () => { /* ... */ });
test('first good', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
test('second flaky', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
test('third good', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });

        Without retries, the tests after the failing one are skipped:

        • Worker #1: beforeAll → first good passes → second flaky fails → third good is skipped entirely.

        With retries, the whole group is run again:

        • Worker #1: beforeAll → first good passes → second flaky fails → third good is skipped.
        • Worker #2: beforeAll runs again → first good passes again → second flaky passes → third good passes.
        Note. It is usually better to make tests isolated so they can run and be retried independently and efficiently.

        Reuse a single page between tests

        By default each test gets an isolated Page. If you want to share one Page across several tests, create it yourself in beforeAll and close it in afterAll (combined with serial mode).

        import { test, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' });

let page: Page;

test.beforeAll(async ({ browser }) => {
  page = await browser.newPage();
});

test.afterAll(async () => {
  await page.close();
});

test('runs first', async () => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
});

test('runs second', async () => {
  await page.getByText('Get Started').click();
});
        Don't overuse retries. Retries hide flakiness; use the report (the flaky status) to find and fix the root cause instead of just increasing the retry count.

        Key points

        • A failed test => the worker (and browser) is discarded and a new worker starts; beforeAll runs again in the new worker.
        • Retries are off by default; enable them with --retries=N or retries in the config; configure per group with describe.configure.
        • Outcomes: passed, flaky (passed on retry), failed. testInfo.retry tells you which retry attempt this is.
        • retries can be a list of { count, condition } to retry depending on the error (the most recent failure decides).
        • Serial mode: when one test fails, the rest are skipped and the whole group is retried together; prefer isolated tests.

        A test in the middle of the suite fails and retries are enabled. What happens to the worker?

        Playwright always shuts down the worker after a failed test to keep the environment clean; the new worker starts with the retried test (beforeAll runs again).

        A test fails on the 1st attempt and passes on the 2nd (a retry). How does the report classify it?

        flaky = failed on the first run but passed on a retry.

        Timeouts (the different kinds of time limits)

        Playwright Test has several configurable timeouts for different kinds of work: the test, assertions (expect), the whole run, actions, navigation, hooks, and fixtures. Knowing which one applies where helps you read timeout errors and adjust the right setting.

        TimeoutDefaultDescriptionConfigure / override
        Test timeout30_000 msTimeout for each testConfig: { timeout: 60_000 }
        Test: test.setTimeout(120_000)
        Expect timeout5_000 msTimeout for each assertionConfig: { expect: { timeout: 10_000 } }
        Assertion: expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 })

        Test timeout

        Each test has a timeout, 30 seconds by default. The time spent in the test function, fixture setup, and the beforeEach hooks counts toward the test timeout. A test that runs over the limit produces this error:

        example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================

Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded.

        A separate timeout (with the same value) is shared by fixture teardown and afterEach after the test function has finished. The same timeout value also applies to beforeAll/afterAll, but they do not share time with any test.

        1. Fixture setupCounts toward the test timeout
        2. beforeEachCounts toward the test timeout
        3. Test functionCounts toward the test timeout
        4. afterEach + fixture teardownUse a separate budget with the same value
        5. beforeAll/afterAllSeparate timeout, not shared with tests

        Set the test timeout in the config

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  timeout: 120_000,
});

        Set the timeout for a single test

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('slow test', async ({ page }) => {
  test.slow(); // A quick way to triple the default timeout
  // ...
});

test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => {
  test.setTimeout(120_000);
  // ...
});

        Change the timeout from a beforeEach hook

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // Extend the timeout by 30 seconds for every test that runs this hook.
  testInfo.setTimeout(testInfo.timeout + 30_000);
});

        Change the timeout for beforeAll/afterAll

        beforeAll and afterAll have their own timeout, which defaults to the test timeout. Change it per hook by calling setTimeout inside the hook.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeAll(async () => {
  // Set the timeout for this hook.
  test.setTimeout(60000);
});

        Expect timeout

        Auto-retrying assertions such as toHaveText have their own timeout, 5 seconds by default, that is unrelated to the test timeout. A sample error:

        example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================

Error: expect(received).toHaveText(expected)

Expected string: "my text"
Received string: ""
Call log:
  - expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms
  - waiting for "locator('button')"

        Set the expect timeout in the config

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    timeout: 10_000,
  },
});

        Set the expect timeout for a single assertion

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('example', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.locator('button')).toHaveText('hello', { timeout: 10_000 });
});

        Global timeout

        A time limit for the entire test run, to avoid wasting resources when everything is broken. There is no default; you should set a sensible value (e.g. one hour). A sample error:

        Running 1000 tests using 10 workers

  514 skipped
  486 passed
  Timed out waiting 3600s for the test suite to run
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  globalTimeout: 3_600_000,
});

        Advanced: low-level timeouts

        These are low-level timeouts that the runner has already configured, and you usually don't need to change them. If you came here because of a flaky test, the cause is most likely somewhere else.

        TimeoutDefaultDescriptionConfigure / override
        Action timeoutno limitEach actionConfig: { use: { actionTimeout: 10_000 } }
        Per call: locator.click({ timeout: 10_000 })
        Navigation timeoutno limitEach navigation actionConfig: { use: { navigationTimeout: 30_000 } }
        Per call: page.goto('/', { timeout: 30_000 })
        Global timeoutno limitThe whole runConfig: { globalTimeout: 3_600_000 }
        beforeAll/afterAll timeout30_000 msEach hookIn the hook: test.setTimeout(60_000)
        Fixture timeoutno limit (shares the test timeout)A single fixtureIn the fixture: { scope: 'test', timeout: 30_000 }

        Set action and navigation timeouts in the config
