        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    actionTimeout: 10 * 1000,
    navigationTimeout: 30 * 1000,
  },
});

        Set the timeout for a single action

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('basic test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev', { timeout: 30000 });
  await page.getByText('Get Started').click({ timeout: 10000 });
});

        Fixture timeout

        By default a fixture shares the timeout with the test. For slow fixtures, especially worker-scoped ones, give them their own timeout so you can keep the overall test timeout small while allowing the slow fixture more time.

        import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const test = base.extend<{ slowFixture: string }>({
  slowFixture: [async ({}, use) => {
    // ... slow operation ...
    await use('hello');
  }, { timeout: 60_000 }],
});

test('example test', async ({ slowFixture }) => {
  // ...
});
        Tip. The test timeout (30s) and the expect timeout (5s) are independent. For a slow assertion, adjust expect.timeout; for a long test, use test.slow()/test.setTimeout(); don't change the action/navigation timeouts to "cure" flakiness.

        Key points

        • The 30s test timeout covers the test function + fixture setup + beforeEach; afterEach + teardown have a separate budget with the same value.
        • The 5s expect timeout is independent of the test timeout; the global, action, and navigation timeouts have no limit by default.
        • test.slow() triples it; test.setTimeout()/testInfo.setTimeout() set a new value (including inside hooks).
        • A slow fixture can have its own timeout instead of raising the timeout of every test.
        • You should set a sensible globalTimeout on CI to avoid runs that never end.

        An expect(locator).toHaveText() reports "with timeout 5000ms". What do you do to relax just this assertion?

        The expect timeout is independent of the test timeout and the global timeout.

        Does the time spent in beforeEach count toward the test timeout?

        beforeEach is part of the test timeout; it is beforeAll/afterAll that have their own timeout, not shared with tests.

        Reporters (test result reports)

        Playwright Test ships with many built-in reporters (list, line, dot, failures, html, blob, json, junit, perfetto, github) and lets you write custom reporters. They differ mainly in how much detail they give for passing tests; every reporter prints error details.

        Introduction

        The quickest way to try one is to pass --reporter on the command line; for finer control, configure it in the config file.

        npx playwright test --reporter=line
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: 'line',
});

        Multiple reporters at once

        For example, list to watch the terminal and json to get a full results file.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    ['list'],
    ['json', { outputFile: 'test-results.json' }]
  ],
});

        Reporters on CI

        Use different reporters locally and on CI. dot is compact, avoids too much output, and is the default on CI.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // 'dot' is concise for CI, 'list' is the default when running locally
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'dot' : 'list',
});

        Report only failures (onlyFailures)

        Use onlyFailures with the JSON, JUnit, or HTML reporter to include only tests with unexpected outcomes (including unexpected passes), flaky tests (even if they passed on retry), and interrupted tests. Every attempt of a test is kept, including successful retries.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['html', { onlyFailures: true }]],
});

        onlyFailures is configured independently for each reporter. When merging blob reports, pass the config: npx playwright merge-reports --config=playwright.config.ts ./blob-report.

        Use the failures reporter to get direct diagnostics in the terminal without progress output. For example, keep the full HTML report together with compact terminal output:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['failures'], ['html']],
});

        Built-in reporters: quick comparison

        ReporterCharacteristicsWhen to use
        listOne line per test; the local defaultLocal development
        lineOne line for the test that just finished; prints errors immediatelyLarge suites
        dotOne character per test; the default on CICI, minimal output
        failuresPrints failures and successful retries as they happen, then a summaryCombined with html
        htmlA self-contained report folder, opened like a web pageViewing details/traces
        blobStores all the details so they can be merged laterSharding
        jsonA complete JSON objectProcessing with tools
        junitJUnit-style XMLCI integration
        perfettoTrace Event Format timelinePerformance/worker analysis
        githubFailure annotations on GitHub ActionsGitHub CI
        1. onBeginThe run starts, config + suite are known
        2. onTestBeginEach test starts
        3. onTestEndThe test ends with a status
        4. onEndThe run ends with an overall status
        5. Output the reportterminal / html / json / junit / blob...

        List reporter

        The default (except on CI, where dot is the default). Prints one line for each running test.

        npx playwright test --reporter=list
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: 'list',
});

        Sample output while the run is in progress (failures are listed at the end by default):

        npx playwright test --reporter=list
Running 124 tests using 6 workers

 1  ✓ should access error in env (438ms)
 2  ✓ handle long test names (515ms)
 3  x 1) render expected (691ms)
 4  ✓ should timeout (932ms)
 5    should repeat each:
 6  ✓ should respect enclosing .gitignore (569ms)
 7    should teardown env after timeout:
 8    should respect excluded tests:
 9  ✓ should handle env beforeEach error (638ms)
10    should respect enclosing .gitignore:

        Enable showing each step, print failures inline as they occur, or drop the tags that are automatically added to titles:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['list', { printSteps: true }]],
  // reporter: [['list', { printFailuresInline: true }]],
  // reporter: [['list', { omitTags: true }]],
});
        Environment variableOptionDescriptionDefault
        PLAYWRIGHT_LIST_PRINT_STEPSprintStepsPrint each step on its own line.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_LIST_PRINT_FAILURES_INLINEprintFailuresInlinePrint failure details right after a failed test instead of at the end.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_LIST_OMIT_TAGSomitTagsOmit the tags that are automatically added to test titles.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_FORCE_TTY-Output suited to an interactive terminal. Supports true, 1, false, 0, [WIDTH], [WIDTH]x[HEIGHT].true when it is a TTY
        FORCE_COLOR-Colored output.true when it is a TTY
        NO_COLOR-Disable colors (any non-empty value).not set

        Line reporter

        More compact than list: it uses a single line for the test that just finished and prints failures as they occur. Useful for large suites, as it shows progress without "spamming" the output.

        npx playwright test --reporter=line
        Running 124 tests using 6 workers
  1) dot-reporter.spec.ts:20:1 › render expected ===================================================

    Error: expect(received).toBe(expected) // Object.is equality

    Expected: 1
    Received: 0

[23/124] gitignore.spec.ts - should respect nested .gitignore

        Option: omitTags (env PLAYWRIGHT_LINE_OMIT_TAGS, default false); the same PLAYWRIGHT_FORCE_TTY, FORCE_COLOR, and NO_COLOR variables as list.

        Dot reporter

        Very concise: one character per test. The default on CI.

        npx playwright test --reporter=dot
Running 124 tests using 6 workers
······F·············································
        CharacterMeaning
        ·Passed
        FFailed
        ×Failed or timed out, and will be retried
        ±Passed on retry (flaky)
        TTimed out
        °Skipped

        Option: omitTags (env PLAYWRIGHT_DOT_OMIT_TAGS, default false); the same TTY/color variables as above.

        Failures reporter

        Prints failures and successful retries as soon as they happen, followed by a summary.

        npx playwright test --reporter=failures

        Use quiet in the config to silence the tests' stdout/stderr. Option: omitTags (env PLAYWRIGHT_FAILURES_OMIT_TAGS, default false); the same PLAYWRIGHT_FORCE_TTY, FORCE_COLOR, and NO_COLOR variables.

        HTML reporter

        Produces a self-contained report folder that can be served as a web page.

        npx playwright test --reporter=html

        By default the report opens automatically if any test fails. Control this with the open option or the PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_OPEN variable: always, never, on-failure (the default). You can configure host and port to serve the report.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['html', { open: 'never' }]],
});

        By default the report is written to the playwright-report folder (next to package.json or in the current working directory). Change it with PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_OUTPUT_DIR or the option:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['html', { outputFolder: 'my-report' }]],
});

        If you upload attachments from the data folder to another location, use attachmentsBaseURL so the HTML report knows where to look:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['html', { attachmentsBaseURL: 'https://external-storage.com/' }]],
});

        Quickly open the report from the latest run, a custom folder, or a .zip file (e.g. downloaded from a CI artifact; the zip must have index.html at the top level, and Playwright extracts it to a temporary folder and serves it):

        npx playwright show-report
npx playwright show-report my-report
npx playwright show-report playwright-report.zip
        Environment variableOptionDescriptionDefault
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_TITLEtitleThe title shown in the report.none
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_ONLY_FAILURESonlyFailuresInclude only unexpected, flaky (including successful retries), and interrupted tests.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_OUTPUT_DIRoutputFolderThe folder where the report is saved.playwright-report
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_OPENopenWhen to open the report: always, never, on-failure.on-failure
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_HOSThostThe hostname the report is served on.localhost
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_PORTportThe port the report is served on.9323 or any free port
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_ATTACHMENTS_BASE_URLattachmentsBaseURLWhere attachments from the data folder live when uploaded separately.data/
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_NO_COPY_PROMPTnoCopyPromptDisable the Copy prompt button for errors.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_NO_SNIPPETSnoSnippetsDisable code snippets in the action log (top-level errors still have snippets).false
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_DO_NOT_INLINE_ASSETSdoNotInlineAssetsWrite JS, CSS, and data as separate files instead of embedding them; use this when serving under a strict Content Security Policy.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_MERGE_FILESmergeFilesGroup tests by the title of the top-level test.describe() instead of by file.false

        Blob reporter

        A blob report contains every detail of the run and is used to generate other reports later; its main purpose is to merge the reports of shards.

        npx playwright test --reporter=blob

        By default it is written to the blob-report folder. The file name is report-<hash>.zip, or report-<hash>-<shard_number>.zip when sharding. The hash is computed from --grep, --grep-invert, --project, the tag in the config, and the file filters, which ensures that different command lines produce different report names while staying stable across runs. You can override the file name in the config or with PLAYWRIGHT_BLOB_OUTPUT_FILE.

        When using blob to merge multiple shards, you don't need to pass any options.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: 'blob',
});

        When running on multiple environments, use tag to add a global tag per environment; the tag makes the merged report clearer and produces a unique blob name.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: 'blob',
  tag: process.env.CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME, // for example "@APIv2" or "@linux"
});
        Environment variableOptionDescriptionDefault
        PLAYWRIGHT_BLOB_OUTPUT_DIRoutputDirThe folder where output is saved; existing contents are deleted before writing.blob-report
        PLAYWRIGHT_BLOB_OUTPUT_NAMEfileNameThe report file name.report-<hash>-<shard_number>.zip
        PLAYWRIGHT_BLOB_OUTPUT_FILEoutputFileThe full path; if set, outputDir and fileName are ignored.undefined

        JSON reporter

        Produces a JSON object containing all the information about the run. You usually want to write it to a file; when running with --reporter=json, use the PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_NAME variable:

        PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_NAME=results.json npx playwright test --reporter=json
        set PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_NAME=results.json
npx playwright test --reporter=json
        $env:PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_NAME="results.json"
npx playwright test --reporter=json
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['json', { outputFile: 'results.json' }]],
});
        Environment variableOptionDescriptionDefault
        PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_DIR-The folder where the file is saved; ignored if an output file is specified.cwd or the config folder
        PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_ONLY_FAILURESonlyFailuresInclude only unexpected, flaky, and interrupted tests.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_NAME-The base file name, relative to the output dir.Printed to stdout
        PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_FILEoutputFileThe full path; DIR and NAME are ignored if set.Printed to stdout

        JUnit reporter

        Produces a JUnit-style XML report. Use PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME when running with --reporter=junit:

        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME=results.xml npx playwright test --reporter=junit
        set PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME=results.xml
npx playwright test --reporter=junit
        $env:PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME="results.xml"
npx playwright test --reporter=junit
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['junit', { outputFile: 'results.xml' }]],
});
        Environment variableOptionDescriptionDefault
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_DIR-The folder where the file is saved; ignored if there is an output file.cwd or the config folder
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_ONLY_FAILURESonlyFailuresInclude only unexpected, flaky, and interrupted tests; keeps every attempt regardless of includeRetries.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME-The base file name, relative to the output dir.Printed to stdout
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_FILEoutputFileThe full path; DIR and NAME are ignored.Printed to stdout
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_STRIP_ANSIstripANSIControlSequencesRemove ANSI control sequences from the text.text kept as is
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_INCLUDE_PROJECT_IN_TEST_NAMEincludeProjectInTestNamePrefix each test case name with the project name.not added
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OMIT_TAGSomitTagsOmit the tags that are automatically added to the failure details.false
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_SUITE_ID-The value of the id attribute of the root <testsuites/> element.empty string
        PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_SUITE_NAME-The value of the name attribute of <testsuites/>.empty string

        Perfetto reporter

        Produces a Trace Event Format JSON file that you can open in the Perfetto UI (ui.perfetto.dev) or chrome://tracing. The test run is shown as a timeline with one lane per worker; each test is a slice containing before/after hooks, fixtures, and steps as nested slices. Each slice carries the test/step details in the trace event arguments: source location, params, tags, annotations, errors, stdio, and attachment paths.

        npx playwright test --reporter=perfetto

        By default it is written to test-results/perfetto.json. If the file name ends with .gz, the report is gzip-compressed as it is written (both viewers accept it, which is worthwhile for large runs).

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['perfetto', { outputFile: 'perfetto.json.gz' }]],
});
        Environment variableOptionDescriptionDefault
        PLAYWRIGHT_PERFETTO_OUTPUT_DIR-The folder where the file is saved; ignored if there is an output file.test-results
        PLAYWRIGHT_PERFETTO_OUTPUT_NAME-The base file name.perfetto.json
        PLAYWRIGHT_PERFETTO_OUTPUT_FILEoutputFileThe full path; DIR and NAME are ignored.undefined

        GitHub Actions annotations

        The github reporter automatically creates failure annotations when running on GitHub Actions. All other reporters still work on GitHub Actions but without annotations. It is not recommended with a matrix strategy, because the failure stack traces get multiplied and clutter GitHub's file view.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // 'github' on CI for annotations, 'list' is the default when running locally
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'github' : 'list',
});

        github accepts omitTags (or the PLAYWRIGHT_GITHUB_OMIT_TAGS variable) to omit tags from annotations, for example reporter: [['github', { omitTags: true }]].

        Custom reporters

        Create a custom reporter by implementing a class with some of the methods of the Reporter API.

        import type {
  FullConfig, FullResult, Reporter, Suite, TestCase, TestResult
} from '@playwright/test/reporter';

class MyReporter implements Reporter {
  onBegin(config: FullConfig, suite: Suite) {
    console.log(`Starting the run with ${suite.allTests().length} tests`);
  }

  onTestBegin(test: TestCase, result: TestResult) {
    console.log(`Starting test ${test.title}`);
  }

  onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult) {
    console.log(`Finished test ${test.title}: ${result.status}`);
  }

  onEnd(result: FullResult) {
    console.log(`Finished the run: ${result.status}`);
  }
}

export default MyReporter;

        Use this reporter in the config, or pass the file path via --reporter:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: './my-awesome-reporter.ts',
});
        npx playwright test --reporter="./myreporter/my-awesome-reporter.ts"

        Some open-source reporters for reference: Allure Reporter, GitHub Actions Reporter (estruyf), Mail Reporter, ReportPortal, Monocart.

        Best practice. Local: list or html. CI: dot/github for the terminal + blob (if sharding) or html/junit as an artifact. Set open: 'never' for HTML on CI/headless.

        Key points

        • Choose with --reporter or reporter in the config; use several reporters at once with an array [['list'], ['json', {...}]].
        • Defaults: list locally, dot on CI.
        • HTML opens automatically when there is a failure (open: 'on-failure'); view it again with npx playwright show-report (which also supports .zip files).
        • blob is for sharding followed by merge-reports; json/junit need outputFile (or an environment variable) to write to a file.
        • onlyFailures keeps reports compact (json/junit/html); perfetto gives a worker timeline; github gives annotations.
        • Custom reporters: implement onBegin, onTestBegin, onTestEnd, onEnd.

        Which reporter is suitable for saving each shard's results and then merging them into an HTML report?

        A blob report contains the full run details and attachments so that merge-reports can convert it into another report.

        What does the ± character in the dot reporter mean?

        Skipped is °, failed and will retry is ×, and ± is flaky.

        Web server (starting a dev server before the tests)

        The webServer option in the config lets Playwright automatically launch a local server before running tests, which is very handy when you write tests during development and don't yet have a staging/production URL to test against.

        Introduction

        Playwright runs your command, waits for the server to be ready before running tests, and shuts the server down when it finishes. To start the server only when a specific project runs, configure webServer inside that project. A server declared at the top level always starts regardless of which project is selected; a server shared by multiple projects should be declared at the top level.

        1. CheckIs there already a server at the url/port? (reuseExistingServer)
        2. LaunchRun the command (npm run start) with the configured cwd/env
        3. Wait until readyPoll the url (2xx/3xx/400-403) or match the wait output, up to timeout (60s)
        4. Run testsTests use a baseURL pointing at the server
        5. Shut down the serverSIGKILL by default, or gracefulShutdown

        Configuring the web server

        Use the webServer property in the config:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Run the local dev server before starting the tests
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    stdout: 'ignore',
    stderr: 'pipe',
  },
});
        PropertyDescription
        webServer (TestConfig)Launches one (or several) dev web servers during the tests.
        commandThe shell command that starts your app's dev server.
        cwdThe working directory of the process; defaults to the directory containing the config file.
        envEnvironment variables for the command. Inherits process.env by default and adds PLAYWRIGHT_TEST=1.
        gracefulShutdownHow the process is shut down. By default the whole process group receives SIGKILL. With { signal: 'SIGTERM', timeout: 500 }, it sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL if the process doesn't exit within 500ms (SIGINT can also be used). timeout: 0 means SIGKILL is never sent. Windows doesn't support SIGTERM/SIGINT, so this option is ignored there. Shutting down a Docker container requires SIGTERM.
        ignoreHTTPSErrorsIgnore HTTPS errors when accessing the url. Defaults to false.
        nameA custom name, added as a prefix to the logs. Defaults to [WebServer].
        portDeprecated, use url. The port the http server will appear on; Playwright waits until it accepts connections. Either port or url is required.
        reuseExistingServerIf true, reuses a server that is already running at the port/url; if there is none it runs the command. If false and a process is already listening there, it throws an error. Commonly set to !process.env.CI so that local test runs use the local dev server.
        stderrPipe the command's stderr to the process's stderr, or ignore it. Defaults to "pipe".
        stdout"pipe" forwards the command's stdout to the process's stdout; "ignore" discards it. Defaults to "ignore".
        timeoutHow long to wait for the process to start and become ready (ms). Defaults to 60000.
        urlThe URL of the http server, considered ready when it returns a 2xx, 3xx, 400, 401, 402, or 403 status code. Either port or url is required. If both url and wait are given, the server is considered started as soon as at least one condition is met.
        waitConsider the command started only when matching output appears. Accepts an object with stdout and/or stderr regexes. Named capture groups are stored in the environment, e.g. /Listening on port (?<my_server_port>\d+)/ stores the port in process.env['MY_SERVER_PORT']. With both url and wait, meeting either one is enough.
         
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    // Wait for the "Listening on port 4000" log instead of polling the url
    wait: { stdout: /Listening on port (?<my_server_port>\d+)/ },
    // The captured port is available as process.env.MY_SERVER_PORT
  },
});
        Best practice. Use url (not the deprecated port) and reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI so that local runs reuse an already running server, while CI always starts a clean one.

        Adding a server timeout

        A web server sometimes takes a long time to start. Increase timeout to wait longer.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Rest of the config...

  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    timeout: 120 * 1000,
  },
});

        Adding a baseURL

        It is a good idea to set baseURL in use: {} so tests can use relative URLs instead of repeating the full URL. The functions page.goto(), page.route(), page.waitForURL(), page.waitForRequest(), and page.waitForResponse() all take the base URL into account using the URL() constructor. For example, with a baseURL of http://localhost:3000 and a navigation to /login, the test goes to http://localhost:3000/login.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});

        Now you can use relative paths when navigating:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('test', async ({ page }) => {
  // Navigates to http://localhost:3000/login
  await page.goto('./login');
});

        Multiple web servers

        You can launch several web servers (or background processes) at the same time by passing an array to the webServer config.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  webServer: [
    {
      command: 'npm run start',
      url: 'http://localhost:3000',
      name: 'Frontend',
      timeout: 120 * 1000,
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    },
    {
      command: 'npm run backend',
      url: 'http://localhost:3333',
      name: 'Backend',
      timeout: 120 * 1000,
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    }
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});

        Key points

        • webServer automatically runs the command, waits for the url to be ready (or for output matching wait), and shuts the server down when done.
        • reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI: reuse the local server, CI always starts a new one; with false and a busy port, it errors.
        • timeout defaults to 60000 ms; stdout defaults to ignore, stderr defaults to pipe; port is deprecated.
        • Combine with use.baseURL to use relative URLs (page.goto('./login')).
        • Use an array to run several servers (frontend + backend); a per-project server goes inside the project, a shared server goes at the top level.

        You want local runs to reuse an already running dev server, while CI always starts a fresh one. Which configuration is correct?

        When not on CI (the CI variable is unset), the value is true and the server is reused; on CI it is false, so a new one is always started (and it errors if the port is already taken).

        With baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000', where does page.goto('/login') navigate?

        Playwright uses the URL() constructor to combine the relative path with the base URL.

        Locators

        Locators are the heart of Playwright's auto-waiting and retry-ability: a locator describes how to find an element on the page at any given moment, rather than holding on to one fixed element. Choosing good locators decides whether your tests are robust or flaky.

        Quick Guide – the recommended built-in locators

        MethodUsed for
        page.getByRole()Find by accessibility attributes (explicit or implicit role) + accessible name
        page.getByText()Find by text content
        page.getByLabel()Find a form control by the text of its associated label
        page.getByPlaceholder()Find an input by its placeholder
        page.getByAltText()Find an element (usually an image) by its alternative text (alt)
        page.getByTitle()Find an element by its title attribute
        page.getByTestId()Find by data-testid (the attribute name can be changed)
         
        await page.getByLabel('User Name').fill('John');

await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret-password');

await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

await expect(page.getByText('Welcome, John!')).toBeVisible();
        Tip Use the code generator to produce locators, then adjust them to your liking.

        A locator is re-resolved every time it is used

        Every time a locator is used for an action, Playwright looks up the latest DOM element on the page again. In the example below, the element is looked up twice (before hover and before click). If the DOM changes in between (because of a re-render), the new element matching the locator is used – there is never a "stale element" error.

        const locator = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' });

await locator.hover();
await locator.click();
        1. Create the locatorOnly stores the lookup "recipe"; does not touch the DOM yet
        2. Call an actionclick / fill / expect...
        3. ResolveFind the current element in the DOM
        4. ActionabilityWait for visible, stable, enabled...
        5. PerformIf the checks are not met → retry until timeout

        Chaining locators and FrameLocator

        Every locator-creating method such as getByLabel is also available on Locator and FrameLocator, so you can chain them to narrow the scope step by step.

        const locator = page
    .frameLocator('#my-frame')
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' });

await locator.click();

        Locate by role – getByRole

        getByRole reflects how users and assistive technologies (screen readers) perceive the page: is the element a button or a checkbox? You should usually pass an accessible name as well to pinpoint the right element.

        <h3>Sign up</h3>
<label>
  <input type="checkbox" /> Subscribe
</label>
<br/>
<button>Submit</button>
        await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Sign up' })).toBeVisible();

await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: 'Subscribe' }).check();

await page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i }).click();
        • Role locators cover buttons, checkboxes, headings, links, lists, tables... and follow W3C standards: ARIA roles, ARIA attributes and accessible name.
        • Many HTML tags such as <button> have an implicit role and are recognized by getByRole.
        • Role locators are not a replacement for accessibility audits or compliance testing; they only give early feedback about ARIA guidelines.
        • name accepts a string (by default a case-insensitive substring match) or a RegExp.
        When to use Prefer role locators to find elements: this is the closest approach to how users and assistive technologies perceive the page.

        Locate by label – getByLabel

        Most form controls have their own label. Use getByLabel to find a control through the text of its associated label.

        <label>Password <input type="password" /></label>
        await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret');
        When to use When locating form fields.

        Locate by placeholder – getByPlaceholder

        An input can have a placeholder attribute that hints at the value to enter.

        <input type="email" placeholder="name@example.com" />
        await page
    .getByPlaceholder('name@example.com')
    .fill('playwright@microsoft.com');
        When to use For form elements that have no label but do have a placeholder.

        Locate by text – getByText

        Find an element by the text it contains. Matching can be by substring (default), exact string (exact: true) or regular expression.

        <span>Welcome, John</span>
        // Substring match, case-insensitive
await expect(page.getByText('Welcome, John')).toBeVisible();

// Exact match
await expect(page.getByText('Welcome, John', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();

// Match with a regex
await expect(page.getByText(/welcome, [A-Za-z]+$/i)).toBeVisible();
        Whitespace normalization Text matching always normalizes whitespace, even with exact: multiple spaces become one, line breaks become spaces, and leading/trailing whitespace is removed.
        When to use getByText suits non-interactive elements such as div, span, p. For interactive elements (button, a, input) use a role locator. You can combine it with filtering by text to find an item in a list.

        Locate by alt text – getByAltText

        <img alt="playwright logo" src="/img/playwright-logo.svg" width="100" />
        await page.getByAltText('playwright logo').click();
        When to use When the element supports alt text, such as img and area.

        Locate by title – getByTitle

        <span title='Issues count'>25 issues</span>
        await expect(page.getByTitle('Issues count')).toHaveText('25 issues');
        When to use When the element has a title attribute.

        Locate by test id – getByTestId

        Test ids are the most resilient approach: even if the text or role changes, the test still passes. QA and developers should agree on explicit test ids. However, test ids are not something users see; if role/text matters to you, use user-facing locators.

        <button data-testid="directions">Itinéraire</button>
        await page.getByTestId('directions').click();
        When to use When you have chosen the "test id" approach, or cannot locate by role/text.

        Changing the test id attribute

        By default getByTestId uses data-testid. You can change this in the config or with selectors.setTestIdAttribute().

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    testIdAttribute: 'data-pw'
  }
});
        <button data-pw="directions">Itinéraire</button>
        await page.getByTestId('directions').click();

        Locate by CSS or XPath – page.locator()

        If you must use CSS/XPath, use page.locator(). Playwright automatically detects CSS vs. XPath if you omit the css= / xpath= prefix.

        await page.locator('css=button').click();
await page.locator('xpath=//button').click();

await page.locator('button').click();
await page.locator('//button').click();
        ❌ Avoid
        await page.locator(
    '#tsf > div:nth-child(2) > div.A8SBwf > div.RNNXgb > div > div.a4bIc > input'
).click();

await page
    .locator('//*[@id="tsf"]/div[2]/div[1]/div[1]/div/div[2]/input')
    .click();

        Long CSS/XPath strings are tightly coupled to the DOM structure; change the structure and the test breaks.

        ✅ Prefer
        await page.getByRole('searchbox', { name: 'Search' }).click();
// or an explicit test id
await page.getByTestId('search-input').click();

        Use locators that are close to how users perceive the page, or define a "test contract" with test ids.

        See the less commonly used locator types in Other locators.

        Locating inside Shadow DOM

        By default, every locator in Playwright pierces open shadow roots. Exceptions:

        • XPath does not pierce shadow roots.
        • Closed-mode shadow roots are not supported.
        <x-details role=button aria-expanded=true aria-controls=inner-details>
  <div>Title</div>
  #shadow-root
    <div id=inner-details>Details</div>
</x-details>
        // Click <div>Details</div> inside the shadow root
await page.getByText('Details').click();

// Click <x-details> itself
await page.locator('x-details', { hasText: 'Details' }).click();

// Make sure <x-details> contains the text "Details"
await expect(page.locator('x-details')).toContainText('Details');

        Filtering Locators

        Consider the product list below; we want to click the buy button of the second product card.

        <ul>
  <li>
    <h3>Product 1</h3>
    <button>Add to cart</button>
  </li>
  <li>
    <h3>Product 2</h3>
    <button>Add to cart</button>
  </li>
</ul>

        Filter by text – hasText

        locator.filter({ hasText }) looks for the string anywhere in the element (including child elements), case-insensitively. You can pass a regex.

        await page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasText: 'Product 2' })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
    .click();

// Using a regex
await page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasText: /Product 2/ })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
    .click();

        Filter by not having text – hasNotText

        // 5 in-stock items
await expect(page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasNotText: 'Out of stock' })).toHaveCount(5);

        Filter by child/descendant – has

        Filter elements that have (or do not have) a child element matching another locator. You can use any locator: getByRole, getByTestId, getByText...

        await page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Product 2' }) })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
    .click();

// Assert there is exactly one such product card
await expect(page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Product 2' }) }))
    .toHaveCount(1);
        The filter locator must be relative The locator inside has is queried starting from the element matching the outer locator, not from the document root. That is why the example below is wrong: page.getByRole('list') starts from the <ul> that lies outside the <li>.
        // ✖ WRONG
await expect(page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('list').getByText('Product 2') }))
    .toHaveCount(1);

        Filter by not having child/descendant – hasNot

        await expect(page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasNot: page.getByText('Product 2') }))
    .toHaveCount(1);

        Note that the inner locator is also matched starting from the outer locator, not from the document root.

        filter() optionMeaning
        hasTextContains text (string/regex), case-insensitive
        hasNotTextDoes not contain the text
        hasHas a child element matching the locator (relative)
        hasNotDoes not have a child element matching the locator
        visibleFilter by visibility (set false to find hidden elements)

        Locator operators

        Matching inside a locator – nesting/chaining

        Chain locator-creating methods (getByText, getByRole...) to narrow the search to part of the page. For example, create a product locator and reuse it multiple times.

        const product = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Product 2' });

await product.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();

await expect(product).toHaveCount(1);

        You can also combine two locators with locator.within(), for example to find the "Save" button inside a specific dialog:

        const saveButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' });
// ...
const dialog = page.getByTestId('settings-dialog');
await saveButton.within(dialog).click();

        Matching two locators simultaneously – and()

        locator.and() narrows an existing locator by requiring it to also match another locator (the intersection of two conditions).

        const button = page.getByRole('button').and(page.getByTitle('Subscribe'));

        Matching one of the alternatives – or()

        When you want to target one of two (or more) elements without knowing which will appear, use locator.or(): it matches any of the alternatives, or both. Example: you want to click "New email", but sometimes a security settings dialog shows up first.

        const newEmail = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'New' });
const dialog = page.getByText('Confirm security settings');
await expect(newEmail.or(dialog).first()).toBeVisible();
if (await dialog.isVisible())
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Dismiss' }).click();
await newEmail.click();
        Strict mode If both the "New email" button and the dialog are shown, the or locator matches both and may throw a "strict mode violation" error. In that case use .first() to take only one.

        Matching only visible elements

        Note It is usually better to find a more reliable way to identify the element instead of checking visibility.
        <button style='display: none'>Invisible</button>
<button>Visible</button>
        // Matches both buttons → strictness violation error
await page.locator('button').click();

// Matches only the second button because it is visible, then clicks it
await page.locator('button').visible().click();

        To match hidden elements, use locator.filter({ visible: false }).

        Version The .visible() and within() syntax is a new API in the current docs; check your Playwright version. The long-standing equivalent is the CSS button:visible (see Other locators).

        Lists – working with lists

        <ul>
  <li>apple</li>
  <li>banana</li>
  <li>orange</li>
</ul>

        Counting items in a list

        await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(3);

        Asserting all the text in a list

        toHaveText accepts an array: it checks the count and the order of the texts.

        await expect(page
    .getByRole('listitem'))
    .toHaveText(['apple', 'banana', 'orange']);

        Getting a specific item

        ApproachExampleNotes
        By textpage.getByText('orange').click()Simplest
        Filter by textpage.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'orange' }).click()Restrict to the exact role first
        By test idpage.getByTestId('orange').click()You may need to add the test id to the HTML
        By positionpage.getByRole('listitem').nth(1)Use first(), last(), nth(); be careful
        Be careful with nth When the page changes, the locator may end up pointing to a completely different element. Try to create a unique locator that satisfies strictness.

        Chaining filters

        When elements look alike, chain multiple filter() calls. For example, take a screenshot of the row that has "Mary" and a "Say goodbye" button:

        const rowLocator = page.getByRole('listitem');

await rowLocator
    .filter({ hasText: 'Mary' })
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Say goodbye' }) })
    .screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' });

        Rarely used cases

        Iterating over each element, evaluateAll 
        // Option 1: all()
for (const row of await page.getByRole('listitem').all())
  console.log(await row.textContent());

// Option 2: a plain for loop
const rows = page.getByRole('listitem');
const count = await rows.count();
for (let i = 0; i < count; ++i)
  console.log(await rows.nth(i).textContent());

// Option 3: run in the page with evaluateAll (any DOM API can be called)
const texts = await rows.evaluateAll(
    list => list.map(element => element.textContent));

        Strictness

        Locators are strict: any operation that targets a single element will throw if more than one element matches. In contrast, operations on multiple elements (such as count()) work normally.

        // Throws if there is more than one button
await page.getByRole('button').click();

// OK with multiple elements
await page.getByRole('button').count();

        You can deliberately bypass strictness with first(), last(), nth(), but this is not recommended because when the page changes, Playwright may click the wrong element. Create a uniquely identifying locator instead.

        Other locators

        Less commonly used locators are on the Other locators page.

        Locator priority table

        PriorityLocatorUse when
        1getByRoleInteractive elements (button, link, checkbox, heading...)
        2getByLabelForm fields that have a label
        3getByPlaceholderInputs with no label but with a placeholder
        4getByTextNon-interactive elements (div, span, p)
        5getByAltText / getByTitleImages / elements with a title
        6getByTestIdWhen a user-facing locator cannot be used
        7CSS / XPathLast resort

        Key points

        • A locator re-resolves the DOM on every action → there is no "stale" element.
        • Prefer user-facing: getByRole > label/placeholder/text > test id > CSS/XPath.
        • filter() (hasText/has/hasNot/hasNotText) and chained locators help you locate precisely; the locator inside has must be relative.
        • and() = intersection, or() = union (watch out for strict mode violations).
        • Locators are strict: with multiple matches the action throws; use first/last/nth only when there is no alternative.
        • Locators pierce open shadow DOM (except XPath); change the test id attribute with testIdAttribute.
        Can a locator go "stale"?
        No. Every time it is used, the locator looks up the current element in the DOM again.
        What is the difference between the default hasText and exact in getByText?
        hasText/getByText by default match a substring, case-insensitively; exact: true matches the full string, case-sensitively (whitespace is still normalized).

        You want to click "Add to cart" for the product whose heading is "Product 2" in a list of li elements. Which approach is correct?

        B uses a user-facing locator and filters by child, so it stays robust when the order/structure changes. A and C depend on order/DOM and are therefore fragile.

        What happens with await page.getByRole('button').click() when the page has 3 buttons?

        Locators are strict: an operation targeting a single element fails if there are multiple matches.

        Other locators

        Besides getByRole, getByText..., Playwright also supports extended CSS, XPath, nth=, legacy text, attribute shorthands and chaining with >>. Most of these are fallbacks; prefer user-facing locators.

        CSS locator

        Recommendation Prefer user-visible locators (text, role) over implementation-coupled CSS, because CSS can break when the page changes.
        await page.locator('css=button').click();

        Playwright extends standard CSS in two ways:

        • CSS selectors pierce open shadow DOM.
        • It adds its own pseudo-classes: :visible, :has-text(), :has(), :is(), :nth-match(), etc.

        CSS: matching by text

        Pseudo-classMeaningCase-sensitive
        :has-text("...")An element that contains the text somewhere inside (including children/descendants); substring match, whitespace trimmedNo
        :text("...")The smallest element containing the text; substring matchNo
        :text-is("...")The smallest element whose text is exactly the string (full match)Yes
        :text-matches("regex", "flags")The smallest element whose text matches a JavaScript-style regexDepends on flags
         
        // Wrong: matches many elements, including <body>
await page.locator(':has-text("Playwright")').click();
// Correct: matches only <article>
await page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")').click();

// Find "Home" inside #nav-bar
await page.locator('#nav-bar :text("Home")').click();
        • :text-is("Log") does not match <button>Log in</button> (the text node is "Log in") but does match <button> Log <span>in</span></button> because there is a text node " Log ". :text-is("Download") does not match download.
        • :text-matches("Log\s*in", "i") matches <button>Login</button> and <button>log IN</button>.
        Use :has-text() together with another selector On its own it matches every element that contains the text, including <body>.
        Note Text matching always normalizes whitespace. Inputs of type button and submit are matched by their value instead of text content (e.g. :text("Log in") matches <input type=button value="Log in">).

        CSS: matching only visible elements

        css=button matches every button; css=button:visible matches only buttons that are currently displayed.

        // <button style='display: none'>Invisible</button><button>Visible</button>

// Matches both → strictness violation
await page.locator('button').click();

// Matches only the second button
await page.locator('button:visible').click();
        Tip Prefer the locator.visible() shortcut over the :visible pseudo-class.

        CSS: an element that contains another element – :has()

        // Get the text of the <article> that has a <div class=promo> inside
await page.locator('article:has(div.promo)').textContent();

        CSS: matching one of several conditions

        A comma-separated list of selectors matches every element that belongs to any of the selectors. :is() is useful for specifying a list of secondary conditions.

        // Click the <button> with the text "Log in" or "Sign in"
await page.locator('button:has-text("Log in"), button:has-text("Sign in")').click();

        CSS: matching by layout (deprecated)

        Deprecated Layout selectors are marked as deprecated and may be removed. Layout-based matching can give surprising results (a 1-pixel shift can match a different element). Prefer user-visible locators.

        Layout pseudo-classes use the bounding client rect to compute relative distance/position. Use them together with another tag (e.g. input); on their own you will often get an empty element in the middle.

        Pseudo-classMatches an element...
        :right-of(sel)to the right of the element matching sel (at any vertical position)
        :left-of(sel)to the left
        :above(sel)above (at any horizontal position)
        :below(sel)below
        :near(sel)near (within 50 CSS px)
         
        // Fill the input to the right of "Username"
await page.locator('input:right-of(:text("Username"))').fill('value');

// Click the button near the promo card
await page.locator('button:near(.promo-card)').click();

// Click the radio nearest to "Label 3"
await page.locator('[type=radio]:left-of(:text("Label 3"))').first().click();

// Limit the maximum distance to 120px with the last argument
await page.locator('button:near(:text("Username"), 120)').click();

        Results are sorted by distance to the anchor, so first() picks the nearest element – this only makes sense for lists of similar elements.

        CSS: choosing the n-th match – :nth-match()

        <section><button>Buy</button></section>
<article><div><button>Buy</button></div></article>
<div><div><button>Buy</button></div></div>
        // Click the third "Buy" button (index starts at 1)
await page.locator(':nth-match(:text("Buy"), 3)').click();

// Wait until there are at least 3 buttons
await page.locator(':nth-match(:text("Buy"), 3)').waitFor();
        Unlike :nth-child() The elements do not need to be siblings; they can be anywhere on the page. Being able to tell them apart by attribute/text is usually more robust.

        N-th element locator – nth=

        // Click the first button (index from 0)
await page.locator('button').locator('nth=0').click();

// Click the last button
await page.locator('button').locator('nth=-1').click();
        :nth-match()nth=
        IndexStarts at 1Starts at 0, -1 is the last

        Parent element locator

        It is usually better to filter() by a child locator rather than climbing up to the parent.

        // <li><label>Hello</label></li><li><label>World</label></li>
const child = page.getByText('Hello');
const parent = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child });

// Fallback, less robust
const parent2 = page.getByText('Hello').locator('xpath=..');

        XPath locator

        Recommendation Prefer user-visible locators; XPath is coupled to the implementation and breaks easily.

        An XPath locator is equivalent to calling Document.evaluate.

        await page.locator('xpath=//button').click();
        • A string starting with // or .. is treated as XPath (e.g. '//html/body' becomes 'xpath=//html/body').
        • XPath does not pierce shadow roots.

        XPath union

        The pipe operator | matches every element belonging to any of the selectors.

        // Wait for the confirmation dialog or the loading spinner
await page.locator(
    `//span[contains(@class, 'spinner__loading')]|//div[@id='confirmation']`
).waitFor();

        Label to form control retargeting

        Recommendation Use getByLabel instead of relying on retargeting.

        Input actions that target a label are automatically redirected to the associated control. For example <label for="password">Password:</label><input id="password" type="password">; if you find the label with getByText, the following actions are performed on the input:

        • click() – clicks the label and automatically focuses the input
        • fill() – fills the input
        • inputValue() – returns the input's value
        • selectText() – selects the text in the input
        • setInputFiles() – sets files on an input type=file
        • selectOption() – selects an option in a select
        // Fill the input by targeting the label
await page.getByText('Password').fill('secret');

// But an assertion targets the label itself, not the input
await expect(page.locator('label')).toHaveText('Password');

        Legacy text locator

        Recommendation Use the modern getByText instead of the legacy form.
        SyntaxMeaning
        text=Log inDefault: case-insensitive, whitespace trimmed, substring match (text=Log matches <button>Log in</button>)
        text="Log in"Quoted: exact text node match after trimming, case-sensitive. Escaped like a regular string: text="foo\"bar"
        text=/Log\s*in/iJavaScript-style regex wrapped in /
         
        await page.locator('text=Log in').click();
await page.locator('text="Log in"').click();
await page.locator('text=/Log\\s*in/i').click();
        Note A selector string that starts and ends with a quote (" or ') is treated as a legacy text locator: "Log in" is internally converted to text="Log in". Whitespace is always normalized; input type button/submit is matched by value.

        id, data-testid, data-test-id, data-test selectors

        Recommendation Use getByTestId instead.

        Shorthands for the attributes: id, data-testid, data-test-id, data-test.

        // Fill the input with id "username"
await page.locator('id=username').fill('value');

// Click the element with data-test-id "submit"
await page.locator('data-test-id=submit').click();
        Note Attribute selectors are not CSS, so they do not support :enabled etc. If you need CSS features, use css=[data-test="login"]:enabled.

        Chaining selectors – the >> operator

        Recommendation Prefer chaining locators over chaining selectors.

        Selectors of the form engine=body can be joined with >>; each following selector is queried relative to the result of the previous one.

        css=article >> css=.bar > .baz >> css=span[attr=value]

        is equivalent to:

        document
    .querySelector('article')
    .querySelector('.bar > .baz')
    .querySelector('span[attr=value]');

        If a selector body needs to contain >>, it must be put in a quoted string: text="some >> text".

        Intermediate matches

        By default a selector chain returns the element of the last selector. Add the * prefix to get the element of an intermediate selector: css=article >> text=Hello returns the element containing the text Hello, while *css=article >> text=Hello returns the article that contains an element with the text Hello. (Prefer filter with has instead.)

        Key points

        • Everything on this page is a "fallback"; user-facing locators are always preferred.
        • Playwright's CSS pierces open shadow DOM, XPath does not.
        • :text() matches a substring (case-insensitive), :text-is() matches exactly, :has-text() must be paired with another tag.
        • :nth-match() starts at 1; nth= starts at 0 (-1 is the last).
        • Layout pseudo-classes (:right-of...) are deprecated.

        Which locator matches only visible buttons and is Playwright-specific CSS syntax?

        :visible is a pseudo-class that Playwright adds to CSS (the newer docs recommend the locator.visible() shortcut).

        Actions (input & interaction)

        Playwright can interact with text inputs, checkboxes, radios, selects, mouse clicks, key presses, keyboard shortcuts, file uploads, focus, drag-and-drop and scrolling. (The slug actions returns a 404, so this content comes from the input page, which is titled "Actions".)

        Text input – fill()

        locator.fill() is the easiest way to fill in a form: it focuses the element and fires an input event with the entered text. It works with <input>, <textarea> and [contenteditable].

        // Text input
await page.getByRole('textbox').fill('Peter');

// Date input
await page.getByLabel('Birth date').fill('2020-02-02');

// Time input
await page.getByLabel('Appointment time').fill('13:15');

// Local datetime input
await page.getByLabel('Local time').fill('2020-03-02T05:15');

        Checkbox and radio – check() / setChecked()

        locator.setChecked() (and check()/uncheck()) works with input[type=checkbox], input[type=radio] and [role=checkbox].

        // Check the checkbox
await page.getByLabel('I agree to the terms above').check();

// Assert the checked state
expect(page.getByLabel('Subscribe to newsletter')).toBeChecked();

// Select the radio button
await page.getByLabel('XL').check();
        Forgotten await Web-first assertions such as toBeChecked() are async; in real code write await expect(...).toBeChecked() (the original docs example omits the await).

        Select options – selectOption()

        Select one or more options in a <select>, by value or label.

        // Single selection matching the value or label
await page.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption('blue');

// Single selection matching the label
await page.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption({ label: 'Blue' });

// Multiple selected items
await page.getByLabel('Choose multiple colors').selectOption(['red', 'green', 'blue']);

        Mouse click

        // Generic click
await page.getByRole('button').click();

// Double click
await page.getByText('Item').dblclick();

// Right click
await page.getByText('Item').click({ button: 'right' });

// Shift + click
await page.getByText('Item').click({ modifiers: ['Shift'] });

// Ctrl + click on Windows and Linux
// Meta + click on macOS
await page.getByText('Item').click({ modifiers: ['ControlOrMeta'] });

// Hover over element
await page.getByText('Item').hover();

// Click the top left corner
await page.getByText('Item').click({ position: { x: 0, y: 0 } });

        Under the hood, click and the other pointer methods will:

        1. AttachedWait for the element to be in the DOM
        2. VisibleNot empty, not display:none/visibility:hidden
        3. StableWait for it to stop moving (e.g. a CSS transition)
        4. ScrollScroll the element into view
        5. Receives eventsNot covered by another element at the click point
        6. ClickIf the element is detached midway → retry

        See Auto-waiting for the details of each check.

        Forcing the click

        Sometimes an app has complex logic: hovering over an element shows an overlay that blocks the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug (the element is covered). If you know for certain that this is the case, you can skip the actionability checks:

        await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });

        Programmatic click – dispatchEvent

        If you do not need to test under real conditions and want to simulate a click at all costs, dispatch the click event directly (similar to HTMLElement.click()):

        await page.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');

        Type characters – pressSequentially()

        Note Most of the time you should enter text with fill(). Only type character by character when the page has special keyboard handling.
        // Press keys one by one
await page.locator('#area').pressSequentially('Hello World!');

        This method emits the full keydown, keypress, keyup events. You can pass an optional delay between keys to simulate a real user.

        Keys and shortcuts – press()

        // Hit Enter
await page.getByText('Submit').press('Enter');

// Dispatch Control+Right
await page.getByRole('textbox').press('Control+ArrowRight');

// Press $ sign on keyboard
await page.getByRole('textbox').press('$');

        locator.press() focuses the element and then produces a single key press. It accepts logical key names (the keyboardEvent.key values):

        Backquote, Minus, Equal, Backslash, Backspace, Tab, Delete, Escape,
ArrowDown, End, Enter, Home, Insert, PageDown, PageUp, ArrowRight,
ArrowUp, F1 - F12, Digit0 - Digit9, KeyA - KeyZ, etc.
        • You can pass a single character such as "a" or "#"; characters are case-sensitive ("a" differs from "A").
        • Modifier keys: Shift, Control, Alt, Meta.
        • Combinations such as "Control+o", "Control+Shift+T": the modifiers are held down while the next key is pressed.
        // <input id=name>
await page.locator('#name').press('Shift+A');

await page.locator('#name').press('Shift+ArrowLeft');
        Note You still need to write an uppercase A in Shift+A to get an uppercase character; Shift+a yields a lowercase character as if CapsLock were on.

        Upload files – setInputFiles()

        The first argument points to an <input type="file">. You can pass multiple files in an array. Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory. An empty array clears the selected files.

        // Select one file
await page.getByLabel('Upload file').setInputFiles(path.join(__dirname, 'myfile.pdf'));

// Select multiple files
await page.getByLabel('Upload files').setInputFiles([
  path.join(__dirname, 'file1.txt'),
  path.join(__dirname, 'file2.txt'),
]);

// Select a directory
await page.getByLabel('Upload directory').setInputFiles(path.join(__dirname, 'mydir'));

// Remove all the selected files
await page.getByLabel('Upload file').setInputFiles([]);

// Upload buffer from memory
await page.getByLabel('Upload file').setInputFiles({
  name: 'file.txt',
  mimeType: 'text/plain',
  buffer: Buffer.from('this is test')
});

        If the input element is not readily available (it is created dynamically), catch the filechooser event:

        // Start waiting for file chooser before clicking. Note no await.
const fileChooserPromise = page.waitForEvent('filechooser');
await page.getByLabel('Upload file').click();
const fileChooser = await fileChooserPromise;
await fileChooser.setFiles(path.join(__dirname, 'myfile.pdf'));

        Focus element – focus()

        For dynamic pages that handle focus events:

        await page.getByLabel('Password').focus();

        Drag and Drop – dragTo()

        locator.dragTo() will: hover the element being dragged, press the left mouse button, move the mouse to the drop target element, and release the left mouse button.

        await page.locator('#item-to-be-dragged').dragTo(page.locator('#item-to-drop-at'));

        Dragging manually

        For precise control, use hover, mouse.down, mouse.move, mouse.up:

        await page.locator('#item-to-be-dragged').hover();
await page.mouse.down();
await page.locator('#item-to-drop-at').hover();
await page.mouse.up();
        dragover If the page relies on the dragover event, you need at least two mouse moves to trigger it in every browser: hover the dragged element, mouse down, hover the drop target, hover the drop target a second time, mouse up.

        Scrolling

        Playwright usually scrolls automatically before each action, so you do not need to scroll manually.

        // Scrolls automatically so that button is visible
await page.getByRole('button').click();

        Manual scrolling is rarely needed (e.g. to force an "infinite list" to load more, or to position the page for a screenshot). The most reliable way is to scroll an element into view:

        // Scroll the footer into view, forcing an "infinite list" to load more content
await page.getByText('Footer text').scrollIntoViewIfNeeded();

        For finer control use mouse.wheel or locator.evaluate:

        // Position the mouse and scroll with the mouse wheel
await page.getByTestId('scrolling-container').hover();
await page.mouse.wheel(0, 10);

// Alternatively, programmatically scroll a specific element
await page.getByTestId('scrolling-container').evaluate(e => e.scrollTop += 100);

        Cheat sheet

        PurposeAPI
        Fill a text fieldfill(), clear()
        Type key by keypressSequentially()
        Press a key/shortcutpress('Control+A')
        Checkbox/radiocheck(), uncheck(), setChecked(bool)
        SelectselectOption()
        Mouseclick(), dblclick(), hover(), dragTo()
        UploadsetInputFiles() / filechooser event
        Focus/scrollfocus(), scrollIntoViewIfNeeded(), mouse.wheel()

        Key points

        • Prefer fill() over pressSequentially(); only type key by key when the page has special keyboard handling.
        • Pointer actions automatically wait for attached/visible/stable/receives events and scroll automatically; force: true skips the checks, dispatchEvent('click') only dispatches the event.
        • press() is case-sensitive; modifiers are Shift/Control/Alt/Meta, and ControlOrMeta works across platforms.
        • Upload: setInputFiles or catch filechooser; an empty array clears the files.
        • Drag & drop: dragTo() or manually (hover → down → hover ×2 → up).

        When should you use pressSequentially() instead of fill()?

        The docs recommend fill() for most cases (including date/time); pressSequentially is only needed when the page has its own key handling.

        An overlay blocks the click because the app has special hover logic, and you know it is not a bug. What do you do?

        force skips the non-essential checks such as "Receives Events".

        Auto-waiting (actionability checks)

        Before each action, Playwright runs a series of actionability checks and automatically waits for all of them to pass before acting. If they do not pass within the timeout, the action fails with a TimeoutError. (The slug auto-waiting returns a 404; the real page has the slug actionability and is titled "Auto-waiting".)

        The general mechanism

        Take locator.click() as an example; Playwright ensures that:

        • the locator resolves to exactly one element;
        • the element is Visible;
        • the element is Stable (not animating, or the animation has finished);
        • the element Receives Events (is not covered by another element);
        • the element is Enabled;
        • the element is Not Inert.
        1. ResolveLocator → exactly 1 element
        2. VisibleHas a bounding box, not hidden
        3. StableBounding box steady for ≥ 2 frames
        4. Enabled / Not InertNot disabled, not inert
        5. Receives EventsHit-test at the click point
        6. Perform the actionIf not met → retry until timeout (TimeoutError)

        Actionability checks per action

        ActionVisibleStableReceives EventsEnabledEditableNot Inert
        locator.check()YesYesYesYes-Yes
        locator.click()YesYesYesYes-Yes
        locator.dblclick()YesYesYesYes-Yes
        locator.setChecked()YesYesYesYes-Yes
        locator.tap()YesYesYesYes-Yes
        locator.uncheck()YesYesYesYes-Yes
        locator.hover()YesYesYes---
        locator.dragTo()YesYesYes---
        locator.screenshot()YesYes----
        locator.fill()Yes--YesYesYes
        locator.clear()Yes--YesYesYes
        locator.selectOption()Yes--Yes-Yes
        locator.selectText()Yes-----
        locator.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded()-Yes----
        locator.blur()------
        locator.dispatchEvent()------
        locator.focus()------
        locator.press()------
        locator.pressSequentially()------
        locator.setInputFiles()------

        Forcing actions

        Some actions such as locator.click() support a force option to disable the non-essential actionability checks. For example, passing a truthy force to click() will not check whether the target element actually receives the click event.

        await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });

        Self-retrying assertions

        Like the auto-waiting before actions, web-first expect automatically waits until the condition is true, eliminating flakiness.

        AssertionDescription
        toBeAttachedElement is attached
        toBeCheckedCheckbox is checked
        toBeDisabledElement is disabled
        toBeEditableElement is editable
        toBeEmptyContainer is empty
        toBeEnabledElement is enabled
        toBeFocusedElement is focused
        toBeHiddenElement is not visible
        toBeInViewportElement intersects the viewport
        toBeVisibleElement is visible
        toContainTextElement contains text
        toHaveAttributeElement has a DOM attribute
        toHaveClassElement has a class property
        toHaveCountList has exactly the given count
        toHaveCSSElement has a CSS property
        toHaveIdElement has an ID
        toHaveJSPropertyElement has a JavaScript property
        toHaveTextElement matches text
        toHaveValueInput has a value
        toHaveValuesSelect has the given options selected
        page: toHaveTitlePage has a title
        page: toHaveURLPage has a URL
        response: toBeOKResponse has an OK status

        See also Assertions.

        Visible

        An element is considered visible when it has a non-empty bounding box and its computed style is not visibility:hidden. By this definition:

        • An element with zero size is not visible.
        • An element with display:none is not visible.
        • An element with opacity:0 is still considered visible.

        Stable

        An element is stable when it keeps the same bounding box for at least two consecutive animation frames.

        Enabled

        An element is enabled when it is not disabled. An element is disabled when:

        • it is a <button>, <select>, <input>, <textarea>, <option> or <optgroup> with the [disabled] attribute;
        • it is one of the tags above but sits inside a <fieldset> with [disabled];
        • it is a descendant of an element with [aria-disabled=true].

        Editable

        An element is editable when it is enabled and not readonly. It is readonly when:

        • it is a <select>, <input> or <textarea> with [readonly];
        • it has [aria-readonly=true] and an aria role that supports that attribute.

        Not Inert

        An element is not inert when it is not part of an inert subtree. Inert elements cannot be focused, clicked or interacted with. An element is inert when it has the inert attribute or is a descendant of such an element.

        Receives Events

        An element receives pointer events when it is the hit target of the pointer event at the action point. For example, when clicking at (10;10), Playwright checks whether another element (usually an overlay) would catch the click at that point.

        Example scenario: Playwright will click the Sign Up button regardless of when click() is called:

        • the page is checking whether the username is unique and the Sign Up button is disabled;
        • after querying the server, the disabled Sign Up button is replaced with a new, enabled button.
        Best practice Do not insert waitForTimeout to "wait". Let auto-waiting and web-first assertions do their job; use force only when you clearly understand why.

        Key points

        • 6 checks: Visible, Stable, Receives Events, Enabled, Editable, Not Inert (+ exactly 1 element); each action applies only a subset.
        • fill/clear need Editable but not Stable; hover/click need Stable + Receives Events.
        • opacity:0 is still visible; display:none or zero size is not.
        • When time runs out → TimeoutError; force skips the non-essential checks.

        Which action does NOT require any actionability check?

        focus, blur, press, pressSequentially, dispatchEvent and setInputFiles have no checks in the table.

        An element with opacity:0 is considered?

        Visible = non-empty bounding box and not visibility:hidden; opacity:0 is still visible.

        Assertions

        Playwright provides the expect function with both generic matchers (toEqual, toContain...) and asynchronous web-first matchers that wait until the condition is met. Understanding the difference between retrying and non-retrying assertions is the key to stable tests.

        Introduction

        // generic matcher – runs synchronously
expect(success).toBeTruthy();

// web-first matcher – auto-retries
await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');

        Playwright will keep re-checking the element with the test id status until its text is "Submitted": it re-fetches the element and checks repeatedly until the condition is met or the timeout expires. You can pass the timeout directly or configure it once via TestConfig.expect. The default assertion timeout is 5 seconds.

        1. FetchRe-find the element from the locator
        2. CheckCompare with the expected value
        3. Met?Met → pass immediately
        4. Wait & repeatNot met → wait for the interval, then go back to step 1
        5. TimeoutAfter 5s (default) → fail

        Auto-retrying assertions

        The following assertions retry automatically until they pass or the timeout expires. They are async, so you must await them.

        AssertionDescription
        await expect(locator).toBeAttached()Element is attached to the DOM
        await expect(locator).toBeChecked()Checkbox is checked
        await expect(locator).toBeDisabled()Element is disabled
        await expect(locator).toBeEditable()Element is editable
        await expect(locator).toBeEmpty()Container is empty
        await expect(locator).toBeEnabled()Element is enabled
        await expect(locator).toBeFocused()Element is focused
        await expect(locator).toBeHidden()Element is not visible
        await expect(locator).toBeInViewport()Element intersects the viewport
        await expect(locator).toBeVisible()Element is visible
        await expect(locator).toContainText()Element contains text
        await expect(locator).toContainClass()Element has the specified CSS classes
        await expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleDescription()Matches the accessible description
        await expect(locator).toHaveAccessibleName()Matches the accessible name
        await expect(locator).toHaveAttribute()Element has a DOM attribute
        await expect(locator).toHaveClass()Element has the specified CSS class property
        await expect(locator).toHaveCount()List has exactly the given number of children
        await expect(locator).toHaveCSS()Element has a CSS property
        await expect(locator).toHaveId()Element has an ID
        await expect(locator).toHaveJSProperty()Element has a JavaScript property
        await expect(locator).toHaveRole()Element has the specified ARIA role
        await expect(locator).toHaveScreenshot()Element matches a screenshot
        await expect(locator).toHaveText()Element matches text
        await expect(locator).toHaveValue()Input has a value
        await expect(locator).toHaveValues()Select has the given options selected
        await expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()Element matches an Aria snapshot
        await expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()Page matches an Aria snapshot
        await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()Page matches a screenshot
        await expect(page).toHaveTitle()Page has a title
        await expect(page).toHaveURL()Page has a URL
        await expect(response).toBeOK()Response has an OK status

        Non-retrying assertions

        These assertions test any condition but do not auto-retry. Because web pages usually display information asynchronously, using them on UI data easily causes flakiness. Prefer auto-retrying assertions; for complex checks that need retrying, use expect.poll or expect.toPass.

        AssertionDescription
        toBeValues are identical
        toBeCloseToNumbers are approximately equal
        toBeDefinedValue is not undefined
        toBeFalsyValue is falsy (false, 0, null...)
        toBeGreaterThanNumber is greater
        toBeGreaterThanOrEqualNumber is greater or equal
        toBeInstanceOfObject is an instance of a class
        toBeLessThanNumber is less
        toBeLessThanOrEqualNumber is less or equal
        toBeNaNValue is NaN
        toBeNullValue is null
        toBeTruthyValue is truthy (not false, 0, null...)
        toBeUndefinedValue is undefined
        toContain (string)String contains a substring
        toContain (array/set)Array or set contains an item
        toContainEqualArray/set contains a "similar" item
        toEqualValues are similar – deep equality and pattern matching
        toHaveLengthArray or string has the given length
        toHavePropertyObject has a property
        toMatchString matches a regex
        toMatchObjectObject contains the specified properties
        toStrictEqualSimilar, including property types
        toThrowFunction throws an error
        ❌ Avoid
        // read the text once, then compare – no retry
expect(await page.getByTestId('status').textContent()).toBe('Submitted');

        If the UI has not updated at the moment of reading, the test fails even though the UI would be correct 100ms later.

        ✅ Prefer
        await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');

        A web-first assertion retries automatically until it is correct or times out.

        Asymmetric matchers

        These expressions can be nested inside other assertions for looser matching.

        MatcherDescription
        expect.any()Matches any instance of a class/primitive
        expect.anything()Matches anything
        expect.arrayContaining()Array contains the specified items
        expect.arrayOf()Array contains items of the specified type
        expect.closeTo()Numbers are approximately equal
        expect.objectContaining()Object contains the specified properties
        expect.stringContaining()String contains a substring
        expect.stringMatching()String matches a regex
         
        expect(user).toEqual({
  id: expect.any(Number),
  name: expect.stringContaining('Ann'),
  tags: expect.arrayContaining(['admin']),
});

        Negating matchers

        Add .not before the matcher to expect the opposite.

        expect(value).not.toEqual(0);
await expect(locator).not.toContainText('some text');

        Soft assertions

        By default, a failed assertion stops the test. A soft assertion does not stop the test but still marks the test as failed.

        // Make a few checks that will not stop the test when failed...
