await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Success');
await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('eta')).toHaveText('1 day');

// ... and continue the test to check more things.
await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'next page' }).click();
await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Make another order' })).toBeVisible();

        At any time you can check whether there were any soft failures:

        await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Success');
await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('eta')).toHaveText('1 day');

// Avoid running further if there were soft assertion failures.
expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
        Note Soft assertions only work with the Playwright test runner.

        Custom expect message

        Pass a custom message as the second argument of expect. The message is shown in the reporter for both passing and failing expects.

        await expect(page.getByText('Name'), 'should be logged in').toBeVisible();

// Soft assertions support it too
expect.soft(value, 'my soft assertion').toBe(56);

        When it passes, you see a step like ✅ should be logged in @example.spec.ts:18. When it fails:

            Error: should be logged in

    Call log:
      - expect.toBeVisible with timeout 5000ms
      - waiting for "getByText('Name')"

        expect.configure

        Creates a pre-configured expect instance with its own defaults such as timeout and soft.

        const slowExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 10000 });
await slowExpect(locator).toHaveText('Submit');

// Always do soft assertions.
const softExpect = expect.configure({ soft: true });
await softExpect(locator).toHaveText('Submit');

        expect.poll

        Turns any synchronous expect into an asynchronous polling one. For example, poll a function until it returns HTTP 200:

        await expect.poll(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  return response.status();
}, {
  // Custom expect message for reporting, optional.
  message: 'make sure API eventually succeeds',
  // Poll for 10 seconds; defaults to 5 seconds. Pass 0 to disable timeout.
  timeout: 10000,
}).toBe(200);

        Customize the pause between polls:

        await expect.poll(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  return response.status();
}, {
  // Probe, wait 1s, probe, wait 2s, probe, wait 10s, probe, wait 10s, probe
  // ... Defaults to [100, 250, 500, 1000].
  intervals: [1_000, 2_000, 10_000],
  timeout: 60_000
}).toBe(200);

        Combine expect.soft with expect.poll to get a soft assertion in polling logic (the test continues even if the assertion inside the poll fails):

        await expect.soft.poll(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  return response.status();
}).toBe(200);

// or reuse a configured instance
const softExpect = expect.configure({ soft: true });
await softExpect.poll(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  return response.status();
}).toBe(200);

        expect.toPass

        Retries an entire block of code until it succeeds.

        await expect(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
}).toPass();
        await expect(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
}).toPass({
  // Probe, wait 1s, probe, wait 2s, probe, wait 10s, probe, wait 10s, probe
  // ... Defaults to [100, 250, 500, 1000].
  intervals: [1_000, 2_000, 10_000],
  timeout: 60_000
});
        toPass timeout By default toPass has a timeout of 0 and does not respect a custom expect timeout. Set timeout explicitly.
        expect.pollexpect.toPass
        What is retriedA function that returns a single value, then a matcher is appliedAn entire block of code containing multiple assertions
        Default timeout5 seconds0, does not use the expect timeout
        Default intervals[100, 250, 500, 1000] ms

        Custom matchers – expect.extend

        Extend Playwright's assertions with custom matchers, made available on the expect object. A matcher must return a pass flag and a message callback used when the assertion fails.

        import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { Locator } from '@playwright/test';

export { test } from '@playwright/test';

export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  async toHaveAmount(locator: Locator, expected: number, options?: { timeout?: number }) {
    const assertionName = 'toHaveAmount';
    let pass: boolean;
    let matcherResult: any;
    try {
      const expectation = this.isNot ? baseExpect(locator).not : baseExpect(locator);
      await expectation.toHaveAttribute('data-amount', String(expected), options);
      pass = true;
    } catch (e: any) {
      matcherResult = e.matcherResult;
      pass = false;
    }

    if (this.isNot) {
      pass = !pass;
    }

    const message = pass
      ? () => this.utils.matcherHint(assertionName, undefined, undefined, { isNot: this.isNot }) +
          '\n\n' +
          `Locator: ${locator}\n` +
          `Expected: not ${this.utils.printExpected(expected)}\n` +
          (matcherResult ? `Received: ${this.utils.printReceived(matcherResult.actual)}` : '')
      : () =>  this.utils.matcherHint(assertionName, undefined, undefined, { isNot: this.isNot }) +
          '\n\n' +
          `Locator: ${locator}\n` +
          `Expected: ${this.utils.printExpected(expected)}\n` +
          (matcherResult ? `Received: ${this.utils.printReceived(matcherResult.actual)}` : '');

    return {
      message,
      pass,
      name: assertionName,
      expected,
      actual: matcherResult?.actual,
    };
  },
});

        Use toHaveAmount in a test:

        import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('amount', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.locator('.cart')).toHaveAmount(4);
});

        Generic custom matchers

        TypeScript cannot propagate type parameters from the matcher implementation to the call site; if a matcher is generic over the received value, the type parameter becomes unknown. To get the type of the received value in the matcher parameters, declare the signature in the PlaywrightTest.Matchers interface (the second type parameter T is the type of the value passed to expect). Generic matchers also need an explicit this type declaration to access this.utils.

        import { expect as baseExpect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { ExpectMatcherState } from '@playwright/test';

export const expect = baseExpect.extend({
  toSatisfy<T>(this: ExpectMatcherState, received: T, predicate: (value: T) => boolean) {
    const pass = predicate(received);
    return {
      message: () => `expected ${this.utils.printReceived(received)} to satisfy the predicate`,
      pass,
    };
  },
});

declare global {
  namespace PlaywrightTest {
    interface Matchers<R, T = unknown> {
      toSatisfy(predicate: (value: T) => boolean): R;
    }
  }
}
        import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('generic matcher', async () => {
  expect('hello').toSatisfy(value => value.startsWith('h'));
  expect(42).toSatisfy(value => value > 40);
});

        Compatibility with the expect library

        Do not confuse them Playwright's expect is not the expect library (Jest). That library is not fully integrated with the Playwright test runner; use Playwright's expect.

        Merging custom matchers from multiple modules

        import { mergeTests, mergeExpects } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as dbTest, expect as dbExpect } from 'database-test-utils';
import { test as a11yTest, expect as a11yExpect } from 'a11y-test-utils';

export const expect = mergeExpects(dbExpect, a11yExpect);
export const test = mergeTests(dbTest, a11yTest);
        import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('passes', async ({ database }) => {
  await expect(database).toHaveDatabaseUser('admin');
});

        Key points

        • Auto-retrying (async, await, default timeout 5s) vs non-retrying (synchronous, no retry) – prefer the former for UI data.
        • .not inverts a matcher; expect.soft does not stop the test but still makes it fail; check test.info().errors.
        • A custom message is the second argument of expect; expect.configure creates an instance with its own defaults (timeout/soft).
        • expect.poll retries a single value; expect.toPass retries a whole block of code (default timeout 0).
        • expect.extend adds matchers (return pass + message); mergeExpects/mergeTests combine multiple modules.
        What is the default assertion timeout?
        5 seconds; change it via expect.timeout in the config or the option on each assertion.
        When should you use expect.poll?
        When you need to retry an async function that returns a value (e.g. an API status) and then apply a generic matcher such as toBe(200).

        Which of the following assertions does NOT auto-retry?

        toBe is a generic matcher that runs synchronously on an already-fetched value; textContent() reads only once, so it is prone to flakiness.

        What happens when a soft assertion fails?

        expect.soft records the error without throwing; the test fails at the end.

        Pages (pages, tabs, popups)

        Each BrowserContext can hold multiple Pages; a Page is a tab or a popup window. A Page is used to navigate to URLs and interact with the page content.

        Page

        // Create a page.
const page = await context.newPage();

// Navigate explicitly, similar to entering a URL in the browser.
await page.goto('http://example.com');
// Fill an input.
await page.locator('#search').fill('query');

// Navigate implicitly by clicking a link.
await page.locator('#submit').click();
// Expect a new url.
console.log(page.url());
        In @playwright/test The page fixture already creates a fresh page in its own context for each test; use context.newPage() when you need additional pages.

        Multiple pages

        Each browser context can hold multiple pages (tabs).

        • Each page behaves like a focused, active page. There is no need to "bring to front".
        • Pages in a context follow the context-level emulation: viewport, custom network routes, locale...
        // Create two pages
const pageOne = await context.newPage();
const pageTwo = await context.newPage();

// Get pages of a browser context
const allPages = context.pages();

        Handling new pages

        The page event on the browser context lets you get a page newly created in the context, for example a page opened by a target="_blank" link.

        // Start waiting for new page before clicking. Note no await.
const pagePromise = context.waitForEvent('page');
await page.getByText('open new tab').click();
const newPage = await pagePromise;
// Interact with the new page normally.
await newPage.getByRole('button').click();
console.log(await newPage.title());

        If you do not know which action triggers the new page, listen to the event:

        // Get all new pages (including popups) in the context
context.on('page', async page => {
  await page.waitForLoadState();
  console.log(await page.title());
});
        Do not await before the click Create the waitForEvent promise before clicking (without await on that line), and only await it afterwards; otherwise you may miss the event.

        Handling popups

        If a page opens a popup (e.g. a target="_blank" link), listen to the popup event on the page. This event is emitted in addition to the browserContext.on('page') event, but only for popups related to this page.

        // Start waiting for popup before clicking. Note no await.
const popupPromise = page.waitForEvent('popup');
await page.getByText('open the popup').click();
const popup = await popupPromise;
// Interact with the new popup normally.
await popup.getByRole('button').click();
console.log(await popup.title());

        If you do not know which action triggers the popup:

        // Get all popups when they open
page.on('popup', async popup => {
  await popup.waitForLoadState();
  console.log(await popup.title());
});
        EventEmitted byWhen
        pageBrowserContextAny new page in the context (tab, popup)
        popupPageA popup opened by that very page
        1. Create the promiseconst p = context.waitForEvent('page') – no await
        2. Actawait click on a target=_blank link
        3. Await the promiseconst newPage = await p
        4. InteractnewPage.getByRole(...)

        Key points

        • One context, many pages; pages share the context's emulation/network routes/locale.
        • New page: context.waitForEvent('page'); popup: page.waitForEvent('popup').
        • Always create the promise that waits for the event before performing the triggering action.
        • Call waitForLoadState() when handling a page/popup in an event listener.

        A target="_blank" link opens a new tab. What is the standard way to get the new page?

        Waiting for an event must be registered before the action so you do not miss it; approach A has a race condition.

        Frames (iframe)

        A Page has a main frame and can have many additional Frames attached through iframe tags. Page-level interactions (such as click) operate in the main frame by default; to act inside an iframe you need to access that frame.

        Frame locator – frameLocator()

        The recommended approach: use page.frameLocator() and then chain locators such as getByLabel.

        // Locate element inside frame
const username = page.frameLocator('.frame-class').getByLabel('User Name');
await username.fill('John');
        Note The original docs example writes await before frameLocator(...).getByLabel(...); in reality the locator is created synchronously and you only need await on the action (fill).

        Frame objects – page.frame()

        Access a Frame object via page.frame():

        // Get frame using the frame's name attribute
const frame = page.frame('frame-login');

// Get frame using frame's URL
const frame = page.frame({ url: /.*domain.*/ });

// Interact with the frame
await frame.fill('#username-input', 'John');
        Note page.frame() may return null if the frame is not found, and the methods directly on Frame (e.g. frame.fill) use the legacy selector style. Prefer frameLocator + locators when possible. (The two const frame declarations above illustrate two approaches; in real code give them different names.)
        page.frameLocator(sel)page.frame(...)
        ReturnsFrameLocatorFrame object
        Selected bySelector (CSS...)name or url

        Key points

        • The main frame is the default; an iframe needs frameLocator() or page.frame().
        • page.frame('name') selects by the name attribute; page.frame({ url }) selects by URL.
        • Locators inside a frame are used like regular locators: getByLabel, getByRole...

        How do you fill "User Name" inside the iframe .frame-class?

        Page-level locators only search the main frame; you must go through frameLocator to enter the iframe.

        Navigations

        Playwright navigates to URLs and handles navigations caused by interactions on the page. Understanding "when is the page loaded", hydration, and the navigation lifecycle helps you avoid flaky tests.

        Basic navigation

        // Navigate the page
await page.goto('https://example.com');

        The code above loads the page and waits for it to fire the load event, meaning the whole page has finished loading, including dependent resources such as stylesheets, scripts, iframes, and images.

        Redirect If the page performs a client-side redirect before load, page.goto() waits for the redirected page to fire load.
        Firefox On Firefox, a navigation triggered by the page can interrupt page.goto() with the error NS_BINDING_ABORTED. This is a known Firefox limitation.

        When is the page loaded?

        Modern pages do a lot of work after the load event: lazy-loading data, building the UI, fetching heavy resources, and so on. There is no general way to know that a page is fully "loaded"; it depends on the page and the framework. So when should you start interacting? In Playwright, you can interact at any time: it automatically waits for the element to be actionable.

        // Navigate and click element
// Click will auto-wait for the element
await page.goto('https://example.com');
await page.getByText('Example Domain').click();

        Playwright waits for the text to be visible, waits for the remaining actionability checks to pass, and then clicks. It behaves like a very fast user: as soon as it sees the button, it clicks, and in general you don't need to worry about whether every resource has finished loading.

        Hydration

        Sometimes Playwright performs an action but nothing seems to happen, or the text you typed disappears. The cause is usually poor hydration.

        • With hydration, a static version of the page is sent to the browser first, then the dynamic part is sent and the page comes "alive".
        • If a button is already enabled but its listener hasn't been attached yet, Playwright still clicks it, but nothing happens.
        • How to check: open Chrome DevTools, select "Slow 3G" in the Network tab, and reload the page. As soon as you see the element, interact with it: the click is ignored and the text you type is reset by code from the later load.
        • The right fix: make sure all interactive controls are disabled until hydration completes, when the page is fully functional.

        Waiting for navigation

        Clicking an element can trigger several navigations. In that case, explicitly wait for a specific URL with page.waitForURL().

        await page.getByText('Click me').click();
await page.waitForURL('**/login');

        Back/Forward Cache (BFCache)

        Modern browsers use BFCache to load a page instantly when the user navigates back/forward: the DOM and JS heap are "frozen" in memory and then "thawed" when the user returns.

        • By default, Playwright disables BFCache in all browsers to keep the test environment consistent and clean.
        • Even if you enable BFCache yourself, testing restoration from BFCache is not supported: a BFCache restore skips the network load, so the browser does not fire the standard lifecycle events (commit, domcontentloaded, load); the internal state of Page relies on these events.
        • Consequence: calling page.goBack() in a way that causes a BFCache restore bypasses Playwright's lifecycle tracking, leading to timeouts and a Page object whose state is out of sync, so subsequent interactions fail.

        Navigation events

        Playwright splits the process of displaying a new document into navigation and loading.

        • Navigation starts: by changing the URL or interacting with the page (e.g. clicking a link). The navigation intent may be canceled (e.g. DNS fails to resolve) or turn into a file download.
        • Navigation is committed: when the response headers have been parsed and the session history has been updated. Only after a successful commit does the page start loading.
        • Loading: loading the rest of the response body, parsing, running scripts, and firing the load event.
        1. Navigation startsgoto / click link
        2. CommittedHeaders parsed, history updated
        3. New page.url()The URL is updated
        4. Parse contentLoad the body over the network and parse it
        5. DOMContentLoadedPage.DOMContentLoaded event
        6. Load resourcesScripts, stylesheets, images...
        7. loadPage.load event
        8. Dynamic scriptsThe page runs late-loading scripts

        Key takeaways

        • page.goto() waits for the load event (even after a client-side redirect).
        • You don't need to wait for the "page to finish loading"; auto-waiting takes care of waiting for elements to be actionable.
        • Poor hydration leads to lost clicks/input; fix it by disabling controls until hydration finishes.
        • Multiple navigations after a click: use page.waitForURL() to wait for the target URL.
        • BFCache is disabled by default; testing BFCache restore is not supported.

        You click a button but "nothing happens" on an SSR page whose JS loads slowly. What is the most likely cause?

        Playwright acts like a very fast user; the right fix is to disable the control until hydration is finished.

        After a click, the page goes through several redirects. What should you do?

        waitForURL explicitly waits for the target URL, which is more stable than a fixed wait.

        Dialogs

        Playwright can handle browser dialogs: alert, confirm, prompt, and beforeunload confirmations; there is also a way to verify print dialogs.

        alert(), confirm(), prompt() dialogs

        By default, dialogs are automatically dismissed by Playwright, so you don't have to handle them. However, you can register a handler before the action that triggers the dialog in order to accept or dismiss it.

        page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept());
await page.getByRole('button').click();
        The listener must handle the dialog A page.on('dialog') listener must accept/dismiss the dialog, otherwise the action (a click or anything else) will hang. Dialogs on the Web are modal, so they block page execution until they are handled.
        ❌ Avoid (WRONG)
        page.on('dialog', dialog => console.log(dialog.message()));
await page.getByRole('button').click(); // Will hang here

        The listener only logs and never accepts/dismisses, so the click will never resolve.

        ✅ Prefer
        page.on('dialog', async dialog => {
  console.log(dialog.message());
  await dialog.accept();
});
await page.getByRole('button').click();

        Always handle the dialog inside the listener.

        Note If there is no listener for page.on('dialog'), every dialog is automatically dismissed.
        MemberDescription
        dialog.accept()Accepts (OK); for a prompt you can pass the text to enter
        dialog.dismiss()Rejects/closes (Cancel)
        dialog.message()The message text
        dialog.type()alert, confirm, prompt, or beforeunload

        beforeunload dialog

        When you call page.close() with a truthy runBeforeUnload, the page runs its unload handlers. This is the only case where page.close() does not wait for the page to actually close, because the page may in the end remain open.

        Register a dialog handler to handle the beforeunload dialog yourself:

        page.on('dialog', async dialog => {
  assert(dialog.type() === 'beforeunload');
  await dialog.dismiss();
});
await page.close({ runBeforeUnload: true });

        Print dialogs

        To assert that a print dialog (via window.print) was triggered:

        await page.goto('<url>');

await page.evaluate('(() => {window.waitForPrintDialog = new Promise(f => window.print = f);})()');
await page.getByText('Print it!').click();

await page.waitForFunction('window.waitForPrintDialog');

        This snippet waits for the print dialog to open after the button is clicked. Make sure to run evaluate before clicking the button and after the page has loaded.

        Key takeaways

        • No listener means the dialog is dismissed automatically.
        • If you add a listener, you must call accept() or dismiss(), otherwise the action hangs.
        • Register the handler before the action that triggers the dialog.
        • beforeunload: page.close({ runBeforeUnload: true }) + a handler; verify a print dialog by overriding window.print.

        You have page.on('dialog', d => console.log(d.message())) and then click a button that opens a confirm. What happens?

        Once a listener exists, Playwright no longer dismisses automatically; the listener must handle the dialog.

        Downloads

        For every attachment downloaded by the page, a download event is emitted. You get the URL, file name, and payload stream from the Download object.

        Introduction

        All attachments are downloaded to a temporary directory. You can specify where to save them with the downloadsPath option of browserType.launch().

        Note Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

        The simplest way

        // Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.
const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download');
await page.getByText('Download file').click();
const download = await downloadPromise;

// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.
await download.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/' + download.suggestedFilename());
        1. Create the promisepage.waitForEvent('download') – no await
        2. Triggerclick the download button/link
        3. Receive Downloadawait downloadPromise
        4. Save the filedownload.saveAs(path)

        Variations

        If you don't know what triggers the download, you can still handle it with an event:

        page.on('download', download => download.path().then(console.log));
        Mind the control flow Event-based handling "forks" the control flow and makes the script harder to follow. Your script may finish while the file is still downloading because the main flow does not wait for this operation to complete.
        Upload To upload files, see the Upload files section.
        Download memberDescription
        download.suggestedFilename()The file name suggested by the page/server
        download.saveAs(path)Waits for the download to finish and saves it to the given path
        download.path()Path of the temporary file
        download.url()URL of the file

        Key takeaways

        • Register waitForEvent('download') before clicking (don't await it right away).
        • Use saveAs() to keep the file permanently; the temp file is deleted when the context closes.
        • Configure the download directory with downloadsPath at launch.
        • A page.on('download') handler splits the control flow; the test may end before the download finishes.

        What is the correct order to capture a download?

        You must register the wait for the event before clicking so you don't miss it; only then await it and save.

        Network

        Playwright lets you monitor and modify all of the browser's HTTP/HTTPS traffic, including XHR and fetch. This is the foundation for mocking APIs, blocking resources, adding proxies, HTTP authentication, and tracking WebSockets.

        Mock APIs

        This page is the "advanced" part about networking. If you just want to mock quickly, see Mock APIs to learn how to:

        • mock API requests and never hit the real API;
        • call the real API and then modify the response;
        • use HAR files to mock the network.

        Network mocking

        No configuration is needed: just define a custom Route on the browser context to mock the network for the whole context.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ context }) => {
  // Block any css requests for each test in this file.
  await context.route(/.css$/, route => route.abort());
});

test('loads page without css', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  // ... test goes here
});

        Or use page.route() to mock in a single page only:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('loads page without images', async ({ page }) => {
  // Block png and jpeg images.
  await page.route(/(png|jpeg)$/, route => route.abort());

  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  // ... test goes here
});

        HTTP Authentication

        Perform HTTP Authentication (Basic/Digest...) with the httpCredentials option.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    httpCredentials: {
      username: 'bill',
      password: 'pa55w0rd',
    }
  }
});
        const context = await browser.newContext({
  httpCredentials: {
    username: 'bill',
    password: 'pa55w0rd',
  },
});
const page = await context.newPage();
await page.goto('https://example.com');

        HTTP Proxy

        You can configure pages to load over an HTTP(S) or SOCKSv5 proxy. The proxy can be set globally for the whole browser or separately for each browser context. You can additionally specify a username/password for an HTTP(S) proxy and a list of hosts that bypass the proxy (bypass) – see the proxy option of browser.newContext().

        Global proxy:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    proxy: {
      server: 'http://myproxy.com:3128',
      username: 'usr',
      password: 'pwd'
    }
  }
});
        const browser = await chromium.launch({
  proxy: {
    server: 'http://myproxy.com:3128',
    username: 'usr',
    password: 'pwd'
  }
});

        Per-context proxy:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('should use custom proxy on a new context', async ({ browser }) => {
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    proxy: {
      server: 'http://myproxy.com:3128',
    }
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();

  await context.close();
});
        const browser = await chromium.launch();
const context = await browser.newContext({
  proxy: { server: 'http://myproxy.com:3128' }
});

        Network events

        You can monitor every Request and Response through page events:

        // Subscribe to 'request' and 'response' events.
page.on('request', request => console.log('>>', request.method(), request.url()));
page.on('response', response => console.log('<<', response.status(), response.url()));

await page.goto('https://example.com');

        Or wait for a response after clicking a button with page.waitForResponse():

        // Use a glob URL pattern. Note no await.
const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse('**/api/fetch_data');
await page.getByText('Update').click();
const response = await responsePromise;
        Watch the "no await": you must start waiting before the action that causes the response (without an immediate await), and only then await the promise; otherwise you may miss the response.

        Variations

        page.waitForResponse() accepts a glob, a RegExp, or a predicate that receives the Response object:

        // Use a RegExp. Note no await.
const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(/\.jpeg$/);
await page.getByText('Update').click();
const response = await responsePromise;

// Use a predicate taking a Response object. Note no await.
const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(response => response.url().includes(token));
await page.getByText('Update').click();
const response = await responsePromise;

        Handle requests

        Mock an API endpoint by handling the request in your Playwright script; route.fulfill() returns a fake response without touching the network.

        await page.route('**/api/fetch_data', route => route.fulfill({
  status: 200,
  body: testData,
}));
await page.goto('https://example.com');

        Variations

        Set a route on the whole browser context with browserContext.route() or on a single page with page.route(). A context-level route also applies to popups and links opened from the page.

        await browserContext.route('**/api/login', route => route.fulfill({
  status: 200,
  body: 'accept',
}));
await page.goto('https://example.com');

        Modify requests

        Use route.continue() to let a request go through with modifications (headers, method, postData, url...).

        // Delete header
await page.route('**/*', async route => {
  const headers = route.request().headers();
  delete headers['x-secret'];
  await route.continue({ headers });
});

// Continue requests as POST.
await page.route('**/*', route => route.continue({ method: 'POST' }));

        The first example removes an HTTP header from every outgoing request.

        Abort requests

        Block requests with page.route() and route.abort(): by URL pattern or by resource type (resourceType()).

        await page.route('**/*.{png,jpg,jpeg}', route => route.abort());

// Abort based on the request type
await page.route('**/*', route => {
  return route.request().resourceType() === 'image' ? route.abort() : route.continue();
});

        Modify responses

        To modify a response: use route.fetch() (via APIRequestContext) to get the original response, then pass it to route.fulfill(). You can override individual fields (body, headers, status...).

        await page.route('**/title.html', async route => {
  // Fetch original response.
  const response = await route.fetch();
  // Add a prefix to the title.
  let body = await response.text();
  body = body.replace('<title>', '<title>My prefix:');
  await route.fulfill({
    // Pass all fields from the response.
    response,
    // Override response body.
    body,
    // Force content type to be html.
    headers: {
      ...response.headers(),
      'content-type': 'text/html'
    }
  });
});
        1. Page sends a requestfetch / XHR / navigation / image load...
        2. Route handler runsbefore the request enters the browser's network stack
        3a. route.continue()let it through (optionally modifying header/method/url)
        3b. route.fulfill()return a fake response, without touching the network
        3c. route.abort()make the request fail
        4. Network stackadds Cookie, Host, Sec-Fetch-*... and then sends to the server

        How request interception works

        A route sits between the page and the browser's network stack. The handler runs before the network stack processes the request: route.continue() forwards it, route.fulfill() answers without touching the network, and route.abort() makes the request fail.

        Headers owned by the network stack

        Some headers are attached by the network stack right before sending: Cookie, Host, Accept-Encoding, Content-Length, Sec-Fetch-*, and a few others. This is a security boundary (for example, HttpOnly cookies are never exposed to the page). Because the handler runs before this step:

        • these headers are not guaranteed to appear in request.headers() / request.allHeaders(), and they cannot be overridden;
        • a cookie header passed to route.continue() is ignored, and the browser's cookie store is always used;
        • on the response side, the network stack has already finished processing, so response.allHeaders() returns the headers exactly as the server sent them, including Set-Cookie for HttpOnly cookies;
        • to see the real headers on the wire: observe the request without routing it – when there is no route, request.allHeaders() is complete.

        Redirects

        Playwright treats a request together with its redirects as a single unit. The handler is called only once for the original request; the browser follows the redirects itself. response.request() returns the last request in the chain, and request.redirectedFrom() walks back to the request you intercepted. Headers passed to route.continue() apply to every hop (except cookie).

        Fulfilling with a 3xx: this gives you no second chance to intercept. Chromium and Firefox follow the redirect themselves without calling the handler, and WebKit rejects the call. If you want to return different content, fulfill with that content directly; if you want to redirect the request, pass url to route.continue() or route.fallback().

        Glob URL patterns

        Playwright uses simple globs to match URLs in page.route(), page.waitForResponse(), and so on:

        CharacterMeaning
        *matches any characters except /
        **matches any characters including /
        ?matches only the literal ? character (to match any single character, use *)
        {}a comma-separated list of alternatives
        \escapes special characters (escape itself with \\)
        • https://example.com/*.js matches https://example.com/file.js but not https://example.com/path/file.js
        • https://example.com/?page=1 matches https://example.com/?page=1 but not https://example.com
        • **/*.js matches both https://example.com/file.js and https://example.com/path/file.js
        • **/*.{png,jpg,jpeg} matches all image requests
        Important note: the glob must match the entire URL (including the protocol and path separators), not just a part of it. For more complex requirements, use a RegExp.

        WebSockets

        Playwright supports inspecting, mocking, and modifying WebSockets out of the box (see Mock APIs, the Mock WebSockets section). Whenever a WebSocket is created, the page.on('websocket') event is fired with a WebSocket object so you can inspect its frames:

        page.on('websocket', ws => {
  console.log(`WebSocket opened: ${ws.url()}>`);
  ws.on('framesent', event => console.log(event.payload));
  ws.on('framereceived', event => console.log(event.payload));
  ws.on('close', () => console.log('WebSocket closed'));
});

        Missing Network Events and Service Workers

        Playwright's built-in browserContext.route() and page.route() let you route requests, mock, and intercept natively. If you use them and notice missing network events, disable Service Workers by setting the serviceWorkers option to 'block'.

        You may be using a mocking tool such as Mock Service Worker (MSW): it works well for mocking responses, but it adds its own Service Worker that "takes over" network requests, making them invisible to context.route() / page.route(). If you care about both network testing and mocking, use the built-in routes for response mocking.

        If you want to route/listen to requests made by the Service Worker itself, see Service Workers.

        Key takeaways

        • route.continue() / fulfill() / abort() are the 3 main actions; route.fetch() + fulfill({ response, ... }) modifies a real response.
        • A route on the context also applies to popups; a route on the page applies only to that page.
        • A glob matches the whole URL; * does not cross /, ** does.
        • Headers such as Cookie and Host are attached by the network stack and cannot be overridden.
        • Redirects: the handler runs only once for the original request.
        • Missing events, or a route not catching a request? Try serviceWorkers: 'block'.

        Which glob pattern matches both https://example.com/file.js and https://example.com/path/file.js?

        ** matches / as well, while a single * does not. ? matches only a literal question mark.

        You call route.continue({ headers: { cookie: 'a=b' } }). What happens to the cookie header?

        Cookie is a header owned by the network stack and attached after the route handler runs, so it cannot be overridden.

        Mock APIs

        Web APIs are usually HTTP endpoints. Playwright lets you mock and modify HTTP/HTTPS traffic (XHR, fetch) and even replay it from a HAR file containing many requests – making tests stable, fast, and independent of the backend.

        Mock API requests

        The code below intercepts every call to */**/api/v1/fruits and returns a custom response; no request reaches the real API. The test opens the URL that uses the mocked route and checks that the mock data is displayed.

        test("mocks a fruit and doesn't call api", async ({ page }) => {
  // Mock the api call before navigating
  await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => {
    const json = [{ name: 'Strawberry', id: 21 }];
    await route.fulfill({ json });
  });
  // Go to the page
  await page.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking');

  // Assert that the Strawberry fruit is visible
  await expect(page.getByText('Strawberry')).toBeVisible();
});
        Trace: in the test's trace you will see that the API was never called; the request was fulfilled with the mock data. The json option of route.fulfill() serializes the data automatically and sets the JSON content-type.
        Order: you must register the route before page.goto() (or before the action that produces the request), otherwise the first request may already have gone out to the real network.

        See also Network for advanced techniques.

        Modify API responses

        Sometimes you need to call the real API but "patch" the response so the test is repeatable. Instead of mocking completely, perform the request and then fulfill with the modified response. For example, add a "Loquat" fruit to the data:

        test('gets the json from api and adds a new fruit', async ({ page }) => {
  // Get the response and add to it
  await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => {
    const response = await route.fetch();
    const json = await response.json();
    json.push({ name: 'Loquat', id: 100 });
    // Fulfill using the original response, while patching the response body
    // with the given JSON object.
    await route.fulfill({ response, json });
  });

  // Go to the page
  await page.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking');

  // Assert that the new fruit is visible
  await expect(page.getByText('Loquat', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
});

        In the trace, the API is called and the response has been modified (the new fruit is added to the list).

        ❌ Mocking everything when you need real data
        await route.fulfill({ json: [{ name: 'Strawberry', id: 21 }] });

        You lose all the real data; there is no more integration check against the backend.

        ✅ fetch, then patch the response
        const response = await route.fetch();
const json = await response.json();
json.push({ name: 'Loquat', id: 100 });
await route.fulfill({ response, json });

        Keeps the real data intact and only adds what is needed to make the test reproducible.

        Mocking with HAR files

        A HAR (HTTP Archive) is a file containing a record of all network requests made when loading a page: request/response headers, cookies, content, timing, and so on. The workflow:

        1. RecordrouteFromHAR with update: true (or recordHar / CLI)
        2. Modifyedit the data in the HAR file and commit it with the test
        3. ReplayrouteFromHAR with update: false or without the option

        Recording a HAR file

        Use page.routeFromHAR() or browserContext.routeFromHAR(): they take the path to the HAR file and an optional options object. The url option (a glob) restricts serving from the HAR to matching requests only; if omitted, all requests are served from the HAR. Setting update: true will create/update the HAR file with real network information instead of serving from the HAR – use it when writing a test to fill in real data.

        Alternatively, you can record a HAR with the recordHar option of browser.newContext(): it records all of the context's traffic until the context is closed.

        test('records or updates the HAR file', async ({ page }) => {
  // Get the response from the HAR file
  await page.routeFromHAR('./hars/fruit.har', {
    url: '*/**/api/v1/fruits',
    update: true,
  });

  // Go to the page
  await page.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking');

  // Assert that the fruit is visible
  await expect(page.getByText('Strawberry')).toBeVisible();
});

        Modifying a HAR file

        After recording, you can edit it by opening the .txt file (with a hashed name) in the hars folder and modifying the JSON. This file should be committed to source control. Each time you run the test with update: true, the HAR file is refreshed from the API.

        [
  {
    "name": "Playwright",
    "id": 100
  },
  // ... other fruits
]

        Replaying from HAR

        Once you have a HAR (and have edited the mock data), turn off or remove the update option so the test runs against the HAR instead of calling the API.

        test('gets the json from HAR and checks the new fruit has been added', async ({ page }) => {
  // Replay API requests from HAR.
  // Either use a matching response from the HAR,
  // or abort the request if nothing matches.
  await page.routeFromHAR('./hars/fruit.har', {
    url: '*/**/api/v1/fruits',
    update: false,
  });

  // Go to the page
  await page.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking');

  // Assert that the Playwright fruit is visible
  await expect(page.getByText('Playwright', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
});

        Matching rules during replay:

        • The URL and HTTP method must match strictly; for POST, the payload must also match strictly.
        • If multiple records match, the one with the most matching headers is chosen.
        • Entries that lead to a redirect are followed automatically.
        • If the HAR file name ends with .zip, it is an archive containing the HAR along with separate payloads. You can unzip it, edit the payloads or the HAR log manually, and then point to the unzipped HAR file; all payloads are resolved relative to that HAR file.
        What if nothing matches? As the comment in the example says: use the matching response from the HAR, or abort the request if nothing matches.

        Recording HAR with CLI

        Using the update option to record a HAR for tests is recommended, but you can also record with the Playwright CLI: open a browser with --save-har; additionally use --save-har-glob to save only the requests you need (e.g. API endpoints). If the HAR file name ends with .zip, the artifacts are recorded as separate files and then compressed into a single zip.

        # Save API requests from example.com as "example.har" archive.
npx playwright open --save-har=example.har --save-har-glob="**/api/**" https://example.com

        Mock WebSockets

        The following snippet intercepts a WebSocket connection and mocks all communication instead of connecting to the server. For example, it replies "response" to every "request":

        await page.routeWebSocket('wss://example.com/ws', ws => {
  ws.onMessage(message => {
    if (message === 'request')
      ws.send('response');
  });
});

        Or connect to the real server but intercept in the middle to modify/block messages. For example, modify some messages the page sends to the server and leave the rest untouched:

        await page.routeWebSocket('wss://example.com/ws', ws => {
  const server = ws.connectToServer();
  ws.onMessage(message => {
    if (message === 'request')
      server.send('request2');
    else
      server.send(message);
  });
});

        For details, see the WebSocketRoute class in the API reference.

        GoalAPI
        Return completely fake dataroute.fulfill({ json })
        Modify a real responseroute.fetch() + route.fulfill({ response, json })
        Replay from HARpage.routeFromHAR(path, { url, update })
        Record a HAR for the whole contextrecordHar option / CLI --save-har
        Mock a WebSocketpage.routeWebSocket(url, handler)

        Key takeaways

        • Register the route before the navigation/action that produces the request.
        • route.fulfill({ json }) to mock; route.fetch() + fulfill({ response, json }) to patch a response.
        • HAR: record (update: true) -> edit -> replay (update: false); URL/method/POST payload matching is strict.
        • A .zip HAR holds separate payloads and can be unzipped for manual editing.
        • routeWebSocket mocks everything or sits between the client and the real server via connectToServer().

        You want to get real data from the API and add an element before returning it to the page. What should you do?

        route.fetch() performs the real request; fulfill with the original response and the new json patches the body.

        When replaying from a HAR (update: false), what happens to a request that matches no record?

        According to the comment in the docs: use the matching response from the HAR, or abort the request if nothing matches.

        Mock browser APIs

        For experimental APIs or APIs that are not yet fully supported by every browser, Playwright usually has no dedicated automation API. You can use mocks to verify the app's behavior. This page illustrates the approach with the Battery API.

        Introduction

        Suppose a web app uses the battery API to display battery status. We will mock this API and check that the page shows the battery status correctly.

        Creating mocks

        Since the page may call the API very early while loading, every mock must be set up before the page starts loading. The easiest way is page.addInitScript():

        await page.addInitScript(() => {
  const mockBattery = {
    level: 0.75,
    charging: true,
    chargingTime: 1800,
    dischargingTime: Infinity,
    addEventListener: () => { }
  };
  // Override the method to always return mock battery info.
  window.navigator.getBattery = async () => mockBattery;
});

        Then navigate and check the UI state:

        // Configure mock API before each test.
test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    const mockBattery = {
      level: 0.90,
      charging: true,
      chargingTime: 1800, // seconds
      dischargingTime: Infinity,
      addEventListener: () => { }
    };
    // Override the method to always return mock battery info.
    window.navigator.getBattery = async () => mockBattery;
  });
});

test('show battery status', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-percentage')).toHaveText('90%');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-status')).toHaveText('Adapter');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-fully')).toHaveText('00:30');
});

        Mocking read-only APIs

        Some APIs are read-only, so you can't assign to properties of navigator:

        // Following line will have no effect.
navigator.cookieEnabled = true;

        However, if the property is configurable, you can still override it with plain JavaScript:

        await page.addInitScript(() => {
  Object.defineProperty(Object.getPrototypeOf(navigator), 'cookieEnabled', { value: false });
});

        Verifying API calls

        Sometimes you need to verify that the page makes all the expected API calls. You can record every call and then compare it with a "golden" result. page.exposeFunction() is useful for sending messages from the page back to the test code:

        test('log battery calls', async ({ page }) => {
  const log = [];
  // Expose function for pushing messages to the Node.js script.
  await page.exposeFunction('logCall', msg => log.push(msg));
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    const mockBattery = {
      level: 0.75,
      charging: true,
      chargingTime: 1800,
      dischargingTime: Infinity,
      // Log addEventListener calls.
      addEventListener: (name, cb) => logCall(`addEventListener:${name}`)
    };
    // Override the method to always return mock battery info.
    window.navigator.getBattery = async () => {
      logCall('getBattery');
      return mockBattery;
    };
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-percentage')).toHaveText('75%');

  // Compare actual calls with golden.
  expect(log).toEqual([
    'getBattery',
    'addEventListener:chargingchange',
    'addEventListener:levelchange'
  ]);
});

        Updating mock

        To verify that the app reacts correctly when the battery status changes, the mock must fire the right events like the browser's real implementation. The example below uses a mock class that can notify listeners, and then the test triggers changes through page.evaluate():

        test('update battery status (no golden)', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    // Mock class that will notify corresponding listeners when battery status changes.
    class BatteryMock {
      level = 0.10;
      charging = false;
      chargingTime = 1800;
      dischargingTime = Infinity;
      _chargingListeners = [];
      _levelListeners = [];
      addEventListener(eventName, listener) {
        if (eventName === 'chargingchange')
          this._chargingListeners.push(listener);
        if (eventName === 'levelchange')
          this._levelListeners.push(listener);
      }
      // Will be called by the test.
      _setLevel(value) {
        this.level = value;
        this._levelListeners.forEach(cb => cb());
      }
      _setCharging(value) {
        this.charging = value;
        this._chargingListeners.forEach(cb => cb());
      }
    }
    const mockBattery = new BatteryMock();
    // Override the method to always return mock battery info.
    window.navigator.getBattery = async () => mockBattery;
    // Save the mock object on window for easier access.
    window.mockBattery = mockBattery;
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-percentage')).toHaveText('10%');

  // Update level to 27.5%
  await page.evaluate(() => window.mockBattery._setLevel(0.275));
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-percentage')).toHaveText('27.5%');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-status')).toHaveText('Battery');

  // Emulate connected adapter
  await page.evaluate(() => window.mockBattery._setCharging(true));
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-status')).toHaveText('Adapter');
  await expect(page.locator('.battery-fully')).toHaveText('00:30');
});
        1. addInitScriptinstall the mock before the page runs its scripts
        2. gotothe page calls the API (already mocked)
        3. exposeFunction(optional) the page reports calls back to the test
        4. evaluatethe test changes the mock's state, and the mock fires events
        5. expectverify the UI reflects it correctly

        Key takeaways

        • Install mocks with page.addInitScript() so they run before any of the page's scripts.
        • Read-only properties: use Object.defineProperty on the prototype if configurable.
        • page.exposeFunction() helps record API calls to compare against a "golden" result.
        • Stateful mocks should be installed on window and controlled with page.evaluate(); remember to fire events just like the real browser.

        Why should you install the mock with addInitScript instead of page.evaluate after goto?

        The init script runs before any of the page's scripts, ensuring the mock is ready when the page calls the API early.

        API testing

        Playwright can access your application's REST API directly from Node.js without opening a page: to test the API server, to prepare server-side state before a UI test, or to verify post-conditions after actions in the browser. Everything is based on APIRequestContext.

        Introduction

        Example use cases:

        • Testing the server API.
        • Preparing server-side state before entering the web app in a test.
        • Validating server-side post-conditions after running some actions in the browser.

        Writing API Test

        APIRequestContext can send all kinds of HTTP(S) requests. For example, a test that creates issues via the GitHub API: create a repository before running the tests, create a few issues and check the server state, then delete the repository after the run.

        Configuration

        The GitHub API requires authorization, so configure the token once for all tests and also set baseURL. Put it in the config file or in the test file with test.use().

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // All requests we send go to this API endpoint.
    baseURL: 'https://api.github.com',
    extraHTTPHeaders: {
      // We set this header per GitHub guidelines.
      'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
      // Add authorization token to all requests.
      // Assuming personal access token available in the environment.
      'Authorization': `token ${process.env.API_TOKEN}`,
    },
  }
});

        Proxy configuration: if your tests run behind a proxy, declare it in the config; the request fixture picks it up automatically:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    proxy: {
      server: 'http://my-proxy:8080',
      username: 'user',
      password: 'secret'
    },
  }
});

        Writing tests

        Playwright Test comes with a built-in request fixture that respects configured options such as baseURL and extraHTTPHeaders.

        const REPO = 'test-repo-1';
const USER = 'github-username';

test('should create a bug report', async ({ request }) => {
  const newIssue = await request.post(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`, {
    data: {
      title: '[Bug] report 1',
      body: 'Bug description',
    }
  });
  expect(newIssue.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  const issues = await request.get(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`);
  expect(issues.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  expect(await issues.json()).toContainEqual(expect.objectContaining({
    title: '[Bug] report 1',
    body: 'Bug description'
  }));
});

test('should create a feature request', async ({ request }) => {
  const newIssue = await request.post(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`, {
    data: {
      title: '[Feature] request 1',
      body: 'Feature description',
    }
  });
  expect(newIssue.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  const issues = await request.get(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`);
  expect(issues.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  expect(await issues.json()).toContainEqual(expect.objectContaining({
    title: '[Feature] request 1',
    body: 'Feature description'
  }));
});

        Setup and teardown

        The tests above assume the repository already exists. Usually you want to create a new one before running and delete it afterwards, using the beforeAll / afterAll hooks:

        test.beforeAll(async ({ request }) => {
  // Create a new repository
  const response = await request.post('/user/repos', {
    data: {
      name: REPO
    }
  });
  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();
});

test.afterAll(async ({ request }) => {
  // Delete the repository
  const response = await request.delete(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}`);
  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();
});

        Using request context

        Under the hood, the request fixture calls APIRequest.newContext(). You can call it yourself for more control. This is a standalone script equivalent to the beforeAll/afterAll above:

        import { request } from '@playwright/test';
const REPO = 'test-repo-1';
const USER = 'github-username';

(async () => {
  // Create a context that will issue http requests.
  const context = await request.newContext({
    baseURL: 'https://api.github.com',
  });

  // Create a repository.
  await context.post('/user/repos', {
    headers: {
      'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
      // Add GitHub personal access token.
      'Authorization': `token ${process.env.API_TOKEN}`,
    },
    data: {
      name: REPO
    }
  });

  // Delete a repository.
  await context.delete(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}`, {
    headers: {
      'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
      // Add GitHub personal access token.
      'Authorization': `token ${process.env.API_TOKEN}`,
    }
  });
})();

        Sending API requests from UI tests

        While running tests inside the browser, you can call your application's HTTP API to prepare server state before a test or verify post-conditions after actions in the browser – all with APIRequestContext.

        Establishing preconditions

        The test below creates a new issue via the API, then opens the issue list and checks that it is at the top of the list.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const REPO = 'test-repo-1';
const USER = 'github-username';

// Request context is reused by all tests in the file.
let apiContext;

test.beforeAll(async ({ playwright }) => {
  apiContext = await playwright.request.newContext({
    // All requests we send go to this API endpoint.
    baseURL: 'https://api.github.com',
    extraHTTPHeaders: {
      // We set this header per GitHub guidelines.
      'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
      // Add authorization token to all requests.
      // Assuming personal access token available in the environment.
      'Authorization': `token ${process.env.API_TOKEN}`,
    },
  });
});

test.afterAll(async ({ }) => {
  // Dispose all responses.
  await apiContext.dispose();
});

test('last created issue should be first in the list', async ({ page }) => {
  const newIssue = await apiContext.post(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`, {
    data: {
      title: '[Feature] request 1',
    }
  });
  expect(newIssue.ok()).toBeTruthy();

  await page.goto(`https://github.com/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`);
  const firstIssue = page.locator(`a[data-hovercard-type='issue']`).first();
  await expect(firstIssue).toHaveText('[Feature] request 1');
});

        Validating postconditions

        The test below creates an issue through the browser UI and then verifies via the API that it exists:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const REPO = 'test-repo-1';
const USER = 'github-username';

// Request context is reused by all tests in the file.
let apiContext;

test.beforeAll(async ({ playwright }) => {
  apiContext = await playwright.request.newContext({
    // All requests we send go to this API endpoint.
    baseURL: 'https://api.github.com',
    extraHTTPHeaders: {
      // We set this header per GitHub guidelines.
      'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
      // Add authorization token to all requests.
      // Assuming personal access token available in the environment.
      'Authorization': `token ${process.env.API_TOKEN}`,
    },
  });
});

test.afterAll(async ({ }) => {
  // Dispose all responses.
  await apiContext.dispose();
});

test('last created issue should be on the server', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto(`https://github.com/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`);
  await page.getByText('New Issue').click();
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Title' }).fill('Bug report 1');
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Comment body' }).fill('Bug description');
  await page.getByText('Submit new issue').click();
  const issueId = new URL(page.url()).pathname.split('/').pop();

  const newIssue = await apiContext.get(
      `https://api.github.com/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues/${issueId}`
  );
  expect(newIssue.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  expect(await newIssue.json()).toEqual(expect.objectContaining({
    title: 'Bug report 1'
  }));
});
        1. Create the contextplaywright.request.newContext({ baseURL, extraHTTPHeaders })
        2. Precondition via APIPOST creates data quickly, bypassing the UI
        3. UI actionspage.goto / click / fill
        4. Postcondition via APIGET confirms the server state
        5. DisposeapiContext.dispose() in afterAll

        Reusing authentication state

        Web apps use cookie-based or token-based authentication, and the signed-in state is stored as cookies. apiRequestContext.storageState() retrieves the storage state from an authenticated context so you can create a new context with that state. Storage state is interchangeable between BrowserContext and APIRequestContext: sign in via the API and then create a browser context that already has the cookies.

        const requestContext = await request.newContext({
  httpCredentials: {
    username: 'user',
    password: 'passwd'
  }
});
await requestContext.get(`https://api.example.com/login`);
// Save storage state into the file.
await requestContext.storageState({ path: 'state.json' });

// Create a new context with the saved storage state.
const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'state.json' });

        Context request vs global request

        There are two kinds of APIRequestContext:

        Tied to a BrowserContextStandalone instance
        How to get itbrowserContext.request, page.requestplaywright.request.newContext()
        Cookie headerTaken from the browser contextIts own isolated cookie storage
        Set-Cookie in the responseAutomatically updates the browser context's cookiesDoes not affect the browser context; export via storageState()

        Example of a context request sharing cookie storage with its browser context:

        test('context request will share cookie storage with its browser context', async ({
  page,
  context,
}) => {
  await context.route('https://www.github.com/', async route => {
    // Send an API request that shares cookie storage with the browser context.
    const response = await context.request.fetch(route.request());
    const responseHeaders = response.headers();

    // The response will have 'Set-Cookie' header.
    const responseCookies = new Map(responseHeaders['set-cookie']
        .split('\n')
        .map(c => c.split(';', 2)[0].split('=')));
    // The response will have 3 cookies in 'Set-Cookie' header.
    expect(responseCookies.size).toBe(3);
    const contextCookies = await context.cookies();
    // The browser context will already contain all the cookies from the API response.
    expect(new Map(contextCookies.map(({ name, value }) =>
      [name, value])
    )).toEqual(responseCookies);

    await route.fulfill({
      response,
      headers: { ...responseHeaders, foo: 'bar' },
    });
  });
  await page.goto('https://www.github.com/');
});

        If you don't want APIRequestContext to use and update the browser context's cookies, create a new instance with isolated cookies:

        test('global context request has isolated cookie storage', async ({
  page,
  context,
  browser,
  playwright
}) => {
  // Create a new instance of APIRequestContext with isolated cookie storage.
  const request = await playwright.request.newContext();
  await context.route('https://www.github.com/', async route => {
    const response = await request.fetch(route.request());
    const responseHeaders = response.headers();

    const responseCookies = new Map(responseHeaders['set-cookie']
        .split('\n')
        .map(c => c.split(';', 2)[0].split('=')));
    // The response will have 3 cookies in 'Set-Cookie' header.
    expect(responseCookies.size).toBe(3);
    const contextCookies = await context.cookies();
    // The browser context will not have any cookies from the isolated API request.
    expect(contextCookies.length).toBe(0);

    // Manually export cookie storage.
    const storageState = await request.storageState();
    // Create a new context and initialize it with the cookies from the global request.
    const browserContext2 = await browser.newContext({ storageState });
    const contextCookies2 = await browserContext2.cookies();
    // The new browser context will already contain all the cookies from the API response.
    expect(
        new Map(contextCookies2.map(({ name, value }) => [name, value]))
    ).toEqual(responseCookies);

    await route.fulfill({
      response,
      headers: { ...responseHeaders, foo: 'bar' },
    });
  });
  await page.goto('https://www.github.com/');
  await request.dispose();
});

        Key takeaways

        • The request fixture respects baseURL, extraHTTPHeaders, and proxy from the config.
        • Use beforeAll/afterAll to create and clean up server-side data; remember apiContext.dispose() for contexts you create yourself.
        • storageState can be used back and forth between APIRequestContext and BrowserContext.
        • page.request/context.request share cookies with the browser; playwright.request.newContext() is isolated.

        You want an API request that does not change the browser context's cookies. What do you use?

        An instance created with newContext() has isolated cookie storage; page.request and context.request share cookies with the browser context.

        Authentication

        Playwright runs tests in isolated environments called browser contexts. Tests can load a pre-authenticated state, so you don't have to sign in in every test and tests run much faster.

        Core concepts

        Whichever strategy you choose, you will usually save the authenticated browser state to the file system. It is a good idea to create a playwright/.auth directory and add it to .gitignore. The authentication step generates the state and saves it there; later tests reuse this state and start out signed in.

        Danger: the browser state file may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test accounts. Never commit it to a repository (public or private).
        mkdir -p playwright/.auth
echo $'\nplaywright/.auth' >> .gitignore
        md playwright\.auth
echo. >> .gitignore
echo "playwright/.auth" >> .gitignore
        New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path playwright\.auth
Add-Content -path .gitignore "`r`nplaywright/.auth"

        Basic: shared account in all tests

        This is the recommended approach for tests with no server-side state. Authenticate once in a setup project, save the state, and then reuse it so that every test starts out signed in.

        When to useWhen NOT to use
        When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account without affecting each other. Your tests modify server-side state (e.g. one test checks the rendering of the settings page while another changes a setting, running in parallel) – in that case you must use different accounts. Or the authentication is browser-specific.

        Create tests/auth.setup.ts to prepare the state for all other tests:

        import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const authFile = path.join(__dirname, '../playwright/.auth/user.json');

setup('authenticate', async ({ page }) => {
  // Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.
  await page.goto('https://github.com/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('username');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  // Wait until the page receives the cookies.
  //
  // Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.
  // Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.
  await page.waitForURL('https://github.com/');
  // Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'View profile and more' })).toBeVisible();

  // End of authentication steps.

  await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile });
});

        Create a setup project in the config and declare it as a dependency of all your test projects. This project always runs and authenticates before all the tests. Every test project uses that state as its storageState.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    // Setup project
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/ },

    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        // Use prepared auth state.
        storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
      },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },

    {
      name: 'firefox',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Firefox'],
        // Use prepared auth state.
        storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
      },
      dependencies: ['setup'],
    },
  ],
});

        Tests start out authenticated because storageState is declared in the config:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('test', async ({ page }) => {
  // page is authenticated
});
        IndexedDB: if your app stores tokens in IndexedDB (e.g. Firebase Authentication), enable the indexedDB option when saving state: await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile, indexedDB: true }). IndexedDB is not part of the snapshot by default.

        Note: you must delete the saved state when it expires. If you don't need to keep the state between runs, write it to TestProject.outputDir – this directory is cleaned automatically before every test run.

        1. setup projectruns auth.setup.ts before the other projects (dependencies)
        2. Sign infill in the form, wait for the cookies to be set (waitForURL / expect)
        3. Save statecontext.storageState({ path }) into playwright/.auth
        4. Test projectuse.storageState loads that file
        5. Every testthe page is already signed in

        Authenticating in UI mode

        UI mode does not run the setup project by default, to speed things up. You should run auth.setup.ts manually from time to time, when the login session expires: first enable the setup project in the filters, click the triangle button next to the auth.setup.ts file, and then disable the setup project in the filters again. See UI mode.

        Moderate: one account per parallel worker

        This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state. Each parallel worker process authenticates once with its own account; all tests in that worker share that state. You need multiple test accounts, one per worker.

        When to useWhen NOT to use
        Tests modify shared server-side state (e.g. one test checks the settings page while another changes a setting). Tests do not modify shared server-side state – in that case use a single shared account for everything.

        Create playwright/fixtures.ts to override the storageState fixture so it authenticates once per worker, using testInfo.parallelIndex to tell workers apart.

        import { test as baseTest, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

export * from '@playwright/test';
export const test = baseTest.extend<{}, { workerStorageState: string }>({
  // Use the same storage state for all tests in this worker.
  storageState: ({ workerStorageState }, use) => use(workerStorageState),

  // Authenticate once per worker with a worker-scoped fixture.
  workerStorageState: [async ({ browser }, use) => {
    // Use parallelIndex as a unique identifier for each worker.
    const id = test.info().parallelIndex;
    const fileName = path.resolve(test.info().project.outputDir, `.auth/${id}.json`);

    if (fs.existsSync(fileName)) {
      // Reuse existing authentication state if any.
      await use(fileName);
      return;
    }

    // Important: make sure we authenticate in a clean environment by unsetting storage state.
    const page = await browser.newPage({ storageState: undefined });

    // Acquire a unique account, for example create a new one.
    // Alternatively, you can have a list of precreated accounts for testing.
    // Make sure that accounts are unique, so that multiple team members
    // can run tests at the same time without interference.
    const account = await acquireAccount(id);

    // Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.
    await page.goto('https://github.com/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill(account.username);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(account.password);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    // Wait until the page receives the cookies.
    //
    // Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.
    // Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.
    await page.waitForURL('https://github.com/');
    // Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.
    await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'View profile and more' })).toBeVisible();

    // End of authentication steps.

    await page.context().storageState({ path: fileName });
    await page.close();
    await use(fileName);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

        Each test file imports test from the fixtures file instead of @playwright/test. No config changes are needed.

        // Important: import our fixtures.
import { test, expect } from '../playwright/fixtures';

test('test', async ({ page }) => {
  // page is authenticated
});

        Advanced scenarios

        Authenticate with API request

        When to use: your web app supports authentication via an API that is easier/faster than driving the UI. Send the request with APIRequestContext and then save the state as usual. In the setup project:

        import { test as setup } from '@playwright/test';

const authFile = 'playwright/.auth/user.json';

setup('authenticate', async ({ request }) => {
  // Send authentication request. Replace with your own.
  await request.post('https://github.com/login', {
    form: {
      'user': 'user',
      'password': 'password'
    }
  });
  await request.storageState({ path: authFile });
});

        Or in a worker fixture:

        import { test as baseTest, request } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

export * from '@playwright/test';
export const test = baseTest.extend<{}, { workerStorageState: string }>({
  // Use the same storage state for all tests in this worker.
  storageState: ({ workerStorageState }, use) => use(workerStorageState),

  // Authenticate once per worker with a worker-scoped fixture.
  workerStorageState: [async ({}, use) => {
    // Use parallelIndex as a unique identifier for each worker.
    const id = test.info().parallelIndex;
    const fileName = path.resolve(test.info().project.outputDir, `.auth/${id}.json`);

    if (fs.existsSync(fileName)) {
      // Reuse existing authentication state if any.
      await use(fileName);
      return;
    }

    // Important: make sure we authenticate in a clean environment by unsetting storage state.
    const context = await request.newContext({ storageState: undefined });

    // Acquire a unique account, for example create a new one.
    // Alternatively, you can have a list of precreated accounts for testing.
    // Make sure that accounts are unique, so that multiple team members
    // can run tests at the same time without interference.
    const account = await acquireAccount(id);

    // Send authentication request. Replace with your own.
    await context.post('https://github.com/login', {
      form: {
        'user': 'user',
        'password': 'password'
      }
    });

    await context.storageState({ path: fileName });
    await context.dispose();
    await use(fileName);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

        Multiple signed in roles

        When to use: you have multiple roles in your end-to-end tests but can reuse the accounts across all tests. Authenticate multiple times in the setup project:

        import { test as setup, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const adminFile = 'playwright/.auth/admin.json';

setup('authenticate as admin', async ({ page }) => {
  // Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.
  await page.goto('https://github.com/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('admin');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  // Wait until the page receives the cookies.
  //
  // Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.
  // Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.
  await page.waitForURL('https://github.com/');
  // Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'View profile and more' })).toBeVisible();

  // End of authentication steps.

  await page.context().storageState({ path: adminFile });
});

const userFile = 'playwright/.auth/user.json';

setup('authenticate as user', async ({ page }) => {
  // Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.
