  await page.goto('https://github.com/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('user');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  // Wait until the page receives the cookies.
  //
  // Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.
  // Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.
  await page.waitForURL('https://github.com/');
  // Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'View profile and more' })).toBeVisible();

  // End of authentication steps.

  await page.context().storageState({ path: userFile });
});

        Then specify storageState for each test file or group of tests, instead of setting it in the config:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });

test('admin test', async ({ page }) => {
  // page is authenticated as admin
});

test.describe(() => {
  test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' });

  test('user test', async ({ page }) => {
    // page is authenticated as a user
  });
});

        See also authenticating in UI mode.

        Testing multiple roles together

        When to use: you need to test several roles interacting with each other in a single test. Use multiple BrowserContexts and Pages with different storage states:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('admin and user', async ({ browser }) => {
  // adminContext and all pages inside, including adminPage, are signed in as "admin".
  const adminContext = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });
  const adminPage = await adminContext.newPage();

  // userContext and all pages inside, including userPage, are signed in as "user".
  const userContext = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' });
  const userPage = await userContext.newPage();

  // ... interact with both adminPage and userPage ...

  await adminContext.close();
  await userContext.close();
});

        Testing multiple roles with POM fixtures

        You can create fixtures that provide an authenticated page for each role. For example, create a fixture for two Page Object Models: an admin POM and a user POM. This assumes the admin.json and user.json files have already been created by the setup step.

        import { test as base, type Page, type Locator } from '@playwright/test';

// Page Object Model for the "admin" page.
// Here you can add locators and helper methods specific to the admin page.
class AdminPage {
  // Page signed in as "admin".
  page: Page;

  // Example locator pointing to "Welcome, Admin" greeting.
  greeting: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.greeting = page.locator('#greeting');
  }
}

// Page Object Model for the "user" page.
// Here you can add locators and helper methods specific to the user page.
class UserPage {
  // Page signed in as "user".
  page: Page;

  // Example locator pointing to "Welcome, User" greeting.
  greeting: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.greeting = page.locator('#greeting');
  }
}

// Declare the types of your fixtures.
type MyFixtures = {
  adminPage: AdminPage;
  userPage: UserPage;
};

export * from '@playwright/test';
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({
  adminPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });
    const adminPage = new AdminPage(await context.newPage());
    await use(adminPage);
    await context.close();
  },
  userPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' });
    const userPage = new UserPage(await context.newPage());
    await use(userPage);
    await context.close();
  },
});
        // Import test with our new fixtures.
import { test, expect } from '../playwright/fixtures';

// Use adminPage and userPage fixtures in the test.
test('admin and user', async ({ adminPage, userPage }) => {
  // ... interact with both adminPage and userPage ...
  await expect(adminPage.greeting).toHaveText('Welcome, Admin');
  await expect(userPage.greeting).toHaveText('Welcome, User');
});

        Session storage

        Reusing authenticated state covers cookies, local storage, IndexedDB, and passkeys (WebAuthn). Rarely, an app uses session storage to hold information tied to the signed-in state. Session storage is specific to each domain and is not persisted across page loads. Playwright has no API for persisting session storage, but the snippet below can save/load it manually:

        // Get session storage and store as env variable
const sessionStorage = await page.evaluate(() => JSON.stringify(sessionStorage));
fs.writeFileSync('playwright/.auth/session.json', sessionStorage, 'utf-8');

// Set session storage in a new context
const sessionStorage = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('playwright/.auth/session.json', 'utf-8'));
await context.addInitScript(storage => {
  if (window.location.hostname === 'example.com') {
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(storage))
      window.sessionStorage.setItem(key, value);
  }
}, sessionStorage);

        Avoid authentication in some tests

        You can reset the storage state in a test file to avoid the authentication that was set up for the whole project:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

// Reset storage state for this file to avoid being authenticated
test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } });

test('not signed in test', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});
        StrategyUse whenHow
        Shared account (Basic)Tests have no server-side statesetup project + storageState in the config
        One account per workerTests modify server-side stateworker-scoped fixture + parallelIndex
        API requestSigning in via the API is faster than the UIrequest.post() + request.storageState()
        Multiple rolesSeveral roles, accounts reusedmultiple state files + test.use({ storageState })
        Multiple roles in one testThe roles interact with each othermultiple BrowserContexts or POM fixtures

        Key takeaways

        • Save state into playwright/.auth and add it to .gitignore – never commit it.
        • The recommended default: setup project + dependencies: ['setup'] + storageState.
        • If tests modify server state, use one account per worker (testInfo.parallelIndex).
        • Wait until cookies are actually set (waitForURL or an assertion) before saving state.
        • IndexedDB needs indexedDB: true; session storage must be saved/loaded yourself with addInitScript.
        • Reset with storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } for tests that need a signed-out state.

        Your tests all modify the same setting on the server and run in parallel. Which authentication strategy fits?

        When tests modify shared server-side state, parallel tests must use different accounts so they don't affect each other; use parallelIndex to tell workers apart.

        The app stores its login token in IndexedDB (like Firebase Auth). What do you need to do when saving state?

        IndexedDB is not part of the snapshot by default; you must enable the indexedDB option.

        Events

        Playwright lets you listen to many kinds of events that happen on the page, such as network requests, creation of child pages (popups), dedicated workers, and more. You can wait for an event or add/remove listeners.

        Waiting for event

        Most scripts need to wait for a specific event to happen. These are the typical waiting patterns.

        Wait for a request with a given URL using page.waitForRequest():

        // Start waiting for request before goto. Note no await.
const requestPromise = page.waitForRequest('**/*logo*.png');
await page.goto('https://wikipedia.org');
const request = await requestPromise;
console.log(request.url());

        Wait for a popup window:

        // Start waiting for popup before clicking. Note no await.
const popupPromise = page.waitForEvent('popup');
await page.getByText('open the popup').click();
const popup = await popupPromise;
await popup.goto('https://wikipedia.org');
        The "no await" pattern: start waiting before the triggering action (without an immediate await), then perform the action and await the promise. This avoids a race condition that would make you miss the event.
        1. Start waitingconst p = page.waitForEvent('popup') – not awaited yet
        2. Triggerclick / goto produces the event
        3. await the promisereceive the event object (popup, request...)

        Adding/removing event listener

        Sometimes events happen at random times and need to be handled rather than waited for. Playwright uses the language's familiar mechanism to subscribe/unsubscribe:

        page.on('request', request => console.log(`Request sent: ${request.url()}`));
const listener = request => console.log(`Request finished: ${request.url()}`);
page.on('requestfinished', listener);
await page.goto('https://wikipedia.org');

page.off('requestfinished', listener);
await page.goto('https://www.openstreetmap.org/');
        Tip: to remove a listener, you must keep a reference to the same function (listener) and pass it to page.off().

        Adding one-off listeners

        If an event only needs to be handled once, use page.once(). For example, accepting a prompt() dialog with a value:

        page.once('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept('2021'));
await page.evaluate("prompt('Enter a number:')");
        NeedAPI
        Wait for one event after an actionpage.waitForEvent(), waitForRequest(), waitForResponse()
        Handle every occurrence of an eventpage.on() / page.off()
        Handle exactly oncepage.once()

        Key takeaways

        • Start waiting before triggering the action, await afterwards.
        • on/off for random events; once for one-time handling.
        • Removing a listener requires the same function reference.

        To capture a popup created by a click, what is the correct approach?

        If you wait after clicking, the popup may already have appeared and the event is missed.

        Handles

        A handle is a "grip" living in the Playwright process that points to a real object living in the browser. There is JSHandle for any JavaScript object and ElementHandle for DOM elements. However, ElementHandle is discouraged – prefer Locator.

        Introduction

        Playwright can create handles that point to DOM elements or to any object in the page. The handle lives in the Playwright process, while the real object lives in the browser. There are two kinds:

        • JSHandle: a reference to any JavaScript object in the page.
        • ElementHandle: a reference to a DOM element; it has extra methods for interacting with the element and inspecting its properties.

        Every DOM element is a JavaScript object, so every ElementHandle is also a JSHandle. Handles are used to operate on the real object: evaluate on the handle, get properties, pass the handle as an evaluate argument, serialize the object to JSON... The easiest way to get a JSHandle:

        const jsHandle = await page.evaluateHandle('window');
//  Use jsHandle for evaluations.

        Element Handles

        Discouraged: using ElementHandle is discouraged; use Locator and web-first assertions instead.

        When you really need an ElementHandle, it is best to obtain it with page.waitForSelector() or frame.waitForSelector(); these APIs wait for the element to be attached and visible.

        // Get the element handle
const elementHandle = await page.waitForSelector('#box');

// Assert bounding box for the element
const boundingBox = await elementHandle.boundingBox();
expect(boundingBox.width).toBe(100);

// Assert attribute for the element
const classNames = await elementHandle.getAttribute('class');
expect(classNames.includes('highlighted')).toBeTruthy();

        Handles as parameters

        Handles can be passed into page.evaluate() and similar methods. The following snippet creates a new array in the page, initializes it with data, returns a handle to Playwright, and then uses that handle in subsequent evaluations:

        // Create new array in page.
const myArrayHandle = await page.evaluateHandle(() => {
  window.myArray = [1];
  return myArray;
});

// Get the length of the array.
const length = await page.evaluate(a => a.length, myArrayHandle);

// Add one more element to the array using the handle
await page.evaluate(arg => arg.myArray.push(arg.newElement), {
  myArray: myArrayHandle,
  newElement: 2
});

// Release the object when it's no longer needed.
await myArrayHandle.dispose();

        Handle Lifecycle

        Handles are created by page methods such as page.evaluateHandle(), page.$() (querySelector), page.$$() (querySelectorAll), or their frame equivalents (frame.evaluateHandle(), frame.querySelector(), frame.querySelectorAll()). Once created, a handle keeps the object from being garbage collected until the page navigates or the handle is released manually with jsHandle.dispose().

        1. CreateevaluateHandle / $ / $$
        2. Useevaluate, getAttribute, pass as an argument
        3. ReleasejsHandle.dispose() or page navigation
        Related API reference
        • JSHandle, ElementHandle
        • ElementHandle.boundingBox(), getAttribute(), innerText(), innerHTML(), textContent()
        • JSHandle.evaluate(), Page.evaluateHandle(), Page.querySelector(), Page.querySelectorAll()

        Locator vs ElementHandle

        Use ElementHandle only rarely: when you need to do a lot of DOM traversal on a static page. For all user actions and assertions, use locators.

        The difference: an ElementHandle points to one specific element, while a Locator holds the logic for finding that element. In the example below, the handle points to one specific DOM element; if the element changes its text or React re-renders it into a completely different component, the handle still points to the old (stale) element, which can cause unexpected behavior.

        ❌ ElementHandle (can go stale)
        const handle = await page.$('text=Submit');
// ...
await handle.hover();
await handle.click();

        The handle is permanently bound to one DOM element; if the DOM re-renders, it becomes stale.

        ✅ Locator
        const locator = page.getByText('Submit');
// ...
await locator.hover();
await locator.click();

        Each time it is used, the locator re-finds the latest element in the DOM (here the element is located 2 times).

        LocatorElementHandle
        NatureLogic for finding an elementReference to 1 specific element
        When the DOM changesRe-finds the new elementMay go stale
        Auto-waiting & assertionsYes (web-first)Discouraged
        RecommendationDefaultRarely (DOM traversal on static pages)

        Key Takeaways

        • JSHandle is for any object; ElementHandle (which is a JSHandle) is for DOM elements.
        • Handles can be passed to evaluate; inside the function they are converted to the values they represent.
        • A handle keeps its object from being garbage collected until navigation or dispose() – remember to dispose.
        • Prefer Locator; avoid ElementHandle.

        What is the main difference between Locator and ElementHandle?

        A Locator stores the logic for retrieving the element; an ElementHandle holds a reference to one specific DOM element.

        Evaluating JavaScript

        Playwright test scripts and page scripts run in two different environments. page.evaluate() is the bridge: it runs a function in the web page context and brings the result back to the Playwright environment.

        Introduction

        Playwright scripts run in your Playwright environment; page scripts run in the browser's page environment. These two environments do not intersect: they run in different virtual machines, different processes, and may even be on different machines.

        page.evaluate() runs a JavaScript function in the page context and returns the result to Playwright. You can use browser globals such as window and document.

        const href = await page.evaluate(() => document.location.href);

        If the result is a Promise or the function is async, evaluate automatically waits until it resolves:

        const status = await page.evaluate(async () => {
  const response = await fetch(location.href);
  return response.status;
});

        Different environments

        Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in the testing environment. Because of this, you cannot use test variables inside the page and vice versa; you must pass them explicitly via arguments.

        ❌ WRONG: using the variable directly
        const data = 'some data';
const result = await page.evaluate(() => {
  // WRONG: there is no "data" in the web page.
  window.myApp.use(data);
});

        There is no data variable in the page.

        ✅ RIGHT: pass it as an argument
        const data = 'some data';
// Pass |data| as a parameter.
const result = await page.evaluate(data => {
  window.myApp.use(data);
}, data);

        The value is serialized and passed to the page as an argument.

        Evaluation Argument

        Playwright's evaluate methods such as page.evaluate() take one optional argument. This argument can be a mix of Serializable values and JSHandle instances. Handles are automatically converted to the value they represent.

        // A primitive value.
await page.evaluate(num => num, 42);

// An array.
await page.evaluate(array => array.length, [1, 2, 3]);

// An object.
await page.evaluate(object => object.foo, { foo: 'bar' });

// A single handle.
const button = await page.evaluateHandle('window.button');
await page.evaluate(button => button.textContent, button);

// Alternative notation using JSHandle.evaluate.
await button.evaluate((button, from) => button.textContent.substring(from), 5);

// Object with multiple handles.
const button1 = await page.evaluateHandle('window.button1');
const button2 = await page.evaluateHandle('window.button2');
await page.evaluate(
    o => o.button1.textContent + o.button2.textContent,
    { button1, button2 });

// Object destructuring works. Note that property names must match
// between the destructured object and the argument.
// Also note the required parenthesis.
await page.evaluate(
    ({ button1, button2 }) => button1.textContent + button2.textContent,
    { button1, button2 });

// Array works as well. Arbitrary names can be used for destructuring.
// Note the required parenthesis.
await page.evaluate(
    ([b1, b2]) => b1.textContent + b2.textContent,
    [button1, button2]);

// Any mix of serializables and handles works.
await page.evaluate(
    x => x.button1.textContent + x.list[0].textContent + String(x.foo),
    { button1, list: [button2], foo: null });
        Destructuring: for objects, property names must match between the destructuring pattern and the argument; for arrays you can use arbitrary names. Both require parentheses around the parameter.

        Init scripts

        Sometimes you need to run something in the page before it starts loading, for example to set up mocks or test data. Use page.addInitScript() or browserContext.addInitScript(). In this example, Math.random() is replaced with a constant value. First, create a preload.js file containing the mock:

        // preload.js
Math.random = () => 42;

        Then add the init script to the page:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Add script for every test in the beforeEach hook.
  // Make sure to correctly resolve the script path.
  await page.addInitScript({ path: path.resolve(__dirname, '../mocks/preload.js') });
});

        Alternatively, you can pass a function instead of creating a preload file – handy for short, one-off scripts. This approach also lets you pass arguments:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Add script for every test in the beforeEach hook.
test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  const value = 42;
  await page.addInitScript(value => {
    Math.random = () => value;
  }, value);
});
        1. Test (Node.js)calls page.evaluate(fn, arg)
        2. Serializefn and arg are sent to the browser
        3. Page runs fnhas window/document; cannot see test variables
        4. Result returnsPromises are awaited; the value is serialized back to the test

        Key Takeaways

        • page.evaluate() runs a function in the page; async functions/Promises are awaited automatically.
        • Variables from the outer scope are not available in the page: pass them via one argument.
        • The argument can mix serializable values and JSHandles.
        • addInitScript runs before any of the page's scripts (on both page and context).

        Why does page.evaluate(() => window.myApp.use(data)) fail when data is declared in the test?

        The test and the page run in separate environments; use page.evaluate(data => ..., data).

        Clock

        Accurately simulating time-dependent behavior is essential. The Clock API lets you manipulate and control time in tests: verify render times, timeouts, and periodic tasks without waiting for real time and without variability.

        Introduction

        Methods for controlling time:

        MethodPurpose
        setFixedTimeSets a fixed time for Date.now() and new Date()
        installInitializes the clock, unlocking the methods below
          pauseAtPauses time at a specific point
          fastForwardFast-forwards time
          runForRuns time for a specified duration
          resumeResumes time
        setSystemTimeSets the current system time

        Recommended approach: use setFixedTime. If that is not enough for your case, use install (which lets you pause, fast forward, tick... later). setSystemTime is only recommended for advanced cases.

        What gets overridden: page.clock overrides the native time-related globals/classes so they can be controlled manually: Date, Temporal.Now, setTimeout, clearTimeout, setInterval, clearInterval, requestAnimationFrame, cancelAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback, cancelIdleCallback, performance, Event.timeStamp.
        Call order: if you call install at any point in a test, that call MUST happen before any other clock-related calls. Calling in the wrong order leads to undefined behavior. For example, you cannot call setInterval, then install, then clearInterval, because install overrides the native definitions of the clock functions.

        Test with predefined time

        Often you only need to fake Date.now while letting timers keep running. Time still flows naturally, but Date.now always returns a fixed value.

        <div id="current-time" data-testid="current-time"></div>
<script>
  const renderTime = () => {
    document.getElementById('current-time').textContent =
        new Date().toLocaleString();
  };
  setInterval(renderTime, 1000);
</script>
        await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00'));
await page.goto('http://localhost:3333');
await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:00 AM');

await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:30:00'));
// We know that the page has a timer that updates the time every second.
await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:30:00 AM');

        Consistent time and timers

        Sometimes your timers depend on Date.now and get "confused" when Date.now does not change along with time. In that case, install the clock and then fast-forward to the moment you want to test. (The sample HTML is the same as in the previous example.)

        // Initialize clock with some time before the test time and let the page load
// naturally. `Date.now` will progress as the timers fire.
await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2024-02-02T08:00:00') });
await page.goto('http://localhost:3333');

// Pretend that the user closed the laptop lid and opened it again at 10am,
// Pause the time once reached that point.
await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00'));

// Assert the page state.
await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:00 AM');

// Close the laptop lid again and open it at 10:30am.
await page.clock.fastForward('30:00');
await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:30:00 AM');

        Test inactivity monitoring

        Inactivity monitoring is a common feature: logging the user out after a period without interaction. Testing it is hard because you would have to wait a long time; with the clock you can fast-forward time.

        <div id="remaining-time" data-testid="remaining-time"></div>
<script>
  const endTime = Date.now() + 5 * 60_000;
  const renderTime = () => {
    const diffInSeconds = Math.round((endTime - Date.now()) / 1000);
    if (diffInSeconds <= 0) {
      document.getElementById('remaining-time').textContent =
        'You have been logged out due to inactivity.';
    } else {
      document.getElementById('remaining-time').textContent =
        `You will be logged out in ${diffInSeconds} seconds.`;
    }
    setTimeout(renderTime, 1000);
  };
  renderTime();
</script>
<button type="button">Interaction</button>
        // Initial time does not matter for the test, so we can pick current time.
await page.clock.install();
await page.goto('http://localhost:3333');
// Interact with the page
await page.getByRole('button').click();

// Fast forward time 5 minutes as if the user did not do anything.
// Fast forward is like closing the laptop lid and opening it after 5 minutes.
// All the timers due will fire once immediately, as in the real browser.
await page.clock.fastForward('05:00');

// Check that the user was logged out automatically.
await expect(page.getByText('You have been logged out due to inactivity.')).toBeVisible();

        Tick through time manually, firing all the timers consistently

        Rarely, you may want to advance time manually, firing every timer and animation frame along the way, to get fine-grained control over the flow of time.

        // Initialize clock with a specific time, let the page load naturally.
await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2024-02-02T08:00:00') });
await page.goto('http://localhost:3333');

// Pause the time flow, stop the timers, you now have manual control
// over the page time.
await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00'));
await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:00 AM');

// Tick through time manually, firing all timers in the process.
// In this case, time will be updated in the screen 2 times.
await page.clock.runFor(2000);
await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:02 AM');
        ScenarioUseBehavior
        You only need a fixed date/time, timers keep runningsetFixedTimeTime "flows" but Date.now always returns a fixed value
        Timers need Date.now to changeinstall + pauseAt / fastForwardDate.now advances as timers fire
        Testing timeout/inactivityinstall + fastForward('05:00')All due timers fire once immediately, like a real browser
        Control every tickinstall + pauseAt + runFor(ms)Fires all timers/animation frames within that span
        1. install({ time })must be called before any other clock call
        2. gotothe page loads, time advances with the timers
        3. pauseAt(time)stops time, you take control
        4. fastForward / runForfast-forward or tick manually and fire timers
        5. resume(optional) let time run again

        Key Takeaways

        • Start with setFixedTime; when you need timers, use install; setSystemTime is only for advanced cases.
        • install must be called before any other clock call.
        • fastForward('05:00') is like closing the laptop lid and reopening it 5 minutes later: due timers fire once.
        • runFor(ms) ticks step by step, firing every timer along the way.
        • Duration strings look like '30:00' (30 minutes) and '05:00' (5 minutes).

        You want to test logout after 5 minutes of inactivity without really waiting. What is the fastest way?

        install enables fast-forwarding; fastForward makes all due timers fire immediately like a real browser.

        Which statement about setFixedTime is correct?

        That is its purpose: time "flows" naturally but Date.now is fixed; install is not needed.

        Service Workers

        This page covers requests made by the Service Worker itself and how to observe/route them. For ordinary mocking/routing/interception, see Network first.

        Introduction

        Chromium only: Service workers are only supported on Chromium-based browsers.
        Note: if you only need general network mocking/routing/interception, Playwright already has built-in APIs that do not require the information below. Keep reading if you care about requests made by a Service Worker.

        Service Workers are the browser's native way to handle requests made by the page through fetch and other network resources (scripts, CSS, images). They can act as a network proxy between the page and the outside network to cache content or provide an offline experience, if there is a FetchEvent listener.

        Many sites use a Service Worker purely as a transparent optimization technique: users may see things load faster, but the app is unaware of their existence; functionally, it behaves the same with or without the Service Worker.

        How to Disable Service Workers

        Playwright lets you disable Service Workers during tests, which makes tests more predictable and faster. However, if your real page uses a Service Worker, behavior may differ. Set serviceWorkers to 'block':

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    serviceWorkers: 'block'
  },
});

        Accessing Service Workers and Waiting for Activation

        Use browserContext.serviceWorkers() to list the Service Workers, or watch for one specifically if you expect the page to trigger a registration:

        const serviceWorkerPromise = context.waitForEvent('serviceworker');
await page.goto('/example-with-a-service-worker.html');
const serviceworker = await serviceWorkerPromise;

        The BrowserContext.serviceWorker event is fired before the Service Worker controls the page, so before evaluating inside the worker with worker.evaluate() you must wait for it to be activated. There are more idiomatic ways, but the following is an implementation-independent approach:

        await page.evaluate(async () => {
  const registration = await window.navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistration();
  if (registration.active?.state === 'activated')
    return;
  await new Promise(resolve => {
    window.navigator.serviceWorker.addEventListener('controllerchange', resolve);
  });
});

        Network Events and Routing

        Any network request made by a Service Worker is reported through the BrowserContext object:

        • The BrowserContext.request, requestFinished, response, and requestFailed events are fired.
        • browserContext.route() sees the request.
        • request.serviceWorker() returns the Service Worker instance, and request.frame() will throw.

        In addition, for requests made by a Page, response.fromServiceWorker() returns true when the request was handled by the Service Worker's fetch handler.

        Consider a simple service worker that fetches every page request:

        self.addEventListener('fetch', event => {
  // actually make the request
  const responsePromise = fetch(event.request);
  // send it back to the page
  event.respondWith(responsePromise);
});

self.addEventListener('activate', event => {
  event.waitUntil(clients.claim());
});

        If index.html registers this service worker and then fetches data.json, the following Request/Response events are emitted (along with the corresponding network lifecycle events):

        EventOwnerURLRoutedResponse.fromServiceWorker()
        BrowserContext.requestFrameindex.htmlYes
        Page.requestFrameindex.htmlYes
        BrowserContext.requestService Workertransparent-service-worker.jsYes
        BrowserContext.requestService Workerdata.jsonYes
        BrowserContext.requestFramedata.jsonYes
        Page.requestFramedata.jsonYes

        Because the example Service Worker is just a transparent "proxy":

        • There are 2 BrowserContext.request events for data.json: one owned by the Frame and one owned by the Service Worker.
        • Only the request owned by the Service Worker can be routed through browserContext.route(); the Frame-owned events for data.json are not routable, because they cannot reach the outside network once the Service Worker has registered a fetch handler.
        Caution: calling request.frame() or response.frame() will throw an exception if request.serviceWorker() is not null.
        1. Page fetches data.jsonFrame-owned request – not routable
        2. SW fetch handlerintercepts the request, calls fetch(event.request)
        3. SW-owned requestgoes through BrowserContext.route – routable
        4. Response to the pageresponse.fromServiceWorker() = true

        Routing Service Worker Requests Only

        await context.route('**', async route => {
  if (route.request().serviceWorker()) {
    // NB: calling route.request().frame() here would THROW
    await route.fulfill({
      contentType: 'text/plain',
      status: 200,
      body: 'from sw',
    });
  } else {
    await route.continue();
  }
});

        Known Limitations

        Requests that fetch updates to the Service Worker's main script file currently cannot be routed (see issue #14711).

        Key Takeaways

        • Service Workers are only supported on Chromium; they can be disabled with serviceWorkers: 'block'.
        • SW requests are reported through BrowserContext, not Page; request.serviceWorker() is non-null and request.frame() will throw.
        • response.fromServiceWorker() tells you the page's response was handled by the SW.
        • Wait for the SW to be "activated" before evaluating inside the worker.
        • Requests that update the SW's main script cannot be routed yet.

        A request is made by a Service Worker. What happens when you call request.frame()?

        For a request whose serviceWorker() is non-null, request.frame() and response.frame() will throw.

        Extensibility

        Playwright can be extended by registering custom selector engines, so you can define your own way of finding elements (for example tag=button) and use them with every API that accepts a selector.

        Custom selector engines

        Register one with selectors.register(). A selector engine needs to provide:

        • query(root, selector): finds the first element matching selector in the subtree of root.
        • queryAll(root, selector): finds all elements matching the corresponding selector.

        By default the engine runs directly in the frame's JavaScript context, so it can call functions defined by the application. To isolate the engine from the JavaScript in the frame while still accessing the DOM, register it with the { contentScript: true } option. Content-script engines are safer because they are protected against tampering with global objects (for example, modifying methods of Node.prototype). All built-in selector engines run as content scripts.

        Note: running as a content script is not guaranteed when the engine is used together with other custom engines. Also, selectors must be registered before creating the page.

        Example of registering an engine that finds elements by tag name:

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Must be a function that evaluates to a selector engine instance.
const createTagNameEngine = () => ({
  // Returns the first element matching given selector in the root's subtree.
  query(root, selector) {
    return root.querySelector(selector);
  },

  // Returns all elements matching given selector in the root's subtree.
  queryAll(root, selector) {
    return Array.from(root.querySelectorAll(selector));
  }
});

export const test = base.extend<{}, { selectorRegistration: void }>({
  // Register selectors once per worker.
  selectorRegistration: [async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    // Register the engine. Selectors will be prefixed with "tag=".
    await playwright.selectors.register('tag', createTagNameEngine);
    await use();
  }, { scope: 'worker', auto: true }],
});
        import { test, expect } from './baseTest';

test('selector engine test', async ({ page }) => {
  // Now we can use 'tag=' selectors.
  const button = page.locator('tag=button');
  await button.click();

  // We can combine it with built-in locators.
  await page.locator('tag=div').getByText('Click me').click();

  // We can use it in any methods supporting selectors.
  await expect(page.locator('tag=button')).toHaveCount(3);
});
        1. Write the enginea function returning { query, queryAll }
        2. Registerplaywright.selectors.register('tag', fn) – before creating a page
        3. Usepage.locator('tag=button') or combine with built-in locators
        Fixture tip: register inside a fixture with scope: 'worker' and auto: true so each worker registers exactly once and it is automatically applied to every test. See Fixtures.

        Key Takeaways

        • An engine consists of query and queryAll, taking (root, selector).
        • Register with selectors.register(name, engine) before creating a page; selectors are used with the name= prefix.
        • { contentScript: true } isolates the engine from the frame's JS (safer).
        • Works with every API that accepts selectors and can be combined with built-in locators.

        When must selectors.register() be called?

        The docs state it explicitly: selectors must be registered before creating a page.

        Which option makes a custom selector engine run isolated from the frame's JavaScript?

        contentScript: true isolates the engine from the frame's JS while still allowing DOM access.

        Debugging Tests

        Playwright provides several layers of debugging tools: the VS Code extension, Playwright Inspector, Trace Viewer, Browser DevTools, and verbose logs. Knowing how to pick the right tool helps you find the cause of a failing test much faster.

        1. Test failsRead the error message + call log
        2. VS Code / --debugBreakpoints, step, Pick locator
        3. page.pause()Stop exactly where you want to look
        4. Trace ViewerTime-travel when it fails on CI
        5. DEBUG=pw:apiVerbose log of every API call

        VS Code debugger

        The recommended approach: use the VS Code Extension to debug right in your editor: see errors, set breakpoints, and step through.

        Error Messages

        When a test fails, VS Code shows the error message right in the editor: the expected value, the received value, and the full call log.

        Live Debugging

        Run the test with the Show Browser option ticked. Then click any locator in VS Code and it is highlighted in the browser window, and Playwright tells you if multiple elements match. You can also edit the locator directly in VS Code and see the change live in the browser.

        Picking a Locator

        Click the Pick locator button in the Testing sidebar, then click the element you want in the browser. The locator appears in VS Code's Pick locator box; press Enter to copy it to the clipboard (then paste it into your code) or Esc to cancel.

        Playwright analyzes the page and picks the best locator, preferring role, text, and test id. If multiple elements match, it automatically refines the locator to uniquely identify the target element, so you worry less about tests failing because of locators.

        Run in Debug Mode

        Click next to a line number until a red dot appears to set a breakpoint. Right-click the line next to the test you want to run and choose Debug Test. The browser opens, the test runs and stops at the breakpoint; you can step, pause, and rerun from the VS Code menu.

        Debug Tests Using Chrome DevTools

        Instead of Debug Test, choose Run Test with Show Browser enabled. The browser session is reused, so you can open Chrome DevTools to continuously debug both the test and the web app.

        Debug in different Browsers

        By default, debugging uses the Chromium profile. To change it: right-click the debug icon in the testing sidebar, choose Select Default Profile, then pick the profile you want. Every run in debug mode will use that profile.

        Playwright Inspector

        The Inspector is a GUI tool that helps debug tests: run step by step, edit locators live, pick locators, and view actionability logs.

        Run in debug mode (the --debug flag)

        Running a test with the --debug flag opens the Inspector. When you use --debug, Playwright also configures some useful defaults:

        • The browser runs headed.
        • Default timeout = 0 (no timeout).
        GoalCommand
        Debug all tests on every browser (runs tests one at a time, each opening an Inspector + browser)npx playwright test --debug
        Debug 1 test (file + line) on every browser in the confignpx playwright test example.spec.ts:10 --debug
        Debug on 1 specific project/browsernpx playwright test --project=chromium --debug
        Debug 1 test on 1 specific browsernpx playwright test example.spec.ts:10 --project=webkit --debug
         
        npx playwright test --debug
npx playwright test example.spec.ts:10 --debug
npx playwright test --project=chromium --debug
npx playwright test --project="Mobile Safari" --debug
npx playwright test --project="Microsoft Edge" --debug
npx playwright test example.spec.ts:10 --project=webkit --debug

        Project names (chromium, Mobile Safari, Microsoft Edge...) come from the projects in playwright.config.

        Stepping through your tests

        Use the toolbar at the top of the Inspector to play, pause, or step through each action. The current action is highlighted in the code and the matching elements are highlighted in the browser window.

        Run a test from a specific breakpoint: page.pause()

        Add page.pause() so you don't have to step through every action to reach the point you want to debug. When running in debug mode, click Resume in the Inspector and the test will run and stop only at page.pause().

        await page.pause();

        Live editing locators

        While debugging, next to the Pick Locator button there is a box showing the locator the test is currently paused at. You can edit this locator directly and the matching elements will be highlighted in the browser.

        Picking locators

        Click Pick Locator and then hover over an element in the browser: the locator code appears below. Click the element to put its locator into the box, then adjust it or copy it into your code. The locator selection mechanism is the same as in VS Code (prefers role, text, test id; automatically made unique).

        Actionability logs

        When Playwright pauses at a click action, it has already finished the actionability checks and the results are in the log: whether the element is visible, enabled, stable, whether the locator resolved to an element, whether it was scrolled into view... If actionability has not been satisfied yet, the action is shown as pending.

        Trace Viewer

        Trace Viewer is a GUI for exploring a recorded trace of a test: step forward/backward through each action on the left, view the DOM snapshot in the middle, and see action details (time, parameters, return value, log) on the right. You can also view console messages, network requests, and source code.

        Browser Developer Tools (PWDEBUG=console)

        When running with PWDEBUG=console, the playwright object is available in the DevTools console. DevTools helps you inspect the DOM tree and find selectors, view console logs while running, inspect network, and use other DevTools features.

        How to do it: set a breakpoint with await page.pause() in the test, then run with PWDEBUG=console. When the browser opens, open DevTools and the playwright object is in the Console panel.

        PWDEBUG=console npx playwright test
        set PWDEBUG=console
npx playwright test
        $env:PWDEBUG="console"
npx playwright test
        FunctionPurposeExample
        playwright.$(selector)Queries using Playwright's own query engine, returns the first elementplaywright.$('.auth-form >> text=Log in')
        playwright.$$(selector)Same as $ but returns all matching elementsplaywright.$$('li >> text=John')
        playwright.inspect(selector)Shows the element in the Elements panelplaywright.inspect('text=Log in')
        playwright.locator(selector)Creates a locator and queries the matching elementsplaywright.locator('.auth-form', { hasText: 'Log in' })
        playwright.selector(element)Generates a selector for an element (e.g. select it in the Elements panel and pass $0)playwright.selector($0)
         
        playwright.$('.auth-form >> text=Log in');
// <button>Log in</button>

playwright.$$('li >> text=John')
// [<li>, <li>, <li>, <li>]

playwright.locator('.auth-form', { hasText: 'Log in' });
// Locator ()
//   - element: button
//   - elements: [button]

playwright.selector($0)
// "div[id="glow-ingress-block"] >> text=/.*Hello.*/"

        Verbose API logs

        Playwright supports verbose logging via the DEBUG environment variable:

        DEBUG=pw:api npx playwright test
        set DEBUG=pw:api
npx playwright test
        $env:DEBUG="pw:api"
npx playwright test
        WebKit note: opening the WebKit Inspector while running will block the Playwright script from continuing and will reset the user agent and any device emulation that was already configured.

        Headed mode

        Playwright runs headless by default. Use headless: false when launching to change that behavior; add slowMo to slow down each operation by N milliseconds so you can follow along.

        // Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit
await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });
        Cheat sheet: which tool to choose?
        SituationTool
        Coding in VS Code, need breakpointsVS Code extension + Debug Test
        Want to see the actionability log, step through each action--debug (Inspector)
        Want to stop at exactly one pointawait page.pause()
        Test fails on CITrace Viewer (trace: 'on-first-retry')
        Need to try out selectors in DevToolsPWDEBUG=console
        Need a log of every API callDEBUG=pw:api

        Key Takeaways

        • --debug = headed + timeout 0 + opens the Inspector; it can be combined with file:line and --project.
        • page.pause() lets you jump straight to the point you want to debug, then click Resume.
        • Pick locator prefers role/text/test id and automatically makes the locator unique.
        • PWDEBUG=console provides the playwright object in DevTools; DEBUG=pw:api enables verbose logs.
        • Trace Viewer is the number one choice for failures on CI.

        Which defaults does the --debug flag set?

        With --debug, the browser runs headed and the default timeout is set to 0 so you can inspect each step at your leisure.

        What do you need to do to use the playwright.$() object in Chrome DevTools?

        The playwright object is only available in the DevTools console when running with PWDEBUG=console; page.pause() stops the test so you can interact.

        UI Mode

        UI Mode is a visual test runner with a "time travel" experience and watch mode: you explore, run, and debug tests in a single interface, with a full trace for every test.

        Introduction

        All test files appear in the sidebar; you expand each file and describe block to run, view, watch, and debug individual tests. You can filter by name, projects (set in playwright.config), @tag, or passed, failed, skipped status. You see the full trace, hover over each action to see what happened at each step, and can "pop out" the DOM snapshot into its own window.

        Opening UI Mode

        npx playwright test --ui

        Running your tests

        After opening UI Mode you will see the list of test files. Run everything with the triangle icon in the sidebar. You can also run a single file, a block of tests, or a single test by hovering over its name and clicking the triangle next to it.

        Filtering tests

        Filter by text, @tag, passed/failed/skipped, or by project.

        Project dependencies: UI Mode does not take setup tests into account. If you use project dependencies, you must run the setup tests yourself before running the tests that depend on them.

        Timeline view

        At the top of the trace is a timeline with different colors to highlight navigation and actions. Hover back and forth to see the snapshot image for each action. Double-click an action to see its time range. Use the slider on the timeline to expand the selected range of actions; these actions appear in the Actions tab, while the console log and network log are filtered to only the logs of the selected actions.

        Actions

        The Actions tab shows which locator was used for each action and how long it took. Hover over each action to see the DOM snapshot change; go forward/backward in time and click an action to inspect it. Use the Before and After tabs to see the state before and after the action.

        Pop out and inspect the DOM

        Click the pop-out icon above the DOM snapshot to open the snapshot in its own window. There you can open the browser DevTools to inspect HTML, CSS, Console... Back in UI Mode, pick another action and pop it out too to compare two snapshots side by side.

        Pick locator

        Click the pick locator button and then hover over the DOM snapshot to see the locator of each element. Click an element to put it into the locator playground. You can edit the locator and check whether it matches any element in the DOM snapshot; when you are happy with it, use the copy button and paste it into your test.

        Source

        When you hover over an action, the corresponding line of code is highlighted in the Source panel. The Open in VSCode button in the top-right corner opens the test in VS Code at the exact line you clicked.

        Call, Log, Errors, Console, Network

        TabContent
        CallAction information: time, the locator used, whether strict mode applies, which keys were used.
        LogThe full log of what Playwright did behind the scenes: scroll into view, wait for visible/enabled/stable, perform click, fill, press...
        ErrorsError messages when a test fails; the timeline shows a red line at the error position; you can switch to the Source tab to see the failing line.
        ConsoleConsole logs from the browser and from the test file, with icons that distinguish the source.
        NetworkEvery request in the test; sorted by request type, status code, method, request, content type, duration, size. Click to see request/response headers and body.

        Attachments

        The Attachments tab lets you explore attachments. If you do visual regression testing, you compare screenshots via image diff, actual, and expected. Click the expected image to use a slider to drag one image over the other and clearly see the differences.

        Metadata

        Next to the Actions tab is the Metadata tab, which shows the Browser, viewport size, test duration, and more.

        Watch mode

        Next to each test in the sidebar is an eye icon. Click it to enable watch mode: the test reruns whenever you change it. You can watch several tests at once by clicking the eye next to each test, or watch all of them with the eye at the top of the sidebar.

        Docker & GitHub Codespaces

        In Docker and GitHub Codespaces environments, you run UI mode in the browser. To make the endpoint reachable from outside the container, you need to bind to the 0.0.0.0 interface:

        npx playwright test --ui-host=0.0.0.0

        With Codespaces, the port is forwarded automatically, and you click the link in the terminal to open UI mode. If you want a fixed port, use --ui-port:

        npx playwright test --ui-port=8080 --ui-host=0.0.0.0
        Security: when using --ui-host, UI Mode (along with traces, passwords, and secrets) is accessible to anyone who can reach that address and port; with 0.0.0.0 this includes other machines on the network. On Codespaces, the port is by default only accessible from your own account. When using --ui-port, other users on your machine can connect, run your tests, and read project files and traces.

        Key Takeaways

        • npx playwright test --ui opens UI Mode; it has a timeline, full traces, and watch mode.
        • Filter by name, project, @tag, status; setup projects must be run manually first.
        • Pop out DOM snapshot + Pick locator + Open in VSCode shorten the debugging loop.
        • Docker/Codespaces: --ui-host=0.0.0.0 (and --ui-port), but remember the security risks.
        What does the eye icon in UI Mode do?
        Enables watch mode: the test reruns automatically when files change.
        Command to open UI Mode?
        npx playwright test --ui

        You use project dependencies (a setup project). Which statement is true in UI Mode?

        UI Mode does not take setup tests into account, so you need to run them manually first.

        Trace Viewer

        Trace Viewer is a GUI tool that helps you explore recorded traces after a script has finished running. Traces are a great way to debug failing tests on CI: you step forward/backward through each action and see what state the page was in.

        1. Record a tracetrace: 'on-first-retry' / --trace on
        2. Test runsProduces trace.zip in test-results
        3. Open the reportnpx playwright show-report
        4. Open the traceshow-trace or trace.playwright.dev
        5. AnalyzeActions, Snapshots, Network, Console

        Introduction

        Open a trace on your machine (locally) or in the browser at trace.playwright.dev. Trace Viewer lets you go forward/backward through each action of the test and visually see what happened.

        Opening Trace Viewer

        Open a saved trace using the Playwright CLI or in the browser at trace.playwright.dev. Remember to give the full path to the trace.zip file.

        npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip

        Using trace.playwright.dev

        trace.playwright.dev is a statically hosted version of Trace Viewer. You load a trace file by drag-and-drop or the Select file button. The trace is loaded entirely in your browser and no data is transmitted elsewhere.

        Viewing remote traces

        Open a remote trace directly via URL, which is handy for viewing traces from CI without downloading them manually:

        npx playwright show-trace https://example.com/trace.zip

        With trace.playwright.dev, you can also pass the URL of a trace (uploaded somewhere accessible, e.g. in CI) via the trace query param. CORS rules may apply.

        https://trace.playwright.dev/?trace=https://demo.playwright.dev/reports/todomvc/data/e6099cadf79aa753d5500aa9508f9d1dbd87b5ee.zip

        Recording a trace

        Tracing locally

        During development, set the --trace flag to on. UI Mode gives a better experience because it automatically traces every test.

        npx playwright test --trace on

        Then open the HTML report and click the trace icon to open the trace:

        npx playwright show-report

        Tracing on CI

        On CI, you should record a trace on the first retry of a failing test with trace: 'on-first-retry'. This produces one trace.zip for each retried test.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  retries: 1,
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
});
        const browser = await chromium.launch();
const context = await browser.newContext();

// Start tracing before creating / navigating a page.
await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });

const page = await context.newPage();
await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');

// Stop tracing and export it into a zip archive.
await context.tracing.stop({ path: 'trace.zip' });

        Values of the trace option

        ValueMeaning
        'on-first-retry'Records a trace only on the first retry of a test.
        'on-all-retries'Records a trace for every retry.
        'off'Does not record traces.
        'on'Records a trace for every test (not recommended because of the performance cost).
        'retain-on-failure'Records a trace for every test but removes the traces of successful runs.
        Tip: if you don't enable retries but still want traces for failing tests, use trace: 'retain-on-failure'. More detailed options are available in TestOptions.trace. If you are not using the Playwright Test runner, use the browserContext.tracing API.

        Default configuration when creating a project (Getting started)

        On the "Trace viewer" page of the Getting started section: the default playwright.config file already configures trace: 'on-first-retry', and retries is 2 when running on CI and 0 locally. This means a trace is recorded on the first retry of a failing test, not on the first run and not on the second retry either.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0, // set to 2 when running on CI
  // ...
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry', // record traces on first retry of each test
  },
});

        Open the HTML report and click the trace icon next to the test file name to open the trace; or open the test details, scroll down to the Traces tab and click the trace image. Trace Viewer creates interactive DOM snapshots, so you can open the browser DevTools to inspect HTML, CSS...

        npx playwright test --trace on
npx playwright show-report

        Trace Viewer features

        Actions

        Shows the locator used for each action and the run time. Hover over each action to see the DOM snapshot change; click an action to inspect it; use the Before/After tabs. Selecting an action shows: action snapshots, the action log, and the source code location.

        Screenshots

        When screenshots is enabled (the default), each trace records a screencast and displays it as a film strip. Hover over the film strip to see an enlarged image for each action/state. Double-click an action to see its time range; drag the slider to expand the selected range: the Actions tab shows those actions, and the console and network are filtered accordingly.

        Snapshots

        When snapshots is enabled (the default), Playwright captures a complete DOM snapshot for each action. Depending on the action type, it captures:

        TypeDescription
        BeforeThe snapshot at the moment the action is called.
        ActionThe snapshot at the moment the input is performed. Especially useful for knowing exactly where Playwright clicked.
        AfterThe snapshot after the action.

        A typical action snapshot highlights both the DOM node and the exact click position.

        Source, Call, Log, Errors

        • Source: click an action in the sidebar and the corresponding line of code is highlighted in the source panel.
        • Call: time, locator, strict mode, keys used.
        • Log: the full log of what Playwright did behind the scenes (scroll into view, wait for visible/enabled/stable, click, fill, press...).
        • Errors: error messages; the timeline has a red line where the error occurred; switch to the Source tab to see the failing line.

        Console

        View console logs from the browser and from the test file, with icons that distinguish the source. Double-click an action in the sidebar to filter the console to only the logs within that action; click Show all to see everything again. You can also filter by dragging a range on the timeline.

        Network

        The Network tab shows every request in the test, sorted by type, status code, method, request, content type, duration, size. Click a request to see request/response headers, the request body, and the response body. Double-click an action to filter the requests of that action; Show all to see everything again; or drag a range on the timeline.

        Metadata and Attachments

        • Metadata: next to the Actions tab; shows the Browser, viewport size, test duration...
        • Attachments: explore attachments; with visual regression you can compare image diff, actual, expected and use a slider to overlay the two images.
        Best practice: on CI use trace: 'on-first-retry' together with retries; locally use UI Mode or --trace on when needed. Avoid 'on' on CI because of the performance cost.

        Key Takeaways

        • npx playwright show-trace path/trace.zip or drag-and-drop into trace.playwright.dev (processed entirely in the browser).
        • 5 modes: on-first-retry, on-all-retries, off, on, retain-on-failure.
        • Each action has Before / Action / After snapshots; the Action snapshot shows the click position.
        • Outside the test runner, use context.tracing.start()/stop({ path }).

        Which trace value records a trace for every test but deletes the traces of successful tests?

        retain-on-failure records a trace for every test and then discards the traces of passing tests, which suits setups where retries are not enabled.

        Does uploading a trace to trace.playwright.dev send data to an external server?

        The docs state explicitly that Trace Viewer loads the trace in the browser and does not transmit data elsewhere.

        Test generator (Codegen)

        Playwright can generate tests as you interact with the browser, which is very handy for getting started quickly. It picks the best locator (preferring role, text, test id) and automatically makes the locator unique when multiple elements match. (The slug test-generator returns a 404; the content lives at codegen and the introduction at codegen-intro.)

        Introduction

        Running the codegen command opens two windows: a browser window where you interact with the website you want to test, and a Playwright Inspector window where you record the test and then copy it into your editor.

        Generate tests in VS Code

        Install the VS Code extension (available on the VS Code Marketplace) to generate tests directly from VS Code.

        Record a New Test

        1. Click Record new in the Testing sidebar: it creates a test-1.spec.ts file and opens a browser window.
        2. Go to the URL you want to test and click around to record your actions.
        3. Playwright generates the test code right in VS Code. You can generate assertions with the icons on the toolbar and then click an element on the page.
        4. When finished, click cancel or close the browser, then edit the test-1.spec.ts file if needed.
        AssertionChecks
        'assert visibility'the element is visible
        'assert text'the element contains specific text
        'assert value'the element has a specific value

        Record at Cursor

        To continue recording from a specific point: place the cursor where you want to record more, then click Record at cursor in the Testing sidebar. If the browser is not open yet, first run the test with 'Show browser' ticked, then click Record at cursor. The new actions are inserted into the test at the cursor position.

        Generating locators (VS Code)

        • Click Pick locator in the testing sidebar and hover over an element in the browser to see its locator below.
        • Click the element you want: it appears in the Pick locator box.
        • Press Enter to copy it to the clipboard and paste it into your code, or Esc to cancel.

        Generate tests with the Playwright Inspector

        Running Codegen

        Use the codegen command followed by the website's URL. The URL is optional; you can type the URL directly in the browser window.

        npx playwright codegen demo.playwright.dev/todomvc

        Recording a test

        Run codegen and interact with the browser; the code appears in the Inspector window. When finished, stop recording and click copy to paste it into your editor. You can record:

        • Actions such as click and fill simply by interacting with the page.
        • Assertions: click the icon on the toolbar and then click an element to assert (assert visibility, assert text, assert value).

        When you finish interacting, click the record button to stop recording and the copy button to copy the code. The clear button erases the code so you can record again from scratch. When done, close the Inspector window or stop the command in the terminal.

        Generating locators (Inspector)

        1. Click the Record button to stop recording; the Pick Locator button will appear.
        2. Click Pick Locator and then hover over an element in the browser to see the locator highlighted.
        3. Click the element you want to locate: the locator code appears in the box next to the Pick Locator button (the locator playground).
        4. Edit the locator in this box to refine it (matching elements are highlighted), or copy it and paste it into your code.

        Emulation

        The test generator can generate tests with emulation: viewport, devices, color scheme, geolocation, language, timezone; and it can keep the logged-in state.

        Emulate viewport size

        Playwright opens the browser window with a fixed (non-responsive) viewport because tests need to run under the same conditions. Use --viewport-size to generate tests with a different viewport.

        npx playwright codegen --viewport-size="800,600" playwright.dev

        Emulate devices

        Record scripts/tests while emulating a mobile device with --device (sets the viewport, user agent...).

        npx playwright codegen --device="iPhone 13" playwright.dev

        Emulate color scheme

        npx playwright codegen --color-scheme=dark playwright.dev

        Emulate geolocation, language and timezone

        Use --timezone, --geolocation, and --lang. When the page opens: accept cookies, then click the "locate me" button in the top-right corner to see geolocation working.

        npx playwright codegen --timezone="Europe/Rome" --geolocation="41.890221,12.492348" --lang="it-IT" bing.com/maps
        Codegen flagEffect
        --viewport-size="w,h"Sets the viewport size
        --device="iPhone 13"Emulates a device
        --color-scheme=darkEmulates dark/light
        --timezone, --geolocation, --langTimezone, location, language
        --save-storage=auth.jsonSaves cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB at the end of the session
        --load-storage=auth.jsonLoads the saved state back
        --user-data-dir=pathUses a fixed user data directory
        --http-credentials="user:pass"HTTP Basic Authentication

        Preserve authenticated state

        Run codegen with --save-storage to save cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB when the session ends. Useful for recording the login step separately and reusing it in later tests.

        npx playwright codegen github.com/microsoft/playwright --save-storage=auth.json

        Login: after you log in and close the browser, auth.json contains the storage state for you to reuse in tests.

        Security warning: only use auth.json locally because it contains sensitive information. Add it to .gitignore or delete it after you finish generating tests.

        Load authenticated state: run with --load-storage to restore cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB; most web apps will be in the logged-in state, and you can continue generating tests from there.

        npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json github.com/microsoft/playwright

        Use existing userDataDir

        Use --user-data-dir to set a fixed user data directory for the browser session. If you create a dedicated user data directory, codegen uses that profile and has access to any authentication state in the profile.

        Chrome 136+: the default user data directory cannot be accessed by automation tools such as Playwright. You must create a separate user data directory for testing.
        npx playwright codegen --user-data-dir=/path/to/your/browser/data/ github.com/microsoft/playwright

        Authenticate with HTTP credentials

        Use --http-credentials to authenticate HTTP Basic Authentication. Unlike credentials embedded in a URL, they are sent to any origin that requests them during the recording session and are included in the generated code.

        npx playwright codegen --http-credentials="username:password" example.com

        Record using custom setup

        For non-standard setups (e.g. using BrowserContext.route), calling page.pause() opens a separate window containing the codegen controls.

        const { chromium } = require('@playwright/test');

(async () => {
  // Make sure to run headed.
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });

  // Setup context however you like.
  const context = await browser.newContext({ /* pass any options */ });
  await context.route('**/*', route => route.continue());

  // Pause the page, and start recording manually.
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.pause();
})();
        Best practice: codegen produces a good draft, but review it: add meaningful assertions, give tests clear names, and move the login part into storageState instead of recording it every time.

        Key Takeaways

        • npx playwright codegen [url] opens a browser + Inspector; records actions and assertions (visibility/text/value).
        • Pick Locator lets you choose and refine locators; prefers role/text/test id.
        • Emulation: --viewport-size, --device, --color-scheme, --timezone, --geolocation, --lang.
        • --save-storage / --load-storage to reuse the logged-in state; do not commit auth.json.
        • page.pause() opens the codegen controls for custom setups.

        Which flag is used to load the logged-in state saved by codegen?

        --save-storage saves the storage state; --load-storage loads it back so you can continue generating tests in the logged-in state.

        Visual comparisons (image comparison)

        Playwright Test can generate and compare screenshots with await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(). The first run creates a reference image (golden); subsequent runs compare against it to detect UI changes.

        1. First runNo golden yet: test fails, actual is written
        2. Commit the goldenThe *.spec.ts-snapshots folder
        3. Later runsPixel comparison against the golden
        4. Intentional UI change--update-snapshots

        Introduction

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('example test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot();
});
        Environment: browser rendering depends on the OS, version, settings, hardware, power source (battery or adapter), headless mode... To get consistent screenshots, run tests in the same environment in which the baseline was created.

        Generating screenshots

        On the first run, the test runner reports:

        Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

        That is because there is no golden file yet. The method takes multiple screenshots until two consecutive images match, then saves the last image to the file system. This image is ready to be committed to the repository.

        The folder holding the goldens starts with the test file name:

        example.spec.ts
example.spec.ts-snapshots/
  example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png

        The snapshot name example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png consists of:

        • example-test-1.png: an auto-generated name. Or you can pick a name as the first argument of toHaveScreenshot():
        await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('landing.png');
        • chromium-darwin: the browser and platform name. Screenshots differ between browsers/platforms because of rendering, fonts... so separate snapshots are needed. If you use multiple projects in the config, the project name replaces chromium.

        The snapshot name and path can be configured with TestConfig.snapshotPathTemplate in the config.

        PNG and WebP

        PNG is saved by default. Give the name a .webp extension to save WebP (also lossless):

        await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('landing.webp');

        To save all unnamed snapshots as WebP, set type in TestConfig.expect:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot: {
      type: 'webp',
    },
  },
});
        Note: toHaveScreenshot() also accepts an array of path segments, e.g. expect().toHaveScreenshot(['relative', 'path', 'to', 'snapshot.png']). This path must be inside each test file's snapshots folder (e.g. a.spec.js-snapshots), otherwise it will throw.

        Updating screenshots

        When the page changes intentionally, you need to update the reference images with the --update-snapshots flag.

        npx playwright test --update-snapshots

        Hover effects

        Screenshots capture any hover effect that is currently active. To avoid this, move the mouse to a position that does not trigger an effect (or hover an element with no effect) before taking the screenshot:

        await page.mouse.move(-1, -1);
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot();

        Options

        maxDiffPixels and threshold

        Playwright Test uses the pixelmatch library. You can pass options to change the behavior:

        OptionMeaningDefault
        thresholdThe acceptable perceived color difference between the same pixel in the two images, from 0 (strict) to 1 (lenient).0.2
        maxDiffPixelsThe number of pixels allowed to differ.Not set
         
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('example test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot({ maxDiffPixels: 100, threshold: 0.1 });
});

        To share default values across all tests in the project, set them in the config (globally or per project):

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixels: 100, threshold: 0.1 },
  },
});

        stylePath

        Applies a custom stylesheet to the page while taking the screenshot. It lets you filter out dynamic/unstable elements, making screenshots more deterministic.

        iframe {
  visibility: hidden;
}
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('example test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot({ stylePath: path.join(__dirname, 'screenshot.css') });
});

        Shared default values go in the config:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot: {
      stylePath: './screenshot.css'
    },
  },
});

        Non-image snapshots

        Besides screenshots, use expect(value).toMatchSnapshot(snapshotName) to compare text or any binary data. Playwright Test automatically detects the content type and picks a suitable comparison algorithm.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('example test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  expect(await page.textContent('.hero__title')).toMatchSnapshot('hero.txt');
});

        Snapshots are stored next to the test file, in a dedicated folder: my.spec.ts creates a my.spec.ts-snapshots folder. Commit this folder to version control (e.g. git) and review every change in it.

        Best practice: generate and update goldens in the same environment (e.g. the same Docker image on CI); hide dynamic content with stylePath; move the mouse out of hover areas before taking the screenshot.

        Key Takeaways

        • toHaveScreenshot(): the first run creates the golden (test fails), later runs compare.
        • The file name contains the project/browser name + platform; configure it via snapshotPathTemplate.
        • --update-snapshots to update; threshold defaults to 0.2; maxDiffPixels is not set by default.
        • stylePath hides unstable elements; toMatchSnapshot() is for text/binary.

        What happens when you run toHaveScreenshot() for the first time with no golden yet?

        On the first run there is no golden, so the test fails, but the image is written out for you to commit as the baseline.

        Snapshot testing (Aria snapshots)

        Aria snapshots let you assert the page's accessibility tree against a YAML template. The template is a constraint, not necessarily a full serialization of the tree.

        Overview

        await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
await expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
  - banner:
    - heading /Playwright enables reliable end-to-end/ [level=1]
    - link "Get started":
      - /url: /docs/intro
    - link "Star microsoft/playwright on GitHub":
      - /url: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright
    - link /[\\d]+k\\+ stargazers on GitHub/
`);

        Assertion testing vs Snapshot testing

        Assertion testingSnapshot testing
        NatureAsserts specific values/conditions (e.g. toHaveText, toHaveValue), comparing the current state against a predefined expected state.Captures a "snapshot" of the entire state of an element/component/data at a point in time and compares it on later runs.
        ProsClear (the intent is easy to understand); specific (resilient to unrelated changes); easy to debug (failures point at exactly the right spot).Simplifies complex output; gives fast feedback on unintended changes; keeps output consistent as the code evolves.
        ConsVerbose for complex output; costly to maintain when the code changes.Easy to accept a new snapshot without understanding it (hiding bugs); large snapshots are hard to read when they differ; not suited to constantly changing content.
        Best forCore logic, computed values, detailed tests that need exact conditions.Full-page UI and components, broad structural checks, regression testing for output whose structure rarely changes.
        Combine them: use snapshots for broad structural checks and assertions for specific functionality to get a balanced testing strategy.

        Aria snapshots (YAML format)

        An aria snapshot is a YAML representation of the accessibility tree. The syntax is tree-shaped: each node is an accessible element, and indentation shows nesting. Each node looks like this:

        - role "name" [attribute=value]
        • role: an ARIA or HTML role (e.g. heading, list, listitem, button).
        • "name": the accessible name. A quoted string is an exact value; /pattern/ is used for a regex.
