        • [attribute=value]: ARIA attributes such as checked, disabled, expanded, invalid, level, pressed, selected; you can constrain a specific value, e.g. [pressed=mixed].

        Values come from ARIA attributes or are computed from HTML semantics. To inspect the accessibility tree structure, use the Accessibility tab in Chrome DevTools.

        Snapshot matching

        The PageAssertions.toMatchAriaSnapshot assertion compares the page's accessible structure against a template. Use LocatorAssertions.toMatchAriaSnapshot to match just part of the page. For example, with the DOM <h1>title</h1>:

        await expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
  - heading "title"
`);

        Matching rules:

        • If the tree structure matches the template, the assertion passes; otherwise it fails.
        • The comparison is case-sensitive and normalizes whitespace in names/text. YAML indentation determines nesting.
        • The comparison is order-sensitive: the order in the template must match the order in the accessibility tree.
        • A single-node template can match at any depth within the selected page/locator. Multiple top-level nodes must match under the same parent, in order.

        Partial matching

        Omit attributes or the accessible name to match partially, which is useful for dynamic or irrelevant parts.

        ✅ Match the role, omit the name
        <button>Submit</button>
        - button

        Matches the button role regardless of its label.

        ✅ Omit an attribute
        <input type="checkbox" checked>
        - checkbox

        The checked attribute is ignored, so this passes regardless of the state.

        You can also match just part of the children in a list/group by leaving out some items:

        <ul>
  <li>Feature A</li>
  <li>Feature B</li>
  <li>Feature C</li>
</ul>
        - list:
  - listitem: Feature B

        Strict matching (the /children property)

        By default, a template containing a subset of the children still matches. The /children property controls how children are matched for the node where it appears:

        ValueMeaning
        contain (default)Matches if every specified child is present, in order.
        equalMatches if the direct children exactly match the specified list, in order.
        deep-equalMatches if the children and the deeply nested children exactly match the specified list, in order.

        When no children are expected: contain allows any children, while equal and deep-equal require no children. Add /children: contain to a nested node to override an inherited deep-equal and allow extra children there.

        The following snapshot will fail because Feature C is not in the template:

        - list:
  - /children: equal
  - listitem: Feature A
  - listitem: Feature B

        Setting children mode globally

        Set the default for every toMatchAriaSnapshot in the config; each snapshot can still override it with an explicit /children.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toMatchAriaSnapshot: {
      children: 'equal',
    },
  },
});

        Matching with regular expressions

        Accessible names and text support regex for dynamic content.

        <h1>Issues 12</h1>
        - heading /Issues \d+/

        Generating snapshots

        With the Playwright code generator

        • "Assert snapshot" action: automatically creates a snapshot assertion for the selected element, right in the recording flow.
        • "Aria snapshot" tab: visually shows the aria snapshot of the selected locator, so you can explore/inspect roles, attributes and accessible names.

        See also Code Generator.

        Updating with --update-snapshots (-u)

        Running without the flag uses the default mode: missing snapshots are generated, but the test that generates them fails (so a run with a new snapshot doesn't silently pass). missing generates missing snapshots and keeps the test passing. -u uses the changed mode and updates snapshots that don't match. all regenerates every snapshot, even matching ones. none prevents any update.

        ModeBehavior
        defaultGenerates missing snapshots, but the tests that generate them fail.
        missingGenerates missing snapshots and keeps the test passing.
        changed (when using -u)Updates snapshots that don't match.
        allRegenerates everything, including snapshots that match.
        noneDoesn't update any snapshots.
         
        npx playwright test --update-snapshots

        Playwright retries the assertion until the expect timeout runs out. Adjust --timeout if generating the snapshot takes longer than the test timeout.

        Empty template

        Passing an empty string as the template generates the snapshot immediately; it works without -u because the default mode generates missing snapshots.

        await expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot('');

        Snapshot patch files and --update-source-method

        For inline templates, Playwright creates a patch file recording the differences so you can review and apply them. Separate .aria.yml snapshots are written directly to the configured path. Change how the source is updated with --update-source-method:

        • "patch" (default): generates a unified diff that you apply with git apply.
        • "3way": generates merge conflict markers in the source so you can choose whether to accept them.
        • "overwrite": overwrites the source with the new snapshot value.
        npx playwright test --update-snapshots --update-source-method=3way

        Snapshots as separate files

        Use the name option with a .aria.yml extension to store the snapshot in a separate file:

        await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toMatchAriaSnapshot({ name: 'main.aria.yml' });

        By default, snapshots for example.spec.ts live in the example.spec.ts-snapshots folder. Because snapshots are identical across browsers, only one copy is stored even when you test multiple browsers. Customize this with pathTemplate:

        export default defineConfig({
  expect: {
    toMatchAriaSnapshot: {
      pathTemplate: '__snapshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',
    },
  },
});

        Page.ariaSnapshot() and Locator.ariaSnapshot()

        Generates, at run time, a YAML representation of the accessible elements within the locator's scope, which is useful for generating snapshots dynamically:

        const snapshot = await page.ariaSnapshot();
console.log(snapshot);

        Accessibility tree examples

        PatternHTMLAria snapshot
        Heading + level<h1>Title</h1><h2>Subtitle</h2>- heading "Title" [level=1]
        - heading "Subtitle" [level=2]
        Text node<div>Sample accessible name</div>- text: Sample accessible name
        Multiline text (normalized)<p>Line 1<br>Line 2</p>- paragraph: Line 1 Line 2
        Text box<input type="text" value="Enter your name">- textbox: Enter your name
        Group (details)<details><summary>Summary</summary><p>Detail content here</p></details>- group: Summary
        Checkbox checked<input type="checkbox" checked>- checkbox [checked]
        Button pressed<button aria-pressed="true">Toggle</button>- button "Toggle" [pressed=true]

        Links and /url

        A link displays its text or content assembled from pseudo-elements. The link's destination is matched with the /url property, whose value can also be a regex.

        <a href="#more-info">Read more about Accessibility</a>
        - link "Read more about Accessibility":
    - /url: "#more-info"
        <a href="https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC46Zj8pDH5tDosqm1gd7WTg">YouTube channel</a>
        - link:
  - /url: /https://www.youtube.com/channel/.*/

        Lists

        <ul aria-label="Main Features">
  <li>Feature 1</li>
  <li>Feature 2</li>
</ul>
        - list "Main Features":
  - listitem: Feature 1
  - listitem: Feature 2

        aria-invalid

        The aria-invalid value is represented directly: true shows [invalid], grammar and spelling show [invalid=grammar] and [invalid=spelling]; false is omitted.

        <input type="text" aria-label="Email" aria-invalid="true" value="not-an-email">
        - textbox "Email" [invalid]: not-an-email
        <input type="text" aria-label="Bio" aria-invalid="spelling">
        - textbox "Bio" [invalid=spelling]

        Key points

        • toMatchAriaSnapshot compares the accessibility tree as YAML; the template is a constraint (partial matching is allowed).
        • Case- and order-sensitive; supports regex in name/text//url.
        • /children: contain (default) / equal / deep-equal; set it globally in expect.toMatchAriaSnapshot.children.
        • Generating snapshots: codegen, -u (modes default/missing/changed/all/none), empty template, --update-source-method (patch/3way/overwrite).
        • Store them as separate .aria.yml files with name; get the YAML with ariaSnapshot().

        A template with - list: + /children: equal + 2 listitems is compared against a list with 3 items. What is the result?

        equal requires the list of direct children to match exactly; the third item makes the test fail.

        What is the default /children mode?

        The default is contain: the listed children must be present in order, and extra children are allowed.

        Screenshots

        Capture a page or element with page.screenshot() / locator.screenshot(): save it to a file or get a buffer for further processing.

        Introduction

        A quick way to take a screenshot and save it to a file:

        await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' });

        The Screenshots API accepts many parameters: image format, clip area, quality, and so on. Be sure to read through it.

        Full page screenshots

        A full page screenshot is an image of the entire scrollable area, as if you had a very tall screen that fits the whole page.

        await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true });

        Capture into buffer

        Instead of writing to a file, you can get a buffer containing the image for post-processing or to feed into a third-party pixel diff tool.

        const buffer = await page.screenshot();
console.log(buffer.toString('base64'));

        Element screenshot

        Sometimes you need to capture an individual element.

        await page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' });
        NeedHow
        Capture the viewport, save to a filepage.screenshot({ path })
        Capture the whole scrollable pagepage.screenshot({ path, fullPage: true })
        Get a bufferconst buffer = await page.screenshot()
        Capture a single elementpage.locator(...).screenshot({ path })
        Related: to automatically compare images against a baseline, use toHaveScreenshot() instead of taking screenshots and comparing them manually.

        Key points

        • page.screenshot({ path }) saves a file; fullPage: true captures the entire scrollable page.
        • If you don't pass path, you get a buffer back.
        • locator.screenshot() captures a single element.

        How do you capture the entire page, including the parts you have to scroll to?

        The fullPage: true option captures the page's entire scrollable area.

        Videos

        Playwright can record video for your tests, controlled by the video option in the config. Video is off by default.

        Record video

        The values for video:

        ValueMeaning
        'off'Do not record video.
        'on'Record video for every test.
        'retain-on-failure'Record video for every test, but delete the video of runs that pass.
        'on-first-retry'Record only when retrying a test for the first time.

        Video files are placed in the test output directory, usually test-results. See TestOptions.video for advanced configuration.

        Note: videos are saved when the browser context closes at the end of the test. If you create contexts manually, make sure to await context.close().
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    video: 'on-first-retry',
  },
});
        const context = await browser.newContext({ recordVideo: { dir: 'videos/' } });
// Make sure to await close, so that videos are saved.
await context.close();

        Video size and annotations

        The default video size equals the viewport scaled down to fit within 800x800. The viewport's video is placed in the top-left corner of the output video, scaled down if necessary. You may need to set the viewport to match the video size you want.

        • When you specify show: { actions }, each action is visually highlighted in the video with an element outline and an action title caption. The optional duration property controls how long each annotation is shown (default 500ms).
        • When you specify show: { test }, the video is annotated with information about the current test, with a configurable level.
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    video: {
      mode: 'on-first-retry',
      size: { width: 640, height: 480 },
      show: {
        actions: {
          duration: 500,
          position: 'top-right',
          fontSize: 14,
        },
        test: {
          level: 'step',
          position: 'top-left',
          fontSize: 12,
        }
      },
    },
  },
});

        Accessing a page's video file

        In multi-page scenarios, get the video file associated with a page via page.video():

        const path = await page.video().path();
        Note: the video is only available after the page or browser context has closed.

        Key points

        • The video option: off (default) / on / retain-on-failure / on-first-retry.
        • Videos are saved when the context closes; if you create a context yourself, you must await context.close().
        • Advanced configuration: size, show.actions, show.test.
        • page.video().path() only works after the page/context has closed.

        When is a test's video file finished being written?

        The video is saved when the context closes; if you create the context yourself, you must await context.close().

        Accessibility testing

        Playwright works with @axe-core/playwright (the axe engine) to automatically detect many kinds of accessibility issues right inside your tests.

        Introduction

        Examples of issues it can catch:

        • Text that is hard to read for users with low vision because of poor color contrast.
        • UI controls and form elements without labels that screen readers can pick up.
        • Interactive elements with duplicate IDs that confuse assistive technologies.

        The examples use the @axe-core/playwright package, which lets you run axe as part of your Playwright tests.

        Disclaimer: automated accessibility testing can only detect some common issues (missing or incorrect attributes, etc.). Many problems can only be found through manual testing. Combine automated testing, manual assessment and testing with real users. For manual assessment, the docs suggest Accessibility Insights for Web (free, open source, with guided assessment against WCAG 2.1 AA).

        Example accessibility tests

        Accessibility tests run like any other Playwright test: create dedicated test cases, or integrate scans and assertions into your existing tests.

        Scanning an entire page

        Steps: (1) import @axe-core/playwright; (2) define the test; (3) navigate to the page; (4) await AxeBuilder.analyze() to run the scan; (5) use regular assertions to confirm there are no violations.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright'; // 1

test.describe('homepage', () => { // 2
  test('should not have any automatically detectable accessibility issues', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('https://your-site.com/'); // 3

    const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze(); // 4

    expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]); // 5
  });
});

        Configuring axe to scan a specific part of a page

        @axe-core/playwright supports many configuration options through AxeBuilder's Builder pattern. For example, AxeBuilder.include() limits the scan to one part of the page.

        AxeBuilder.analyze() scans the page in its current state. To scan parts that only appear after a UI interaction, use Locators to interact before calling analyze():

        test('navigation menu should not have automatically detectable accessibility violations', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('https://your-site.com/');

  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Navigation Menu' }).click();

  // It is important to waitFor() the page to be in the desired
  // state *before* running analyze(). Otherwise, axe might not
  // find all the elements your test expects it to scan.
  await page.locator('#navigation-menu-flyout').waitFor();

  const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .include('#navigation-menu-flyout')
      .analyze();

  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);
});

        Scanning for WCAG violations

        By default axe checks many rules; some correspond to WCAG success criteria, while others are "best practice" rules that WCAG doesn't require. Use AxeBuilder.withTags() to run only the rules tagged with specific WCAG tags. To match the "Automated Checks" in Accessibility Insights (WCAG A and AA), use the tags wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa. Note that automated testing can't detect every kind of WCAG violation.

        test('should not have any automatically detectable WCAG A or AA violations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://your-site.com/');

  const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
      .analyze();

  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);
});

        For the full list of tags, see the "Axe-core Tags" section in axe's API documentation.

        Handling known issues

        A common question: "how do I exclude violations I already know about?"

        Excluding individual elements from a scan

        Use AxeBuilder.exclude() to leave an element with a known issue out of the scan until it is fixed. This is usually the simplest option, but it has important drawbacks:

        • exclude() excludes the specified element and all of its children; avoid it with components that have many children.
        • exclude() prevents all rules from running on that element, not just the rule for the known issue.
        test('should not have any accessibility violations outside of elements with known issues', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('https://your-site.com/page-with-known-issues');

  const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .exclude('#element-with-known-issue')
      .analyze();

  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);
});

        If the element is reused across many pages, consider using a test fixture.

        Disabling individual scan rules

        If you have many existing violations of one specific rule, use AxeBuilder.disableRules() to temporarily turn that rule off. The rule ID is in the violation's id property; the full list of rules is in the axe-core documentation.

        test('should not have any accessibility violations outside of rules with known issues', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto('https://your-site.com/page-with-known-issues');

  const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .disableRules(['duplicate-id'])
      .analyze();

  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);
});

        Using snapshots to allow specific known issues

        To allow a set of known violations in more detail, use Snapshots to verify that the set of existing violations doesn't change. This avoids the drawbacks of exclude() but is slightly more complex and brittle.

        ❌ Avoid
        // Don't do this! This is fragile.
expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toMatchSnapshot();

        The violations array contains implementation details (e.g. HTML snippets), so the test breaks whenever the component changes for unrelated reasons.

        ✅ Prefer
        // This is less fragile than snapshotting the entire violations array.
expect(violationFingerprints(accessibilityScanResults)).toMatchSnapshot();

// my-test-utils.js
function violationFingerprints(accessibilityScanResults) {
  const violationFingerprints = accessibilityScanResults.violations.map(violation => ({
    rule: violation.id,
    // These are CSS selectors which uniquely identify each element with
    // a violation of the rule in question.
    targets: violation.nodes.map(node => node.target),
  }));

  return JSON.stringify(violationFingerprints, null, 2);
}

        Create a "fingerprint" containing just enough information to uniquely identify the violation.

        Exporting scan results as a test attachment

        Scan results contain more than just violations: they also include rules that passed and elements with inconclusive results. This information is useful for debugging a test that doesn't detect enough violations. To include the entire result in the test results, attach it with testInfo.attach(); reporters can embed or link the full result.

        test('example with attachment', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  await page.goto('https://your-site.com/');

  const accessibilityScanResults = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze();

  await testInfo.attach('accessibility-scan-results', {
    body: JSON.stringify(accessibilityScanResults, null, 2),
    contentType: 'application/json'
  });

  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);
});

        Using a test fixture for common axe configuration

        Test fixtures are a good way to share common AxeBuilder configuration. Useful scenarios: sharing a single set of rules; excluding known violations in shared elements that appear on many pages; attaching a consistent accessibility report for multiple scans.

        Creating a fixture

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

type AxeFixture = {
  makeAxeBuilder: () => AxeBuilder;
};

// Extend base test by providing "makeAxeBuilder"
//
// This new "test" can be used in multiple test files, and each of them will get
// a consistently configured AxeBuilder instance.
export const test = base.extend<AxeFixture>({
  makeAxeBuilder: async ({ page }, use) => {
    const makeAxeBuilder = () => new AxeBuilder({ page })
        .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa'])
        .exclude('#commonly-reused-element-with-known-issue');

    await use(makeAxeBuilder);
  }
});
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

        Using a fixture

        Replace new AxeBuilder({ page }) with the makeAxeBuilder fixture:

        const { test, expect } = require('./axe-test');

test('example using custom fixture', async ({ page, makeAxeBuilder }) => {
  await page.goto('https://your-site.com/');

  const accessibilityScanResults = await makeAxeBuilder()
      // Automatically uses the shared AxeBuilder configuration,
      // but supports additional test-specific configuration too
      .include('#specific-element-under-test')
      .analyze();

  expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);
});
        AxeBuilder methodUsed to
        include(selector)Limit the scan to a specific part of the page
        exclude(selector)Exclude an element (and its children) from the scan
        withTags([...])Run only rules matching the tags (e.g. WCAG A/AA)
        disableRules([...])Disable rules by ID
        analyze()Run the scan and return the results

        Key points

        • Use new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze() and then expect(results.violations).toEqual([]).
        • Wait for the UI to be in the right state before analyze() (it scans the current state).
        • Handle known issues with exclude() (excludes children too and turns off every rule), disableRules(), or a "fingerprint" snapshot.
        • Don't snapshot the whole violations array; use a fixture to share configuration.
        • Automated testing does not replace manual testing.

        Why shouldn't you toMatchSnapshot() the entire violations array?

        Create a fingerprint containing only the rule id and target selectors so the snapshot stays stable.

        Emulation

        Playwright can emulate real devices (phones, tablets) and the user's environment: userAgent, screenSize, viewport, hasTouch, geolocation, locale, timezone, permissions, colorScheme... for all tests or for individual tests.

        Introduction

        You configure the device you want to emulate and Playwright simulates browser behavior such as userAgent, screenSize, viewport, hasTouch. You can also emulate geolocation, locale, timezone, set permissions (e.g. to show notifications), or change the colorScheme.

        Devices

        Playwright ships a registry of device parameters via playwright.devices for many desktop, tablet and mobile devices. Use it to simulate the user agent, screen size, viewport and touch support. All tests run with the chosen device's parameters.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test'; // import devices

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'Mobile Safari',
      use: {
        ...devices['iPhone 13'],
      },
    },
  ],
});
        const { chromium, devices } = require('playwright');
const browser = await chromium.launch();

const iphone13 = devices['iPhone 13'];
const context = await browser.newContext({
  ...iphone13,
});
        Note: preconfigured devices assume a specific platform; for example, "Desktop Chrome" provides a Windows-specific user agent. If you want the user agent to match the platform the tests run on, unset the user agent property.
        const context = await browser.newContext({
  ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
  userAgent: undefined,
});

        Viewport

        The viewport is already part of the device, but you can override it for some tests with page.setViewportSize() or via config/test.use.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        // It is important to define the `viewport` property after destructuring `devices`,
        // since devices also define the `viewport` for that device.
        viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
      },
    },
  ]
});
        Spread order: you must set viewport AFTER destructuring devices, because the device also defines a viewport; if you set it first, it gets overwritten.

        In a test file:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  viewport: { width: 1600, height: 1200 },
});

test('my test', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        It also works inside a describe block:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('specific viewport block', () => {
  test.use({ viewport: { width: 1600, height: 1200 } });

  test('my test', async ({ page }) => {
    // ...
  });
});

        With the library, you can change the viewport per page and emulate high-DPI screens:

        // Create context with given viewport
const context = await browser.newContext({
  viewport: { width: 1280, height: 1024 }
});

// Resize viewport for individual page
await page.setViewportSize({ width: 1600, height: 1200 });

// Emulate high-DPI
const context = await browser.newContext({
  viewport: { width: 2560, height: 1440 },
  deviceScaleFactor: 2,
});

        isMobile

        Specifies whether the meta viewport tag is taken into account and whether touch events are enabled.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        // It is important to define the `isMobile` property after destructuring `devices`,
        // since devices also define the `isMobile` for that device.
        isMobile: false,
      },
    },
  ]
});

        Locale & Timezone

        Emulate the browser's locale and timezone; set them globally in the config and then override them per test.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Emulates the browser locale.
    locale: 'en-GB',

    // Emulates the browser timezone.
    timezoneId: 'Europe/Paris',
  },
});
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  locale: 'de-DE',
  timezoneId: 'Europe/Berlin',
});

test('my test for de lang in Berlin timezone', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://www.bing.com');
  // ...
});
        Note: this only affects the browser's timezone and locale, not the test runner's timezone. To set the test runner's timezone, use the TZ environment variable.

        Permissions

        Allow the app to show system notifications.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Grants specified permissions to the browser context.
    permissions: ['notifications'],
  },
});

        Allow notifications for a specific domain:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ context }) => {
  // Runs before each test and signs in each page.
  await context.grantPermissions(['notifications'], { origin: 'https://skype.com' });
});

test('first', async ({ page }) => {
  // page has notifications permission for https://skype.com.
});

        Revoke all permissions with context.clearPermissions():

        // Library
await context.clearPermissions();

        Geolocation

        Grant the "geolocation" permission and set the location to a specific area.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Context geolocation
    geolocation: { longitude: 12.492507, latitude: 41.889938 },
    permissions: ['geolocation'],
  },
});
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  geolocation: { longitude: 41.890221, latitude: 12.492348 },
  permissions: ['geolocation'],
});

test('my test with geolocation', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        Change the location later:

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  geolocation: { longitude: 41.890221, latitude: 12.492348 },
  permissions: ['geolocation'],
});

test('my test with geolocation', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // overwrite the location for this test
  await context.setGeolocation({ longitude: 48.858455, latitude: 2.294474 });
});
        Note: you can only change the geolocation for all pages in the context.

        Color Scheme and Media

        Emulate the user's colorScheme: 'light', 'dark', 'no-preference'. You can also emulate the media type with page.emulateMedia().

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    colorScheme: 'dark',
  },
});
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  colorScheme: 'dark' // or 'light'
});

test('my test with dark mode', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});
        // Create context with dark mode
const context = await browser.newContext({
  colorScheme: 'dark' // or 'light'
});

// Create page with dark mode
const page = await browser.newPage({
  colorScheme: 'dark' // or 'light'
});

// Change color scheme for the page
await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' });

// Change media for page
await page.emulateMedia({ media: 'print' });

        reducedMotion, forcedColors, contrast

        The "reducedMotion", "forcedColors" and "contrast" options similarly emulate the prefers-reduced-motion, forced-colors and prefers-contrast media features. page.emulateMedia() changes them for a single page.

        OptionValues
        reducedMotion'reduce', 'no-preference'
        forcedColors'active', 'none'
        contrast'more', 'no-preference'
         
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    reducedMotion: 'reduce',
    forcedColors: 'active',
    contrast: 'more',
  },
});
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({
  reducedMotion: 'reduce', // or 'no-preference'
  forcedColors: 'active', // or 'none'
  contrast: 'more', // or 'no-preference'
});

test('my test with reduced motion, forced colors and more contrast', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});
        // Change the media features for the page
await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce', forcedColors: 'active', contrast: 'more' });

        User Agent

        The User Agent is already part of the device, so you rarely need to change it; if you need to test a different user agent, override it with the userAgent property.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({ userAgent: 'My user agent' });

test('my user agent test', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});

        Offline

        Emulate an offline network.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    offline: true
  },
});
        Limitation: offline emulation only affects requests that go through the browser's regular network stack (navigations, fetch(), XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket). It does not affect WebRTC: an already established RTCPeerConnection keeps sending/receiving media over UDP. To test WebRTC connectivity loss, cut the connection outside the browser (e.g. stop the TURN server or use an OS-level firewall).

        JavaScript Enabled

        Emulate a scenario where the user has disabled JavaScript.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({ javaScriptEnabled: false });

test('test with no JavaScript', async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});
        OptionExamplePurpose
        devices...devices['iPhone 13']A set of device parameters
        viewport, deviceScaleFactor{ width: 1280, height: 720 }Size, DPI
        isMobilefalseMeta viewport + touch
        locale, timezoneId'de-DE', 'Europe/Berlin'Language, timezone
        permissions['notifications']Grant permissions
        geolocation{ longitude, latitude }Location
        colorScheme, reducedMotion, forcedColors, contrast'dark'...Media features
        userAgent'My user agent'Override the UA
        offlinetrueNetwork loss
        javaScriptEnabledfalseDisable JS

        Key points

        • Use ...devices['Device name'] in a project's use; set viewport/isMobile AFTER the spread to override them.
        • Options can be set in the config (global/project), test.use() (file/describe) or newContext().
        • Geolocation needs permissions: ['geolocation'] alongside it; setGeolocation applies to the whole context.
        • Timezone/locale only change the browser; to change the runner's, use the TZ environment variable.
        • Offline does not affect WebRTC.

        Why must you set viewport after ...devices['Desktop Chrome']?

        A later spread overwrites keys set earlier; to make your custom viewport win, put it after the spread.

        Component testing

        Playwright Test can test your web app's components in isolation: a component test is a regular end-to-end test that runs against a small story gallery page served by your own dev server, using the built-in mount fixture of @playwright/test.

        Introduction

        There is no separate component-testing runtime, no bundler integration, and no extra npm package: the built-in mount fixture does it all.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('click should expand', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount('components/Expandable/Stateful');
  await component.getByRole('button').click();
  await expect(component.getByTestId('expanded')).toHaveValue('true');
});

        The test runs in Node.js while the component runs in a real browser: real clicks, real layout, and you can do visual regression. The test also gets everything Playwright Test offers: parallelism, parametrization, retries and post-mortem tracing.

        Experimental packages removed: the @playwright/experimental-ct-react, -ct-react17 and -ct-vue packages have been removed and are no longer published. If you still use them, stay on Playwright 1.62 until you have followed the migration guide below.

        Why a framework-agnostic approach

        The @playwright/experimental-ct-* packages let you write inline JSX, for example mount(<Button onClick={spy} />). To make that work, Playwright had to control the entire pipeline: scan tests for components, compile a bundle with its own copy of Vite and its own config, serve it from its own server, and marshal props/callbacks across the Node.js/browser boundary. That design kept the packages experimental forever:

        • It only works when your setup matches Playwright's. Path aliases, plugins and CSS handling had to be copied by hand into ctViteConfig. Projects using webpack, Next.js or a custom pipeline couldn't use the separate build. Every framework needed its own package.
        • The Node.js/browser boundary leaks. JSX written in a test is compiled in Node.js and then reassembled in the browser. Live objects can't cross it, callbacks only half work, and mocked modules silently don't apply.

        The alternative design inverts control:

        • You own the pipeline. Components are built and served by your dev server, with your plugins, aliases and CSS. Playwright doesn't compile or serve anything; it just navigates to a page like any other test.
        • Framework-agnostic. The only framework-dependent part is the gallery page that you own. React, Vue, Svelte, Solid or anything else: if your dev server can render it, Playwright can test it.
        • Stable. Tests import plain test and expect from @playwright/test; mount is a documented built-in fixture. No experimental packages, no separate config dialect.

        How it works

        1. StoryComponent + fixed props/mocks/providers/callbacks
        2. GalleryA page that serves window.mount / window.unmount
        3. mount fixtureNavigates to baseURL, calls window.mount({ story, props })
        4. Root locatorReturns a Locator for #root to query
        5. TestInteract + assert via DOM/URL/network
        • Story: a small wrapper component that puts the component under test into a specific scenario: fixed props, mock data, providers, recorded callbacks. Stories live next to the component in *.story.tsx files (or .ts/.jsx/.js/.vue); each named export is a story.
        • Gallery: a single page served by your dev server that exposes the window.mount(params) and window.unmount() functions to render a story (resolved from the story files) into the #root element. It depends on your framework and you own it.
        • The mount fixture navigates to the gallery (TestOptions.baseURL), calls window.mount() with the story id and props, and then returns a Locator for the gallery root. You query from there: component.getByRole('button').click().

        Everything the component needs is set up inside the story (which runs in the browser). Everything the test asserts is observable through the page: DOM, URL, network.

        Getting started

        Step 1: Point your coding agent at the skill

        The gallery is application code that belongs to you. The fastest way is to ask a coding agent (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot...) to do it: Playwright ships this approach as an agent skill.

        npx playwright init-skills
        Set up component testing using the playwright-component-testing skill.

        The agent detects your framework and bundler, installs the gallery for your stack, adds a Playwright project to the config, and writes the first story + spec. The contract the gallery fulfills:

        • It is a single page under playwright/gallery/, served by your dev server: Vite apps use their existing dev server; other setups run a small standalone Vite server next to the app.
        • It discovers *.story.* files and exposes two functions: window.mount({ story, props }) renders a story by id into #root, and window.unmount() removes it. A story that doesn't exist or fails to render rejects, which shows up as the test's mount() call throwing.
        • It reuses the render root between calls, so component.update(props) reconciles instead of remounting, preserving state.
        • It imports global CSS the same way as the app's entry; the body of window.mount is the natural place for app-wide setup, equivalent to the old beforeMount/afterMount hooks.

        If you'd rather write the gallery yourself, the installed skill has a complete spec with React and Vue examples in references/gallery-spec.md; the whole page is only a few dozen lines.

        Step 2: Configure Playwright

        Add a project to playwright.config.ts and point baseURL at the gallery:

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'components',
      testDir: './tests/components',
      use: {
        ...devices['Desktop Chrome'],
        baseURL: 'http://localhost:5173/playwright/gallery/index.html',
        serviceWorkers: 'block',
        reuseContext: true,
      },
    },
  ],
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run dev',
    url: 'http://localhost:5173/playwright/gallery/index.html',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
  },
});
        • mount navigates to baseURL, so it must point at the gallery.
        • serviceWorkers: 'block' stops the app's service worker from serving cached responses that would hide your page.route() mocks.
        • reuseContext: true reuses the browser context between tests in a worker: a big speedup for component suites, the same optimization the experimental packages applied implicitly.

        Step 3: Write a story

        Stories live next to the component; each named export is a scenario.

        import { Button } from './Button';

export const Primary = () => <Button title='Submit' />;

export const Disabled = () => <Button title='Submit' disabled />;

        Step 4: Write a test

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('renders primary button', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount('components/Button/Primary');
  await expect(component.getByRole('button')).toHaveText('Submit');
});

test('disabled button is disabled', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount('components/Button/Disabled');
  await expect(component.getByRole('button')).toBeDisabled();
});

        Step 5: Run

        npx playwright test --project=components

        Stories as a methodology

        Stories aren't just a workaround for testing: they are grep-able, reviewable documentation of a component's states, following these conventions:

        • One export per scenario. Prefer creating a new story export over parameterizing an existing one. A Button.story.tsx that exports Primary, Disabled and WithLongTitle reads like a spec for the component.
        • Stories live next to the component. src/components/Button.story.tsx describes src/components/Button.tsx; renames and refactors update both together.
        • Story ids are generated from the file path: the path under src/ without the .story.* suffix, plus the export name, for example components/Button/Primary. Any unique suffix also works: mount('Button/Primary').
        • The story owns everything the component needs: providers, mock data, state, callbacks. The test owns only the interactions and assertions.

        Because every story is a named, addressable page state, the gallery is also a living catalog: open the gallery URL in a browser and render any story to look at it.

        Testing patterns

        Record state for assertions

        A component takes callbacks, and the test wants to assert that the callback ran. Instead of marshaling callbacks between Node.js and the browser, the story owns the state and supplies the callbacks, then records the observable result into a hidden form next to the component:

        import { useState } from 'react';
import { Expandable } from './Expandable';

export const Stateful = () => {
  const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(false);
  return <>
    <Expandable expanded={expanded} setExpanded={setExpanded} title='Title'>Details</Expandable>
    <form hidden><input data-testid='expanded' readOnly value={String(expanded)} /></form>
  </>;
};
        import { defineComponent, h, ref } from 'vue';
import Expandable from './Expandable.vue';

export const Stateful = defineComponent(() => {
  const expanded = ref(false);
  return () => h('div', [
    h(Expandable, {
      'expanded': expanded.value,
      'onUpdate:expanded': (value: boolean) => expanded.value = value,
      'title': 'Title',
    }),
    h('form', { hidden: true }, [
      h('input', { 'data-testid': 'expanded', 'readonly': true, 'value': String(expanded.value) }),
    ]),
  ]);
});
        test('click should expand', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount('components/Expandable/Stateful');
  await component.getByRole('button').click();
  await expect(component.getByTestId('expanded')).toHaveValue('true');
});

        This is the heart of the methodology:

        • The whole scenario runs in the browser: no marshaled callbacks, no Node.js/browser boundary leaks.
        • toHaveValue() is a web-first assertion: it retries until the state updates, with no manual awaiting or polling.
        • Record each observed value into its own data-testid input: String(...) for scalars, JSON.stringify(...) for payloads. The reverse works too: perform an action and assert that the value did not change.
        • The recorded state is visible when you open the story in the gallery: click by hand and watch the value change; the story doubles as a manual test page for exactly the scenario the automated test covers. Keep the form hidden for clean screenshot baselines, or remove hidden while developing.

        Per-test props

        When a scenario needs parameterization, pass plain serializable props as the second argument of mount; the gallery hands them to the story as props.

        import { Button } from './Button';

export const WithTitle = ({ title = 'Default' }: { title?: string }) =>
  <Button title={title} />;
        import type { WithTitle } from '../../src/components/Button.story';

const component = await mount<typeof WithTitle>('Button/WithTitle', { title: 'Hello' });

        mount is generic over the story: pass the story type as the template argument and the props (and update()) are type-checked against the story's signature. Keep props as serializable data; callbacks belong inside the story.

        Prop transitions with update()

        To test how a component reacts when a prop changes without remounting (preserving state), call component.update(newProps): it re-renders the same story with new props on the existing root.

        const component = await mount('components/Counter/Default', { value: 1 });
await expect(component.getByTestId('value')).toHaveText('1');
await component.update({ value: 2 });
await expect(component.getByTestId('value')).toHaveText('2');

        Multiple states and visual comparison

        Every mount() is a fresh navigation, so tests are fully isolated and mounting several stories in one test is very cheap:

        await expect(await mount('Button/Primary')).toHaveScreenshot('primary.png');
await expect(await mount('Button/Disabled')).toHaveScreenshot('disabled.png');

        Screenshot the returned root locator, not the page, to avoid asserting on anything else you might put in the gallery. See Visual comparisons.

        Handling network requests

        Use page.route() as usual, and register the route before mount() because mount navigates the page:

        test('renders the error state', async ({ page, mount }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/items', route => route.fulfill({ status: 500 }));
  const component = await mount('components/ItemList/Default');
  await expect(component.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Something went wrong');
});

        The serviceWorkers: 'block' option in the config stops the app's service worker from returning cached responses that would hide the route. Teams with a library of MSW handlers can start the worker inside a story or decorator.

        Debugging stories

        Open the gallery URL in a browser and call await window.mount({ story: 'components/Button/Primary' }) from the DevTools console: it's exactly what the mount fixture does. A story that doesn't exist or fails to render makes window.mount reject, which surfaces as the test's mount() throwing with the real stack. To browse without the console, add an index page that lists every discovered story.

        Migration from the experimental packages

        The experimental packages compile JSX in the test file and then marshal it into the browser. The gallery pattern moves the scenario into a story export that runs natively in the browser. The concept mapping:

        @playwright/experimental-ct-*Story gallery
        mount(<Button onClick={spy} />)A stateful story: the story supplies onClick and records the effect into a hidden input; the test asserts with toHaveValue()
        Plain data props from the testSame in spirit: mount(id, props)
        JSX children / slots from the testOne story export per composition (Vue: a .story.vue file for multi-slot scenarios)
        component.update(<Button count={2} />)component.update({ count: 2 })
        component.unmount()component.unmount()
        beforeMount / afterMount hooksThe gallery's window.mount body (global) or story decorators (per story)
        Per-test hooksConfig variantsProps: mount('App/Routing', { route: '/dashboard' }), interpreted by the story
        router fixture / MSW handlers in Node.jspage.route() in the test, or MSW setupWorker in the story
        playwright/index.html (styles, theme)The gallery's index.html and imports in the entry module
        ctViteConfig, ctPort, ctTemplateDirGone: the gallery runs through your dev server; the port lives in webServer and baseURL
        defineConfig from the ct packagePlain defineConfig from @playwright/test

        A typical spec is converted like this:

        ❌ Before: button.spec.tsx
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';
import Button from '../src/components/Button';

test('counts clicks', async ({ mount }) => {
  let clicks = 0;
  const component = await mount(<Button title='Submit' onClick={() => ++clicks} />);
  await component.getByRole('button').click();
  expect(clicks).toBe(1);
});

        The callback has to be marshaled across the Node.js/browser boundary.

        ✅ After: story + test
        import { useState } from 'react';
import { Button } from './Button';

export const CountsClicks = () => {
  const [clicks, setClicks] = useState(0);
  return <>
    <Button title='Submit' onClick={() => setClicks(count => count + 1)} />
    <form hidden><input data-testid='click-count' readOnly value={String(clicks)} /></form>
  </>;
};
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('counts clicks', async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount('components/Button/CountsClicks');
  await component.getByRole('button').click();
  await expect(component.getByTestId('click-count')).toHaveValue('1');
});

        The story holds the state; the test only interacts and asserts through the DOM.

        Migrate incrementally: while still pinned to Playwright 1.62, set up the gallery and a components project alongside the old CT project, convert specs one at a time, then drop the @playwright/experimental-ct-* dependency together with playwright/index.html, playwright/index.ts and playwright/.cache, and upgrade.

        Things to watch out for:
        • Story ids are strings. Renaming or moving a story breaks specs at runtime, not compile time. Using mount<typeof Story> at least ties the props to the story at compile time.
        • Per-test JSX is gone. A test that used to build different JSX trees becomes one story export per composition, which is intentional: every composition worth testing is worth naming and reviewing.

        Frequently asked questions

        How do I access a component's methods or instance?

        Accessing a component's internal methods or its instance from test code is neither recommended nor supported. Instead, observe and interact with the component from the user's point of view: click, look at the page, and record internal effects into the DOM through the story. Tests become less brittle and more valuable when they avoid implementation details. If a test fails when run from the user's perspective, the automated test has most likely caught a real bug.

        Can I keep my own bundler plugins, aliases and CSS?

        Yes, that is the core of the design. The gallery is served by your dev server, so whatever your app can render, your stories can render. There is no second bundler config to keep in sync.

        What about frameworks other than React and Vue?

        Ask a coding agent to set up the gallery following the contract for your framework: resolve a story id to a component, render it into #root, and reuse the root between calls so update() preserves state. The mount fixture doesn't know or care which framework is on the other side.

        Best practice: the story owns state/callbacks/mocks, and the test only interacts + makes web-first assertions through the DOM; one story export per scenario; register page.route() before mount(); screenshot the root locator instead of the page.

        Key points

        • Component test = a regular Playwright test + the mount fixture + a gallery page that you own; the experimental-ct-* packages are gone.
        • Story = a named export for one scenario; the story id comes from the path (components/Button/Primary).
        • Config: baseURL pointing at the gallery, serviceWorkers: 'block', reuseContext: true, webServer.
        • Record state into a hidden data-testid input and assert with toHaveValue(); plain props via the second argument; update() changes props without remounting.
        • Callbacks don't cross the Node.js/browser boundary: let the story own them.
        Which fixture mounts a story?
        mount (built into @playwright/test); it returns a Locator for the gallery root.
        How do you change props while keeping state?
        component.update(newProps) — re-renders the same story on the existing root, without remounting.
        Why register page.route() before mount()?
        Because mount() navigates the page; the route must be in place before the component makes network calls.

        How do you assert that a component's onClick callback was called?

        Callbacks don't cross the Node.js/browser boundary; the "record state" pattern keeps the whole scenario in the browser and asserts through the DOM.

        Which project option reuses the browser context between tests in a worker to speed things up?

        reuseContext: true reuses the context; serviceWorkers: 'block' blocks service workers; reuseExistingServer belongs to webServer.

        Best Practices

        A guide to writing durable, low-flakiness tests: test user-visible behavior, isolate tests, use locators and web-first assertions properly, set up sensible debugging/CI configuration, and make the most of Playwright's tooling.

        Testing philosophy

        Test user-visible behavior

        Automated tests should verify that the application works correctly for the end user, and avoid depending on implementation details such as function names, whether a variable is an array, or an element's CSS class. Users only see and interact with what is rendered on the page, so your tests should only look at and interact with that same rendered output.

        Make tests as isolated as possible

        Each test must be completely independent of the others and run on its own with its own local storage, session storage, data, cookies, and so on. Test isolation makes results reproducible, easier to debug, and avoids cascading failures.

        To avoid repeating a chunk of setup, use beforeEach/afterEach hooks (for example, navigating to a URL or signing in). Tests stay isolated because no test relies on another. That said, accept a little code repetition if the tests are simple and it makes the code easier to read.

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
  // Runs before each test and signs in each page.
  await page.goto('https://github.com/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('username');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
});

test('first', async ({ page }) => {
  // page is signed in.
});

test('second', async ({ page }) => {
  // page is signed in.
});

        You can also reuse a signed-in state with a setup project (see auth – shared account): sign in once, then skip the login step in every test.

        Avoid testing third-party dependencies

        Only test what you control. Don't test links to external sites or third-party servers: it wastes time, slows your tests down, and you don't control content (cookie banners, overlays...) that could make the test fail. Instead, use the Network API (page.route) to guarantee the responses you need.

        await page.route('**/api/fetch_data_third_party_dependency', route => route.fulfill({
  status: 200,
  body: testData,
}));
await page.goto('https://example.com');

        Testing with a database

        If you work with a database, keep control of the data: test against a staging environment and make sure the data doesn't change. For visual regression tests, the operating system and browser version must be the same.

        Best Practices

        Use locators

        To write E2E tests you first need to find elements. Use Playwright's built-in locators: they have auto-waiting (they perform actionability checks, such as the element being visible and enabled, before clicking) and retry-ability. To keep tests durable, prefer user-facing attributes and "explicit contracts".

        // 👍
page.getByRole('button', { name: 'submit' });

        Use chaining and filtering

        Locators can be chained to narrow the search down to one part of the page, and can be filtered by text or by another locator.

        const product = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Product 2' });
        await page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ hasText: 'Product 2' })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
    .click();

        Prefer user-facing attributes to XPath or CSS selectors

        The DOM changes easily, so tests that depend on the DOM structure are brittle. For example, selecting a button by CSS class: if a designer changes the class, the test breaks.

        ❌ Avoid
        page.locator('button.buttonIcon.episode-actions-later');

        Depends on a CSS class – change the styling and the test breaks.

        ✅ Prefer
        page.getByRole('button', { name: 'submit' });

        Relies on the role + accessible name, resilient to DOM changes.

        Generate locators

        Playwright has a test generator that can generate tests and pick locators for you. It analyzes the page and picks the best locator, prioritizing role, text and test id. If several elements match, the generator refines the locator to uniquely identify the target element.

        Use codegen to generate locators

        Run codegen with the URL you want to get locators from:

        npx playwright codegen playwright.dev
        yarn playwright codegen playwright.dev
        pnpm exec playwright codegen playwright.dev

        The command opens a browser window and the Playwright Inspector. By default codegen starts a new recording session; to pick a locator, press the Record button to stop recording, and the Pick Locator button becomes available. Hover over an element to see its locator highlighted, and click to add the locator to the Inspector. You can copy it into your test file or keep refining the locator right in the Inspector (for example, edit the text) and see the result in the browser.

        Use the VS Code extension to generate locators

        The VS Code extension can also generate locators and record tests, and gives you a great experience for writing, running and debugging tests.

        Use web first assertions

        Assertions verify that the expected result matches the actual one. With web first assertions, Playwright waits until the condition is met. For example, if an alert appears after half a second, toBeVisible() waits and retries as needed.

        Don't use manual assertions

        When you use isVisible(), the test doesn't wait even a second: it checks instantly and returns right away. Putting await inside expect is the wrong approach.

        ❌ Avoid
        expect(await page.getByText('welcome').isVisible()).toBe(true);

        No auto-wait/retry; prone to flakiness.

        ✅ Prefer
        await expect(page.getByText('welcome')).toBeVisible();

        A web-first assertion waits until the condition is true or the timeout expires.

        Configure debugging

        Local debugging

        We recommend debugging live in VS Code with the VS Code extension. Run a test in debug mode by right-clicking the line next to the test; the browser opens and stops at your breakpoint. You can click/edit locators in VS Code to highlight the locator in the browser and see which other locators match on the page.

        Or debug with the Playwright Inspector using the --debug flag:

        npx playwright test --debug
        yarn playwright test --debug
        pnpm exec playwright test --debug

        You can step through the test, view the actionability log, edit locators live and see the number of matching elements. To debug a specific test, add the file name and the test's line number:

        npx playwright test example.spec.ts:9 --debug
        yarn playwright test example.spec.ts:9 --debug
        pnpm exec playwright test example.spec.ts:9 --debug

        Debugging on CI

        When a test fails on CI, use the Trace Viewer instead of relying on video and screenshots alone. The Trace Viewer is a local PWA that's easy to share, and shows the timeline, DOM snapshots of each action (with dev tools), network requests, and more.

        Traces are configured in the config file, and on CI they typically run with on-first-retry (the first retry of a failed test). Setting on (trace every test) is not recommended because it is very expensive performance-wise. During local development you can use the --trace flag:

        npx playwright test --trace on
        yarn playwright test --trace on
        pnpm exec playwright test --trace on

        Each test's trace can then be viewed directly in the HTML report:

        npx playwright show-report
        yarn playwright show-report
        pnpm exec playwright show-report

        Open a trace by clicking the icon next to the test file name, or open an individual test report and scroll down to the traces section.

        Use Playwright's Tooling

        • VS Code extension: a great experience for writing, running and debugging tests.
        • Test generator (codegen): generates tests and picks locators.
        • Trace viewer: the full trace as an easily shared local PWA (timeline, DOM snapshots, network...).
        • UI Mode: explore, run and debug tests "time travel" style with watch mode; all test files are loaded into the sidebar so you can run/view/watch/debug each test or describe block.
        • TypeScript: works out of the box, with better IDE suggestions. You aren't required to write TS code; just use the .ts extension.

        Test across all browsers

        Playwright can test on every browser regardless of the platform you're on. Configure projects in the config with a name and the corresponding browser/device.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'firefox',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'webkit',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] },
    },
  ],
});

        Keep your Playwright dependency up to date

        Updating Playwright lets you test on the latest browsers and catch bugs before those browsers are widely released.

        npm install -D @playwright/test@latest
        yarn add --dev @playwright/test@latest
        pnpm install --save-dev @playwright/test@latest

        See the release notes for the latest version. Check the version you're using:

        npx playwright --version
        yarn playwright --version
        pnpm exec playwright --version

        Run tests on CI

        Set up CI/CD and run your tests frequently – the more often the better, ideally on every commit and pull request. Playwright ships a ready-made GitHub Actions workflow (no extra setup needed) and can be configured on any CI (see Continuous Integration).

        Use Linux on CI because it's cheaper; developers can use whatever environment they like when running locally. Consider sharding to make CI faster.

        Optimize browser downloads on CI

        Only install the browsers you actually need, especially on CI. For example, if you only test with Chromium, install only Chromium – it saves download time and disk space.

        # Instead of installing all browsers
npx playwright install --with-deps

# Install only Chromium
npx playwright install chromium --with-deps

        Lint your tests

        We recommend using TypeScript and ESLint to catch errors early. Use the @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises rule to make sure no await is missing before Playwright API's async calls. On CI you can run tsc --noEmit to check that functions are called with the correct signatures.

        Use parallelism and sharding

        Playwright runs tests in parallel by default. Tests in the same file run sequentially in the same worker. If a file has many independent tests, you can run them in parallel:

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' });

test('runs in parallel 1', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
test('runs in parallel 2', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });

        Playwright can also shard a test suite to run across multiple machines:

        npx playwright test --shard=1/3
        yarn playwright test --shard=1/3
        pnpm exec playwright test --shard=1/3

        Productivity tips: Use soft assertions

        When a test fails, Playwright reports which part failed (VS Code, terminal, HTML report, trace viewer). With soft assertions, the test doesn't stop immediately when an assertion fails; instead it collects a list of errors and shows them when the test ends.

        // Make a few checks that will not stop the test when failed...
await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Success');

// ... and continue the test to check more things.
await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'next page' }).click();
        1. Pick a locatorgetByRole / getByText, use codegen
        2. Actauto-wait + actionability
        3. Web-first assertionawait expect(...) retries automatically
        4. DebugVS Code / --debug / UI Mode
        5. CItrace on-first-retry, shard, Linux

        Key points

        • Test user-visible behavior; prefer getByRole/text/test id, and avoid DOM-dependent CSS/XPath.
        • Isolate every test (its own browser context); use hooks or a setup project to reuse login.
        • Always use web-first assertions (await expect(locator)...), never expect(await ...isVisible()).
        • Mock/stub third-party services with page.route; control your DB data.
        • CI: Linux, trace on-first-retry, install only the browsers you need, shard, lint with no-floating-promises + tsc --noEmit.
        • expect.soft collects multiple failures without stopping the test.

        Which way of writing an assertion is correct according to best practices?

        B is a web-first assertion: it waits and retries automatically. A checks instantly without waiting, and C is missing await so it isn't guaranteed to finish waiting.

        On CI, which trace configuration is recommended?

        Trace on is very heavy; on-first-retry only records a trace on the first retry of a failed test, which is enough to debug while using few resources.

        Page object models

        The Page Object Model (POM) is a way to structure a large test suite: each page or section of the application is encapsulated in a class, which makes tests easier to write and easier to maintain.

        Introduction

        Large test suites should be organized so they are easy to write and easy to maintain; the Page Object Model is one such approach. A page object represents a part of your web app. For example, an e-commerce app might have a home page, a listings page, and a checkout page – each of them is a page object model.

        Page objects:

        • Simplify writing tests by creating a higher-level API that fits your application.
        • Simplify maintenance by keeping element selectors in one place and creating reusable code to avoid repetition.

        Implementation

        We create a helper class PlaywrightDevPage that encapsulates common operations on the playwright.dev page. Internally it uses the page object. The class stores the locators (getStartedLink, gettingStartedHeader, pomLink, tocList) in its constructor and provides the methods goto(), getStarted(), and pageObjectModel().

        import { expect, type Locator, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export class PlaywrightDevPage {
  readonly page: Page;
  readonly getStartedLink: Locator;
  readonly gettingStartedHeader: Locator;
  readonly pomLink: Locator;
  readonly tocList: Locator;

  constructor(page: Page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.getStartedLink = page.locator('a', { hasText: 'Get started' });
    this.gettingStartedHeader = page.locator('h1', { hasText: 'Installation' });
    this.pomLink = page.locator('li', {
      hasText: 'Guides',
    }).locator('a', {
      hasText: 'Page Object Model',
    });
    this.tocList = page.locator('article div.markdown ul > li > a');
  }

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  }

  async getStarted() {
    await this.getStartedLink.first().click();
    await expect(this.gettingStartedHeader).toBeVisible();
  }

  async pageObjectModel() {
    await this.getStarted();
    await this.pomLink.click();
  }
}
        Library version (JavaScript, no test runner)

        When using the Playwright Library (require('playwright')), a similar class is written in CommonJS and exported via module.exports:

        class PlaywrightDevPage {
  /**
   * @param {import('playwright').Page} page
   */
  constructor(page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.getStartedLink = page.locator('a', { hasText: 'Get started' });
    this.gettingStartedHeader = page.locator('h1', { hasText: 'Installation' });
    this.pomLink = page.locator('li', {
      hasText: 'Playwright Test',
    }).locator('a', {
      hasText: 'Page Object Model',
    });
    this.tocList = page.locator('article div.markdown ul > li > a');
  }
  async getStarted() {
    await this.getStartedLink.first().click();
    await expect(this.gettingStartedHeader).toBeVisible();
  }

  async pageObjectModel() {
    await this.getStarted();
    await this.pomLink.click();
  }
}
module.exports = { PlaywrightDevPage };
        const { PlaywrightDevPage } = require('./playwright-dev-page');

// In the test
const page = await browser.newPage();
await playwrightDev.goto();
await playwrightDev.getStarted();
await expect(playwrightDev.tocList).toHaveText([
  `How to install Playwright`,
  `What's installed`,
  `How to run the example test`,
  `How to open the HTML test report`,
  `Write tests using web-first assertions, fixtures and locators`,
  `Run single or multiple tests; headed mode`,
  `Generate tests with Codegen`,
  `View a trace of your tests`,
]);

        Using the page object in tests

        Now you can use PlaywrightDevPage in a test: create an instance from page, then call the high-level methods.

        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { PlaywrightDevPage } from './playwright-dev-page';

test('getting started should contain table of contents', async ({ page }) => {
  const playwrightDev = new PlaywrightDevPage(page);
  await playwrightDev.goto();
  await playwrightDev.getStarted();
  await expect(playwrightDev.tocList).toHaveText([
    `How to install Playwright`,
    `What's installed`,
    `How to run the example test`,
    `How to open the HTML test report`,
    `Write tests using web-first assertions, fixtures and locators`,
    `Run single or multiple tests; headed mode`,
    `Generate tests with Codegen`,
    `View a trace of your tests`,
  ]);
});

test('should show Page Object Model article', async ({ page }) => {
  const playwrightDev = new PlaywrightDevPage(page);
  await playwrightDev.goto();
  await playwrightDev.pageObjectModel();
  await expect(page.locator('article')).toContainText('Page Object Model is a common pattern');
});
        Tip: combine POM with fixtures to create a page object automatically for each test (test.extend), so you don't have to call new manually in every test. Locators should be readonly properties declared in the constructor, while actions are async methods.
        1. Testnew PlaywrightDevPage(page)
        2. Page objectholds locators + high-level methods
        3. pagethe Playwright Page executes
        4. Assertionexpect(...) in the test

        Key takeaways

        • A page object is a class representing a page or UI region, wrapping around Page.
        • Benefits: a high-level API makes tests easier to write; selectors live in one place, so they are easier to maintain and avoid repetition.
        • Locators are declared in the constructor; methods like goto() and getStarted() perform actions.
        • A test only creates the page object, then calls methods and expect.

        What is the main benefit of the Page Object Model?

        POM simplifies writing and maintaining tests by gathering selectors and reusable code into page objects.

        Browsers

        Each Playwright version needs the exact matching browser binaries; this page covers how to install and configure them (Chromium, Chrome/Edge, Firefox, WebKit), install behind a firewall/proxy, and manage and remove binaries.

        Introduction

        Each version of Playwright needs specific versions of browser binaries to operate; you use the Playwright CLI to install them. Every Playwright release updates the supported browser versions, so the latest Playwright always supports the latest browsers. This means that every time you update Playwright, you may need to re-run the install command.

        Install browsers

        Running it with no arguments installs the default browsers:

        npx playwright install

        Install a specific browser by passing an argument:

        npx playwright install webkit

        See all supported browsers:

        npx playwright install --help

        Install system dependencies

        System dependencies can be installed automatically – useful for CI environments.

        npx playwright install-deps

        Install dependencies for a single browser only:

        npx playwright install-deps chromium

        You can combine install-deps with install to install the browsers and OS dependencies with a single command:

        npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

        See the system requirements for the officially supported operating systems.

        Update Playwright regularly

        Keep Playwright up to date so you can use new features and test your app on the latest browsers, catching bugs before those browsers are widely released.

        # Update playwright
npm install -D @playwright/test@latest

# Install new browsers
npx playwright install

        Check the release notes for the latest version, and check your current version:

        # See what version of Playwright you have by running the following command
npx playwright --version

        Configure Browsers

        Playwright runs tests on Chromium, WebKit, Firefox, as well as branded browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, and on emulated tablet/mobile devices. See the registry of device parameters for the list of devices.

        Run tests on different browsers

        Set up projects in the config to run tests on multiple browsers/configurations; each project can have its own options.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    /* Test against desktop browsers */
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'firefox',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'webkit',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] },
    },
    /* Test against mobile viewports. */
    {
      name: 'Mobile Chrome',
      use: { ...devices['Pixel 5'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'Mobile Safari',
      use: { ...devices['iPhone 12'] },
    },
    /* Test against branded browsers. */
    {
      name: 'Google Chrome',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], channel: 'chrome' }, // or 'chrome-beta'
    },
    {
      name: 'Microsoft Edge',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Edge'], channel: 'msedge' }, // or 'msedge-dev'
    },
  ],
});

        By default Playwright runs all projects:

        npx playwright test

Running 7 tests using 5 workers

  ✓ [chromium] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [webkit] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Mobile Chrome] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Mobile Safari] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Google Chrome] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)
  ✓ [Microsoft Edge] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)

        Use --project to run a single project:

        npx playwright test --project=firefox

Running 1 test using 1 worker

  ✓ [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)

        With the VS Code extension, you run tests on different browsers by ticking the checkbox next to a project name in the Playwright sidebar (names come from the projects section of the config). The default config has 3 projects, Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit; the first project is selected by default. Select multiple projects to run on multiple browsers.

        Chromium

        For Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other Chromium-based browsers, Playwright uses the open-source Chromium build by default. Chromium is ahead of the branded browsers: when the world is on Chrome N, Playwright already supports Chromium N+1, which will arrive in Chrome/Edge a few weeks later.

        Chromium: headless shell
