        Playwright ships a regular Chromium build for headed mode and a separate chromium headless shell for headless. If you only run tests in the headless shell (that is, you do not specify a channel), for example on CI, you can avoid downloading the full Chromium by using --only-shell:

        # only running tests headlessly
npx playwright install --with-deps --only-shell

        Chromium: new headless mode

        Enable new headless mode with the 'chromium' channel. According to the Chrome docs: "New Headless is the real Chrome browser, so it is more authentic, reliable, and has more features; it is better suited for high-fidelity end-to-end tests or browser extension tests". See issue #33566.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], channel: 'chromium' },
    },
  ],
});

        With new headless mode, you can skip downloading the headless shell by using --no-shell:

        # only running tests headlessly
npx playwright install --with-deps --no-shell

        Installing Google Chrome & Microsoft Edge

        If Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge is not installed on your machine, install it with the Playwright CLI:

        npx playwright install msedge
        Warning: Chrome/Edge will be installed to the OS's default global location, overwriting your existing browser installation.

        Run with --help to see the full list of installable browsers.

        When to use Google Chrome & Microsoft Edge and when not to?

        SituationRecommendation
        DefaultsUsing the default configuration with the latest Chromium is a good idea in most cases. Playwright is ahead of the Stable channel, so you can be confident that the upcoming Chrome/Edge release won't break your site; you find problems early and have plenty of time to fix them.
        Regression testingTesting policies often require regression testing on the currently public browsers: pick the stable channel "chrome" or "msedge".
        Media codecsChromium does not have all the codecs that Chrome/Edge have, due to licensing issues. If your site depends on codecs (rare), use an official channel.
        Enterprise policyChrome/Edge respect enterprise policies (capability restrictions, network proxies, mandatory extensions) that may get in the way of tests. If your organization uses policies, use the bundled Chromium for local tests; you can still choose the stable channel on bots that are not restricted.

        Firefox

        Playwright's Firefox matches a recent Firefox Stable build. Playwright does not work with branded Firefox because it depends on patches. Note that some platform-dependent features may differ between OSes (for example, media codecs differ significantly across Linux, macOS, and Windows).

        WebKit

        Playwright's WebKit is taken from the latest main branch of the WebKit source, usually before updates make it into Apple Safari and WebKit-based browsers – giving you plenty of time to react to issues in new browser releases. Playwright does not work with branded Safari because it depends on patches; test with the latest WebKit build instead. Running WebKit on Linux CI is usually the cheapest, but to get closest to Safari (for example, video playback) you should run WebKit on a Mac.

        Install behind a firewall or a proxy

        By default Playwright downloads browsers from Microsoft's CDN. Many companies have internal proxies that block direct access; in that case, configure downloads to go through the proxy:

        HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1 npx playwright install
        set HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1
npx playwright install
        $Env:HTTPS_PROXY="https://192.0.2.1"
npx playwright install

        If the proxy intercepts requests with an untrusted custom CA and causes the error Error: self signed certificate in certificate chain during download, set the root certificate via the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS variable before installing:

        export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS="/path/to/cert.pem"
        set NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS="C:\certs\root.crt"
        $Env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS="C:\certs\root.crt"

        If downloads are slow or hang, increase the socket timeout (in ms) with PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT. Despite the name "connection timeout", it is actually an idle timeout – the limit on how long a download may go without receiving data; the default is 30 seconds:

        PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=120000 npx playwright install
        set PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=120000
npx playwright install
        $Env:PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT="120000"
npx playwright install

        If you install dependencies and need a proxy on Linux, you must run the command as root; otherwise Playwright will try to become root itself and will not pass environment variables such as HTTPS_PROXY to the Linux package manager.

        sudo HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1 npx playwright install-deps

        Download from artifact repository

        A company may have an internal artifact repository that hosts browser binaries. In that case, configure downloads from the custom location using the PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST variable:

        PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=http://192.0.2.1 npx playwright install
        set PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=http://192.0.2.1
npx playwright install
        $Env:PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST="http://192.0.2.1"
npx playwright install

        You can also use a separate host for each browser: PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_DOWNLOAD_HOST, PLAYWRIGHT_FIREFOX_DOWNLOAD_HOST, PLAYWRIGHT_WEBKIT_DOWNLOAD_HOST – they take higher priority than PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST.

        PLAYWRIGHT_FIREFOX_DOWNLOAD_HOST=http://203.0.113.3 PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=http://192.0.2.1 npx playwright install
        set PLAYWRIGHT_FIREFOX_DOWNLOAD_HOST=http://203.0.113.3
set PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=http://192.0.2.1
npx playwright install
        $Env:PLAYWRIGHT_FIREFOX_DOWNLOAD_HOST="http://203.0.113.3"
$Env:PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST="http://192.0.2.1"
npx playwright install

        Managing browser binaries

        Playwright downloads Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox into an OS-specific cache folder:

        OSPath
        Windows%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\ms-playwright
        macOS~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright
        Linux~/.cache/ms-playwright

        The browsers take up several hundred MB of disk space once installed:

        du -hs ~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/*
281M  chromium-XXXXXX
187M  firefox-XXXX
180M  webkit-XXXX

        You can override the default behavior using environment variables. When installing, download browsers into a specific location:

        PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=$HOME/pw-browsers npx playwright install
        set PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=%USERPROFILE%\pw-browsers
npx playwright install
        $Env:PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH="$Env:USERPROFILE\pw-browsers"
npx playwright install

        When running scripts, tell Playwright to look for browsers in the shared location:

        PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=$HOME/pw-browsers npx playwright test
        set PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=%USERPROFILE%\pw-browsers
npx playwright test
        $Env:PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH="$Env:USERPROFILE\pw-browsers"
npx playwright test

        Playwright keeps track of the packages that need those browsers and will garbage collect them when you upgrade Playwright to a new version.

        Note: developers can enable this mode by exporting PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=$HOME/pw-browsers in .bashrc.

        Hermetic install

        You can opt in to a "hermetic" install – placing the binaries in the project's local folder:

        # Places binaries to node_modules/playwright-core/.local-browsers
PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0 npx playwright install
        # Places binaries to node_modules\playwright-core\.local-browsers
set PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0
npx playwright install
        # Places binaries to node_modules\playwright-core\.local-browsers
$Env:PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0
npx playwright install
        Note: PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH does not change the installation path of Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge.

        Stale browser removal

        Playwright keeps track of the clients that use its browsers. When no clients need a browser version any more, that version is removed from the system. This lets you use multiple Playwright versions side by side without wasting disk space on browsers that are no longer used. To disable this removal, set PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_GC=1 or pass --no-remove:

        npx playwright install --no-remove

        List all installed browsers

        Print the list of browsers from every Playwright installation on the machine:

        npx playwright install --list

        Uninstall browsers

        Remove the browsers (chromium, firefox, webkit) of the current Playwright installation:

        npx playwright uninstall

        To also remove browsers from other Playwright installations, add --all:

        npx playwright uninstall --all

        Command & environment variable cheat sheet

        Command / variableEffect
        npx playwright install [browser]Install the default browsers or the specified browser
        install-deps / install --with-depsInstall system dependencies (CI)
        --only-shell / --no-shellHeadless shell only / skip the headless shell
        --no-remove, PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_GC=1Do not remove old browsers
        install --list, uninstall [--all]List / uninstall browsers
        HTTPS_PROXY, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTSDownload through a proxy / custom CA
        PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST (+ PLAYWRIGHT_{CHROMIUM|FIREFOX|WEBKIT}_DOWNLOAD_HOST)Download from an internal mirror
        PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_CONNECTION_TIMEOUTIdle timeout for downloads (ms, default 30s)
        PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH (0 = hermetic)Where browsers are stored

        Key takeaways

        • When you update Playwright, re-run npx playwright install; on CI use install --with-deps.
        • The open-source Chromium is used by default; use channel: 'chrome' | 'msedge' when you need regression testing on stable builds, codecs, or a branded browser.
        • Playwright's Firefox/WebKit are patched builds, not the branded releases.
        • Behind a firewall: HTTPS_PROXY, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST.
        • Binaries live in an OS-specific cache; change it with PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH (0 = hermetic inside node_modules).

        On CI you want to run only headless and avoid downloading the full Chromium. Which flag do you use (without specifying a channel)?

        --only-shell installs only the headless shell and skips the full Chromium. --no-shell does the opposite (used with new headless mode, channel chromium).

        Isolation (Test isolation)

        Playwright tests run in clean, isolated environments called browser contexts – the foundation for reproducibility and for preventing cascading failures. (The "isolation" page in the sidebar has the actual slug browser-contexts.)

        Introduction

        Tests written with Playwright run in isolated "clean-slate" environments called a browser context. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures.

        What is Test Isolation?

        Test Isolation means each test is completely isolated from the others; each test runs independently, with its own local storage, session storage, cookies, and so on. Playwright achieves this with BrowserContext – the equivalent of an incognito-style profile, which is fast and cheap to create and fully isolated even when running within a single browser. Playwright creates one context per test and provides a default Page in that context.

        Why is Test Isolation Important?

        • No failure propagation: one failing test does not affect the others.
        • Easy to debug errors/flakiness: you can run a single test as many times as you like.
        • No need to care about ordering when running in parallel, sharding, and so on.

        Two Ways of Test Isolation

        There are two isolation strategies: start from scratch or cleanup in between. The problem with cleaning up between tests is that it is easy to forget to clean up, and some things cannot be cleaned up, such as "visited links". State from one test can leak into the next, causing failures and making debugging harder because the problem comes from a different test. Starting from scratch means everything is new; if a test fails, you only need to look inside that test.

        StrategyProsCons
        Cleanup in betweenReuses the environmentEasy to forget cleanup; some things can't be cleaned (visited links); state leaks between tests
        Start from scratch (Playwright)Every test is clean; debugging stays within that testNeeds setup again (solved with hooks / setup projects)

        How Playwright Achieves Test Isolation

        Every test gets its own Browser Context; running a test creates a new browser context each time. When using Playwright Test, the browser context is created by default. Otherwise, you create it manually.

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('example test', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // "context" is an isolated BrowserContext, created for this specific test.
  // "page" belongs to this context.
});

test('another test', async ({ page, context }) => {
  // "context" and "page" in this second test are completely
  // isolated from the first test.
});
        const browser = await chromium.launch();
const context = await browser.newContext();
const page = await context.newPage();

        Browser contexts are also used to emulate multi-page scenarios with mobile devices, permissions, locale, and color scheme. See the Emulation guide.

        Multiple Contexts in a Single Test

        Playwright can create multiple browser contexts within a single scenario – useful when testing multi-user functionality, such as chat.

        import { test } from '@playwright/test';

test('admin and user', async ({ browser }) => {
  // Create two isolated browser contexts
  const adminContext = await browser.newContext();
  const userContext = await browser.newContext();

  // Create pages and interact with contexts independently
  const adminPage = await adminContext.newPage();
  const userPage = await userContext.newPage();
});
        const { chromium } = require('playwright');

// Create a Chromium browser instance
const browser = await chromium.launch();

// Create two isolated browser contexts
const userContext = await browser.newContext();
const adminContext = await browser.newContext();

// Create pages and interact with contexts independently
const adminPage = await adminContext.newPage();
const userPage = await userContext.newPage();
        1. Browsershared between tests in a worker
        2. newContext()created fresh for each test
        3. newPage()the default page in the context
        4. Test runsits own cookies/storage
        5. Close contextstate is completely discarded

        Key takeaways

        • Each test = a new BrowserContext (like an incognito profile), containing a default page.
        • Isolation prevents failures from spreading, makes debugging easier, and lets parallel/sharded runs be order-independent.
        • "Start from scratch" is better than "cleanup in between".
        • You can create multiple contexts in one test to simulate multiple users (admin & user).

        How does Playwright Test isolate tests?

        Each test gets a fresh, clean browser context – there is no old state to clean up.

        Chrome extensions

        How to load and test Chrome extensions (Manifest v3) in Playwright's Chromium using a persistent context, a service worker, and a fixture.

        Introduction

        Note: extensions only work in Chromium when launched with a persistent context. Use custom browser args at your own risk, as some of them may break Playwright functionality. Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge have removed the command-line flags needed to side-load extensions, so use the Chromium that ships with Playwright.

        The code below gets the service worker of a Manifest v3 extension whose source is in ./my-extension. Note that it uses the chromium channel so the extension can run in headless mode; alternatively you can run headed.

        const { chromium } = require('playwright');

(async () => {
  const pathToExtension = require('path').join(__dirname, 'my-extension');
  const userDataDir = '/tmp/test-user-data-dir';
  const browserContext = await chromium.launchPersistentContext(userDataDir, {
    channel: 'chromium',
    args: [
      `--disable-extensions-except=${pathToExtension}`,
      `--load-extension=${pathToExtension}`
    ]
  });
  let [serviceWorker] = browserContext.serviceWorkers();
  if (!serviceWorker)
    serviceWorker = await browserContext.waitForEvent('serviceworker');

  // Test the service worker as you would any other worker.
  await browserContext.close();
})();

        Service worker idle suspension (MV3)

        Chrome's MV3 service workers are automatically suspended after ~30 seconds of inactivity and restarted when needed. When this happens, Playwright keeps the same Worker object – there is no new 'serviceworker' event. New evaluate() calls made during the restart hang until the new context is ready, and then continue automatically:

        const sw = await context.waitForEvent('serviceworker');

// ... SW suspends after 30 s of inactivity and is restarted by the browser ...

// The existing handle is transparent across the restart.
await sw.evaluate(() => sendMessage({ type: 'ping' })); // just works
        Caution: evaluate() calls that are in flight at the exact moment of suspension throw a "Service worker restarted" error, similar to the behavior when a navigation happens mid-call.

        Testing

        To load the extension when running tests, use a test fixture to set up the context. You can also dynamically retrieve the extension id and use it to load and test the popup page. Note that the chromium channel allows running headless.

        First, add a fixture that loads the extension:

        import { test as base, chromium, type BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

export const test = base.extend<{
  context: BrowserContext;
  extensionId: string;
}>({
  context: async ({ }, use) => {
    const pathToExtension = path.join(__dirname, 'my-extension');
    const context = await chromium.launchPersistentContext('', {
      channel: 'chromium',
      args: [
        `--disable-extensions-except=${pathToExtension}`,
        `--load-extension=${pathToExtension}`,
      ],
    });
    await use(context);
    await context.close();
  },
  extensionId: async ({ context }, use) => {
    // for manifest v3:
    let [serviceWorker] = context.serviceWorkers();
    if (!serviceWorker)
      serviceWorker = await context.waitForEvent('serviceworker');

    const extensionId = serviceWorker.url().split('/')[2];
    await use(extensionId);
  },
});
export const expect = test.expect;

        Then use the fixture in your tests:

        import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

test('example test', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://example.com');
  await expect(page.locator('body')).toHaveText('Changed by my-extension');
});

test('popup page', async ({ page, extensionId }) => {
  await page.goto(`chrome-extension://${extensionId}/popup.html`);
  await expect(page.locator('body')).toHaveText('my-extension popup');
});
        1. launchPersistentContextchannel 'chromium' + --load-extension
        2. Get the service workerserviceWorkers() or waitForEvent
        3. Get the extensionIdserviceWorker.url().split('/')[2]
        4. Testchrome-extension://id/popup.html

        Key takeaways

        • Chromium only + launchPersistentContext; branded Chrome/Edge can no longer side-load via flags.
        • Use channel: 'chromium' to run headless; args --disable-extensions-except and --load-extension.
        • The MV3 SW is suspended after ~30s, the Worker handle remains usable; an in-flight evaluate() fails with "Service worker restarted".
        • The extensionId fixture is derived from the service worker URL so you can open the popup.

        What is required to load an extension in Playwright?

        Extensions only work in Chromium with a persistent context; Chrome/Edge have removed the side-loading flags.

        WebView2

        Use Playwright to automate Windows applications that embed Microsoft Edge WebView2 through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).

        Introduction

        Microsoft Edge WebView2 is a WinForms control that uses Microsoft Edge under the hood to render web content. It is part of Edge and is available on Windows 10/11. Playwright can automate WebView2 apps and test the web content inside WebView2. To connect to WebView2, Playwright uses BrowserType.connectOverCDP(), which connects through CDP.

        Overview

        You can make the WebView2 control listen for CDP connections in one of two ways:

        • Set the environment variable WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS to --remote-debugging-port=9222.
        • Or call EnsureCoreWebView2Async with the argument --remote-debugging-port=9222 (via AdditionalBrowserArguments in CoreWebView2EnvironmentOptions, in C# code).

        This starts the WebView2 process with CDP enabled, letting Playwright control it. 9222 is just an example port; you can use any other unused port.

        Once the application containing WebView2 is running, connect with Playwright:

        const browser = await playwright.chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222');
const context = browser.contexts()[0];
const page = context.pages()[0];

        To make sure the WebView2 control is ready, wait for the CoreWebView2InitializationCompleted event (in the .NET application code).

        Writing and running tests

        By default WebView2 uses the same user data directory for all instances, so if you run several tests in parallel they will interfere with each other. To avoid this, set the WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER variable (or use WebView2.EnsureCoreWebView2Async) to a different folder for each test so every test runs with its own user data directory.

        The fixture below runs the WebView2 application as a sub-process, assigns a unique user data directory and CDP port to each worker, and provides a Page instance to the test:

        import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'fs';
import os from 'os';
import path from 'path';
import childProcess from 'child_process';

const EXECUTABLE_PATH = path.join(
    __dirname,
    '../../webview2-app/bin/Debug/net8.0-windows/webview2.exe',
);

export const test = base.extend({
  browser: async ({ playwright }, use, testInfo) => {
    const cdpPort = 10000 + testInfo.workerIndex;
    // Make sure that the executable exists and is executable
    fs.accessSync(EXECUTABLE_PATH, fs.constants.X_OK);
    const userDataDir = path.join(
        fs.realpathSync.native(os.tmpdir()),
        `playwright-webview2-tests/user-data-dir-${testInfo.workerIndex}`,
    );
    const webView2Process = childProcess.spawn(EXECUTABLE_PATH, [], {
      shell: true,
      env: {
        ...process.env,
        WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS: `--remote-debugging-port=${cdpPort}`,
        WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER: userDataDir,
      }
    });
    await new Promise<void>(resolve => webView2Process.stdout.on('data', data => {
      if (data.toString().includes('WebView2 initialized'))
        resolve();
    }));
    const browser = await playwright.chromium.connectOverCDP(`http://127.0.0.1:${cdpPort}`);
    await use(browser);
    await browser.close();
    childProcess.execSync(`taskkill /pid ${webView2Process.pid} /T /F`);
    fs.rmdirSync(userDataDir, { recursive: true });
  },
  context: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = browser.contexts()[0];
    await use(context);
  },
  page: async ({ context }, use) => {
    const page = context.pages()[0];
    await use(page);
  },
});

export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
        import { test, expect } from './webView2Test';

test('test WebView2', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev');
  const getStarted = page.getByText('Get Started');
  await expect(getStarted).toBeVisible();
});
        How it works: each worker uses port 10000 + workerIndex and its own user data dir; the fixture waits for the app to print a line containing WebView2 initialized before calling connectOverCDP; after the test it runs taskkill on the process and deletes the data directory.

        Debugging

        In the WebView2 control, right-click to open the context menu and choose Inspect to open DevTools, or press F12. You can also use the WebView2.CoreWebView2.OpenDevToolsWindow method to open DevTools from code. To debug the test itself, see Playwright's Debugging guide.

        1. Spawn appenv: remote-debugging-port + user data folder
        2. Wait for init"WebView2 initialized"
        3. connectOverCDPhttp://127.0.0.1:port
        4. Testcontexts()[0].pages()[0]
        5. Cleanuptaskkill + delete user data dir

        Key takeaways

        • Connect to WebView2 with chromium.connectOverCDP(url).
        • Enable CDP: WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS=--remote-debugging-port=PORT or via EnsureCoreWebView2Async.
        • Parallel tests need a separate WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER and port for each worker.
        • Debug: right-click > Inspect, F12, or OpenDevToolsWindow.

        Why does each WebView2 test/worker need its own WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER?

        Sharing a user data directory makes parallel tests affect one another; each worker needs its own folder.

        Docker

        Playwright's official Docker images (on the Microsoft Artifact Registry) come with browsers and system dependencies preinstalled, helping you run tests reliably in containers and CI.

        Introduction

        Dockerfile.noble can be used to run Playwright scripts in a Docker environment. The image includes Playwright's browsers and the browsers' system dependencies. The Playwright package/dependency is not in the image and must be installed separately.

        Usage

        The image is published to the Microsoft Artifact Registry.

        Caution: the image is intended for testing and development only; it is not recommended for accessing untrusted websites.

        Pull the image

        docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
        Note: v1.65.0 is only an example version (the original docs use the placeholder %%VERSION%%); use the exact Playwright version of your project.

        Run the image

        By default the image uses the root user to run browsers, which disables the Chromium sandbox (it is not available with root). If you run trusted code (for example E2E tests) and don't want to manage a separate user, root may be acceptable. For web scraping/crawling, it is recommended to create a dedicated user in the container and use a seccomp profile.

        End-to-end tests

        For trusted websites, you can use root because you trust the code running in the browser:

        docker run -it --rm --ipc=host mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble /bin/bash

        Crawling and scraping

        For untrusted websites, you should use a dedicated user to run the browser, combined with a seccomp profile. Inside the container, or when using the image as a base image, you must use adduser to create the user.

        docker run -it --rm --ipc=host --user pwuser --security-opt seccomp=seccomp_profile.json mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble /bin/bash

        seccomp_profile.json is required to run Chromium with the sandbox. It is Docker's default seccomp profile plus permission for user namespace cloning:

        {
  "comment": "Allow create user namespaces",
  "names": [
    "clone",
    "setns",
    "unshare"
  ],
  "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW",
  "args": [],
  "includes": {},
  "excludes": {}
}

        Recommended Docker Configuration

        1. Use the --init flag: avoids special handling of the PID=1 process – a common cause of zombie processes.
        2. Use --ipc=host when running Chromium: otherwise Chromium may run out of memory and crash.
        3. If you hit odd errors when launching Chromium, try running the container with docker run --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN during local development.

        Using on CI

        See the Continuous Integration guides for sample configs.

        Remote Connection

        You can run the Playwright Server in Docker while tests run on the host machine or another machine – useful when using an unsupported Linux distro or running remotely.

        Running the Playwright Server

        docker run -p 3000:3000 --rm --init -it --workdir /home/pwuser --user pwuser mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble /bin/sh -c "npx -y playwright@1.65.0 run-server --port 3000 --host 0.0.0.0"

        Connecting to the Server

        There are two ways to connect to a remote Playwright server:

        1. Use an environment variable with @playwright/test: 
          PW_TEST_CONNECT_WS_ENDPOINT=ws://127.0.0.1:3000/ npx playwright test
        2. Use the BrowserType.connect API for other applications: 
          const browser = await playwright['chromium'].connect('ws://127.0.0.1:3000/');

        Network Configuration

        If you need to access a local server from inside the Docker container:

        docker run --add-host=hostmachine:host-gateway -p 3000:3000 --rm --init -it --workdir /home/pwuser --user pwuser mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble /bin/sh -c "npx -y playwright@1.65.0 run-server --port 3000 --host 0.0.0.0"

        This makes hostmachine point to the host's localhost. Tests should use hostmachine instead of localhost when accessing the local server.

        Caution: when running tests remotely, the Playwright version in your tests must match the version running in the Docker container.

        Connecting using noVNC and GitHub Codespaces

        With Docker and GitHub Codespaces, you can view and generate tests using the noVNC viewer built into the image. To make the VNC web viewer reachable from outside the container, enable the desktop-lite feature and specify webPort in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json:

        {
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble",
  "forwardPorts": [6080],
  "features": {
    "desktop-lite": {
      "webPort": "6080"
    }
  }
}

        Once enabled, open the specified port in a new browser tab to access the noVNC web viewer – it lets you record tests, pick selectors, and use codegen right on the container.

        Image tags

        The tags currently published (where %%VERSION%% is the Playwright version):

        TagDescription
        :v<VERSION>Release image based on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble Numbat)
        :v<VERSION>-nobleUbuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble Numbat)
        :v<VERSION>-jammyUbuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)
        :v<VERSION>-resoluteUbuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon)
        Best practice: always pin the Docker image to a specific version when possible. If the Playwright version in the image doesn't match your project/tests, Playwright will not find the browser executable.

        Base images

        • Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon) – tags containing resolute
        • Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble Numbat) – tags containing noble
        • Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) – tags containing jammy

        Alpine

        The Firefox and WebKit builds are built for the glibc library. Alpine Linux and other musl-based distros are not supported.

        Build your own image

        To run Playwright in Docker you need Node.js, Playwright's browsers, and the browsers' system dependencies. Example Dockerfile:

        FROM node:26-bookworm

RUN npx -y playwright@1.65.0 install --with-deps
        1. Pull imagemcr.microsoft.com/playwright:vX-noble
        2. Install packagesnpm ci (Playwright is not preinstalled in the image)
        3. Run--init --ipc=host (+ pwuser, seccomp for scraping)
        4. Remote (optional)run-server + PW_TEST_CONNECT_WS_ENDPOINT

        Key takeaways

        • The image has browsers + system deps but not the Playwright package; pin a version matching your project.
        • Always use --init and --ipc=host; --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN when debugging Chromium launch errors locally.
        • Root disables the sandbox – only for trusted code; for scraping use pwuser + seccomp_profile.json.
        • Remote: run-server in Docker, connect with PW_TEST_CONNECT_WS_ENDPOINT or browserType.connect; versions must match.
        • Alpine/musl is not supported.

        Which Docker flag is recommended so Chromium does not run out of memory and crash?

        --ipc=host prevents Chromium from running out of shared memory. --init is used to avoid zombie processes caused by PID 1.

        Continuous Integration

        How to run Playwright tests in a CI environment, with sample configurations for GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, CircleCI, Jenkins, Bitbucket, GitLab CI, Google Cloud Build, and Drone; plus notes on workers, global timeout, caching, debugging, and headed mode.

        Introduction

        Playwright tests can run on CI. Playwright provides sample configurations for popular CI providers. There are 3 steps to running tests on CI:

        1. Make sure the CI agent can run browsers: use the Docker image on a Linux agent, or install dependencies with the CLI.
        2. Install Playwright: 
          # Install NPM packages
npm ci

# Install Playwright browsers and dependencies
npx playwright install --with-deps
        3. Run the tests: 
          npx playwright test
        1. Agent can run browsersDocker image or install-deps
        2. Installnpm ci + playwright install --with-deps
        3. Run testsnpx playwright test
        4. Upload reportplaywright-report / JUnit

        Workers

        We recommend setting workers to 1 on CI to prioritize stability and reproducibility. Running sequentially ensures each test has enough system resources and avoids conflicts. However, if your self-hosted CI is powerful, you can enable parallel tests. For broader parallelization, consider sharding – splitting tests across multiple CI jobs.

        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Opt out of parallel tests on CI.
  workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined,
});

        Global timeout

        Always set a global timeout on CI. By default, a test run has no upper limit, so a suite that hangs, or that gradually exceeds the CI provider's job limit, will be killed by the runner midway and no test report will be produced. With globalTimeout, Playwright stops the run on its own.

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  // Fail the run after an hour, so that the reporters still produce a report.
  globalTimeout: 60 * 60 * 1000,
});
        Note: for this reason the examples below do not set a job-level timeout such as GitHub Actions' timeout-minutes. If you add one, keep it comfortably larger than globalTimeout so Playwright always stops first.

        CI configurations

        The Command line tools can be used to install all OS dependencies on CI.

        GitHub Actions

        On push/pull_request

        Tests run on a push or pull request to the main/master branch. The workflow installs dependencies, installs Playwright, and then runs the tests, while also producing an HTML report.

        name: Playwright Tests
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
      with:
        node-version: lts/*
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    - name: Install Playwright Browsers
      run: npx playwright install --with-deps
    - name: Run Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
      with:
        name: playwright-report
        path: playwright-report/
        retention-days: 30
        Tip: if: ${{ !cancelled() }} ensures the report is still uploaded when tests fail (it is only skipped when the job is cancelled).

        On push/pull_request (sharded)

        GitHub Actions supports sharding tests across multiple jobs using a matrix. See the sharding doc for more, and the GitHub Actions example on how to configure jobs to run tests on multiple machines and merge the HTML reports.

        Via Containers

        GitHub Actions supports running jobs in a container via the jobs.<job_id>.container option. This is useful for keeping the host environment clean and having a consistent environment, for example for screenshots/visual regression across different operating systems.

        name: Playwright Tests
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
jobs:
  playwright:
    name: 'Playwright Tests'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
      options: --user 1001
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: lts/*
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run your tests
        run: npx playwright test

        On deployment

        Start tests after a GitHub Deployment moves to the success state. Services such as Vercel use this pattern so you can run E2E tests against the deployed environment.

        name: Playwright Tests
on:
  deployment_status:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success'
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
      with:
        node-version: lts/*
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    - name: Install Playwright
      run: npx playwright install --with-deps
    - name: Run Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test
      env:
        PLAYWRIGHT_TEST_BASE_URL: ${{ github.event.deployment_status.target_url }}

        Fail-Fast

        Large suites can take a very long time to run. By first doing a trial run with the --only-changed flag, you run the test files most likely to fail first, which gives faster feedback and slightly reduces CI cost when working on PRs. --only-changed analyzes the suite's dependency graph to determine which test files are affected by the changeset. This is a heuristic and can miss tests, so always run the entire suite after the trial run.

        name: Playwright Tests
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      with:
        # Force a non-shallow checkout, so that we can reference $GITHUB_BASE_REF.
        # See https://github.com/actions/checkout for more details.
        fetch-depth: 0
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
      with:
        node-version: lts/*
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    - name: Install Playwright Browsers
      run: npx playwright install --with-deps
    - name: Run changed Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test --only-changed=origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF
      if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    - name: Run Playwright tests
      run: npx playwright test
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v5
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
      with:
        name: playwright-report
        path: playwright-report/
        retention-days: 30

        Docker

        Playwright has a prebuilt Docker image that you can use directly or as a reference for updating your existing Docker definition. Follow the Recommended Docker Configuration (--init, --ipc=host...) for the best performance.

        Azure Pipelines

        On Windows or macOS agents no extra configuration is needed; just install Playwright and run the tests. On Linux agents, you can use Playwright's Docker container with Azure Pipelines containerized jobs, or use the Command line tools to install all the necessary dependencies. A pipeline task that runs the tests:

        trigger:
- main

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

steps:
- task: UseNode@1
  inputs:
    version: '22'
  displayName: 'Install Node.js'
- script: npm ci
  displayName: 'npm ci'
- script: npx playwright install --with-deps
  displayName: 'Install Playwright browsers'
- script: npx playwright test
  displayName: 'Run Playwright tests'
  env:
    CI: 'true'

        Uploading playwright-report folder with Azure Pipelines

        The configuration above makes the pipeline fail if any test fails. If you want to integrate test results with Azure DevOps, use the PublishTestResults task:

        trigger:
- main

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

steps:
- task: UseNode@1
  inputs:
    version: '22'
  displayName: 'Install Node.js'

- script: npm ci
  displayName: 'npm ci'
- script: npx playwright install --with-deps
  displayName: 'Install Playwright browsers'
- script: npx playwright test
  displayName: 'Run Playwright tests'
  env:
    CI: 'true'
- task: PublishTestResults@2
  displayName: 'Publish test results'
  inputs:
    searchFolder: 'test-results'
    testResultsFormat: 'JUnit'
    testResultsFiles: 'e2e-junit-results.xml'
    mergeTestResults: true
    failTaskOnFailedTests: true
    testRunTitle: 'My End-To-End Tests'
  condition: succeededOrFailed()
- task: PublishPipelineArtifact@1
  inputs:
    targetPath: playwright-report
    artifact: playwright-report
    publishLocation: 'pipeline'
  condition: succeededOrFailed()

        Note: the JUnit reporter must be configured in playwright.config.ts:

        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [['junit', { outputFile: 'test-results/e2e-junit-results.xml' }]],
});

        Azure Pipelines (sharded)

        Use strategy.matrix to run each project × shard combination as its own job (here 3 browsers × 3 shards = 9 jobs):

        trigger:
- main

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

strategy:
  matrix:
    chromium-1:
      project: chromium
      shard: 1/3
    chromium-2:
      project: chromium
      shard: 2/3

    firefox-1:

    firefox-2:

    firefox-3:
