steps:
- task: UseNode@1
  inputs:
    version: '22'
  displayName: 'Install Node.js'

- script: npm ci
  displayName: 'npm ci'
- script: npx playwright install --with-deps
  displayName: 'Install Playwright browsers'
- script: npx playwright test --project=$(project) --shard=$(shard)
  displayName: 'Run Playwright tests'
  env:
    CI: 'true'

        Azure Pipelines (containerized)

        trigger:
- main

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest
container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble

steps:
- task: UseNode@1
  inputs:
    version: '22'
  displayName: 'Install Node.js'

- script: npm ci
  displayName: 'npm ci'
- script: npx playwright test
  displayName: 'Run Playwright tests'
  env:
    CI: 'true'

        CircleCI

        Running Playwright on CircleCI is very similar to GitHub Actions. To use the prebuilt Docker image, modify the agent definition with docker::

        executors:
  pw-noble-development:
    docker:
      - image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
        Caution: when using a docker agent, you are specifying the resource class as the medium tier. By default Playwright sets the number of workers to the number of detected cores (2 for the medium tier). Overriding the worker count to a value higher than this will cause unnecessary timeouts and failures.

        Sharding in CircleCI

        Sharding in CircleCI is indexed from 0, so you need to override the default parallelism variable. The example below runs Playwright with parallelism 4, adding 1 to CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX to pass it to --shard:

        playwright-job-name:
  executor: pw-noble-development
  parallelism: 4
  steps:
    - run: SHARD="$((${CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX}+1))"; npx playwright test --shard=${SHARD}/${CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL}

        Jenkins

        Jenkins supports Docker agents for pipelines. Use the Playwright Docker image to run tests on Jenkins:

        pipeline {
   agent { docker { image 'mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble' } }
   stages {
      stage('e2e-tests') {
         steps {
            sh 'npm ci'
            sh 'npx playwright test'
         }
      }
   }
}

        Bitbucket Pipelines

        Bitbucket Pipelines can use public Docker images as build environments. To run Playwright tests on Bitbucket, use Playwright's public image:

        image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble

        GitLab CI

        To run Playwright tests on GitLab, use the public Docker image:

        stages:
  - test

tests:
  stage: test
  image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
  script:
  ...

        Sharding (GitLab)

        GitLab CI supports sharding tests across multiple jobs using the parallel keyword. The job is split into several smaller jobs that run in parallel, named sequentially job_name 1/N through job_name N/N.

        stages:
  - test

tests:
  stage: test
  image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
  parallel: 7
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx playwright test --shard=$CI_NODE_INDEX/$CI_NODE_TOTAL

        GitLab CI also supports sharding with parallel:matrix: a job runs multiple times in parallel within a single pipeline with different variable values. The example below has 2 PROJECT values and 10 SHARD values, for a total of 20 jobs:

        stages:
  - test

tests:
  stage: test
  image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - PROJECT: ['chromium', 'webkit']
        SHARD: ['1/10', '2/10', '3/10', '4/10', '5/10', '6/10', '7/10', '8/10', '9/10', '10/10']
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx playwright test --project=$PROJECT --shard=$SHARD

        Google Cloud Build

        To run Playwright tests on Google Cloud Build, use the public Docker image:

        steps:
- name: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
  script:
  ...
  env:
  - 'CI=true'

        Drone

        To run Playwright tests on Drone, use the public Docker image:

        kind: pipeline
name: default
type: docker

steps:
  - name: test
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.0-noble
    commands:
      - npx playwright test
        CIHow to runSharding
        GitHub Actionsubuntu runner or container: with the Playwright imagematrix (see test-sharding)
        Azure Pipelinesscript or container:strategy.matrix + --project=$(project) --shard=$(shard)
        CircleCIexecutor with the Playwright docker imageparallelism + CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX+1
        Jenkinsagent { docker { image ... } }-
        Bitbucketimage: Playwright-
        GitLab CIimage: Playwrightparallel / parallel:matrix
        Google Cloud Buildstep name: Playwright image-
        Droneimage: Playwright-

        Caching browsers

        Caching browser binaries is not recommended, because the time to restore the cache is comparable to the time to download the binaries. On Linux in particular, the OS dependencies must be installed and cannot be cached. If you still want to cache, cache these folders in your CI configuration, keyed by a hash of the Playwright version.

        Debugging browser launches

        Playwright supports the DEBUG environment variable to print debug logs while running. Setting pw:browser is useful when debugging Error: Failed to launch browser errors:

        DEBUG=pw:browser npx playwright test

        Running headed

        By default Playwright runs browsers in headless mode. See the Running tests guide for running headed. On Linux agents, running headed requires Xvfb. Playwright's Docker image and GitHub Action have Xvfb preinstalled. Prefix the command with xvfb-run to run headed browsers with Xvfb:

        xvfb-run npx playwright test

        Key takeaways

        • 3 steps: an agent that can run browsers → npm ci + playwright install --with-deps → npx playwright test.
        • CI: workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined for stability; always set globalTimeout so you still get a report.
        • GitHub Actions: upload playwright-report/ with if: ${{ !cancelled() }}; variants for containers, deployment_status, and --only-changed.
        • Other CIs use the Docker image mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:vX-noble; shard with --shard=i/N using each CI's matrix/parallel feature.
        • Don't cache browsers; debug launches with DEBUG=pw:browser; for headed on Linux use xvfb-run.

        Why should you set globalTimeout on CI?

        Without a limit, a hung suite gets killed midway by CI and there is no report. globalTimeout lets Playwright stop first.

        On CircleCI, why do you need CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX+1 when using --shard?

        Playwright shards are of the form 1/N through N/N, while CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX starts from 0.

        Selenium Grid (experimental)

        Connect Playwright to a Selenium Grid Hub (Selenium 4) to run Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge remotely instead of locally – an experimental feature.

        Introduction

        Playwright can connect to a Selenium Grid Hub running Selenium 4 to launch Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge browsers, instead of running the browser locally. This feature is experimental and is prioritized accordingly.

        Warning: there is a risk that Playwright's integration with Selenium Grid Hub will break in the future; weigh the risks and benefits before using it.
        Details

        Under the hood, Playwright connects to the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol websocket. Selenium 4 currently supports this capability, but it may be dropped in the future. If Selenium removes this capability, Playwright will stop working with it.

        Before connecting Playwright to Selenium Grid, make sure the grid works with Selenium WebDriver: for example, run an example and pass the SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL variable. If the webdriver example doesn't work, check the errors in the hub/node/standalone output and search the Selenium issues.

        Starting Selenium Grid

        If you run a distributed Selenium Grid, Playwright needs the selenium nodes to be registered with an accessible address so it can connect to the browsers. Set the SE_NODE_GRID_URL variable pointing to the hub when starting the selenium nodes:

        # Start selenium node
SE_NODE_GRID_URL="http://<selenium-hub-ip>:4444" java -jar selenium-server-<version>.jar node

        Connecting Playwright to Selenium Grid

        To connect Playwright to Selenium Grid 4, set the SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL variable pointing to the Hub. It only works with Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge.

        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://<selenium-hub-ip>:4444 npx playwright test

        No code changes are needed; just use the test harness or BrowserType.launch as usual.

        Passing additional capabilities

        If the grid requires additional capabilities (for example when using an external service), set SELENIUM_REMOTE_CAPABILITIES to JSON-serialized capabilities:

        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://<selenium-hub-ip>:4444 SELENIUM_REMOTE_CAPABILITIES="{'mygrid:options':{os:'windows',username:'John',password:'secure'}}" npx playwright test

        Passing additional headers

        If the grid requires additional headers (for example an authorization token), set SELENIUM_REMOTE_HEADERS to JSON-serialized headers:

        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://<selenium-hub-ip>:4444 SELENIUM_REMOTE_HEADERS="{'Authorization':'Basic b64enc'}" npx playwright test

        Detailed logs

        Run with DEBUG=pw:browser* to see how Playwright connects to Selenium Grid. If you file an issue, attach this log.

        DEBUG=pw:browser* SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://internal.grid:4444 npx playwright test

        Using Selenium Docker

        An easy way to use Selenium Grid is to run the official Docker containers (see the selenium docker images; for the tag conventions see the tagging convention).

        Standalone mode

        An example of running selenium standalone and connecting Playwright. The hub and node are on the same localhost, and you pass SE_NODE_GRID_URL pointing to it. First start Selenium:

        docker run -d -p 4444:4444 --shm-size="2g" -e SE_NODE_GRID_URL="http://localhost:4444" selenium/standalone-chromium:latest

        Then run Playwright:

        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://localhost:4444 npx playwright test

        Hub and nodes mode

        An example of running a selenium hub and one node, connecting Playwright to the hub. The hub and node have different IPs, and you pass SE_NODE_GRID_URL pointing to the hub when starting the node container. First start the hub and one or more node containers:

        docker run -d -p 4442-4444:4442-4444 --name selenium-hub selenium/hub:4.25.0
docker run -d -p 5555:5555 \
    --shm-size="2g" \
    -e SE_EVENT_BUS_HOST=<selenium-hub-ip> \
    -e SE_EVENT_BUS_PUBLISH_PORT=4442 \
    -e SE_EVENT_BUS_SUBSCRIBE_PORT=4443 \
    -e SE_NODE_GRID_URL="http://<selenium-hub-ip>:4444"
    selenium/node-chromium:4.25.0

        Then run Playwright:

        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://<selenium-hub-ip>:4444 npx playwright test

        Selenium 3

        Playwright connects to the browser over the CDP websocket. Selenium 4 exposes this capability; Selenium 3 does not. Therefore Selenium 3 is supported on a best-effort basis: Playwright tries to connect directly to the grid node, so the grid nodes must be directly reachable from the machine running Playwright.

        Environment variableRole
        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URLURL of the Selenium Grid Hub (enables the integration)
        SELENIUM_REMOTE_CAPABILITIESAdditional capabilities as JSON
        SELENIUM_REMOTE_HEADERSAdditional headers as JSON (e.g. Authorization)
        SE_NODE_GRID_URLSet when starting a node: the hub address that Playwright can reach
        DEBUG=pw:browser*Detailed connection logs

        Key takeaways

        • Experimental; only Chrome/Edge through Selenium Grid 4 (relies on the CDP websocket).
        • Run: SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL=http://hub:4444 npx playwright test – no code changes needed.
        • Add SELENIUM_REMOTE_CAPABILITIES/SELENIUM_REMOTE_HEADERS for cloud grids; debug with DEBUG=pw:browser*.
        • Distributed grid: set SE_NODE_GRID_URL when starting nodes. Selenium 3: best-effort, nodes must be directly reachable.

        Which environment variable enables Playwright's connection to Selenium Grid?

        SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL points to the hub. SE_NODE_GRID_URL is set when starting a Selenium node; variable C is for the Playwright Server.

        Library

        Playwright Library (playwright) provides a unified API for launching and controlling browsers; Playwright Test (@playwright/test) adds a full test runner on top. This page compares the two approaches and shows how to use the Library.

        Introduction

        Playwright Library provides a unified API for launching and interacting with browsers, while Playwright Test provides all of that plus a fully managed Test Runner. For most E2E testing, you should use @playwright/test rather than using playwright directly. To get started with Playwright Test, see Getting Started.

        Differences when using library

        Library Example

        An example that uses the Library directly to open Chromium, navigate to a page, and check the title:

        import { chromium, devices } from 'playwright';
import assert from 'node:assert';

(async () => {
  // Setup
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext(devices['iPhone 11']);
  const page = await context.newPage();

  // The actual interesting bit
  await context.route('**.jpg', route => route.abort());
  await page.goto('https://example.com/');

  assert(await page.title() === 'Example Domain'); // 👎 not a Web First assertion

  // Teardown
  await context.close();
  await browser.close();
})();
        CommonJS version (JavaScript) 
        const assert = require('node:assert');
const { chromium, devices } = require('playwright');

(async () => {
  // Setup
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext(devices['iPhone 11']);
  const page = await context.newPage();

  // The actual interesting bit
  await context.route('**.jpg', route => route.abort());
  await page.goto('https://example.com/');

  assert(await page.title() === 'Example Domain'); // 👎 not a Web First assertion

  // Teardown
  await context.close();
  await browser.close();
})();

        Run it with node my-script.js.

        Test Example

        A test that achieves the same behavior:

        import { expect, test, devices } from '@playwright/test';

test.use(devices['iPhone 11']);

test('should be titled', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await context.route('**.jpg', route => route.abort());
  await page.goto('https://example.com/');

  await expect(page).toHaveTitle('Example');
});

        Run it with npx playwright test.

        Key Differences

        LibraryTest
        Installationnpm install playwrightnpm init playwright@latest (note install vs init)
        Install browsersInstall @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox and/or @playwright/browser-webkitnpx playwright install, or npx playwright install chromium for a single browser
        import fromplaywright@playwright/test
        InitializationYou must do it yourself: (1) pick a browser, e.g. chromium; (2) call BrowserType.launch; (3) create a context with Browser.newContext and pass context options explicitly, e.g. devices['iPhone 11']; (4) create a page with BrowserContext.newPageEach test is given an isolated page and context along with other built-in fixtures; you don't create them explicitly. If a test references them in its parameters, the Test Runner creates them (lazy initialization)
        AssertionsNo built-in Web-First AssertionsWeb-First assertions such as toHaveTitle, toHaveScreenshot – they wait and retry automatically
        TimeoutsDefault 30s for most operationsMost operations have no individual timeout, but each test has a timeout that makes it fail (default 30s)
        CleanupYou must do it yourself: close the context (BrowserContext.close) and the browser (Browser.close)Built-in fixtures are not closed explicitly; the Test Runner handles it
        RunningRun the code as a node script, possibly compiling it firstUse the npx playwright test command; with the same config, the Test Runner handles compilation and decides what to run and how

        In addition, Playwright Test is a full-featured Test Runner that also includes:

        • Configuration Matrix and Projects: in the Library example, running with a different device/browser means editing the script; with Playwright Test you just declare the configuration matrix in one place and the runner runs the tests under each configuration.
        • Parallelization
        • Web-First Assertions
        • Reporting
        • Retries
        • Easily Enabled Tracing
        • and much more…

        Usage

        Use npm or Yarn to install the Playwright library into a Node.js project (see system requirements).

        npm i -D playwright

        You also need to install browsers – either manually or by adding helper packages that install them for you:

        # Download the Chromium, Firefox and WebKit browser
npx playwright install chromium firefox webkit

# Alternatively, add packages that will download a browser upon npm install
npm i -D @playwright/browser-chromium @playwright/browser-firefox @playwright/browser-webkit

        See managing browsers for more options. Once installed, import Playwright in a Node.js script and launch one of the 3 browsers (chromium, firefox, webkit).

        const { chromium } = require('playwright');

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  // Create pages, interact with UI elements, assert values
  await browser.close();
})();

        The Playwright API is asynchronous and returns Promises. The examples use the async/await pattern for readability; the code is wrapped in a self-invoking anonymous async arrow function:

        (async () => { // Start of async arrow function
  // Function code
  // ...
})(); // End of the function and () to invoke itself

        First script

        The first script: go to https://playwright.dev/ and take a screenshot in WebKit.

        const { webkit } = require('playwright');

(async () => {
  const browser = await webkit.launch();
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
  await page.screenshot({ path: `example.png` });
  await browser.close();
})();

        By default Playwright runs browsers in headless mode. To see the UI, pass headless: false when launching; use slowMo to slow down execution (see debugging tools).

        firefox.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 50 });

        Record scripts

        Command line tools can record user interactions and generate JavaScript code:

        npx playwright codegen wikipedia.org

        Browser downloads

        Download the Playwright browsers:

        # Explicitly download browsers
npx playwright install

        Or add the @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox, @playwright/browser-webkit packages to download the corresponding browser automatically when the package is installed:

        # Use a helper package that downloads a browser on npm install
npm install @playwright/browser-chromium

        Download behind a firewall or a proxy

        Pass the HTTPS_PROXY variable to download through a proxy.

        # Manual
HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1 npx playwright install

# Through @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1 npm install
        # Manual
set HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1
npx playwright install

# Through @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
set HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1
npm install
        # Manual
$Env:HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1
npx playwright install

# Through @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
$Env:HTTPS_PROXY=https://192.0.2.1
npm install

        Download from artifact repository

        By default Playwright downloads browsers from Microsoft's CDN. Pass PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST to download from an internal artifact repository.

        # Manual
PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=192.0.2.1 npx playwright install

# Through @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=192.0.2.1 npm install
        # Manual
set PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=192.0.2.1
npx playwright install

# Through @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
set PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=192.0.2.1
npm install
        # Manual
$Env:PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=192.0.2.1
npx playwright install

# Through @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
$Env:PLAYWRIGHT_DOWNLOAD_HOST=192.0.2.1
npm install

        Skip browser download

        In some cases you want to avoid downloading browsers entirely because the binaries are managed separately. Set the PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD variable before installing the packages.

        # When using @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1 npm install
        # When using @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
set PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1
npm install
        # When using @playwright/browser-chromium, @playwright/browser-firefox
# and @playwright/browser-webkit helper packages
$Env:PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1
npm install

        TypeScript support

        Playwright has built-in TypeScript support; type definitions are imported automatically. Type-checking is recommended for a better IDE experience.

        In JavaScript

        Add the following line at the top of your JavaScript file to get type-checking in VS Code or WebStorm:

        // @ts-check
// ...

        Or use JSDoc to set the type of a variable:

        /** @type {import('playwright').Page} */
let page;

        In TypeScript

        TypeScript support works out of the box. Types can also be imported explicitly:

        let page: import('playwright').Page;

        Key takeaways

        • playwright (Library) = only the browser-control API; @playwright/test = Library + runner, fixtures, web-first assertions, parallelism, retries, reporters, tracing.
        • Library: you must launch/newContext/newPage yourself and close the context + browser; there are no web-first assertions.
        • Test: page/context are provided and cleaned up automatically; run with npx playwright test.
        • Browsers for the Library: npx playwright install or the @playwright/browser-* packages; PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1 to skip downloading.
        • For E2E testing, prefer Playwright Test.

        Which difference between Library and Test is correct?

        Library has no runner or web-first assertions; you do every setup/cleanup step yourself. Playwright Test handles it all through fixtures.

        Supported languages

        Playwright is available for multiple languages, all sharing the same core implementation. Browser automation features are identical across languages; the main difference is the accompanying test runner ecosystem.

        Overview

        The core features (browser control, locators, network, auto-waiting...) work in every language. What differs is the test ecosystem integration (runner, assertions, reporters, parallelism). Choose a language based on your team's experience, familiarity with that language's test ecosystem, and your project's constraints.

        Quick comparison table

        LanguageRecommended test runnerHighlights
        JavaScript / TypeScript@playwright/test (Playwright's own runner)Built-in parallelization, screenshot assertions, HTML reporter, automatic tracing
        Pythonpytest-playwright pluginPer-test context isolation, running with multiple browser configurations
        JavaAny: JUnit, TestNG...Pick the framework that fits your project requirements
        .NETBase classes for MSTest, NUnit, xUnit, xUnit v3Inherit from PageTest to get Page and Expect out of the box

        JavaScript and TypeScript

        Playwright for Node.js ships with its own test runner: parallel execution, screenshot comparison, HTML reporter, automatic traces. This is the most fully featured language and is the scope of most of this documentation.

        Python

        The recommended way to run E2E tests is the Pytest plugin. The plugin provides the page fixture, isolates contexts, and lets you run across multiple browsers via command-line options.

        Java

        You can use any framework such as JUnit or TestNG; you manage the lifecycle of Playwright / Browser / BrowserContext yourself.

        .NET

        Playwright for .NET provides ready-made base classes for MSTest, NUnit, xUnit and xUnit v3. See the installation comparison at Playwright for Python/Java/.NET.

        Note Some features are only available in the Node.js runner (for example UI Mode, component testing, built-in sharding, the full VS Code extension). If you need the entire ecosystem, choose TypeScript.

        Key takeaways

        • 4 language groups: JS/TS, Python, Java, .NET – all on the same core.
        • The difference is in the test runner: Node has its own runner, Python uses pytest, Java uses JUnit/TestNG, .NET uses MSTest/NUnit/xUnit.

        Which language has a test runner provided by Playwright itself (parallelization, HTML reporter, automatic tracing)?

        Only the Node.js version has @playwright/test. The other languages rely on their own ecosystem's test frameworks (pytest, JUnit, NUnit...).

        Playwright for Python / Java / .NET (installation comparison and minimal examples)

        Each language has its own installation method and test runner, but the API is nearly parallel (goto, get_by_role/getByRole/GetByRole...). This section collects the install commands, minimal test examples and system requirements for each language.

        Comparison table

        PythonJava.NET
        Install packagepytest-playwrightcom.microsoft.playwright:playwright (Maven)Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit (or MSTest/xUnit)
        Install browsersplaywright installDownloaded automatically on the first run of the example (see Browsers)pwsh bin/Debug/net8.0/playwright.ps1 install
        Run testspytestmvn compile exec:java ... / JUnitdotnet test
        Test runnerpytestJUnit, TestNG...MSTest, NUnit, xUnit, xUnit v3
        Minimum versionPython 3.8+Java 8+.NET Standard 2.0 (.NET 8 recommended)

        Python

        Install the Pytest plugin with a package manager, then install the browsers.

        pip install pytest-playwright
playwright install
        poetry add pytest-playwright
playwright install
        uv add pytest-playwright
playwright install

        Create a test_example.py file (both the file name and the function names must start with test_):

        import re
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_has_title(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://playwright.dev/")
    # Expect a title "to contain" a substring.
    expect(page).to_have_title(re.compile("Playwright"))

def test_get_started_link(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://playwright.dev/")
    # Click the get started link.
    page.get_by_role("link", name="Get started").click()
    # Expects page to have a heading with the name of Installation.
    expect(page.get_by_role("heading", name="Installation")).to_be_visible()
        pytest
# Default: Chromium, headless. Change browser/options via the pytest-playwright CLI.

# Update Playwright
pip install pytest-playwright playwright -U

        Besides pytest, the library can also be used as a general automation tool with both the sync and async APIs.

        Java

        Add the dependency to pom.xml (the page uses version 1.64.0):

        <dependency>
  <groupId>com.microsoft.playwright</groupId>
  <artifactId>playwright</artifactId>
  <version>1.64.0</version>
</dependency>

        A minimal program (prints the page title):

        package org.example;

import com.microsoft.playwright.*;

public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Playwright playwright = Playwright.create()) {
            Browser browser = playwright.chromium().launch();
            Page page = browser.newPage();
            page.navigate("https://playwright.dev");
            System.out.println(page.title());
        }
    }
}
        mvn compile exec:java -D exec.mainClass="org.example.App"

        The first run downloads the Playwright package and installs the Chromium, Firefox and WebKit binaries. By default the browser runs headless; to see the UI or slow down actions:

        playwright.firefox().launch(new BrowserType.LaunchOptions().setHeadless(false).setSlowMo(50));

        When writing tests with JUnit/TestNG, create Playwright and Browser once per class (@BeforeAll/@AfterAll), and create a fresh BrowserContext and Page for each test (@BeforeEach/@AfterEach) to isolate state. When running in parallel, use one Playwright per thread. With Gradle, the test task uses useJUnitPlatform().

        import com.microsoft.playwright.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;

class ExampleTest {
    static Playwright playwright;
    static Browser browser;
    BrowserContext context;
    Page page;

    @BeforeAll static void launchBrowser() {
        playwright = Playwright.create();
        browser = playwright.chromium().launch();
    }
    @AfterAll static void closeBrowser() { playwright.close(); }

    @BeforeEach void createContextAndPage() {
        context = browser.newContext();
        page = context.newPage();
    }
    @AfterEach void closeContext() { context.close(); }

    @Test void hasTitle() {
        page.navigate("https://playwright.dev");
        Assertions.assertTrue(page.title().contains("Playwright"));
    }
}

        .NET

        dotnet new nunit -n PlaywrightTests
cd PlaywrightTests
dotnet add package Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit
dotnet build
# replace net8.0 with your .NET version; requires PowerShell (pwsh)
pwsh bin/Debug/net8.0/playwright.ps1 install

        Replace UnitTest1.cs with a class that inherits from PageTest (NUnit):

        using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Microsoft.Playwright;
using Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit;
using NUnit.Framework;

namespace PlaywrightTests;

[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Self)]
[TestFixture]
public class ExampleTest : PageTest
{
    [Test]
    public async Task HasTitle()
    {
        await Page.GotoAsync("https://playwright.dev");

        // Expect a title "to contain" a substring.
        await Expect(Page).ToHaveTitleAsync(new Regex("Playwright"));
    }

    [Test]
    public async Task GetStartedLink()
    {
        await Page.GotoAsync("https://playwright.dev");

        // Click the get started link.
        await Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Link, new() { Name = "Get started" }).ClickAsync();

        // Expects page to have a heading with the name of Installation.
        await Expect(Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Heading, new() { Name = "Installation" })).ToBeVisibleAsync();
    }
}
        MSTest version 
        using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using Microsoft.Playwright;
using Microsoft.Playwright.MSTest;

namespace PlaywrightTests;

[TestClass]
public class ExampleTest : PageTest
{
    [TestMethod]
    public async Task HasTitle()
    {
        await Page.GotoAsync("https://playwright.dev");
        await Expect(Page).ToHaveTitleAsync(new Regex("Playwright"));
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public async Task GetStartedLink()
    {
        await Page.GotoAsync("https://playwright.dev");
        await Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Link, new() { Name = "Get started" }).ClickAsync();
        await Expect(Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Heading, new() { Name = "Installation" })).ToBeVisibleAsync();
    }
}
        dotnet test
# By default runs Chromium headless. Change the browser with the BROWSER environment variable
BROWSER=firefox dotnet test

        Side-by-side mapping of the same action

        ActionTypeScriptPythonJava.NET
        Navigationpage.goto(url)page.goto(url)page.navigate(url)Page.GotoAsync(url)
        Locator by rolegetByRole('link', {name})get_by_role("link", name=...)getByRole(AriaRole.LINK, ...)GetByRole(AriaRole.Link, new() {...})
        Assertionawait expect(loc).toBeVisible()expect(loc).to_be_visible()assertThat(loc).isVisible()await Expect(loc).ToBeVisibleAsync()
        Heads up Naming conventions differ: Python uses snake_case, .NET uses the Async suffix and PascalCase, and Java names options through Options classes (setters). Each language's API documentation is the authoritative source.

        Common system requirements

        • Windows 11+, Windows Server 2019+ or WSL.
        • macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later.
        • Debian 12/13 or Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04 (x86-64 or arm64).

        Key takeaways

        • Python: pip install pytest-playwright + playwright install, run with pytest.
        • Java: add the Maven dependency; browsers are downloaded automatically on the first run.
        • .NET: dotnet add package Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit, build, then run playwright.ps1 install; tests inherit from PageTest.
        • All three run Chromium headless by default.

        In .NET, why must you run dotnet build before installing the browsers?

        The playwright.ps1 script is generated in bin/Debug/netX.0/ after the build; then you run pwsh ... playwright.ps1 install.

        With Java + JUnit, which objects should be created fresh for each test to isolate state?

        Playwright and Browser are created once per class; BrowserContext/Page are created one per test.

        Release notes (latest versions)

        A summary of versions 1.65 through 1.60 plus the highlights of 1.59/1.58. This is a digest of the main features, not a copy of every older release; always check the original page when upgrading.

        Timeline

        1.58Timeline report, UI theme
        1.59Screencast, browser.bind
        1.60HAR tracing, locator.drop
        1.61WebAuthn passkeys
        1.62retryStrategy, WebP
        1.63Test locks
        1.64WebMCP, shuffle, within
        1.65Bun, failures reporter

        Version 1.65

        • Bun: run tests with Bun using bunx --bun playwright test (without --bun the runner uses Node.js). Limitations: no watch mode, --tsconfig and JSX options are ignored, stack traces lack async frames, test console output is not written to the trace.
        • Failure-focused reporters: the failures reporter prints failures and successful retries as soon as they happen; the HTML/JSON/JUnit reporters have an onlyFailures option (keeps only unexpected, flaky and interrupted tests).
        • Test runner: special -exclusive- lock; test.skip()/fixme()/fail()/slow() accept just a description (stored as an annotation); the PLAYWRIGHT_TRANSFORM_CACHE_DIR variable.
        • New APIs: timeout and signal for cdpSession.send(); testRun.mode() for reporters.
        • Announcements: Node.js 20 is no longer supported; the Docker image uses Node.js 26. Chromium 158.0.8127.18, Firefox 159.0, WebKit 27.2.
        import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    ['failures'],
    ['html', { onlyFailures: true }],
  ],
});
        test('restart the server', { lock: '-exclusive-' }, async () => {
  // No other test runs while this one is running.
});

test('upload a file', async ({ page }) => {
  test.skip('Not implemented yet');
});
        Breaking changes 1.65
        • Class fields follow useDefineForClassFields: a field initializer that reads a constructor parameter property will fail.
        • Actions wait for the element to leave the inert state and time out if it doesn't.
        • Running a shard where no shard has a matching test fails, unless --pass-with-no-tests is used.
        • Cookie matching follows RFC 6265; proxy credentials only answer proxy challenges.
        • Text that the browser does not render is excluded from the accessible name and the aria snapshot.
        • params of APIRequestContext are appended to the existing query string.
        • CSS/LESS/SCSS imports become empty modules (the file must still exist); the blob reporter clears the output directory before writing.

        Version 1.64

        • WebMCP: page.webmcp / frame.webmcp expose the tools a page registers through the WebMCP API (experimental); Playwright MCP supports it by default, and playwright-cli gains webmcp-list and webmcp-call.
        • Video: fps and style options (CSS for click points, highlights, titles; replaces the deprecated fontSize); video uses VP9.
        • Runner: testProject.default, --shuffle, lock in test.describe.configure(), type for toHaveScreenshot (WebP).
        • Locator: locator.within(), page.getByRef() (find by an aria ref such as e2 taken from page.ariaSnapshot() in 'ai' mode), includeShadow for content().
        • Other: signCount for virtual credentials, fullConfig.filteredProjects, cookie methods on apiRequestContext.
        • Browsers: Chromium 156.0.8078.4, Firefox 157.0, WebKit 27.2.
        import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    { name: 'firefox', use: devices['Desktop Firefox'], default: false },
    { name: 'webkit', use: devices['Desktop Safari'], default: false },
  ],
});
        npx playwright test                     # runs chromium only
npx playwright test --project=firefox   # runs firefox
npx playwright test --project="*"       # runs all three, e.g. on CI

npx playwright test --shuffle           # shuffle the test order
npx playwright test --shuffle 271828182 # reproduce a previous order
        test.describe.configure({ lock: 'user-settings' });

const saveButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' });
const dialog = page.getByTestId('settings-dialog');
await saveButton.within(dialog).click();
        import { chromium } from 'playwright';

const browser = await chromium.launch({ args: ['--enable-features=WebMCP'] });
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto('https://example.com');

for (const tool of await page.webmcp.tools())
  console.log(tool.name, tool.description);

const result = await page.webmcp.callTool('add', { a: 2, b: 40 });
console.log(result.content[0].text); // "42"
        Breaking changes 1.64 The screen property is forwarded from the device descriptor (set it to undefined to drop it); JSX follows tsconfig.json; --update-snapshots=missing now lets the run pass (by default it still writes missing snapshots and fails); elements inside a hidden iframe count as hidden.

        Version 1.63

        • Test locks: tests sharing a named lock never run concurrently (across files, workers, projects); a test can hold multiple locks, and test.describe() accepts a lock for the whole group.
        • Cross-frame: frameLocator() without a selector searches every frame in the tree; locator.visible() replaces the :visible pseudo-class.
        • Step & trace: test.step() accepts subtitle and params; the trace snapshots option accepts an object (DOM, aria, screen); the trace viewer has a "Display Aria" mode.
        • New APIs: httpCredentials as an array, opfs storage state, the dialogclosed event, ariaSnapshotJSON(), typed get<T>(), reducedMotion/forcedColors/contrast, --add-reporter, omitTags, codegen --http-credentials, the perfetto reporter, a duration waterfall in the HTML report.
        • Announcements: the experimental ct-react, ct-react17, ct-vue packages are no longer updated; Ubuntu 20.04 is no longer supported; Linux arm64 uses Chrome for Testing. Chromium 153, Firefox 155, WebKit 26.6.

        Version 1.62

        • Component testing: components are organized into stories in a gallery; the mount fixture navigates to the story by id and returns a locator for the root (see Migrating from Testing Library).
        • Cancelling operations: actions, navigations, waits and assertions accept an AbortSignal via signal (the default timeout still applies unless timeout: 0).
        • WebP: names ending in .webp save snapshots as WebP; screenshot() accepts the webp type with a quality.
        • Reporter: reporter.preprocess() runs before onBegin() and can skip/exclude/fix/fail tests through the TestRun object.
        • Retries: retryStrategy: 'isolated' runs all retries at the end in a single worker (default is 'immediate').
        • Other: credentials in storage state, the scroll option, apiResponse.timing(), locator.waitForFunction(), npx playwright mcp and npx playwright cli, mergeFiles for the HTML reporter. The clipboard is decoupled from the OS in headless mode; Debian 11 support is dropped. Chromium 151, Firefox 153, WebKit 26.5.
        export default defineConfig({
  retries: 2,
  retryStrategy: 'isolated',
});

        Version 1.61

        • WebAuthn passkeys: browserContext.credentials is a virtual authenticator that answers navigator.credentials create/get without a hardware key.
        • Web storage: page.localStorage and page.sessionStorage read/write the storage of the current origin.
        • Other: apiResponse.securityDetails()/serverAddr(), artifactsDir for connectOverCDP(), the 'on-all-retries' video mode, expect.soft.poll(...), failOnFlakyTests, the -G shorthand for --grep-invert; Ubuntu 26.04 support; HAR/trace also record WebSocket traffic. No breaking changes. Chromium 149, Firefox 151, WebKit 26.5.
        const context = await browser.newContext();

await context.credentials.create('example.com', {
  id: credentialId,
  userHandle,
  privateKey,
  publicKey,
});
await context.credentials.install();

const page = await context.newPage();
await page.goto('https://example.com/login');

        Version 1.60

        • HAR on tracing: tracing.startHar() / stopHar(), with the same options as recordHar.
        • Drop API: locator.drop() simulates dragging and dropping files or data onto an element (cross-browser upload tests).
        • Aria snapshot: assertions work on the whole page; the boxes option adds bounding boxes.
        • test.abort(): aborts the current test from a fixture, hook or route handler, with an optional message.
        • New APIs: browser.on('context'), the description option for getByRole(), pseudo for toHaveCSS(), page.hideHighlight(), webSocketRoute.protocols(), webError.location(), errorContext, the {testFileBaseName} token for snapshot paths.
        • Breaking: removed Locator.ariaRef(), the handle option of exposeBinding, the logger option of the connect methods, and the videosPath/videoSize context options. Chromium 148, Firefox 150.0.2, WebKit 26.4.

        Versions 1.59 and 1.58 (highlights)

        • 1.59: page.screencast (recording, action annotations, chapter titles, overlays, real-time frame capture); browser.bind() lets playwright-cli and Playwright MCP connect to an already running browser; --debug=cli; npx playwright trace explores traces from the command line; await using with async disposables.
        • 1.58: the HTML report's Speedboard tab gains a Timeline for merged reports; UI Mode and Trace Viewer get a system theme, search in the code editor, and formatted JSON responses; removed the _react/_vue selectors and the devtools launch option.
        When upgrading Read the breaking changes section first, re-run npx playwright install to get the correct browser versions, and try a canary release first if you need an unreleased feature.

        Key takeaways

        • Recent trends: test locks, shuffle, retryStrategy, failures-only reporters, WebMCP/MCP/CLI for agents, WebAuthn, WebP, locator.within().
        • 1.65 drops Node.js 20 and adds support for running with Bun.
        • Always read the Breaking changes section (e.g. 1.60 removed Locator.ariaRef(), 1.65 changed cookie matching).

        What do you use so that tests touching the same shared resource never run concurrently (even across different workers)?

        Test locks (1.63) guarantee that tests sharing a lock do not run at the same time across files, workers and projects; --shuffle only changes the order.

        Which version added retryStrategy: 'isolated'?

        1.62 added retryStrategy: 'isolated' runs all retries at the end in a single worker, and the default is 'immediate'.

        Migrating from Puppeteer

        A guide to moving from Puppeteer to Playwright Library or Playwright Test. Most Puppeteer APIs carry over almost unchanged, but Playwright encourages Locators and web-first assertions instead of ElementHandle and manual waiting.

        Migration principles

        • Most Puppeteer APIs can be reused with few changes.
        • Avoid ElementHandle; use Locator and web-first assertions.
        • Playwright is cross-browser (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit); Puppeteer is not.
        • You usually don't need explicit waits thanks to auto-waiting.

        Puppeteer → Playwright cheat sheet

        PuppeteerPlaywright
        puppeteer.launch()playwright.chromium.launch() (Firefox and WebKit through their own launchers; Puppeteer has no WebKit)
        Incognito contextbrowser.newContext()
        Set the viewportpage.setViewportSize()
        Wait for XPathpage.waitForSelector() (selectors support XPath)
        Wait for networkidle2page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')
        page.$eval()Use assertions instead
        page.$(), page.$x()Discouraged; use Locator
        Checkbox/radiolocator.check(), locator.uncheck() (no direct equivalent)
        Click, focus, hover, select, tapThe corresponding Locator methods
        page.type()locator.fill()
        File uploadlocator.setInputFiles()
        Cookiescookies, clearCookies, addCookies on the browser context
        Intercept requestspage.route()
        Strict mode Locators are strict: an action throws an error if the selector matches more than one element.

        Examples

        Automation example

        ❌ Puppeteer
        const puppeteer = require('puppeteer');

(async () => {
  const browser = await puppeteer.launch();
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.setViewport({ width: 1280, height: 800 });
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle2' });
  await page.screenshot({ path: 'example.png' });
  await browser.close();
})();
        ✅ Playwright
        const { chromium } = require('playwright');

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.setViewportSize({ width: 1280, height: 800 });
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
  await page.screenshot({ path: 'example.png' });
  await browser.close();
})();

        Prefer using a browser context to isolate state.

        Test example

        ❌ Jest + Puppeteer
        it('should work', async () => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
  const title = await page.$eval('.hero__title', (el) => el.textContent);
  expect(title).toContain('Playwright');
});

        $eval reads the text once, with no auto-waiting/retry.

        ✅ Playwright Test
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('should work', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://playwright.dev/');
  await expect(page.locator('.hero__title')).toContainText('Playwright');
});

        Locator + web-first assertion wait and retry automatically.

        Testing

        Use Locators and web-first assertions instead of page.evaluate()/page.$eval() to check elements. Playwright Test is the recommended runner: it supports the Page Object Model, parallel execution, fixtures and reporters (see Fixtures, POM).

        Playwright Test "super powers"

        • Zero-config TypeScript support.
        • Test on Chrome, Firefox, Safari on Windows, macOS, Ubuntu.
        • Multiple origins, frames, tabs, contexts.
        • Parallel, isolated execution.
        • Automatically collected artifacts (screenshots, video, trace).
        • Bundled tools: Inspector, codegen, Tracing.

        Key takeaways

        • page.type() becomes locator.fill(); networkidle2 becomes 'networkidle'; page.$eval becomes an assertion.
        • Avoid ElementHandle; use Locator (strict, auto-wait, retry).
        • A new context replaces incognito; page.route() replaces request interception.

        What is the Playwright equivalent of Puppeteer's page.type(selector, text)?

        Per the cheat sheet: typing text into an input maps to locator.fill().

        Migrating from Protractor

        Protractor is no longer maintained. This page explains how to move Angular/AngularJS tests to Playwright Test: ElementFinder becomes Locator, and waitForAngular becomes auto-waiting.

        Principles

        • No need for webdriver-manager / Selenium.
        • Protractor's ElementFinder corresponds to Playwright Test's Locator.
        • waitForAngular is replaced by auto-waiting.
        • Remember to await almost every Playwright call.

        Cheat sheet

        ProtractorPlaywright Test
        element(by.buttonText('...'))page.locator('button, input[type="button"], input[type="submit"] >> text="..."')
        element(by.css('...'))page.locator('...')
        element(by.cssContainingText('..1..', '..2..'))page.locator('..1.. >> text=..2..')
        element(by.id('...'))page.locator('#...')
        element(by.model('...'))page.locator('[ng-model="..."]')
        element(by.repeater('...'))page.locator('[ng-repeat="..."]')
        element(by.xpath('...'))page.locator('xpath=...')
        element.allpage.locator
        browser.get(url)await page.goto(url)
        browser.getCurrentUrl()page.url()

        Example (AngularJS todo list)

        ❌ Protractor
        describe('angularjs homepage todo list', function() {
  it('should add a todo', function() {
    browser.get('https://angularjs.org');

    element(by.model('todoList.todoText')).sendKeys('first test');
    element(by.css('[value="add"]')).click();

    const todoList = element.all(by.repeater('todo in todoList.todos'));
    expect(todoList.count()).toEqual(3);
    expect(todoList.get(2).getText()).toEqual('first test');

    // You wrote your first test, cross it off the list
    todoList.get(2).element(by.css('input')).click();
    const completedAmount = element.all(by.css('.done-true'));
    expect(completedAmount.count()).toEqual(2);
  });
});
        ✅ Playwright Test
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('should add a todo', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://angularjs.org');

  await page.locator('[ng-model="todoList.todoText"]').fill('first test');
  await page.locator('[value="add"]').click();

  const todoList = page.locator('[ng-repeat="todo in todoList.todos"]');
  await expect(todoList).toHaveCount(3);
  await expect(todoList.nth(2)).toHaveText('first test');

  // You wrote your first test, cross it off the list
  await todoList.nth(2).getByRole('checkbox').click();
  const completedAmount = page.locator('.done-true');
  await expect(completedAmount).toHaveCount(2);
});

        Key differences:

        1. Each test file must explicitly import test and expect.
        2. The test function is async.
        3. The test receives the page fixture.
        4. Almost every Playwright call must be awaited.
        5. page.locator() is one of the few synchronous methods.

        The waitForAngular polyfill

        Auto-waiting usually makes waitForAngular unnecessary, but in a few edge cases it can still be useful:

        1. Keep Protractor in package.json and use a polyfill that runs the client-side waitForAngular script via page.evaluate.
        2. A simpler approach, for Angular 2+ only: wait on each element's whenStable in getAllAngularTestabilities().
        3. Call it after navigation, for example right after page.goto(...).
        // Angular 2+ only: wait until all testabilities are stable
async function waitForAngular(page: import('@playwright/test').Page) {
  await page.evaluate(async () => {
    const testabilities = (window as any).getAllAngularTestabilities();
    await Promise.all(testabilities.map((t: any) => new Promise<void>(resolve => t.whenStable(resolve))));
  });
}

await page.goto('https://example.com');
await waitForAngular(page);

        Playwright Test "super powers"

        • Zero-config TypeScript; cross-browser; multiple origins/frames/tabs/contexts.
        • Parallel execution; automatic artifact collection; Inspector, codegen, Tracing.

        Key takeaways

        • No Selenium/webdriver-manager needed; by.model/by.repeater become CSS attribute selectors.
        • Forgetting await is the most common mistake when migrating.
        • Use web-first assertions (toHaveCount, toHaveText) instead of expect(x.count()).toEqual.

        Which mechanism mainly replaces Protractor's waitForAngular in Playwright?

        Auto-waiting waits for the element to be ready; the polyfill is only needed for edge cases.

        Migrating from Testing Library

        A guide to moving from DOM Testing Library, React Testing Library or Vue Testing Library to Playwright component testing, which is built on the concepts of stories and a gallery.

        Principles

        Note If you run DOM Testing Library in the browser for E2E tests, you can switch straight to Playwright Test: replace await mount with page.goto() to the page under test.

        Playwright renders a component through a story; the dev server serves the stories from a gallery page. Where Testing Library calls render() inside the test, Playwright moves that setup into the story and references it by id in the test. See also Component testing.

        Cheat sheet

        Testing LibraryPlaywright
        screenpage and component
        Queries (getBy..., findBy...)Locators (component.getBy...)
        Async helpersAssertions
        User eventsActions
        await user.click(screen.getByText('Click me'))await component.getByText('Click me').click()
        await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Password'), 'secret')await component.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret')
        expect(screen.getByLabelText('Password')).toHaveValue('secret')await expect(component.getByLabel('Password')).toHaveValue('secret')
        render(<Component />)Story export + await mount('Component/Default')
        const { unmount } = render(...)await component.unmount()
        const { rerender } = render(...)await component.update(props)

        Example: a sign-in test

        ❌ Testing Library
        import React from 'react';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';

test('sign in', async () => {
  // Setup the page.
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<SignInPage />);

  // Perform actions.
  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Username'), 'John');
  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Password'), 'secret');
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }));

  // Verify signed in state by waiting until "Welcome" message appears.
  expect(await screen.findByText('Welcome, John')).toBeInTheDocument();
});
        ✅ Playwright
        import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('sign in', async ({ mount }) => {
  // Setup the page.
  const component = await mount('pages/SignInPage/Default');

  // Perform actions.
  await component.getByLabel('Username').fill('John');
  await component.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret');
  await component.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

  // Verify signed in state by waiting until "Welcome" message appears.
  await expect(component.getByText('Welcome, John')).toBeVisible();
});

        The story file lives next to the component:

        import { SignInPage } from './SignInPage';

export const Default = () => <SignInPage />;
        1. Move the scenario into a story export next to the component.
        2. All imports come from @playwright/test.
        3. The test function receives the mount fixture, which renders the story in an isolated page.
        4. mount('pages/SignInPage/Default') returns a locator for the component, scoped to the gallery root.
        5. The story runs in the browser, so you can no longer pass live objects into the test.

        Converting queries

        Every getBy..., findBy..., queryBy... variant (and the multi-element forms) becomes component.getBy.... Locators wait and retry automatically, so you don't have to pick a query type based on when the element appears; operations on multiple elements are handled automatically too.

        Replacing waitFor

        Playwright assertions wait for the condition automatically, so waitFor and waitForElementToBeRemoved are usually unnecessary.

        // Testing Library
await waitFor(() => {
  expect(getByText('the lion king')).toBeInTheDocument();
});
await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => queryByText('the mummy'));

// Playwright
await expect(page.getByText('the lion king')).toBeVisible();
await expect(page.getByText('the mummy')).toBeHidden();

        When there is no suitable assertion, use expect.poll:

        await expect.poll(async () => {
  const response = await page.request.get('https://api.example.com');
  return response.status();
}).toBe(200);

        Replacing within

        Nest locators with locator.locator() or chain calls directly.

        // Testing Library
const messages = screen.getByTestId('messages');
const helloMessage = within(messages).getByText('hello');

// Playwright
const messages = component.getByTestId('messages');
const helloMessage = messages.getByText('hello');
        Tip Since 1.64 there is also locator.within() to scope one locator inside another (see Release notes).

        Playwright Test "super powers"

        • Test runner: zero-config TypeScript; cross-browser on Windows/macOS/Ubuntu; multiple origins, iframes, tabs, contexts; isolated parallel execution; automatic artifact collection.
        • Tooling: VS Code integration, UI Mode (time-travel debugging, watch mode), Inspector, codegen, Tracing.

        Key takeaways

        • render() becomes a story + mount('id'); screen becomes component/page.
        • Queries become locators, user events become actions, async helpers become assertions.
        • waitFor is almost never needed; when there is no matching assertion, use expect.poll.

        What replaces within(messages).getByText('hello') in Playwright?

        Locators can be chained: call getByText on the messages locator to narrow the scope.

        Getting started – VS Code (Playwright extension for VS Code)

        The official extension lets you run, debug and generate Playwright tests right in the editor: click play next to a test, set breakpoints, view traces and record tests with CodeGen.

        Installation

        Requirements: Node.js (LTS recommended) and Visual Studio Code.

        1. Open Extensions (Ctrl+Shift+X / Cmd+Shift+X), search for "Playwright" and install the official Microsoft extension.
        2. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P) and run Test: Install Playwright.
        3. Choose browsers (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit); you can also add a GitHub Actions workflow for CI. Change these later in playwright.config.ts.

        Click the Testing icon in the Activity Bar to open the Test Explorer, along with the Playwright sidebar (projects, tools, settings).

        Running tests

        • A single test: click the green play icon next to the test; the icon turns into a green check (pass) or a red X (fail), along with the duration. The Test Results panel shows the total run/passed/failed/skipped.
        • Multiple tests: click play next to a file to run that file, or the icon at the top of the Test Explorer to run the whole project.
        • Multiple browsers: tick the projects in the sidebar (each project is a browser configuration with its own viewport and device emulation).
        • Show Browser: turn it on to watch the test run in a real browser; turn it off to run headless.

        Debugging tests

        • Breakpoints: click the gutter next to a line number, right-click the test and choose Debug Test; execution stops at the breakpoint so you can inspect variables and step through the code.
        • Live debugging: with Show Browsers on, click a locator in the code and Playwright highlights the matching element in the browser.
        • Error messages: shown right in the editor with expected vs received and the full call log.
        • Fix with AI: the sparkle icon next to an error asks Copilot to analyze it and suggest a fix.
        • Trace Viewer: turn on Show Trace Viewer and the trace opens automatically after the test finishes (step-by-step analysis, DOM snapshots, network, console, source mapping, screenshots). Especially useful for flaky tests.

        Generating tests with CodeGen

        • Record new: records your interactions as code with locators; add assertions from the recording toolbar.
        • Record at cursor: place the cursor inside an existing test to insert actions there.
        • Pick locator: click an element in the browser and Playwright picks the best locator and copies it to the clipboard.

        See also Test generator.

        Advanced features

        • Project dependencies: setup tests (for example logging in) run before other tests and reuse the authenticated state; they appear in the Test Explorer and can be run on their own.
        • Global setup: run global setup/teardown manually from the sidebar (e.g. seeding a database).
        • Multiple configs: if you have several playwright.config.ts files, switch between them with the gear icon in the sidebar.

        Quick reference

        TaskHow to do it in VS Code
        Install PlaywrightCommand Palette, Test: Install Playwright
        Run a testClick the play icon next to the test
        Debug a testSet a breakpoint, right-click the test, Debug Test
        Watch the browser liveTurn on Show Browsers
        Record a new testRecord new
        Pick a locatorPick locator
        View a traceTurn on Show Trace Viewer

        Key takeaways

        • Install the extension, then run Test: Install Playwright.
        • Show Browsers + Pick locator + Show Trace Viewer are the most useful trio when debugging.
        • Each project in the config is a browser configuration you can tick to run on its own.

        Which feature do you use to pick a locator by clicking an element in the browser?

        Pick locator chooses the best locator for the clicked element and copies it to the clipboard.

        Canary releases

        Playwright for Node.js publishes a canary release every day so you can try unreleased features and give feedback to the maintainers.

        npm dist tags

        Every commit that changes code on main triggers a daily canary release under the next tag.

        TagMeaning
        latestThe stable release
        nextThe canary published daily
        betaAfter the release branch is cut (usually about a week before stable), every commit is published under this tag

        Using a canary release

        npm install -D @playwright/test@next
        Is it safe? Using a canary in production sounds risky but in practice it isn't, because canaries pass the entire automated test suite. Playwright itself uses canaries to E2E-test the HTML report, Trace Viewer and Inspector. Still, behavior may change before it becomes stable.

        Documentation

        Both the stable and next docs are available on playwright.dev. To view the next docs, press the Shift key five times.

        Key takeaways

        • @playwright/test@next = daily canary; @latest = stable; beta = about 1 week before stable.
        • Use canaries to try things early and report bugs.

        Which command installs the daily canary release?

        The next tag holds the daily canary; beta only appears after the release branch is cut.

        Touch events (legacy)

        For web apps that handle legacy touch events (swipe, pinch, tap), you can dispatch TouchEvents into the page yourself with locator.dispatchEvent() and a set of Touch points.

        Introduction

        This approach does not set Event.isTrusted, so if the page checks that property, the test has to disable that check.

        1. touchstartthe touch point is placed down
        2. touchmove ×Nmoves step by step
        3. touchendthe finger lifts

        Simulating a pan gesture

        Panning is used to move a map. The pan helper reads the element's center, dispatches touchstart, a series of touchmove events step by step, then touchend. It only sets clientX and clientY because the app only needs those two values.

        import { test, expect, devices, type Locator } from '@playwright/test';

test.use({ ...devices['Pixel 7'] });

async function pan(locator: Locator, deltaX?: number, deltaY?: number, steps?: number) {
  const { centerX, centerY } = await locator.evaluate((target: HTMLElement) => {
    const bounds = target.getBoundingClientRect();
    const centerX = bounds.left + bounds.width / 2;
    const centerY = bounds.top + bounds.height / 2;
    return { centerX, centerY };
  });

  // Providing only clientX and clientY as the app only cares about those.
  const touches = [{ identifier: 0, clientX: centerX, clientY: centerY }];
  await locator.dispatchEvent('touchstart', { touches, changedTouches: touches, targetTouches: touches });

  steps = steps ?? 5;
  deltaX = deltaX ?? 0;
  deltaY = deltaY ?? 0;
  for (let i = 1; i <= steps; i++) {
    const touches = [{ identifier: 0, clientX: centerX + deltaX * i / steps, clientY: centerY + deltaY * i / steps }];
    await locator.dispatchEvent('touchmove', { touches, changedTouches: touches, targetTouches: touches });
  }

  await locator.dispatchEvent('touchend');
}

test('should pan the map', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('https://www.google.com/maps');
  // Dismiss the "Keep using web" prompt if shown, then:
  const map = page.locator('[data-test-id="met"]');
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    await pan(map, 200, 100);
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot();
});
        Note The Google Maps page in the original example may change its UI; treat it as a sample of how to dispatch events, and replace the selector/URL with your own app.

        Simulating a pinch gesture

        A pinch moves two touch points toward each other to zoom out. The pinch helper dispatches touchstart with two touches, moves both step by step, then sends touchend with empty touch lists. The test repeats the pinch 5 times and compares a screenshot of the zoomed-out map.

        async function pinch(locator: Locator, deltaX = 40, steps = 5) {
  const { centerX, centerY } = await locator.evaluate((target: HTMLElement) => {
    const b = target.getBoundingClientRect();
    return { centerX: b.left + b.width / 2, centerY: b.top + b.height / 2 };
  });

  const start = [
    { identifier: 0, clientX: centerX - deltaX, clientY: centerY },
    { identifier: 1, clientX: centerX + deltaX, clientY: centerY },
  ];
  await locator.dispatchEvent('touchstart', { touches: start, changedTouches: start, targetTouches: start });

  for (let i = 1; i <= steps; i++) {
    const offset = deltaX - (deltaX * i) / (steps * 2); // the two points move closer together
    const touches = [
      { identifier: 0, clientX: centerX - offset, clientY: centerY },
      { identifier: 1, clientX: centerX + offset, clientY: centerY },
    ];
    await locator.dispatchEvent('touchmove', { touches, changedTouches: touches, targetTouches: touches });
  }

  await locator.dispatchEvent('touchend', { touches: [], changedTouches: [], targetTouches: [] });
}
        Hint The pinch helper above was rewritten from the documentation's description (two touches moving closer together, touchend with empty lists); the exact numbers may differ from the original. For ordinary touch interactions (tap), use locator.tap() together with hasTouch: true in emulation.

        Key takeaways

        • Manually dispatch touchstart, touchmove, touchend with locator.dispatchEvent().
        • The events are not "trusted" (isTrusted is not set).
        • Pan = 1 touch point moving; pinch = 2 touch points moving closer together.

        What is the limitation of dispatching touch events with locator.dispatchEvent()?

        Events created by script are not trusted events; if the app checks isTrusted, that check has to be disabled in the test.

        Supported syntax

        Lab: Auto-waiting & Actionability

        Before click(), Playwright waits for the element to pass the actionability checks. Toggle the “page” conditions while the test runs to watch Playwright retry until the conditions are met or the timeout expires.

        Button state (you can change it at any time):
        Click the run button to start.
        Remember The checks run in order; if one fails, Playwright waits and retries the whole sequence until actionTimeout/test timeout runs out, then throws a TimeoutError with a “waiting for…” log.

        Lab: Workers, fullyParallel & Sharding

        Simulates how tests are distributed across workers and shards. By default tests in the same file run sequentially on 1 worker; fullyParallel: true lets them be split per test.

        Observe With fullyParallel off, a file with many long tests becomes a “bottleneck”. Turn it on (or split the file) and raise shards to see the total time drop; but once workers outnumber work units there is no further benefit.
        npx playwright test --workers=3
npx playwright test --shard=1/4

        Lab: Retries, Flaky & Web-first Assertion

        Two experiments: (1) retries turn an intermittently failing test into “flaky”; (2) expect(locator) keeps polling until it is right or times out, while expect(await ...) checks only once.

        Experiment 1 – Retries

        Outcomes: passed (passed on the first run), flaky (failed, then passed on a retry) and failed (failed on every attempt).

        Experiment 2 – Self-retrying assertion

        Time
        ✅ Web-first (auto-retry)
        await expect(page.getByText('Done')).toBeVisible();
        ❌ One-shot check
        expect(await page.getByText('Done').isVisible()).toBe(true);
